fate: Merged with Alcatel, 2006; Alcatel-Lucent acquired by Nokia, 2016
tagline: Bell Labs Walks Out the Door
dek: Lucent built the switches, phones and network gear that carried the world's calls, with Bell Labs behind it.
lede: The biggest IPO in American history up to then came wrapped in a red brushstroke logo. In April 1996 AT&T sold a slice of its equipment arm as Lucent Technologies, raising about $3 billion at $27 a share. Lucent got the switches, the phones, the network gear and about three-quarters of Bell Labs, the research house behind the transistor. AT&T kept 82.4 percent of the stock and promised to hand the rest to its own shareholders by the end of the year.

sections.heading: AT&T Splits in Three
sections.body: In 1995 AT&T decided to break itself into three companies. Lucent took the business of building telephone networks. It sold switching systems, transmission gear, business phone systems and home phones, mostly to the regional Bell companies that had once been part of AT&T. Its 1995 revenue was $21.4 billion. The bet was simple. A gear maker free of AT&T could win orders from phone companies that refused to buy from a rival.

sections.heading: From Bubble Giant to Penny Stock
sections.body: Lucent priced at $27 a share in April 1996 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as LU. AT&T spun off its remaining stake that fall. The stock climbed for years and became one of the most widely held in America. Then the telecom boom ended, carriers stopped buying, and the shares fell below $1 in 2002. Lucent merged with France's Alcatel in 2006. Nokia bought Alcatel-Lucent in 2016, and the lab became Nokia Bell Labs.

cover.artwork: The Evening Bell of the Clock (Tokei no bansho), from the series "Eight Views of the Parlor (Zashiki hakkei)"

dek: Pets.com shipped dog food, cat litter and toys to your door, sold by a talking sock puppet.
lede: A sock puppet with a microphone was the most famous thing about Pets.com, and it outlived the company. The San Francisco online pet store went public in February 2000 at $11 a share, weeks before the dot-com peak. The company had been formed only a year earlier. In its first eleven months it booked $5.8 million in sales and lost $61.8 million. Its largest shareholder was Amazon.com.

sections.heading: Heavy Bags, Thin Margins
sections.body: Pets.com bet that pet owners would rather click than haul. It sold food, toys, litter and supplies online and shipped them to the door. The trouble sat inside the boxes. Pet food is heavy, cheap and costly to ship, so each order earned little or lost money. The company spent big on advertising to build its brand around the sock puppet, and it leaned on Amazon.com and GO.com to send it shoppers.

sections.heading: Nine Months on Nasdaq
sections.body: Pets.com priced its IPO at $11 a share in February 2000 and traded on Nasdaq as IPET. That spring investors turned on web stores that lost money on every sale, and the stock sank with them. In November 2000 the company said it would wind down. It laid off most of its staff and sold its assets, the sock puppet included. The shell company, renamed IPET Holdings, deregistered its stock in 2005.

tagline: The Search Engine Behind the Search Engines
dek: Inktomi ran the search and caching behind other companies' websites, Yahoo's search results among them.
lede: In 1998, when you searched on Yahoo, the results came from a company most people had never heard of. Inktomi, named for a trickster spider in Lakota legend, grew out of research at UC Berkeley and ran search for Yahoo, HotBot and others. Its 31-year-old chief scientist, Eric Brewer, built it on clusters of ordinary computers. When it filed to go public, Inktomi was selling the plumbing of the web to the brands people saw.

sections.heading: A Spider From Berkeley
sections.body: Brewer and his graduate student Paul Gauthier founded Inktomi in February 1996 to turn their research into a business. Their idea was that many cheap workstations, tied together, could index the web faster than one giant machine. Inktomi kept its own name off the screen. It licensed search to portals and sold Traffic Server, software that cached web pages close to users. Revenue for the six months to March 1998 was $5.9 million.

sections.heading: Peak, Crash, Yahoo
sections.body: Inktomi priced at $18 a share in June 1998 and traded on Nasdaq as INKT. The stock rose with the bubble as portals and phone carriers bought its search and caching software. The crash hit those customers hard. In 2000 Yahoo moved its web search to a young company called Google. Yahoo came back for Inktomi itself in 2003, buying it for about $235 million.

cover.theme: a giant spider (the Lakota trickster Iktomi)
cover.artwork: The Earth Spider Slain by Brave Samurai Watanabe no Tauna (center image)

dek: Sonos put wireless speakers in every room and let one app play music through all of them.
lede: By the spring of 2018, Sonos owners had registered more than 19 million speakers in about 6.9 million homes. The Santa Barbara company started in 2002 as Rincon Audio, with a plan to fill every room with music over home Wi-Fi. It spent years teaching people that speakers could talk to each other. When it filed to go public, smart speakers from Amazon and Google were flooding the market at a fraction of its prices.

sections.heading: Rincon Audio's Big Idea
sections.body: John MacFarlane and three co-founders started the company in August 2002 and renamed it Sonos in 2004. Their bet was that people wanted music all over the house without running wires through the walls. Sonos built speakers that joined into one system and played from many streaming services. It sold premium hardware and kept owners buying more rooms. Its customers, the filing said, listened to about 80 percent more music after buying their first Sonos.

sections.heading: Speakers on Nasdaq
sections.body: Sonos priced its IPO at $15 a share in August 2018 and listed on Nasdaq as SONO. The shares jumped more than 30 percent on the first day. Sonos later sued Google over its speaker patents. In 2024 a redesign of its app broke features owners relied on, and chief executive Patrick Spence left in January 2025. Sonos remains a public company on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a child playing a flute (sound filling the room)
cover.artwork: The Flute (Hichiriki), from the series "Fashionable Musical Amusements of Children (Furyu kodomo asobi ongaku)"

dek: Sohu gave Chinese readers a web directory, news and email in their own language, early.
lede: Sohu's name means "search fox" in Chinese, a nod to Yahoo, the American directory it set out to match. Charles Zhang, a physicist trained at MIT, returned to Beijing and started the company in 1996, when few people in China had ever been online. Sohu launched a Chinese-language directory, then grew into a portal with news, email and chat. In July 2000 it went public on Nasdaq, one of the first Chinese internet companies to list in New York.

sections.heading: Yahoo, in Chinese
sections.body: Zhang's bet was that China would come online fast and would want a home page built for it. Sohu started as a hand-sorted directory of Chinese websites and added news, free email, chat rooms and shopping links. It earned money by selling ads to companies that wanted to reach China's first wave of internet users. Its rivals Sina and Netease were making the same bet, and all three listed on Nasdaq in 2000.

sections.heading: Games, Search and Survival
sections.body: Sohu priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as SOHU. The dot-com crash followed within months and the shares fell hard. Sohu survived by adding new lines of business. It built an online game studio, Changyou, and a search engine, Sogou, and later took both public on their own. Sohu remains listed on Nasdaq, with Zhang still in charge.

cover.artwork: Fox, from The Picture Book of Realistic Paintings of Hokusai (Hokusai shashin gafu)

dek: JD.com sold electronics and then everything else online, and delivered it with its own couriers.
lede: When JD.com filed to go public, it had 24,412 couriers of its own. Most Chinese online stores handed parcels to outside delivery firms. JD built 86 warehouses and 1,620 delivery stations across China so it could control every step from shelf to door. Richard Liu started the business in 1998 as a shop selling electronics in Beijing. By its 2014 IPO, it was the largest direct online retailer in China and a rival to Alibaba.

sections.heading: From Market Stall to Warehouses
sections.body: Liu began by selling electronics and home appliances, and he moved the business online after the SARS outbreak kept shoppers home. JD added general merchandise at the end of 2008, then clothing, groceries and books, and opened a marketplace for outside sellers in 2010. The bet was that buyers in China would pay for genuine goods and fast, reliable delivery. That meant owning the trucks, the warehouses and the people. Liu kept 83.7 percent of the voting power.

sections.heading: A Tencent Deal, Then Nasdaq
sections.body: JD.com priced its ADSs at $19 in May 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as JD, raising about $1.8 billion. Tencent had taken a stake weeks earlier and folded its own e-commerce sites into JD. The stock rose in its debut. JD went on to build one of the largest logistics networks in the world, and it added a second listing in Hong Kong in 2020. It remains public in New York and Hong Kong.

cover.theme: a galloping courier (JD's own delivery force)

dek: Tencent Music runs China's biggest music apps, where people stream songs, sing karaoke and tip live performers.
lede: In 2018 most of Tencent Music's money came from people singing karaoke and tipping live performers. Song subscriptions were the smaller business. The company ran QQ Music, Kugou, Kuwo and WeSing, the four most-used music apps in China, with more than 800 million monthly users. It was formed in 2016, when Tencent merged its QQ Music business with China Music Corporation. It filed to go public in New York two years later.

sections.heading: Paying for Songs in China
sections.body: For years Chinese listeners downloaded music for free, often from pirated sites. Tencent Music's bet was that licensed catalogs and a big enough audience would get people to pay. It signed deals with the major record labels and grew its paying users from 18.3 million to 24.9 million in a year. The bigger business was social. Users sang along in WeSing, watched live music streams, and bought virtual gifts for the performers.

sections.heading: A Quiet Debut, a Second Home
sections.body: Tencent Music priced its ADSs at $13 in December 2018 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as TME. The shares edged up on the first day. Tencent kept control, and the offering raised about $1.1 billion. In 2022 the company added a second listing in Hong Kong. It remains public in both cities, with paid subscriptions now the core of its music business.

cover.theme: a songbird singing in a plum tree
cover.artwork: Beauty Admiring a Bush Warbler Singing in a Plum Tree

tagline: The Day the Web Went Public
dek: Netscape made Navigator, the browser that first brought most people onto the World Wide Web.
lede: Netscape's bankers first planned to sell its stock for about $14 a share. Demand pushed the price to $28, and on its first morning of trading in August 1995 it opened at $71. The company was 16 months old and had never made a profit. Its product was Navigator, a web browser built by 24-year-old Marc Andreessen and a team from the University of Illinois. Many people date the dot-com boom to that one day.

sections.heading: Mosaic Moves West
sections.body: As a student, Andreessen co-wrote Mosaic, a browser that put pictures and links on the same page. Jim Clark, who had founded Silicon Graphics, flew to meet him, and in April 1994 the two started Mosaic Communications in Mountain View. A name dispute with the university turned it into Netscape. The bet was that the web would become the way people used computers. Navigator was free to try, and within a year most web users ran it.

sections.heading: The Browser War
sections.body: Netscape priced at $28 a share on August 8, 1995, and closed its first day at $58.25 on Nasdaq. Microsoft answered with Internet Explorer and bundled it free with Windows. Netscape's share of the browser market shrank year by year. In 1998 it released its source code, the seed of the Mozilla project and later Firefox. AOL bought Netscape in a stock deal valued at $4.2 billion when it was announced, and the purchase closed in 1999.

cover.theme: a sailboat at sunrise (a navigator on a new horizon)
cover.artwork: Calendar print: sailboat, Mount Fuji, and sunrise

dek: MarketWatch brought fast, free stock market news to anyone with a browser and a brokerage account.
lede: MarketWatch.com sold its shares at $17 on a Thursday night in January 1999. By the close of trading on Friday they were worth $97.50, a gain of 474 percent. The site covered the stock market in real time for a new crowd of online traders. It was owned by CBS and Data Broadcasting Corporation, and its newsroom was run by Larry Kramer, a former executive editor of the San Francisco Examiner.

sections.heading: A Newsroom for Day Traders
sections.body: Kramer's idea was a financial news site that updated all day, as markets moved. CBS lent its brand and its TV and radio reach, and Data Broadcasting supplied the market data. Editor-in-chief Thom Calandra and a staff of experienced reporters filled the front page at CBS.MarketWatch.com from the open to the close. The bet was that advertisers would follow the readers, and that the readers were people with money to invest.

sections.heading: Bubble Darling, Dow Jones Prize
sections.body: Demand for the IPO was so strong that the price range rose twice before the deal priced at $17. Only theglobe.com had ever posted a bigger first-day gain. The stock fell back with the dot-com crash, but the site kept its readers. In 2004 MarketWatch merged with Pinnacor, and in early 2005 Dow Jones, publisher of The Wall Street Journal, bought the company. The site is still published today.

cover.theme: a stock exchange (a newsroom watching the market)

tagline: The Most Efficient Panel on the Roof
dek: SunPower made high-efficiency solar cells and panels that squeezed more power from every square foot of roof.
lede: SunPower was twenty years old before it sold a single share to the public. Stanford professor Richard Swanson started the company in 1985 to build better silicon solar cells. Cypress Semiconductor rescued and then bought it, and when SunPower went public in November 2005, Cypress still owned 87 percent of its shares. Solar power was a small, subsidy-driven business, and SunPower's pitch was simple: its cells turned more sunlight into electricity than anyone else's.

sections.heading: A Professor's Solar Cell
sections.body: Swanson's design put all the electrical contacts on the back of the cell, so nothing shaded the front. That made SunPower panels more efficient and better looking, at a higher price. Cypress chief T.J. Rodgers backed the company with chip-industry money and manufacturing know-how. The bet was that homeowners and businesses with limited roof space would pay a premium for the most power per panel.

sections.heading: Boom, Bust and Bankruptcy
sections.body: SunPower priced at $18 a share in November 2005 and listed on Nasdaq as SPWR. It rode the solar boom, then struggled as cheaper Chinese panels flooded the market. French oil company Total bought a majority stake in 2011. SunPower spun off its panel factories as Maxeon in 2020 and focused on selling and installing home solar. It filed for bankruptcy in August 2024, and Complete Solaria bought its brand and key assets.

dek: TTM made custom printed circuit boards fast, so electronics makers could test and ship new designs sooner.
lede: TTM's name stands for time to market, and its best trick was building a custom circuit board in as little as 24 hours. Engineers at networking and computer companies needed prototypes the next day, then thousands of boards a few weeks later. TTM did both. The company began in 1978 as Pacific Circuits, a board shop near Seattle, and took the TTM name in December 1999, months before its IPO in September 2000.

sections.heading: Speed Was the Product
sections.body: Every phone, router and server is built on a printed circuit board, a layered sheet of copper paths that ties the chips together. Most board makers competed on price. TTM competed on speed. Its plants handled quick-turn prototypes and then moved the same designs into volume production without a handoff to another supplier. The bet was that customers racing to launch new gear would pay extra to get their boards days or weeks sooner.

sections.heading: Bought Its Way to the Top
sections.body: TTM priced at $16 a share in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as TTMI, just as the telecom spending boom turned to bust. It survived by buying rivals. TTM took over Tyco's circuit board unit in 2006, Hong Kong's Meadville in 2010 and Viasystems in 2015, and grew into one of the largest board makers in the world. It now builds boards for defense, data centers and cars, and it remains public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a maze of beams and stairways (layers of circuit traces)
cover.artwork: The Drawbridge, plate 7 from Imaginary Prisons

tagline: Never Store the Same Byte Twice
dek: Data Domain shrank company backups by keeping one copy of repeated data, so disks could replace tape.
lede: Most of what a company backs up each week is the same data it backed up the week before. Data Domain built boxes that noticed. Its appliances stored each repeated chunk only once, shrinking backups by 10 to 30 times. That made it cheap enough to back up to disk instead of tape, which was slow and easy to lose. The Santa Clara company started shipping in 2004 and went public in June 2007.

sections.heading: A Professor's Compression Trick
sections.body: Princeton computer scientist Kai Li co-founded Data Domain in October 2001 with Ben Zhu and Brian Biles. The company called its method Global Compression. Today the idea goes by a plainer name, deduplication. Data Domain packed it into appliances built from standard parts that plugged into a company's existing backup software. The bet was that IT departments would happily retire their tape libraries if disk cost about the same and restored files far faster.

sections.heading: A Bidding War Ends It
sections.body: Data Domain priced at $15 a share in June 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as DDUP. The shares rose sharply on the first day. Two years later NetApp agreed to buy the company. EMC jumped in with a higher all-cash offer, and after weeks of rival bids EMC won in July 2009 for about $2.1 billion. Data Domain lived on as EMC's backup line, and later as part of Dell.

fate: Bankrupt, 2009; assets bought by Warner Bros.
dek: Midway made arcade hits like Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam, then brought them home to consoles.
lede: Mortal Kombat 3 was the best-selling home video game in the United States in 1995, and Midway had only just started publishing its own home games. Before that it licensed its arcade hits to Acclaim for a modest royalty. The Chicago studio behind Defender, Joust and NBA Jam now wanted that money for itself. In October 1996 its parent, the pinball maker WMS Industries, sold about 13 percent of Midway to the public.

sections.heading: From Arcade to Living Room
sections.body: Midway had been making coin-operated games since the 1970s, from Space Invaders and Pac-Man in America to its own Mortal Kombat, whose home versions had sold more than 10 million copies. It had just bought Atari Games, maker of Gauntlet. The bet was simple. As players left the arcades for the Sony PlayStation and the Nintendo 64, Midway would follow them and publish its hits on every console.

sections.heading: Game Over in 2009
sections.body: Midway priced at $20 a share in October 1996 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MWY. WMS spun off its remaining stake two years later. The arcade business faded, and Midway's home games rarely matched its old hits. Losses piled up through the 2000s. Midway filed for bankruptcy in February 2009, and Warner Bros. bought most of its assets, including Mortal Kombat, later that year.

fate: Taken private by a Warburg Pincus-led group, 2020
tagline: The Classifieds of a Thousand Cities
dek: 58.com let people in China find a plumber, an apartment, a used car or a job from local listings.
lede: If you needed a mover, a nanny or a room to rent in a Chinese city in 2013, you probably looked on 58.com. It was the largest online marketplace for local merchants and consumers in China, a home for classified ads much like Craigslist. Jinbo Yao started it in Beijing in 2005. When it filed to go public, the company was already profitable and had offices in 27 Chinese cities.

sections.heading: Craigslist, With Salespeople
sections.body: 58.com's bet was that China's small local businesses would pay to be found online. Listings for jobs, homes, cars and household services were free to browse. Merchants paid for memberships and for ads that put their listings near the top. Unlike Craigslist, 58.com built a large sales force to sign up those merchants city by city. In the quarter before its IPO it earned $8.5 million.

sections.heading: Merged, Then Taken Private
sections.body: 58.com priced its ADSs at $17 in October 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as WUBA. The stock jumped on its first day. Tencent bought a large stake in 2014. In 2015 58.com took control of its biggest rival, Ganji, and became the clear leader in Chinese classifieds. A group led by Warburg Pincus took the company private in September 2020.

cover.theme: a crowded street of shop signs (local listings)

fate: Merged with NetZero to form United Online, 2001
tagline: Free Email, Paid for by Ads
dek: Juno gave people free email over a dial-up phone call, paid for by ads, before most homes had the web.
lede: Juno was born inside a hedge fund. D. E. Shaw & Co., the New York quant firm run by computer scientist David E. Shaw, launched it to give people email for free. You did not need web access. Juno's software dialed a local number, swapped your messages and hung up, showing ads while you read. By the time Juno went public in May 1999, it was selling full internet access too.

sections.heading: Email for the Rest of Us
sections.body: Juno's bet was that millions of people wanted email before they wanted the web, and that advertisers would pay to reach them. The basic service was free. Juno Gold let users send pictures and files, and Juno Web offered full dial-up internet access for a monthly fee. The company designed its software for people just starting to explore the internet, and planned to move them up to the paid plans.

sections.heading: Two Free Services Join Up
sections.body: Juno priced at $13 a share in May 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as JWEB. Free and cheap dial-up turned into a crowded fight, and ad money dried up after the dot-com crash. In 2001 Juno merged with its rival NetZero to form United Online. The combined company kept both brands, and B. Riley Financial bought United Online in 2016.

cover.theme: a peacock (the bird of the goddess Juno)

dek: LightInTheBox sold Chinese-made dresses, gadgets and home goods straight to shoppers around the world.
lede: A bride in Europe or America could order a custom wedding dress from LightInTheBox and have it made and shipped from China. That was the company's pitch: cut out the importers and the stores, and sell factory goods to the world at factory prices. Five co-founders started it in Beijing in June 2007, led by chairman and chief executive Alan Guo. By its 2013 IPO it was selling apparel, electronics and home goods in many countries and languages.

sections.heading: Factory to Front Door
sections.body: LightInTheBox bet that the internet could link Chinese suppliers directly to overseas consumers. It ran websites in many languages, bought ads on search engines and social networks to find shoppers, and shipped orders by international courier. Made-to-order dresses were a signature product, since they could be cut to a buyer's measurements. A sister site, MiniInTheBox, sold small gadgets and accessories. The model needed cheap traffic from Google and Facebook to work.

sections.heading: Small Cap, Still Standing
sections.body: LightInTheBox priced its ADSs at $9.50 in June 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as LITB. Rising ad costs and tough competition from bigger cross-border sellers squeezed its growth, and its market value shrank. In late 2024 the NYSE warned that it had fallen below listing standards. In June 2026 the exchange confirmed it had cured the deficiency, and the stock remains listed.

dek: Aerohive let companies run office Wi-Fi from the cloud, with no costly central controller box.
lede: Office Wi-Fi in the 2000s usually depended on a single controller, an expensive box that every access point reported to. Aerohive got rid of it. Its access points worked together like bees in a hive, sharing the job of running the network, and customers managed them all from the cloud. The Sunnyvale company was founded in 2006. When it went public in March 2014, phones and tablets were flooding offices and schools with new demands for wireless.

sections.heading: A Hive Mind for Access Points
sections.body: David Flynn and Changming Liu built Aerohive around what it called a distributed, controller-less design. Each access point carried its own intelligence, so a school or retailer could add coverage one unit at a time. Cloud management meant an IT team could run hundreds of sites from a browser. The bet was that schools, stores and branch offices would choose simpler, cheaper wireless over the controller-based gear sold by Cisco and Aruba.

sections.heading: Swallowed by Extreme
sections.body: Aerohive priced at $10 a share in March 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as HIVE. Competition stayed fierce, and Cisco's purchase of cloud-managed rival Meraki in 2012 had already put a giant on the same path. Aerohive grew slowly and never turned a steady profit. In August 2019 Extreme Networks completed a cash tender offer for the company, buying it for about $272 million.

cover.artwork: Broad Bottom Drones Storming the Hive

tagline: The Call Center Moves to the Cloud
dek: Five9 moved call centers into the cloud, so companies could answer customers without owning phone hardware.
lede: Five9 is named for five nines, the 99.999 percent uptime that phone networks promise. The company spent its first eleven years selling call center software over the internet, back when most call centers still ran on racks of hardware bought from Avaya and Cisco. Agents logged in from a browser. Phone, chat and email arrived in one place. When Five9 went public in April 2014, cloud software for the front desk of customer service was still a young market.

sections.heading: Renting the Call Center
sections.body: Five9 was incorporated in 2001 and is based in San Ramon, California, and when it went public it had engineering and support offices in Russia and Asia. Its bet was that companies would rather pay a monthly fee per agent than buy and maintain their own phone systems. Cloud delivery let a business add agents for a busy season, or seat them at home. It also let Five9 ship new features to every customer at once.

sections.heading: The Zoom Deal That Wasn't
sections.body: Five9 priced at $7 a share in April 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as FIVN. The stock grew for years as call centers moved to the cloud. In July 2021 Zoom agreed to buy Five9 in an all-stock deal valued at about $14.7 billion. Zoom's shares fell, Five9 shareholders balked, and the two companies called it off that September. Five9 joined the S&P SmallCap 600 in August 2026 and remains public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a clock tower (five nines of uptime)

dek: N2K ran Music Boulevard, an online record store that sold CDs and even early digital downloads.
lede: In July 1997 a New York company called N2K began selling single songs as digital downloads. Its main business was Music Boulevard, an online record store, wrapped in fan sites like Rocktropolis and Jazz Central Station. N2K was run by music veterans, including Larry Rosen, co-founder of the jazz label GRP Records. It went public that October, betting that the record store of the future would live on the web.

sections.heading: Record Men Meet the Web
sections.body: N2K came out of Telebase Systems, an online information company founded in 1984 that turned to music in 1994. Its leaders included Rosen and producer Phil Ramone, who had made records with Billy Joel and Paul Simon. The bet was that fans would buy where they read and listened. N2K built genre sites for rock, jazz and classical, all feeding shoppers into Music Boulevard's catalog of CDs.

sections.heading: Merged Into CDnow
sections.body: N2K priced at $19 a share in October 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as NTKI. America Online bought shares at the same time. Online music retail turned into a costly fight, with Amazon entering the market in 1998. N2K and its rival CDnow agreed to merge that October and completed the deal in March 1999, under the CDnow name. Bertelsmann bought CDnow the next year.

dek: Broadbase pulled customer data from sales, service and web systems together so companies could see the whole picture.
lede: In 1999 a company's sales team, call center and website each kept their own records of the same customer, and none of them talked to each other. Broadbase sold software that pulled those records into one place and analyzed them. Its pitch was speed: customers could be up and running in less than 30 days. Founded in 1995 by Mark Kremer and backed by Benchmark Capital, the Menlo Park company went public in September 1999.

sections.heading: Data Marts for the Web Era
sections.body: Kremer started Broadbase in November 1995 as BroadBase Information Systems. Its product, Broadbase EPM, sat on top of a company's existing systems and gave marketing, sales and service managers ready-made analysis of their customers. The bet was that the web would multiply the ways customers reached a company, and that businesses would pay to see them as one person again. Over 80 customers had licensed the software by its IPO.

sections.heading: Boom, Bust, Kana
sections.body: Broadbase priced at $14 a share in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as BBSW. It rode the dot-com boom and bought other customer software firms with its soaring stock. When the bubble burst, its customers cut spending and the shares collapsed. In 2001 Broadbase merged with Kana Communications, a maker of customer service software, and the combined company took the Kana name.

cover.theme: a broad plain under a wide sky
cover.artwork: Kogane Plain in Shimosa Province (Shimosa Koganehara), from the series "Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji (Fuji sanjurokkei)"

fate: Became The Meet Group; taken private by NuCom Group, 2020
dek: Quepasa.com built a Spanish-language web portal for Latinos, with search, free email, news and chat.
lede: Quepasa.com's founder was 26 years old when the company went public, and its website had barely any revenue. Jeffrey Peterson had started the Phoenix company in 1997 as Internet Century. He renamed it in December 1998 to chase a market the big portals ignored: Spanish speakers in the United States and Latin America. Between February and June 1999 its email users grew from 201 to about 34,000. In June it raised $48 million on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Yahoo, en Español
sections.body: Quepasa.com offered a Spanish-language search engine, free email, news feeds, chat rooms and message boards. Its bet was that Hispanic internet users would make up a fast-growing audience, and that advertisers would pay to reach them. To lead the company, Peterson brought in Gary Trujillo, a Harvard MBA who had founded a Hispanic-owned consulting firm. Trujillo became chairman and chief executive just before the IPO, and the company had 45 employees.

sections.heading: From Portal to Dating Apps
sections.body: Quepasa priced at $12 a share in June 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as PASA. The dot-com crash crushed the stock, and the portal never found a business. The company kept going, rebuilt itself around social apps, bought myYearbook in 2011 and took the name MeetMe. Renamed The Meet Group, it was bought in 2020 by NuCom Group, owned by ProSiebenSat.1 and General Atlantic, for $6.30 a share.

cover.theme: a Mexican fair (a gathering place for Spanish speakers)
cover.artwork: The San Juan de los Lagos Fair

dek: Pivotal gave mid-sized companies one system to track every sale, campaign and service call.
lede: Pivotal started life in 1990 as Pen Magic Software, a British Columbia company betting on computers you wrote on with a stylus. Pen computing fizzled. By 1995 the company had renamed itself Pivotal Software and turned to customer relationship software, a tool for tracking every contact a business had with its buyers. When it went public in August 1999, Pivotal had licensed its applications to over 540 customers from its home in North Vancouver.

sections.heading: Pen Magic Changes Course
sections.body: Co-founders Norman Francis and Keith Wales led the company through its turn. Pivotal aimed at mid-sized businesses, below the giant corporations that bought from Siebel. It sold through a network of more than 95 partners that installed and serviced its products. In 1998 it co-founded the Enterprise 360 group with KPMG, Microsoft and Hewlett-Packard. The bet was that CRM would spread from the largest corporations down to everyone else.

sections.heading: A Bidding War at the End
sections.body: Pivotal priced at $12 a share in August 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as PVTL. The dot-com crash hit its customers, and the stock fell. In 2003 Pivotal agreed to sell itself to investor Oak Investment Partners. Rival Onyx Software then made its own offer, and CDC Software, a unit of chinadotcom, topped both. CDC closed the purchase in February 2004 for about $59 million.

cover.artwork: The Windmill, from Old English Masters

tagline: Keeping Handhelds and PCs in Sync
dek: Puma Technology made software that kept laptops, handhelds and desktop PCs holding the same files and contacts.
lede: Before phones carried your calendar, you kept it on a PC and a handheld and hoped they matched. Puma Technology sold the software that made them match. Its IntelliSync products synced contacts and schedules, and its TranXit software moved files over infrared beams. Puma's code shipped on machines from Compaq, IBM, Toshiba and a dozen other makers. The company went public in December 1996, as the PalmPilot was turning handhelds into a mass market.

sections.heading: The Invisible Middleman
sections.body: Princeton classmates Bradley Rowe and Stephen Nicol started Puma in August 1993. Their bet was that people would carry more and more devices, and every one would need to agree with the PC on the desk. Puma sold mostly through hardware makers, who bundled its software with their laptops and handhelds. Its customer list read like a guide to the computer industry, from Hitachi and Motorola to Sharp and Samsung.

sections.heading: Nokia Picks It Up
sections.body: Puma priced at $9.50 a share in December 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as PUMA. Over the next decade it shortened its name to Pumatech and bought rivals in the sync business. In 2004 it renamed itself Intellisync, after its best-known product, and moved into syncing email to phones. Nokia bought Intellisync in February 2006 for about $430 million, or $5.25 a share.

fate: Delisted, 2023; assets sold to Enghouse Systems, 2024
tagline: Movies on Demand, Ads on Cue
dek: SeaChange built the video servers that let cable companies insert local ads and offer movies on demand.
lede: Cable networks in the early 1990s slipped local commercials into national shows using banks of videotape machines. SeaChange replaced the tapes with digital video servers. Its SPOT System let a cable operator run ads aimed at a single town. William Styslinger, who had run the cable TV unit at Digital Equipment Corporation, started the company near Boston in 1993. By its IPO in November 1996, SeaChange was also selling servers for video on demand.

sections.heading: From Tape Decks to Servers
sections.body: Styslinger and engineer Edward McGrath founded the company in July 1993 as SeaView Technology and renamed it SeaChange two months later. It shipped its first products in 1994. Digital ad insertion paid the bills. The bigger bet was the SeaChange Movie System, which stored films on disk and streamed them to cable subscribers when they pressed play. That turned cable boxes into video stores and gave operators a new source of revenue.

sections.heading: The Long Fade
sections.body: SeaChange priced at $15 a share in November 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as SEAC. Video on demand did take off on cable, and SeaChange became a major supplier to large operators. Then streaming moved the action to the internet, and its old customers shrank. SeaChange left Nasdaq voluntarily in 2023. In 2024 it sold its business to Enghouse Systems for about $39 million, less its cash.

dek: Peregrine sold help desk software that let big companies track IT problems, assets and fixes.
lede: Peregrine Systems sold software to keep big companies' computers honest, and it ended in one of the largest accounting frauds of its era. The San Diego company's ServiceCenter suite ran the IT help desks of firms like Deere, Lufthansa and Procter & Gamble. Its chairman was John Moores, who had founded BMC Software. When Peregrine went public in April 1997, it was a modest outfit raising about $20 million.

sections.heading: Consultants Turned Software Makers
sections.body: Peregrine was founded in 1981 to consult on IT management software. In 1987 it launched its first product, PNMS, for watching over mainframe networks. ServiceCenter came later and became its main line. The suite tracked trouble tickets, changes and equipment across a company's computers and networks. The bet was that as corporate IT grew more complex, every large company would need one system to run its service desk.

sections.heading: Restated Into Bankruptcy
sections.body: Peregrine priced at $9 a share in April 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as PRGN. It grew fast by buying other companies, including Remedy in 2001. In 2002 it admitted it had inflated its revenue for years, and it filed for bankruptcy that September. Several executives were later convicted. Peregrine emerged from bankruptcy in 2003, and Hewlett-Packard bought it in 2005 for about $425 million.

dek: Cheetah Mobile made free apps that cleaned, sped up and protected Android phones, paid for by ads.
lede: By March 2014 Cheetah Mobile's apps had been installed on 502.1 million mobile devices. Its hit was Clean Master, a free Android app that cleared junk files and promised a faster phone. The Beijing company was a spinoff of the Chinese software maker Kingsoft, which kept control after the IPO. Xiaomi and Baidu bought shares alongside the offering. Smartphones were spreading fast across the developing world, and Cheetah wanted to be on all of them.

sections.heading: Security Software Goes Mobile
sections.body: Cheetah Mobile was formed in 2010 by combining Kingsoft's antivirus business with Conew, a startup run by Fu Sheng. As chief executive, Fu saw that cheap Android phones were filling up and slowing down around the world. The bet was to give away tools that fixed that, win hundreds of millions of users, and earn money by showing them ads. In March 2014 its apps had 362 million monthly users, 222.5 million of them on mobile.

sections.heading: From Utilities to Robots
sections.body: Cheetah Mobile priced its ADSs at $14 in May 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as CMCM. The shares ended their first day just above that price. Its ad business later ran into trouble. In 2020 Google removed dozens of its apps from the Play Store over its ad practices. Cheetah turned to AI and service robots, and it remains listed on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a big cat at rest (the cheetah)
cover.artwork: A Tyger (A Recumbent Leopard by a Tree)

dek: Huami designed and built Xiaomi's cheap fitness bands, then sold smartwatches under its own Amazfit brand.
lede: Millions of people wore Huami's products without knowing its name. The company from Hefei, in central China, was Xiaomi's sole partner for designing and making the Mi Band, a fitness tracker that sold for a small fraction of the price of a Fitbit. When Huami went public in February 2018, it was one of the largest wearable makers in the world. It also wanted shoppers to know its own brand, Amazfit.

sections.heading: Riding on Xiaomi
sections.body: Wang Huang founded Huami in 2013 and held 45.8 percent of the company before the IPO. Huami built Xiaomi-branded bands, watches and scales, and it collected heart rate, sleep and step data from a huge base of users. The bet was that low prices and Xiaomi's reach would win the mass market, and that the data and know-how would let Huami launch its own watches and health services.

sections.heading: A Small Gain on a Bad Day
sections.body: Huami priced its ADSs at $11 in February 2018 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as HMI. On a day when the major indexes fell about 4 percent, the stock closed its first day up 2.3 percent. In 2021 the company renamed itself Zepp Health and changed its ticker to ZEPP, putting its own Amazfit watches at the center of the business. It remains listed on the NYSE.

tagline: Chips for the Speed of Light
dek: Inphi made high-speed analog chips that moved data quickly and cleanly between memory, servers and optical networks.
lede: Inphi's chips sat in the gaps between other chips, where signals blur as data moves faster. The Santa Clara company designed high-speed analog parts that kept those signals clean, first for server memory and then for the optical links that tie data centers together. It started in November 2000 as TCom Communications and took the Inphi name a few months later. It went public in November 2010, as cloud companies were building data centers at record pace.

sections.heading: Analog in a Digital World
sections.body: Most chip startups of its era chased digital logic. Inphi chose analog, the hard craft of moving electrical and light signals at the edge of what physics allows. It was fabless, designing chips and paying factories to build them. Its early money came from memory interface chips for servers. The bet was that every jump in data speed would make clean signals harder to deliver, and that the companies that could deliver them would be paid well.

sections.heading: Marvell Buys the Light
sections.body: Inphi priced at $12 a share in November 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as IPHI. The stock rose 27.5 percent on its first day. Inphi then moved deeper into optical chips for cloud data centers and telecom networks. Marvell Technology bought the company in April 2021 in a cash and stock deal worth about $10 billion.

tagline: A Dial Tone for the Web
dek: EarthLink sold ordinary Americans a monthly dial-up connection to the internet, with a phone line to call for help.
lede: Sky Dayton was 23 when he started EarthLink, after a frustrating week trying to get his own computer online. In 1994 the internet still felt like a club for engineers. Getting connected meant odd software, busy signals, and no one to call. Dayton bet that regular people would pay a flat monthly fee for a connection that just worked. By January 1997, when EarthLink went public, the Pasadena company was racing America Online for the millions of homes buying their first modems.

sections.heading: Busy Signals in Pasadena
sections.body: Dayton founded EarthLink in July 1994 in Southern California. The pitch was simple: one monthly price, the software you needed in the box, and real people on the phone to talk you through setup. EarthLink leased network capacity from other carriers and put its money into signing up customers and keeping them. It sold access to the open web, where AOL steered members toward its own walled garden of content.

sections.heading: Merging Toward Atlanta
sections.body: EarthLink priced 2,000,000 shares at $13 a share on Nasdaq in January 1997, raising about $26 million. In 2000 it merged with MindSpring, a rival internet provider, and moved its headquarters to Atlanta. Broadband slowly emptied the dial-up business, and EarthLink turned toward selling network services to companies. Windstream bought it in early 2017 in a stock deal valued at about $1.1 billion. Two years later Windstream sold the EarthLink consumer business to Trive Capital for $330 million.

cover.theme: a figure turning the globe (linking the earth)

dek: Ctrip let Chinese travelers book hotel rooms and plane tickets by phone or online, at a time when few could.
lede: Ctrip's stock jumped 89 percent on its first day, the biggest IPO pop the market had seen in three years. That was December 2003, when most investors still flinched at the word internet. The Shanghai company sold hotel rooms and plane tickets to a new class of Chinese business travelers. Most of its bookings came through a giant call center, with the website growing beside it. Wall Street saw a bet on China's middle class taking to the road.

sections.heading: Four Founders and a Call Center
sections.body: James Liang, Neil Shen, Min Fan and Qi Ji started Ctrip in Shanghai in 1999. Liang had worked at Oracle, and Shen was an investment banker. China had no easy way to compare and reserve hotels across cities. Ctrip signed up hotels, bought rooms at a discount, and earned a commission on each booking. Travelers could book through the website, but many preferred to call, so Ctrip built a large phone operation to answer them.

sections.heading: From CTRP to TCOM
sections.body: Ctrip priced its American depositary shares at $18 in December 2003, above its $14 to $16 range, and listed on Nasdaq as CTRP. The shares opened at $24 and closed the first day at $33.94. Ctrip grew into China's largest online travel agency and bought Skyscanner in 2016. In 2019 it renamed itself Trip.com Group and changed its ticker to TCOM. It added a Hong Kong listing in 2021 and still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a family on a long journey (Chinese travel)

tagline: The Toy Store Without a Floor
dek: eToys let parents shop for toys online and have them shipped to the door in time for the holidays.
lede: eToys priced its shares at $20 and watched them close near $76.50 on day one. It was May 1999, and the online toy store in Santa Monica was suddenly worth more on paper than Toys "R" Us. Parents were just starting to trust websites with their credit cards. eToys promised them a toy store with no lines, no parking lot, and gifts wrapped and shipped. The question was whether it could deliver all those boxes in December without running out of cash.

sections.heading: Toys Without the Aisles
sections.body: Toby Lenk, who had run strategic planning for Disney's theme parks, launched eToys in 1997. He saw that buying toys meant crowded stores and sold-out shelves, while the web could list everything at once. eToys organized its catalog by age and by type of play, and it sold well-known brands alongside harder-to-find toys. The company spent heavily on advertising and on its own warehouses, betting that being first and biggest online would win the holiday season.

sections.heading: One Bad Christmas Too Many
sections.body: eToys sold its shares on Nasdaq on May 20, 1999, raising $166 million. The stock touched $85 that first day. Holiday sales grew, but costs grew faster, and the dot-com crash in 2000 closed the door on new money. In February 2001 eToys announced it would shut down, and it filed for bankruptcy weeks later. KB Toys bought the eToys name and website from the wreckage for about $5 million.

cover.artwork: Yamauba with Kintaro Holding a Toy Mask

dek: NIO built premium electric SUVs for Chinese drivers, with batteries you could swap out in minutes.
lede: NIO went public with a single car model on the road, and it still raised about $1 billion on the New York Stock Exchange. It was September 2018. Tesla was struggling to build its Model 3, and China was pushing hard to clean its city air. NIO, based in Shanghai, sold a seven-seat electric SUV called the ES8 and promised a service network built around the owner. Investors were buying a promise that China would make its own Tesla.

sections.heading: An Internet Founder Builds a Car
sections.body: William Li, who had built the car-shopping website Bitauto, founded NIO in 2014. He lined up backing from Tencent and other Chinese tech investors. NIO designed its cars in-house and had a partner, JAC Motors, build them in Hefei. Its boldest idea was the battery swap station. A driver pulled in, a machine replaced the empty battery with a charged one, and the car left a few minutes later.

sections.heading: One Cent Above the Floor
sections.body: NIO priced 160 million American depositary shares at $6.26 on September 11, 2018, one cent above the bottom of its range. The stock fell as low as $5.35 on its first day, then closed at $6.60. Losses piled up in 2019, and the company came close to running out of cash. A 2020 investment led by the city of Hefei kept it alive, and the stock soared that year. NIO still trades on the New York Stock Exchange under NIO.

dek: Infosys wrote and ran software for big Western companies from engineering centers in India, at a fraction of the cost.
lede: Infosys became the first company registered in India to list on an American stock exchange. In March 1999, Wall Street was scrambling to fix the Y2K bug and hungry for programmers. Infosys had thousands of engineers in Bangalore who wrote and maintained software for American banks, retailers and manufacturers. Clients sent the work over phone lines and satellite links. The Nasdaq listing told the world that a company from India could compete for the largest software contracts.

sections.heading: Started With Borrowed Rupees
sections.body: N. R. Narayana Murthy and six colleagues founded Infosys in Pune in 1981, starting with a small sum Murthy borrowed from his wife, Sudha. They later moved the company to Bangalore. The bet was that Indian engineers, paid far less than their American peers, could do the same work from home with careful process. Infosys built a campus in Bangalore and sent engineers to client sites abroad. Its model came to be called global delivery.

sections.heading: Nasdaq, Then the Big Board
sections.body: Infosys listed its American depositary shares on Nasdaq on March 11, 1999, at $34 a share, raising about $70 million. The Y2K rush and the dot-com boom drove years of fast growth. Infosys grew to hundreds of thousands of employees and served clients around the world. In 2012 it moved its listing from Nasdaq to the New York Stock Exchange. Infosys still trades there under INFY and in Mumbai.

cover.theme: an Indian scholar at work (knowledge workers)
cover.artwork: Portrait of an Artist or Scholar

dek: King made free puzzle games like Candy Crush Saga that people played in short bursts on their phones.
lede: By February 2014, 144 million people a day were playing King's games, more than 1.4 billion times a day. Most of them were swapping striped candies in Candy Crush Saga on a phone. The games were free. King made its money from the small share of players who paid for extra lives and boosters when a level got hard. When it filed to list in New York, investors had to decide whether King was a lasting studio or a company riding one hit.

sections.heading: A Hundred Games, One Hit
sections.body: Riccardo Zacconi, an Italian who had sold online ads for a dating site, started King in 2003 with Sebastian Knutsson, a Swedish product designer, and a small team. For years King built quick skill games for its own website. The method was to launch many games, watch which ones people kept playing, and drop the rest. Candy Crush began as a web game, moved to Facebook, and then took off on phones.

sections.heading: A Crown for Activision
sections.body: King priced its IPO at $22.50 a share in March 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as KING. The stock fell below its offer price on day one, as investors worried about relying on a single game. King kept Candy Crush near the top of the app charts and added sequels. In February 2016 Activision Blizzard bought King for $5.9 billion. Microsoft then bought Activision Blizzard in 2023, and King came with it.

dek: Bilibili gave young Chinese fans of anime, comics and games a video site where they could watch and talk together.
lede: On Bilibili, viewers typed comments that flew across the video while it played, so watching alone felt like watching with a crowd. The Shanghai site began as a home for fans of anime, comics and games. By the end of 2017 it had 71.8 million monthly users, most of them young, and they spent about 76 minutes a day in its mobile app. In March 2018 Bilibili went to Nasdaq to sell American investors on China's next generation of fans.

sections.heading: A Fan Site Grows Up
sections.body: Xu Yi started Bilibili in 2009 as a small fan site for anime videos. Users uploaded clips, and the scrolling comments turned each video into a shared event. Chen Rui, a software entrepreneur, joined as chairman and chief executive and turned the community into a business. Bilibili added live streaming and licensed shows. Most of its revenue at the IPO came from mobile games it ran for its own users.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Hong Kong
sections.body: Bilibili sold 42 million American depositary shares at $11.50 each in March 2018, raising $483 million, and listed on Nasdaq as BILI. The shares slipped below the offer price in early trading. Bilibili kept broadening its videos from anime into music, gaming, science and daily life, and it added advertising and paid memberships. In 2021 it also listed in Hong Kong. Bilibili still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Hokusai's sketchbooks (the root of manga and anime)

tagline: Six Students and a Search Box
dek: Excite let early web users search pages by meaning, then grew into a portal with news, email and weather.
lede: Six Stanford students built Excite's search engine before most people had heard of a web browser. Their software tried to understand what a page was about, so a search could find documents that matched an idea. In April 1996 Excite went public in the same month as Yahoo and Lycos. Search engines were the front door to the young web. Wall Street was betting that whoever owned that door would sell the most ads.

sections.heading: Architext Before Excite
sections.body: Graham Spencer, Joe Kraus, Mark Van Haren, Ryan McIntyre, Ben Lutch and Martin Reinfried started the project at Stanford. They formed Architext Software in June 1994 to sell tools for searching large sets of documents. The web was growing fast, and in 1995 the company launched Excite as a free search site paid for by advertising. Excite soon added news, horoscopes, chat and free email to keep visitors coming back.

sections.heading: Married to @Home
sections.body: Excite sold 2,000,000 shares at $17 each in April 1996 and began trading on Nasdaq as XCIT on April 4. The founders became millionaires. Excite bought rivals and grew into one of the largest portals. In 1999 it merged with @Home Network, a cable broadband company, in a deal valued at about $6.7 billion. The combined Excite@Home burned through cash after the dot-com crash and filed for bankruptcy in 2001.

dek: TheStreet.com gave everyday investors fast, opinionated stock market news online, for a monthly subscription.
lede: A hedge fund manager and a magazine owner paid for TheStreet.com out of their own pockets. Jim Cramer ran money for a living, and Martin Peretz owned The New Republic. By May 1999 more Americans were trading stocks online than ever, and they wanted news as fast as their brokers got it. TheStreet.com had over 51,000 paying subscribers and a newsroom in Manhattan. It went public at the height of the online trading craze.

sections.heading: Cramer and Peretz Pay the Bills
sections.body: Cramer and Peretz organized the company in June 1996 and funded it with their own investments and loans. The first reporters started that year, and the site began publishing in November 1996. Its coverage of the October 1997 market turmoil sent traffic soaring. TheStreet.com charged readers a subscription, which few websites dared to do, and added advertising aimed at its well-off audience. Subscribers grew more than 380 percent in 1998.

sections.heading: Twenty Years to a Sale
sections.body: TheStreet.com sold 5.5 million shares at $19 each in May 1999, raising $104.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as TSCM. News Corp's News America bought $7.5 million of the stock in the offering. The shares fell hard when the dot-com bubble burst. The company kept publishing, and Cramer went on to host a stock show on CNBC. In 2019 TheMaven bought TheStreet for $16.5 million in cash.

cover.artwork: Wall Street Ferry, New York, No. 4579 from the series "Anthony's Instantaneous Views"

fate: Acquired by Verizon, 2016 ($60 a share, about $2.4B)
dek: Fleetmatics showed small businesses where their trucks and vans were, how fast they drove, and how much fuel they burned.
lede: Every day Fleetmatics collected about 30 million data points from the vans and trucks of its customers. A plumber or a landscaping firm could open a web browser and see where every vehicle was, how fast it was going, and how long it had idled. In 2012 software sold over the web was winning over big companies. Fleetmatics, from Dublin, sold it to the small ones, with more than 16,000 customers and 281,000 vehicles when it filed.

sections.heading: Two Irish Trackers Combine
sections.body: Fleetmatics formed in Dublin in 2004 by combining two fleet management companies, WebSoft and Moviltec. From the start it ran its software as a hosted service that customers reached through a web browser. A small device in each vehicle sent location and driving data over cellular networks. Most customers were small and medium-sized businesses with fewer than 1,000 vehicles. Fleetmatics grew by selling hard in the United States, where it opened a base near Boston.

sections.heading: Verizon Pays Sixty
sections.body: Fleetmatics priced its IPO at $17 a share in October 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as FLTX. It kept adding customers and sold more shares in follow-on offerings in 2013. Verizon was building a business around connected vehicles. In 2016 it agreed to buy Fleetmatics for $60 a share in cash, about $2.4 billion. The deal closed in November 2016, and Fleetmatics became part of Verizon Connect.

cover.theme: a train of covered wagons (a fleet on the road)

tagline: A Kung Fu Novel Goes Online
dek: Changyou ran online role-playing games for millions of Chinese players, led by the martial arts epic Tian Long Ba Bu.
lede: In March 2009 more than 800,000 people were logged into one game at the same moment. The game was Tian Long Ba Bu, built on a kung fu novel by Louis Cha that generations of Chinese readers grew up on. Its owner, Changyou, was the online game arm of the internet portal Sohu. Wall Street was still reeling from the financial crisis, and almost no one was going public. Changyou filed anyway, betting that Chinese gamers would keep paying through the downturn.

sections.heading: Two Licensed Flops, Then a Hit
sections.body: Sohu started an online game unit in 2003. Its first two games were licensed from outside developers. The first, Knight Online, came from Korea and never caught on. Sohu then built its own. Tian Long Ba Bu launched in May 2007, drew more than 400,000 players at once in its first month, and ranked among China's most popular games that year. In August 2007 Sohu set up Changyou as a separate company to hold the game business.

sections.heading: Sohu Takes It Back
sections.body: Changyou priced 7.5 million American depositary shares at $16 each on April 2, 2009, and listed on Nasdaq as CYOU. Half the shares came from the company and half from Sohu. Changyou kept Tian Long Ba Bu running for years and added new games, but China's players moved to phones and the old PC titles faded. In April 2020 Sohu bought out the other shareholders, and Changyou left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a hero of Chinese martial legend (the martial arts epic)
cover.artwork: Ma Lin (Tettekisen Barin), from the series "One Hundred and Eight Heroes of the Popular Water Margin"

dek: Baozun ran the online shops of global brands in China, from the website to the warehouse to customer service.
lede: When a shopper in China bought Nike, Philips or Haagen-Dazs online, Baozun was often the company behind the store. Foreign brands wanted China's online shoppers but did not know how to run a shop on Tmall, write the marketing, or ship the parcels. Baozun did all of it for them. By 2015 it served 94 brand partners. That May it listed on Nasdaq as the hired hand behind China's online shopping boom.

sections.heading: A Back Office for Brands
sections.body: Vincent Qiu, Junhua Wu, Michael Zhang and a few other investors founded Baozun in Shanghai in August 2007. The idea was to be the brand's own e-commerce team, rented out. Baozun built and ran official brand stores on Tmall and JD.com, bought ads, answered customer questions, and packed orders in its own warehouses. Some brands paid service fees. For others, Baozun bought the goods and sold them itself. Alibaba became an early investor and a close partner.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars, Then Hong Kong
sections.body: Baozun sold 11 million American depositary shares at $10 each in May 2015, raising $110 million, and listed on Nasdaq as BZUN. Gross merchandise volume on its platforms kept climbing as more Western brands moved into Chinese e-commerce. Baozun also branched into owning brands of its own. In 2020 it added a second listing in Hong Kong, as many Chinese companies on American exchanges did. It still trades on Nasdaq under BZUN.

cover.theme: a peddler showing his wares (selling on behalf of brands)
cover.artwork: A Fan Peddler Showing his Wares to a Young Woman

fate: Acquired by Nvidia, 2020 ($125 a share, about $6.9B)
dek: Mellanox made the chips and switches that let thousands of servers trade data with almost no delay.
lede: Nvidia paid $125 a share for Mellanox, more than seven times its IPO price. In February 2007 that ending was far away. Mellanox was an Israeli chip company betting on InfiniBand, a fast networking standard most data centers had never used. Its chips linked the servers inside supercomputers and big storage systems so they could act like one machine. Most of the world's networks ran on Ethernet, and Mellanox had to prove that speed was worth a second standard.

sections.heading: Galileo Veterans Bet on InfiniBand
sections.body: Eyal Waldman co-founded Mellanox in March 1999 and served as its chief executive and chairman. He had been vice president of engineering at Galileo Technology, an Israeli chip company that Marvell later bought. The InfiniBand Trade Association formed the same year, backed by IBM, Intel, Sun and others. Mellanox designed adapters and switch chips for the new standard. Most of its people and assets sat in Yokneam, in northern Israel, with a US office in Santa Clara.

sections.heading: Nvidia's Data Center Bet
sections.body: Mellanox sold 6 million shares at $17 each in February 2007, raising $102 million, and listed on Nasdaq as MLNX. InfiniBand spread through the world's fastest supercomputers, and Mellanox added high-speed Ethernet products. As cloud and AI data centers grew, fast links between machines mattered more. In March 2019 Nvidia agreed to buy Mellanox for $125 a share in cash. The deal closed in April 2020.

cover.artwork: Two Chinese Women Examining Thread and a Spider's Web in a Bamboo Grove

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2024 ($30 a share)
dek: Model N let drug and chip makers track the prices, contracts and rebates that decide what they actually earn.
lede: A drug company can sell the same pill at dozens of prices, after rebates to insurers, chargebacks to wholesalers, and discounts the government requires. Model N built software to keep track of all of it. Its customers included Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Amgen, Dell and VMware. In March 2013, as cloud software stocks were in demand, Model N went public as the system of record for the money that slipped between a list price and a real one.

sections.heading: From NetDynamics to Rebates
sections.body: Zack Rinat founded Model N in December 1999. He had co-founded NetDynamics, an application software company that Sun Microsystems bought. Model N's first product suite, released in 2002, served medical device makers. It later expanded to pharmaceutical and biotech companies and then to semiconductor and high-tech firms. The software managed pricing, contracts, incentives and rebates, and it could run on a customer's own servers or in the cloud.

sections.heading: Vista Pays Thirty
sections.body: Model N priced its IPO at $15.50 a share in March 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MODN. It spent the next years moving customers from licenses to cloud subscriptions. In 2024 Vista Equity Partners, a private equity firm that buys software companies, agreed to pay $30 a share in cash. The deal closed that June, and Model N left the stock market.

dek: EverQuote let people shop for car, home and life insurance online, then sold those shoppers to insurers and agents.
lede: EverQuote grew to $126 million in revenue while raising less than $10 million in equity. That is rare for an internet company. Its sites let people compare auto, home and life insurance, and it earned money by passing each shopper to a carrier or local agent who paid for the referral. By the spring of 2018 it had turned 240 million visits into 35 million quote requests. In June 2018 it went public from Cambridge, Massachusetts.

sections.heading: Two Founders, One Marketplace
sections.body: Seth Birnbaum and Tomas Revesz started the company in 2008 under the name AdHarmonics. Birnbaum had co-founded Digital Guardian, a data security company, and studied mechanical engineering at MIT. The company renamed itself EverQuote in 2014. Its bet was that buying insurance felt confusing and opaque, and that a single place to start shopping would win consumers. Insurers and agents paid EverQuote for each interested shopper it sent them.

sections.heading: Listing Without Much Funding
sections.body: EverQuote priced its IPO at $18 a share in June 2018, selling 4,687,500 shares, and listed on Nasdaq as EVER. Its revenue rose and fell with how much car insurers wanted to spend on new customers. When auto insurers cut their ad budgets, EverQuote's sales dropped, and when they returned, sales climbed again. EverQuote still trades on Nasdaq under EVER.

cover.theme: a couple sheltered under one umbrella (insurance)
cover.artwork: Young Couple Under an Umbrella in the Snow

tagline: The Matchmaker Who Met Her Husband
dek: Jiayuan gave China's urban singles a place to find someone to marry, through a dating website built on trust and serious intent.
lede: Gong Haiyan started Jiayuan as a graduate student, and she met her own husband on the site. By 2011 Chinese media called her the country's most famous online matchmaker. Millions of young people had left home for big cities, far from the parents and aunts who once arranged introductions. Jiayuan offered them a place to look for a spouse. It held 43.7 percent of China's online dating spending in 2010 when it listed in New York under a fitting ticker: DATE.

sections.heading: A Graduate Student's Side Project
sections.body: Gong founded the business in 2003 while studying at Fudan University. The site aimed at marriage, which set it apart from casual chat rooms. Members filled out detailed profiles, and Jiayuan worked to make the site feel trustworthy to people looking for a spouse, and to their parents. In the first quarter of 2011 it had about 4.7 million active user accounts a month.

sections.heading: A Ticker Called DATE
sections.body: Jiayuan priced its American depositary shares at $11 in May 2011 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as DATE. It arrived in a busy season for Chinese internet listings, and many of those stocks soon fell out of favor with American investors. In December 2015 Jiayuan agreed to be acquired by a group backed by Baihe Network, a rival Chinese dating company. The deal closed in May 2016, and Jiayuan left Nasdaq.

dek: Appian let big companies and government agencies build their own business apps by drawing them, with little hand-written code.
lede: Appian's chief executive designs strategy board games and plays them to win. Matt Calkins said so in his letter to investors, along with this: he and his three co-founders had been friends before they started the company, and they still argued over every decision. In May 2017 they took Appian public after 18 years of slow, self-funded growth. Its pitch was low-code software, which let companies build custom apps by dragging boxes on a screen.

sections.heading: Eighteen Years Near Washington
sections.body: Matt Calkins, Robert Kramer, Marc Wilson and Michael Beckley formed Appian in 1999 in the Washington, D.C. area. They released their first software in 2000. In 2004 they launched a business process management suite with a web-based tool for designing workflows. Government agencies and large companies used it to automate work such as approvals, case management and claims. The founders grew the company mostly on its own revenue and kept building one platform.

sections.heading: Calkins Keeps Control
sections.body: Appian priced its IPO at $12 a share in May 2017 and listed on Nasdaq as APPN. Calkins kept about 54 percent of the voting power through a second class of shares. Low-code became a crowded market, with Microsoft, Salesforce and ServiceNow selling similar tools. Appian moved more customers to cloud subscriptions and added process mining and AI features. It still trades on Nasdaq under APPN.

cover.theme: chess players (a founder who designs strategy games)

fate: Taken private by founder Scott Painter, 2026 ($2.55 a share)
tagline: What Others Paid for the Car
dek: TrueCar showed car buyers what others paid for the same car, then sent them to dealers with a set price.
lede: Haggling at a car dealership was one of the few prices Americans still fought over in person. TrueCar tried to end the fight with data. Its website showed what other buyers had paid for the same car nearby and connected shoppers to certified dealers who agreed to a price up front. It also ran car-buying programs for USAA and Consumer Reports. In May 2014 TrueCar went public, promising to make the dealership a less stressful place.

sections.heading: The CarsDirect Founder Tries Again
sections.body: Scott Painter had already founded CarsDirect, one of the first websites to sell cars online. In 2005 he started TrueCar in Santa Monica, first under the name Zag. The company gathered transaction data to show the real market price of new and used cars. Dealers in its network paid TrueCar when a shopper it sent them bought a car. Some dealers objected to the model, and TrueCar had to adapt its program state by state to local rules.

sections.heading: Painter Comes Back
sections.body: TrueCar priced its IPO at $9 a share in May 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as TRUE. Painter stepped down as chief executive in 2015. Dealer complaints, slower growth and the loss of key partner traffic weighed on the stock for years. In 2025 a company led by Painter, called Fair Holdings, agreed to buy TrueCar for $2.55 a share in cash. The deal closed in January 2026, and TrueCar left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a stagecoach and team (getting a ride)
cover.artwork: A Stagecoach Drawn by Five Horses

dek: SmarterKids.com sold educational toys, books and software online, matched to each child's age and learning needs.
lede: SmarterKids.com spent its first four years making CD-ROM games for children, then threw that business out. In 1998 it turned into an online store for educational toys, books and software, sorted by a child's age and the skills a parent wanted to build. The website launched in November 1998. A year later, with parents flocking to buy holiday gifts online, the Needham, Massachusetts company went public.

sections.heading: From CD-ROMs to a Catalog
sections.body: SmarterKids.com was incorporated in 1994, and Jeff Pucci, its co-founder, served as chairman. Until March 1998 the company developed and sold its own educational CD-ROM software. Then it began moving to online sales of other companies' learning products. It planned to add child assessment tools and educational content so parents could find the right products for each child. The bet was that parents would pay for a store that understood learning.

sections.heading: Merging to Survive
sections.body: SmarterKids.com sold 4.5 million shares at $14 each in November 1999, raising $63 million, and listed on Nasdaq as SKDS. The dot-com crash in 2000 dried up money for online retailers that were still losing it. In 2001 SmarterKids.com combined with Earlychildhood, a seller of supplies to preschools and teachers, under a new holding company called LearningStar. SmarterKids.com stockholders received shares in the new company.

cover.artwork: The Village School Scene (Terakoya), from the series "Sugawara's Secrets of Calligraphy"

dek: Rediff.com gave Indians at home and abroad free email, news, chat and online shopping in one portal.
lede: Rediff believed it ran India's first online bookshop, music shop and gift shop. In June 2000 only a sliver of Indians had internet access, often in cyber cafes, but millions more lived abroad and wanted news from home. Rediff.com, from Mumbai, gave them news, cricket scores, an instant messenger in English and Hindi, and free email with over 650,000 registered users. It went to Nasdaq just as the dot-com bubble began to burst.

sections.heading: A Mumbai Portal for the World
sections.body: Rediff was incorporated in Mumbai in January 1996 as Rediff Communication, with Ajit Balakrishnan as chairman and managing director. It became a public limited company in 1998 and renamed itself Rediff.com India in February 2000. The portal mixed news, chat, email and shopping. It also linked Indian software engineers to jobs overseas through a recruiting site. The plan was to earn from advertising and e-commerce as Indians came online.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and a Long Fade
sections.body: Rediff sold 4.6 million American depositary shares at $12 each in June 2000, raising $55.2 million, and listed on Nasdaq as REDF. The dot-com crash followed within months, and online ads in India grew slower than hoped. Rediff kept running its portal and email service as Google, Yahoo and Facebook pulled Indian users away. In May 2016 the company took its shares off Nasdaq and ended its US registration.

cover.theme: Krishna gathering a crowd with his flute (a portal that draws people in)

tagline: The Trade Paper of the Web
dek: internet.com ran dozens of websites and newsletters that covered the internet business for the people building it.
lede: Alan Meckler sold his company to Penton Media in 1998, then bought back the one piece Penton did not want: the websites. Those sites became internet.com. By June 1999 it ran 61 websites, 43 email newsletters and 55 discussion forums, all about the internet industry itself. Every dot-com needed programmers, marketers and investors who wanted to know what was happening. internet.com went public to sell ads against their attention, at the height of the boom it covered.

sections.heading: Bought Back From Penton
sections.body: Meckler's Mecklermedia ran Internet World trade shows and magazines. Its web arm had operated since December 1994, with sites called MecklerWeb and iWorld. When Penton Media bought Mecklermedia in November 1998, it decided the internet business did not fit. Meckler bought 80.1 percent of a new company, internet.com LLC, that held those sites. He kept building a network of news and how-to sites for developers, webmasters and internet investors, based in Westport, Connecticut.

sections.heading: From Jupiter to QuinStreet
sections.body: internet.com sold 3.4 million shares at $14 each in June 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as INTM. The dot-com crash cut its ad revenue, and the company renamed itself several times, becoming INT Media Group and then Jupitermedia. It sold its Jupiterimages photo business to Getty Images for $96 million and the internet.com sites to QuinStreet for $18 million in 2009. The remaining company became Mediabistro, then Mecklermedia, and ended its SEC registration in 2018.

cover.theme: a man absorbed in the newspaper (trade news)

dek: Multex.com put Wall Street analysts' research reports online, first for professionals and then for individual investors.
lede: Multex.com held more than a million research reports from over 400 banks and brokerages. For decades that research had traveled by fax and courier to big money managers, and small investors rarely saw it. Multex put it on the web, selling reports one at a time or by subscription. In March 1999, with millions of Americans trading online, the New York company went public promising to give the little investor the same reading list as a fund manager.

sections.heading: From Fax Machines to the Web
sections.body: Isaak Karaev co-founded the company in April 1993 as Multex Systems. It began by delivering research electronically from brokerage firms to institutional investors, replacing piles of paper. As the web spread, Multex opened the same library to individuals through Multex.com. By the IPO, more than 600,000 investors and financial professionals had access to its services, and its library held reports from more than 400 firms.

sections.heading: Reuters Buys the Library
sections.body: Multex.com sold 3 million shares at $14 each in March 1999, raising $42 million, and listed on Nasdaq as MLTX. The stock rode the online trading boom and then fell with it when the bubble burst. In February 2003 Reuters agreed to buy Multex.com for $7.35 a share in cash through a tender offer. The deal closed in March 2003.

dek: Beyond.com sold computer software online and let buyers download many programs instantly instead of waiting for a box.
lede: The company that became Beyond.com was first called CyberSource. In 1997 it split in two. The payments business kept the CyberSource name, and the store became software.net. It sold software over the internet and, for many titles, delivered it as a download. When it went public in June 1998, buying software meant driving to a store for a shrink-wrapped box. software.net bet that the people already online were exactly the people who bought software.

sections.heading: A Store Split From CyberSource
sections.body: William McKiernan and John Pettitt founded the company in August 1994, and it began selling software on its website that November. The company built its own tools for credit card processing, fraud screening and electronic delivery.
