In December 1997 it spun those tools off as CyberSource Corporation so the store could focus on selling. For many titles, a customer could pay and start downloading in minutes.

sections.heading: Into Chapter 11
sections.body: software.net sold 5 million shares at $9 each in June 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as SWNT. It renamed itself Beyond.com and spent heavily on advertising to compete with retail chains and other online stores. Losses mounted after the dot-com crash. Beyond.com filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in January 2002 and sold its online store business to Digital River. CyberSource, the spun-off payments company, later became part of Visa.

cover.theme: a bay opening to the far horizon (going beyond)

dek: Fatbrain.com sold technical books, manuals and training materials to engineers and the companies that employed them.
lede: Fatbrain.com went public under a different name: Computer Literacy. In Silicon Valley that name already meant something. Computer Literacy Bookshops ran four stores stocked with programming books and technical manuals for the engineers who built the valley's chips and software. In 1997 a young online store bought those shops for $5.1 million. When it listed in November 1998, it was betting that technical professionals would buy their books online, through their employers and on their own.

sections.heading: Buying the Valley's Bookshop
sections.body: Chris MacAskill, a geophysicist turned entrepreneur, and Kim Orumchian founded the company in June 1995. They sold technical books online and in May 1997 bought Computer Literacy Bookshops, with its four physical stores, for $5.1 million. The company sold books, training materials, manuals and research reports through its website and through co-branded stores for corporate customers. It later renamed itself Fatbrain.com.

sections.heading: Into Barnes & Noble
sections.body: Computer Literacy sold 3 million shares at $10 each in November 1998, raising $30 million, and listed on Nasdaq as CMPL. Amazon and barnesandnoble.com competed hard on price, and Fatbrain lost money as it grew. In September 2000 barnesandnoble.com agreed to buy Fatbrain for $4.25 a share in cash and stock. The deal closed that November, and Fatbrain's store was folded into Barnes & Noble's site.

cover.theme: a bookseller and an author (a bookstore)

dek: Viasat built satellite communications for the US military, then launched its own satellites to sell internet service from space.
lede: When Viasat went public in December 1996, most of its revenue came from one kind of military radio gear. Its UHF DAMA technology let many users share scarce satellite channels, and the Pentagon and its contractors were the main buyers. The Carlsbad, California company raised under $20 million. Few investors would have guessed it would one day launch some of the largest communications satellites ever built and sell internet service to homes and airplanes.

sections.heading: Three Engineers in Carlsbad
sections.body: Mark Dankberg, Steve Hart and Mark Miller founded Viasat in 1986 near San Diego. They designed networking and signal processing gear for satellite links, mostly under Department of Defense programs. In the six months before the IPO, UHF DAMA products made up 71.2 percent of revenue. The plan was to take that defense expertise into commercial satellite markets, where demand for data was growing.

sections.heading: Building Its Own Satellites
sections.body: Viasat sold 2.2 million shares at $9 each in December 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as VSAT. It kept growing in defense while moving into consumer broadband. In 2011 it launched ViaSat-1, a high-capacity satellite for home internet, and it later added in-flight Wi-Fi for airlines. In 2023 Viasat bought Inmarsat, the British satellite operator. It still trades on Nasdaq under VSAT.

cover.theme: the vault of the night sky (satellites)
cover.artwork: I Adore You as I Adore the Vault of the Night Sky, O Vessel of Sadness, O Great Taciturn One

fate: Taken private by Siris Capital and Elliott, 2019 ($15.75 a share)
tagline: The Pipes Behind Every Plane Ticket
dek: Travelport ran the booking systems that travel agents and websites used to find and sell airline seats and hotel rooms.
lede: In 2013 more than $85 billion of travel spending ran through Travelport's computers in Atlanta. Few travelers knew its name. When an agent or a booking site searched for a flight, the request often went through one of its three reservation systems: Travelport, Galileo or Worldspan. The company was built from pieces of the airline industry's oldest technology. In September 2014 its private equity owners took it public, betting that this plumbing still had value.

sections.heading: Born Inside Cendant
sections.body: Travelport grew out of the travel distribution division of Cendant, the company that also owned hotel and car rental brands. In 2006 Blackstone and its partners bought the business, and it took the name Travelport. In 2007 it bought Worldspan, a rival reservation system. Travelport connected airlines and hotel chains with online and offline travel agencies around the world. It earned a fee on each booking that passed through its network.

sections.heading: Elliott's Exit Ticket
sections.body: Travelport sold 30 million shares at $16 each in September 2014, raising $480 million, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as TVPT. Airlines pushed travelers to book on their own websites, which squeezed the fees that systems like Travelport collected. In late 2018 Siris Capital and Evergreen Coast Capital, an affiliate of the activist fund Elliott, agreed to buy Travelport for $15.75 a share in cash. The deal closed in May 2019.

cover.theme: the entrance to a busy port (Travelport)
cover.artwork: Entrance to the Port of Honfleur

fate: Taken private by RedPrairie and New Mountain Capital, 2012 ($45 a share)
tagline: The Back Room of the Store
dek: JDA wrote the software retailers used to decide what to buy, where to ship it, and how to price it.
lede: Sunglass Hut, West Marine, Woolworths and HMV all ran their back rooms on software from a company in Scottsdale, Arizona. JDA's programs tracked merchandise from the buyer's order to the store shelf to the cash register. Retail chains were growing fast across countries, and spreadsheets could not keep up with millions of items. By November 1996 JDA was already public and selling more stock, with its founders still owning more than a third of the company.

sections.heading: From JDA Canada to Scottsdale
sections.body: James Armstrong founded JDA Canada in 1978 and served as its president until 1987. In 1985 he and Frederick Pakis started the company that became JDA Software Group. Its Merchandise Management System let retailers plan purchases, control inventory and manage pricing. A companion system ran the stores themselves. JDA sold to large specialty and department store chains in North America, Europe and Asia, including Seiyu in Japan.

sections.heading: From Retail Code to Blue Yonder
sections.body: JDA went public on Nasdaq as JDAS in March 1996 at $13 a share, and its November 1996 offering followed with the stock above $28. JDA grew by buying other supply chain software makers, including Manugistics and i2 Technologies. In 2012 RedPrairie, backed by New Mountain Capital, paid $45 a share in cash to take JDA private. The combined company kept the JDA name, became Blue Yonder in 2020, and was bought by Panasonic in 2021.

cover.theme: a busy canal-side market (retail and supply)

tagline: A TV Network Learns the Web
dek: Phoenix New Media ran ifeng.com, a Chinese news portal born from the Hong Kong broadcaster Phoenix TV.
lede: In March 2011, ifeng.com drew more page views than the websites of CNN and the BBC. Its parent, Phoenix TV, was a Hong Kong satellite broadcaster that Chinese viewers trusted for news. Phoenix New Media turned that brand into a web portal and mobile service, with 222 million monthly visitors. A research firm it hired found its readers earned over four times the income of the average Chinese internet user. In May 2011 it listed in New York, during a rush of Chinese internet IPOs.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Phoenix TV
sections.body: Phoenix TV had kept a small website since its own Hong Kong listing in 2000. In November 2005 it put Shuang Liu, one of its vice presidents, in charge of a new media business. In 2007 it moved its sites to the domain ifeng.com, and that November it set up Phoenix New Media in the Cayman Islands to hold the business. The company sold advertising on its portal and paid services delivered to mobile phones.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars on the Big Board
sections.body: Phoenix New Media priced its American depositary shares at $11 in May 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as FENG. The offering raised about $140 million, including shares sold by existing holders. Readers moved from portals to apps and social feeds, and growth slowed. Phoenix New Media kept ifeng running as a news brand. It still trades on the New York Stock Exchange under FENG.

cover.artwork: The Phoenix or The Statue Overthrown

tagline: The Phone Company of the North
dek: China Netcom ran the phone lines and broadband in northern China, from Beijing to Liaoning.
lede: China cut its phone monopoly in two along a line on the map, and China Netcom got the north. In 2002 the government gave the old China Telecom's networks in ten northern provinces to Netcom. China Telecom kept the other 21. Netcom became the main provider of phone lines, broadband and business data in Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei, Henan, Shandong and Liaoning. Two years later it sold shares to investors in New York and Hong Kong.

sections.heading: A Startup Saved by a Split
sections.body: The first China Netcom started in 1999 as a wholesaler of fast data networks. Its backers included Jiang Mianheng, the son of President Jiang Zemin, and Liu Chuanzhi, the chairman of Legend Computers. The business struggled because China Telecom held a monopoly. Then the 2002 break-up handed Netcom a third of China Telecom's assets. It also merged in Jitong Communications. The new group could sell phone service anywhere in China, but its strength was the north.

sections.heading: Olympic Lines, Then Unicom
sections.body: The offering priced at $21.82 per American depositary share, which equaled HK$8.48 per share. Each ADS held 20 shares. Trading began on the New York Stock Exchange on November 16, 2004, and in Hong Kong a day later. Netcom carried the fixed lines for the Beijing 2008 Olympic Games. That June it agreed to merge with China Unicom. The deal closed on October 6, 2008, and Netcom's shares left both exchanges that month.

cover.theme: fishermen hauling in their nets (the Netcom network)
cover.artwork: The Fishermen of Katase Hauling in Their Nets: The Purple Shell (Murasakigai)

dek: Williams Communications ran a nationwide fiber network, much of it laid inside old gas pipelines its parent no longer used.
lede: A Tulsa pipeline company found a second use for its empty pipes: it pulled fiber optic cable through them. The Williams Companies started doing this in 1985. By 1999 its communications arm planned 33,120 route miles of fiber linking 125 cities by the end of 2000. Carriers across America were racing to lay new fiber. Williams Communications went public that October to pay for its share of the race.

sections.heading: Pipes Full of Light
sections.body: Pipeline rights of way were the hard part of building a long-haul network, and Williams already owned thousands of miles of them. The communications unit sold voice, data, internet and video services over its network. It also sold rights to unlit "dark" fiber to other carriers. Alongside the offering, SBC Communications, Intel and Telefonos de Mexico agreed to invest at least $725 million at the IPO price. Network centers in Tulsa and St. Louis watched the lines around the clock.

sections.heading: Seven Billion in Debt
sections.body: The shares priced at $23 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as WCG in October 1999. The Williams Companies kept about 85 percent of the stock. Then the telecom boom turned to a glut of fiber and falling prices. Williams Communications filed for Chapter 11 on April 22, 2002, owing $7.15 billion. The old shares were canceled. The company emerged on October 15, 2002 as WilTel Communications, with Leucadia National holding about 44 percent of the new equity.

cover.theme: a railroad line cut across the West (a long-haul route)
cover.artwork: Central Pacific Railroad, California, from the series "Central Pacific Railroad, California"

dek: Intersil made the analog, power and Wi-Fi chips inside laptops, base stations and broadband gateways.
lede: The best-selling Wi-Fi chips of 1999 came out of a Florida defense contractor. Harris Corporation's chip unit made the PRISM chip set, which led the market for wireless office and home networks. In August 1999 Harris sold the unit to a new company backed by Citicorp Venture Capital. The buyers revived an old name, Intersil, first used by a chip firm that Jean Hoerni, one of the "traitorous eight" of Silicon Valley, founded in 1967.

sections.heading: Harris Sells Its Chips
sections.body: Harris had bought the original Intersil in 1988 and folded it into Harris Semiconductor, along with chip units from General Electric and RCA. The 1999 buyout loaded the new Intersil with debt. The plan was to pay it down with an IPO and to grow the fastest parts of the catalog. Those were PRISM wireless chips, analog and mixed-signal parts for communications, and power management chips. Its headquarters stayed on Palm Bay Road in Palm Bay, Florida.

sections.heading: Half a Billion on Day One
sections.body: Intersil sold 20 million shares at $25 in February 2000, raising $500 million, and listed on Nasdaq as ISIL. Most of the money went to repay buyout debt. The company later sold the PRISM Wi-Fi line to GlobespanVirata in 2003 and built its business around power management and precision analog chips. It moved its base to Milpitas, California. Renesas Electronics bought Intersil for $22.50 a share, about $3.2 billion, closing on February 24, 2017.

cover.theme: a rainbow over a bay (the PRISM chip)
cover.artwork: Rainbow over Cascais Bay, Cintra, Portugal

tagline: The Backbone Behind the Storage Room
dek: McDATA built the big switches that let a company's servers reach its shared storage over one fast network.
lede: EMC, the king of storage in 2000, owned 97 percent of the voting power in the company that wired its machines together. McDATA, based in Broomfield, Colorado, built director-class switches for storage area networks, or SANs. Its ED-5000 director sat at the center of a data center, linking hundreds of servers to shared disk arrays. Data was piling up faster than companies could manage it, and McDATA sold mostly through EMC and IBM.

sections.heading: Run Apart From EMC
sections.body: McDATA had operated as a company separate from EMC since October 1, 1997, under a board with a majority of outside directors. Its pitch was size. One large switch with many ports cost less per port than a pile of small switches wired together to do the same job. EMC planned to hand its McDATA shares to EMC's own stockholders six to twelve months after the IPO, setting the company fully free.

sections.heading: Sold to the Rival
sections.body: McDATA sold 12.5 million Class B shares at $28 on August 9, 2000, raising $350 million, and listed on Nasdaq as MCDT. With the over-allotment, net proceeds came to about $377 million. The storage switch market narrowed to a few players, and McDATA's closest rival was Brocade. Brocade agreed to buy McDATA for about $713 million in stock, and McDATA's shares left Nasdaq in January 2007.

cover.artwork: Sun Pictures of Rocky Mountain Scenery

tagline: Small Glass Parts for Big Pipes
dek: Oplink made the fiber optic components and modules that let telecom gear squeeze more light through each strand.
lede: Cisco lent Oplink money before its IPO, and the loan turned into 3.3 million shares the day the company went public. In October 2000 every telecom equipment maker wanted more optical parts than suppliers could build. Oplink, a San Jose company started in 1995, made the small components and integrated optical modules that boost the performance of fiber networks. It sold them to the equipment makers that built the networks.

sections.heading: Parts Inside the Boxes
sections.body: Oplink's customers were the firms that built gear for phone companies. Its components sat inside their optical equipment and raised the performance of the network, so each fiber could do more work. The company was incorporated in California in September 1995 and moved its legal home to Delaware in September 2000, weeks before the offering. Its biggest customers were communications equipment suppliers around the world.

sections.heading: Bust, Then Koch
sections.body: Oplink sold 13.7 million shares at $18 in October 2000, raising $246.6 million, and listed on Nasdaq as OPLK. Within months the telecom bust froze spending on optical gear. Oplink stayed public for another 14 years. In November 2014 Koch Industries agreed to buy it for $24.25 a share in cash, about $445 million. The tender offer closed on December 23, 2014, and Koch put Oplink under its Molex electronics unit.

cover.theme: moonlight through a window (light through glass)

dek: Gaotu put star teachers in front of thousands of Chinese students at once, live, with a tutor for each child.
lede: The stock that sold for $10.50 in 2019 hit $149.05 in January 2021, then fell to $2.40 six months later. Gaotu, first called GSX Techedu, ran live online classes for Chinese students from kindergarten through high school. One star teacher lectured thousands of children at once. A team of tutors answered each child's questions during and after class. In 2018 China's online large-class tutoring market had grown to $2.2 billion in gross billings.

sections.heading: Big Classes, Small Attention
sections.body: Larry Xiangdong Chen founded the company's main operating business in Beijing in June 2014. Its platform, Genshuixue, also sold foreign language and professional courses to adults. The bet was that one great teacher could reach more students online than in any classroom, while tutors kept each child on track. GSX charged more than most rivals for its K-12 large classes. Chen controlled 89.8 percent of the votes after the offering.

sections.heading: Short Sellers and a Ban
sections.body: GSX sold 19.8 million American depositary shares at $10.50 in June 2019 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. In 2020 more than a dozen research reports, including one from Muddy Waters, accused it of inflating revenue, and the SEC opened an investigation. In July 2021 Beijing banned for-profit tutoring in core school subjects. The company renamed itself Gaotu in 2021. It still trades on the NYSE as GOTU.

cover.theme: a teacher among his disciples (live classes)
cover.artwork: The Ten Great Disciples of Confucius (Komon jittetsu), from the series "A Set of Ten Famous Numbers for the Katsushika Circle (Katsushikaren meisu juban)"

tagline: An Optical Network on a Fingernail
dek: Infinera packed dozens of optical parts onto one chip, making long-distance fiber networks cheaper and simpler to run.
lede: Infinera put more than 60 optical components onto a pair of chips about the size of a child's fingernail. Other fiber gear used those parts as separate pieces, wired together. Infinera's photonic integrated circuit, built in indium phosphide, sent and received 100 gigabits a second. In 2007 the company said it was the only large-scale PIC in commercial use anywhere. Phone carriers were buying it to light up their long-haul and metro routes.

sections.heading: Four Years in Stealth
sections.body: Drew Perkins, Jagdeep Singh and David Welch founded the company in December 2000 as Zepton Networks. It raised its first money in April 2001, just as the telecom bust began. The company stayed quiet until it shipped its first products in 2004. The bet was that integrating optics on a chip would do for fiber networks what the integrated circuit did for electronics in the 1950s. Its DTN system turned those chips into equipment carriers could install.

sections.heading: Nokia Takes the Chip
sections.body: Infinera sold 14 million shares at $13 in June 2007, raising $182 million, and listed on Nasdaq as INFN. Goldman Sachs led the deal. Infinera bought Transmode of Sweden in 2015 and Coriant in 2018 to grow its reach. In June 2024 Nokia agreed to buy Infinera for $2.3 billion in cash and stock. The deal closed in February 2025, and Infinera's shares left Nasdaq on February 28.

cover.theme: a calm sea to the horizon (infinity)
cover.artwork: Sea View, Calm Weather (Vue de mer, temps calme)

dek: Nimble sold fast flash storage that watched itself from the cloud and flagged trouble before customers noticed.
lede: Every Nimble storage array sent a steady stream of data about its own health back to the company. A cloud service called InfoSight read those streams, spotted problems and told Nimble's support team before the customer saw anything. Nimble's arrays mixed fast flash memory with cheap spinning disks, using a file system it called CASL. Storage costs were rising as companies piled up data.

sections.heading: Flash Plus Disk
sections.body: Varun Mehta and Umesh Maheshwari founded Nimble Storage in 2008. It showed its first product, the CS200 hybrid array, in July 2010. CASL let customers add speed or capacity on their own, without taking systems offline. Suresh Vasudevan became chief executive in 2011, and Maheshwari became chief technology officer. The bet was that smart software could get high speed out of a mix of flash and cheap disk, and that analytics could catch trouble early.

sections.heading: Bought by HPE
sections.body: Nimble sold 8 million shares at $21 on December 13, 2013, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as NMBL. It added all-flash arrays in 2016 and struck a partnership with Lenovo that October. On March 7, 2017, Hewlett Packard Enterprise agreed to buy Nimble for about $1.09 billion in cash. The deal closed on April 5, 2017, and HPE kept Nimble as a brand.

dek: Blue Martini sold retailers software to run their websites, call centers and mobile sales as one store.
lede: Monte Zweben owned 40 percent of Blue Martini after its IPO, and the company traded under the ticker BLUE. His San Mateo startup sold software that let big retailers and brands sell the same way on a website, a mobile phone or a call center. It was July 2000. Online startups had raised fortunes, and established brands wanted software to sell online themselves.

sections.heading: Two Years to Nasdaq
sections.body: Blue Martini began in June 1998 as a limited liability company and became a corporation in January 1999. Zweben was its chairman, president and chief executive. The software tracked customers and products across every channel, so a brand could see one shopper whether she used the website, a phone or the call center. The pitch to retailers was to build their brand at every point where customers met them. The company also sold services to install and run the software.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to JDA
sections.body: Blue Martini sold 7.5 million shares at $20 in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as BLUE. The dot-com crash followed within months. In 2005 Multi-Channel Holdings, a company owned by Golden Gate Capital, bought Blue Martini. It merged with GERS in 2006 to form Escalate Retail. RedPrairie bought Escalate in 2011, and its software ended up supported by JDA Software.

cover.theme: a glass on a laid table (a blue martini)

fate: Acquired by Brocade, 2016 ($1.5B); now owned by Belden
dek: Ruckus built Wi-Fi gear with smart antennas that steered the signal toward each device for stronger, steadier connections.
lede: Most Wi-Fi access points shout in every direction at once. Ruckus built antennas that point. Its patented BeamFlex system focused the signal toward each phone or laptop and steered it as conditions changed. In 2012 phone carriers were drowning in smartphone traffic and wanted to push some of it onto Wi-Fi. Businesses wanted Wi-Fi that held up in a crowd. Ruckus sold to both.

sections.heading: Born as Video54
sections.body: Ruckus started in 2002 as a project inside Sequoia Capital in Menlo Park. William Kish and Victor Shtrom incorporated it in June 2004 as Video54 Technologies. The first goal was sending TV video around the home over wireless, and in 2007 it showed a wireless adapter for set-top boxes. Selina Lo became chief executive and led the turn to carrier and business Wi-Fi. The bet was that smarter antennas could make cheap Wi-Fi reliable enough for paying customers.

sections.heading: Four Owners in Ten Years
sections.body: Ruckus priced its IPO at $15 a share and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as RKUS on November 16, 2012. Brocade bought it for about $1.5 billion in May 2016. Arris bought Ruckus from Brocade in December 2017 for $800 million. CommScope bought Arris in 2019. In July 2026 Belden completed its purchase of Ruckus for about $1.85 billion.

tagline: The Right Hours on Every Map
dek: Yext let businesses fix their hours and addresses once and have them show up right on Google, Siri and Yelp.
lede: Ask Siri when a store closes, and the answer has to come from somewhere. In 2017 Yext wanted that somewhere to be the business itself. Its software let companies keep their addresses, hours, menus and other facts in one place. Yext then pushed those facts to more than 100 services, including Apple Maps, Bing, Facebook, Google, Instagram, Siri and Yelp. Search was moving to phones and voice assistants.

sections.heading: From Leads to Listings
sections.body: Howard Lerman, Brian Distelburger and Brent Metz founded Yext in New York in 2006 as a local advertising business. It earned $20 million in 2009 by charging businesses for each customer lead. In 2012 it sold its pay-per-call business to IAC's CityGrid Media to focus on listings. Its direct data links to more than 100 apps and maps formed what it called the PowerListings Network. Yext called its platform a knowledge engine and sold it by subscription.

sections.heading: From Maps to AI Answers
sections.body: Yext sold 10.5 million shares at $11 in April 2017 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as YEXT. Lerman stepped down as chief executive in March 2022, and chairman Michael Walrath took over. Yext cut staff in 2023 and 2024 and bought Hearsay Systems. Its newer tools track how brands appear in AI-driven search. Yext is still public, worth about $930 million at the end of January 2026.

cover.theme: a crossroads with a signpost (pointing people to the right place)
cover.artwork: No. 68 (sic; actually 69): Crossroad at Kusatsu (Kusatsu oiwake), from the series "Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaido (Kisokaido rokujukyu tsugi no uchi)"

fate: Left Nasdaq, 2004; still listed in Frankfurt
dek: Intershop sold the software that let European and American companies open online stores in the early web years.
lede: Three years after the Berlin Wall fell, three founders in Jena, a university town in the former East Germany, started selling e-commerce software. They called the company NetConsult. In 1995 it built Germany's first online store. By 2000 Intershop was worth about $11 billion and was a star of Frankfurt's Neuer Markt, Germany's answer to Nasdaq. That September it brought its shares to America, with headquarters in Hamburg and operations run from San Francisco.

sections.heading: Shops in a Box
sections.body: Stephan Schambach, Karsten Schneider and Wilfried Beeck founded the company in 1992. Their bet was that every retailer would need an online store and few could build one. Intershop sold packaged software for running one, and services to install it. It released its current product line in March 1998, and most of its revenue came from software licenses. Development stayed in Jena, while product management sat in San Francisco. Schambach ran the company as chief executive.

sections.heading: Neuer Markt to Penny Stock
sections.body: Intershop sold American depositary shares at $32.09 in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as ISHP. Within months its earnings warnings shook the whole Neuer Markt, and the stock sank to penny levels. About 30 companies spun out of Intershop, including Demandware, which Salesforce later bought. Intershop left Nasdaq in 2004, the year Schambach left. It survived and still trades in Frankfurt, based in Jena.

cover.artwork: Cabaret de l'Homme Armé, Rue des Blancs-Manteaux

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: SLAB); agreed to be acquired by Texas Instruments, 2026 ($231 a share)
tagline: A Modem Part Shrunk to a Chip
dek: Silicon Labs made mixed-signal chips that shrank modems and cell phone radios, and later the chips inside connected devices.
lede: Silicon Labs' first chip took sales from $5.6 million in 1998 to nearly $47 million in 1999. The chip replaced a bulky part every modem needed, the direct access arrangement, which kept power surges on the phone line from harming the network. Three engineers from Crystal Semiconductor started the Austin company in 1996. By early 2000 they also sold a radio-frequency chip for cell phones, just as mobile phones were spreading fast.

sections.heading: Analog Parts in Plain Silicon
sections.body: Nav Sooch, Dave Welland and Jeff Scott bet that circuits usually built from costly, separate analog parts could move onto standard silicon chips. Their silicon DAA cost less and took less space than the parts it replaced. Their RF synthesizer, released in late 1999, generated the high frequency signals a mobile phone needs. The company sold mainly to makers of modems, phones and communications gear, and its offices sat on Boston Lane in Austin.

sections.heading: From Modems to Texas Instruments
sections.body: Silicon Labs priced its IPO at $31 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as SLAB. It moved into timing chips, microcontrollers and FM radio chips. From 2012 it focused on chips for connected devices. In 2021 it sold its infrastructure and automotive business to Skyworks for $2.75 billion. In February 2026 Texas Instruments agreed to buy Silicon Labs for $231 a share in cash, with closing expected in the first half of 2027.

cover.artwork: Looking Over the Sand Dunes - Easthampton

dek: Everbridge sent urgent alerts by call, text and email to the people who needed them during storms, attacks and outages.
lede: When bombs went off at the Boston Marathon in 2013, the city used Everbridge to reach police, firefighters, hospitals and residents during the lockdown that followed. A year earlier the system sent more than 10 million messages to people in the path of Hurricane Sandy. Everbridge sold software for mass alerts. It reached people by phone, text and email, and stopped once they had read the message. In 2015 it sent 1.1 billion communications.

sections.heading: Born After September 11
sections.body: Cinta Putra, Steve Kirchmeier, Patrick Stuver and James Keene started the company in 2002, after the September 11 attacks showed how hard it was to coordinate a crisis. It began as 3n Global. In 2008 it merged with National Notification Network, and in April 2009 it took the name Everbridge. The bet was that every city, hospital and large company needed one system to warn people and to hear back whether they were safe.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Thoma Bravo
sections.body: Everbridge sold shares at $12 in September 2016, raising $90 million, and listed on Nasdaq as EVBG. Revenue grew from $104 million in 2017 to $271 million three years later, and use rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. It bought a string of companies, including Nixle and xMatters. Thoma Bravo agreed to buy Everbridge in 2024, raising its bid to about $1.8 billion after a rival offer. The deal closed in July 2024.

cover.artwork: The La Plataine Bridge at Royan

tagline: Fiber Along the Southern Power Lines
dek: ITC^DeltaCom sold phone, data and internet service to southern businesses over 6,000 miles of its own and utility-owned fiber.
lede: Half of ITC^DeltaCom's fiber network belonged to power companies. Duke Power, Florida Power & Light and Entergy owned about 3,000 route miles, and the West Point, Georgia company managed and sold the capacity. It owned another 3,000 miles itself, running from Georgia to Texas. In 1997 ITC^DeltaCom planned to sell southern businesses local, long distance, data and internet service in one package.

sections.heading: Two Businesses, One Network
sections.body: The company ran two lines of business. Carriers' Carrier Services sold bulk capacity on its fiber to other phone companies. Retail Services sold phone and internet packages to businesses across ten southern states. Its Gulf States FiberNet routes began carrying traffic in 1994 and 1995. ITC Holding Company, an investor in southern telecom businesses, had been its sole stockholder. Pro forma revenue in 1996 was about $85.4 million.

sections.heading: Bankruptcy, Then EarthLink
sections.body: ITC^DeltaCom sold 5 million shares at $16.50 in October 1997, raising $82.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as ITCD. An over-allotment option could lift the total to $94.9 million. In 2002 it filed for Chapter 11 and reorganized. On October 1, 2010, EarthLink agreed to buy the company for $3.00 a share in cash. The deal closed that December, and ITC^DeltaCom became part of EarthLink.

fate: Merged into ScanSoft, 2005, which took the Nuance name; acquired by Microsoft, 2022 ($19.7B)
tagline: Say It, and the Phone Understands
dek: Nuance built the speech software that let callers say what they wanted instead of pressing buttons on a phone menu.
lede: In 1996 Charles Schwab customers could call in, say a company's name, and hear its stock price. The software that understood them, accents and all, came from Nuance, a spinoff of SRI International's speech lab in Menlo Park. A year later UPS used Nuance to answer calls about packages. By the end of 1999 more than 150 businesses had licensed it, from Fidelity and American Airlines to Sears and British Telecommunications.

sections.heading: Out of SRI's Speech Lab
sections.body: Nuance began in 1994, when it took a license to SRI International's patents and software for voice interfaces. That license was exclusive until December 1999, when Nuance let the exclusivity lapse. Its first name was Corona Corporation. The bet was that call centers would pay to replace touch-tone menus with plain speech. Big customers mattered. Schwab alone made up 16 percent of revenue in 1997, and reseller Periphonics made up 25 percent in 1999.

sections.heading: A Name That Outlived It
sections.body: Nuance sold 4.5 million shares at $17 in April 2000, raising $76.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as NUAN. In September 2005 ScanSoft, a scanning and character recognition company, acquired Nuance and adopted its name. The combined Nuance grew into a major speech company with headquarters in Burlington, Massachusetts. Microsoft bought it for $19.7 billion, including debt, in a deal completed in March 2022.

cover.theme: Echo Canyon (a voice that answers back)

dek: EPAM rented out skilled software engineers from Eastern Europe to build and test products for Western companies.
lede: EPAM listed its address as a small office in Newtown, Pennsylvania, but its engineers worked in Belarus, Ukraine, Russia, Hungary, Kazakhstan and Poland. The company sold software development to Western clients: design, building, testing and moving products between platforms. Its pitch was the deep pool of trained engineers across Central and Eastern Europe. When it went public in February 2012, most buyers thought of India for outsourced code. EPAM offered a different map.

sections.heading: Engineers Across the Old Bloc
sections.body: EPAM's predecessor was founded in 1993. Arkadiy Dobkin ran the company as chief executive, president and chairman. The current company was incorporated in Delaware in December 2002. EPAM's delivery centers sat in cities known for engineering schools. The bet was that clients would pay for strong engineers close to Europe's time zones, and that EPAM could manage them as one team from the United States.

sections.heading: Leaving Russia Behind
sections.body: EPAM sold 6 million shares at $12 in February 2012, 2 million of them new, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as EPAM. For years its largest delivery locations were Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. After Russia invaded Ukraine, EPAM announced a phased exit from Russia on April 7, 2022, and agreed that September to sell almost all of its remaining Russian holdings. EPAM is still public on the NYSE.

dek: Fogdog sold sporting goods online, with up to 60,000 items from more than 500 brands across every major sport.
lede: Nike held a warrant for more than 4.1 million Fogdog shares, a sign of how badly old-line brands wanted a foothold online in 1999. Fogdog said it had the largest selection of sporting goods on the web: up to 60,000 items from over 500 brands. The Redwood City company ran specialty shops for soccer, baseball, golf, the outdoors and fan memorabilia. It had a deal with America Online to reach shoppers, and it was losing money fast.

sections.heading: From Cedro to Fogdog
sections.body: The company started in October 1994 in California as Cedro Group. It took the name Fogdog in November 1998. Fogdog bet that shoppers would choose the web for gear they could not find in a local store. It wrote buying guides and product advice to win over serious athletes and weekend players. Keystone Fulfillment handled shipping. Its net loss for the first nine months of 1999 was $15.1 million.

sections.heading: A Year on Nasdaq
sections.body: Fogdog sold 6 million shares at $11 in December 1999, raising $66 million, and listed on Nasdaq as FOGD. The dot-com crash arrived three months later, and online retailers lost their access to new money. In late 2000 Global Sports, a Pennsylvania company that ran online stores for sporting goods retailers, agreed to buy Fogdog. Fogdog deregistered its stock on December 28, 2000, about a year after its IPO.

cover.artwork: Mishima: Morning Mist (Mishima, asagiri), from the series "Fifty-three Stations of the Tokaido Road (Tokaido gojusan tsugi no uchi)," also known as the Hoeido Tokaido

tagline: Consultants for the Dot-Com Gold Rush
dek: Scient built websites and online strategies for companies racing to do business on the internet.
lede: Scient was 18 months old when it went public, and its founder had already started a rival. Eric Greenberg launched Viant in 1996, then left to found Scient in San Francisco in November 1997. He hired Robert Howe, the former head of IBM's consulting business, as chief executive. Scient sold what it called "eBusiness systems innovation": strategy, design and engineering for companies building online. Its clients included REALTOR.com.

sections.heading: Strategy Plus Code
sections.body: The bet was that companies would pay one firm to plan an internet business and then build it fast. Scient hired strategists, designers and engineers and put them on the same teams. In the year ended March 31, 1999, it earned $20.7 million in revenue and lost $11.7 million. Greenberg served as chairman, and Howe brought the credibility of a big consulting firm.

sections.heading: From $133 to Bankruptcy
sections.body: Scient sold 3 million shares at $20 in May 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as SCNT. By fall 2000 it had about 1,180 employees, $100 million in quarterly revenue and a stock price of $133. Then dot-com clients ran out of money. In 2001 Scient merged with its rival iXL, and quarterly revenue had fallen to $11 million. The company filed for bankruptcy in July 2002 and was bought by SBI.

fate: Merged with NEXTLINK, 2000, forming XO Communications
dek: Concentric ran a fast internet network that carried private company networks, websites and home internet service.
lede: Concentric Network started life in Florida in 1991 as Engineered Video Concepts. By 1997 it ran a high-speed internet network from Cupertino, California, built on an ATM backbone. It sold companies virtual private networks, dedicated lines and web hosting, so they could link offices, suppliers and customers with ordinary browsers. On the day of its IPO, Williams Communications and Bay Networks bought about $18 million of its stock in a private deal.

sections.heading: Four Names in Five Years
sections.body: The company became Concentric Research Corporation in 1992 and began running its network in 1994. It took the name Concentric Network Corporation in 1995. Late in 1996 it finished building its current network design. The bet was that businesses would trust the internet for private traffic if one company guaranteed fast, steady service. Concentric also worked with TMI Telemedia, a Telecom Italia unit, on a worldwide network.

sections.heading: Folded Into XO
sections.body: Concentric sold shares at $12 in August 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as CNCX. The internet boom lifted demand for hosting and business connections over the next three years. In June 2000 Concentric merged with NEXTLINK Communications, and the combined company became XO Communications. XO went on to sell fiber-based business services for years. Verizon bought XO's fiber business for $1.8 billion in 2017.

dek: SeeBeyond sold software that let a company's separate systems, and its partners' systems, pass data to each other.
lede: Big companies in 2000 ran dozens of programs that could not talk to each other: billing, inventory, ordering, the new website. The company that became SeeBeyond, then called Software Technologies Corporation, had spent a decade writing the connections. Its e*Gate engine moved data between those programs inside a company and out to suppliers and partners. Customers included Hewlett-Packard, J.P. Morgan, Nike, Northern Trust, PETsMART and UBS. It filed from Monrovia, California.

sections.heading: A Decade Before the Boom
sections.body: James T. Demetriades founded the company in California in December 1989 as STDC Corporation. It became Software Technologies Corporation in June 1992. Then e-business arrived, and every company needed its old systems linked to the web and to trading partners. STC wrapped e*Gate into a suite called e*Xchange, built to link systems with little custom programming. After the offering, Demetriades owned about 44.9 percent of the stock.

sections.heading: Sun Buys the Pipes
sections.body: STC sold 4 million shares at $12 in April 2000, raising $48 million, and listed on Nasdaq as STCS. The underwriters held an option on 600,000 more shares. The company later renamed itself SeeBeyond Technology Corporation. On June 27, 2005, Sun Microsystems agreed to buy SeeBeyond for $4.25 a share in cash. The deal closed that August, and SeeBeyond's software became part of Sun's product line.

cover.theme: looking out to sea from a shrine (seeing beyond)
cover.artwork: Looking out to Sea from the Benten Shrine at Susaki in Fukagawa (Fukagawa Susaki Benten yori kaijo o nozomu), from the series "Eastern Capital (Toto)"

tagline: First Aid for a Crashing PC
dek: CyberMedia sold First Aid, software that diagnosed and fixed common Windows PC problems without a call to tech support.
lede: CyberMedia had sold more than a million copies of a program called First Aid by 1996. Windows PCs of the day crashed when a modem, a video card and a new program refused to get along. First Aid drew on a knowledge base that covered more than 10,000 combinations of problems and fixed many of them on its own. In October 1996 the Santa Monica company released Oil Change, which updated software and drivers over the internet.

sections.heading: Tech Support in a Box
sections.body: Unni Warrier co-founded CyberMedia in November 1991 with Srikanth Chari and Anne Lam. Warrier had earlier co-founded NetLabs, a maker of UNIX network management tools. The bet was that tech support was costly and getting scarce, and that software could do much of the job. First Aid was the core product. Oil Change aimed to keep a PC current by fetching updates online, a chore most users never did.

sections.heading: Bought for Its Fixes
sections.body: CyberMedia sold 2.5 million shares at $16 in October 1996, raising $40 million, and listed on Nasdaq as CYBR. The IPO came the same month Oil Change shipped. In 1998 Network Associates launched a tender offer for CyberMedia at $9.50 a share in cash, well below the IPO price. The offer succeeded, and CyberMedia deregistered its stock that September.

cover.theme: a field surgeon at work (First Aid)
cover.artwork: The Surgeon at Work at the Rear During an Engagement

dek: Luxoft wrote complex software for banks, carmakers and tech firms using engineers across Russia, Ukraine, Romania and Poland.
lede: Deutsche Bank named Luxoft a strategic vendor partner in 2013 and gave it an award for the way it built its teams. That bank, along with UBS, Boeing, Harman, Avaya and AMD, made up much of Luxoft's business. The company wrote and ran complex software from 14 delivery centers, most of them in Russia, Ukraine, Romania and Poland. It sold 45.6 percent of its work to clients in Europe and 42 percent to North America.

sections.heading: Born Inside IBS
sections.body: Luxoft started in Russia in 2000 under Dmitry Loschinin, who led it from the beginning. Its parent and largest shareholder was IBS Group, an Eastern European IT company founded in 1992. Luxoft opened a center in Krakow in 2010 and bought a firm in Bucharest in 2008. The bet was on engineers with deep industry knowledge, especially in finance. About 85 percent of its staff had more than five years of experience.

sections.heading: Sold to DXC
sections.body: Luxoft sold shares at $17 in June 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as LXFT. On January 7, 2019, DXC Technology agreed to buy Luxoft for $59 a share in cash, about $2 billion. The deal closed in June 2019. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, Luxoft left the Russian market and sold its business there to IBS.

cover.theme: a lantern in a portico (lux, light)

tagline: From Travel TV to Online Tickets
dek: Preview Travel let leisure and small business travelers book flights, hotels and cars online through AOL and Excite.
lede: Preview Travel started out making travel shows for television. By 1997 the San Francisco company had become one of the first places to book a trip online, and its logo sat next to AOL's and Excite's on the prospectus cover. Leisure and small business travelers could search fares, reserve flights, hotels and rental cars, and read travel guides. The company still produced travel programs for broadcast and cable TV, and sold online ads to travel brands.

sections.heading: Preview Media Goes Online
sections.body: The company was incorporated in California in March 1985 as Preview Media. It produced travel programming for TV, with sponsors such as MCI. The bet was that the same audience would rather plan and book trips on a computer. Preview Travel built its own booking service and placed it inside America Online and Excite, the busiest doorways to the web. Advertisers paid for banners and links that reached travelers ready to spend.

sections.heading: Folded Into Travelocity
sections.body: Preview Travel sold 2.5 million shares at $11 in November 1997, raising $27.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as PTVL. Hambrecht & Quist and NationsBanc Montgomery Securities led the deal. In 2000 Sabre negotiated a merger of Travelocity with Preview Travel. The combined Travelocity.com listed on Nasdaq, with Sabre owning about 70 percent, and Preview Travel's own stock was deregistered in March 2000.

dek: Sapient built custom business software for big companies at a fixed price and on a fixed schedule.
lede: Most consultants billed by the hour. Sapient promised a price and a deadline up front, and kept its margins by finishing on time. The Cambridge, Massachusetts firm built client/server and internet software for big organizations using QUADD, its own workshop method where clients worked alongside its staff to design the system. Sapient went public in April 1996. Within weeks the stock traded as high as $58.25, and in October it came back to sell more shares at $46.50.

sections.heading: Two Founders, One Promise
sections.body: Jerry Greenberg and J. Stuart Moore founded Sapient on November 6, 1990, and served together as co-chairmen and co-chief executives. Their bet was that clients hated open-ended consulting bills and would pay for certainty. That meant Sapient had to price each job right and keep its people busy. Revenue grew from $950,000 in 1992 to $503 million in 2000. By 1999 internet work made up more than 70 percent of revenue.

sections.heading: Bubble, Bust, Publicis
sections.body: Sapient's IPO priced at $21 a share in April 1996, raising about $32.4 million, and it listed on Nasdaq as SAPE. The October 1996 offering in this filing sold 1,040,000 more shares. The stock soared through the dot-com years, then fell as low as $0.75 when the bubble burst. Sapient rebuilt with engineering teams in India. Publicis Groupe bought it in 2015 for $3.7 billion, and it lives on as Publicis Sapient.

cover.theme: an owl under a crescent moon (sapient, wise)
cover.artwork: Small-horned owl, pine, and crescent moon

dek: Genpact ran finance, claims and other back-office work for big companies from India and other low-cost centers.
lede: Genpact began with 20 people in Gurgaon processing car loans and credit card transactions for GE Capital. Ten years later it had more than 26,500 employees in nine countries. Jack Welch credited the unit with cutting about $1 billion from GE's operating costs. When it went public in August 2007, Genpact had $613 million in 2006 revenue. GE still supplied most of it, under a contract that ran through 2013.

sections.heading: Born Inside GE Capital
sections.body: Pramod Bhasin founded the business in 1997 while working for GE, as GE Capital International Services. It moved back-office work such as accounting, insurance claims and IT support from the United States to India. GE later sold 60 percent of the business to the investment firms General Atlantic and Oak Hill Capital Partners. In January 2005 the company took the name Genpact and began serving other clients. The bet was that the GE playbook could sell to any big company.

sections.heading: One Letter on the NYSE
sections.body: Genpact sold 35.3 million shares at $14 in August 2007, half new and half from existing holders, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the one-letter symbol G. In 2008 its revenue passed $1 billion, with most of it coming from clients other than GE. Genpact later moved its headquarters to New York. It is still public on the NYSE, with 2025 revenue of $5.08 billion.

cover.theme: villagers at shared work (process work in India)
cover.artwork: Villagers Grinding Corn, page from the Fraser Album

tagline: China's Car Showroom on the Web
dek: Autohome was China's top car website, where buyers read reviews, compared prices and traded advice in busy forums.
lede: The founder of China's biggest car website later started his own carmaker. Li Xiang launched autohome.com.cn in 2005 to sell online ads to the auto industry. By 2013 it ranked first among China's automotive websites in daily visitors and time spent. Its forums held 7.7 million registered users. Every day its editors posted about 600 articles and 1,200 photos for car shoppers across China.

sections.heading: Reviews Before Showrooms
sections.body: Li started a computer site, pcpop.com, in 2000 before turning to cars. Autohome tested and reviewed cars itself, instead of relying only on what automakers said. Buyers used it to compare models and prices before visiting a dealer. Automakers and dealers paid to advertise and to reach those buyers. Before the IPO, Australia's Telstra controlled the company, and Li served as its president.

sections.heading: A Founder Who Built Cars
sections.body: Autohome sold American depositary shares at $17 in December 2013, raising about $133 million, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ATHM. Telstra kept control after the offering through Class B shares, whose voting power depended on how much of the company it held. Li Xiang later founded Li Auto, the electric carmaker. Autohome remains a public company and still trades on the NYSE as ATHM.

tagline: A Front Door to the Spanish-Speaking Web
dek: Terra gave Spanish and Portuguese speakers one home page for news, email, search and dial-up access.
lede: Spain's phone company built Terra Networks to own the Spanish-speaking internet before anyone else could. Telefónica gathered its web portals and dial-up access businesses in Spain and Latin America into one company and sent it public in November 1999. The pitch was simple. Hundreds of millions of people read and wrote in Spanish or Portuguese, and few big sites spoke to them. Shares sold in Madrid and New York, with Telefónica keeping control.

sections.heading: One Portal, Two Continents
sections.body: Terra means earth in Portuguese and Latin, and the company wanted that much ground. It ran portals country by country, from Spain to Brazil, Mexico and Chile, and sold internet access through Telefónica's phone lines. Readers came for news, chat, email and search in their own language. Advertisers followed the readers. The plan leaned on its parent: Telefónica owned the wires, the customers and the brand, and Terra would be its face on the web.

sections.heading: Lycos, Then Home Again
sections.body: Terra priced its offering on November 17, 1999, at 13 euros a share, or $13.41 for each American depositary share on Nasdaq. In 2000 it bought Lycos, the American search portal, to become a global player. The dot-com crash cut the value of both businesses, and Terra sold Lycos in 2004. In February 2005 Telefónica proposed folding Terra back into itself. The merger closed that summer, and Terra's shares stopped trading in July 2005.

cover.artwork: Puerta Visagara, Gate of Madrid, Toledo

tagline: The Blackboard That Learned to Listen
dek: SMART put touch-screen whiteboards in classrooms, so teachers could write, tap and drag lessons on the wall.
lede: A husband-and-wife team in Calgary turned the classroom chalkboard into a giant touch screen. David Martin and Nancy Knowlton built the SMART Board, an interactive whiteboard that let a teacher tap, write and drag on a projected computer screen. By 2010 the boards hung in classrooms around the world, paid for mostly by schools and governments. When SMART went public that July, Intel and the buyout firm Apax Partners sat beside the founders as its biggest owners.

sections.heading: Chalk Meets the Computer
sections.body: Martin and Knowlton started SMART in 1987. The SMART Board made a computer feel like a wall a whole class could share. A teacher could circle a word, open a map or save the day's notes with a touch. SMART sold its boards through dealers, then added software, student response systems and flat-panel displays. Its prospectus warned that a cut in government funding for schools could hurt sales.

sections.heading: Tablets Change the Lesson
sections.body: SMART priced its IPO at $17 a share in July 2010 and listed on Nasdaq and the Toronto Stock Exchange. The timing was hard. School budgets tightened, and tablets gave teachers a cheaper screen to share. The stock spent most of its public life below the offer price. In 2016 SMART agreed to be bought by Foxconn, the Taiwanese electronics maker, through a Singapore subsidiary. Its shares left Nasdaq in September 2016.

fate: Bankrupt, 2002; operations sold to Asia Netcom
dek: Asia Global Crossing laid undersea fiber to carry the internet's traffic between Asia's cities and across the Pacific.
lede: Microsoft and Softbank each owned about 16 percent of Asia Global Crossing on the day it went public. The rest of the control sat with Global Crossing, the American cable builder. Together they bet that Asian internet traffic would explode and that whoever owned the fiber under the sea would carry it. In October 2000 the company raised $476 million, laying a trans-Pacific cable and building networks in Japan and Hong Kong.

sections.heading: Three Partners, One Ocean
sections.body: Global Crossing formed the company in September 1999 and brought in Microsoft and Softbank that November. The plan called for a pan-Asian carrier selling internet, data and voice capacity to other carriers and big businesses. It owned a trans-Pacific subsea cable, a data center in Tokyo and the largest all-fiber network in Hong Kong. It was building an East Asian cable to tie the region's cities together. Every piece cost a fortune, and most of it was borrowed.

sections.heading: Seven Dollars and a Glut
sections.body: The IPO priced at $7 a share on October 10, 2000, for 68 million shares. Within months the world had far more fiber than traffic. Prices for capacity collapsed, and its parent Global Crossing filed for bankruptcy in January 2002. Asia Global Crossing followed on November 17, 2002, filing for Chapter 11 as it agreed to sell its operations to Asia Netcom, a group backed by China Netcom. Its shares were deregistered in June 2003.

cover.artwork: Ferry Crossing at Sakasai (Sakasai no watashi), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo"

dek: Despegar let Latin Americans book flights, hotels and package trips online, in their own currency and language.
lede: Despegar means "to take off" in Spanish, and the company spent 18 years getting off the ground before it reached the New York Stock Exchange. The Buenos Aires company started in 1999 as an online travel agency for Latin America. By 2017 it sold flights, hotels and package trips across the region, from Brazil to Mexico. When it listed that September, most Latin Americans still booked their trips through travel agents or directly with airlines.

sections.heading: Born in the Bubble
sections.body: A group of young founders, among them Martín Rastellino, launched Despegar in 1999, just as the dot-com boom peaked. They survived the crash and Argentina's 2001 economic collapse. The bet was that Latin Americans would book travel online if someone handled their currencies, payment habits and installment plans. Despegar built local sites in each country, sold under the Decolar name in Brazil, and added packages and hotels to its airline tickets. Expedia became a major shareholder before the IPO.

sections.heading: From the NYSE to Prosus
sections.body: Despegar priced its IPO at $26 a share on September 20, 2017, and listed on the NYSE as DESP. The pandemic later shut down travel and hit the company hard, and the stock traded far below its offer price for years. In December 2024 Prosus, the Dutch technology investor, agreed to buy Despegar for $19.50 a share in cash. The deal closed in May 2025, and Despegar left the New York Stock Exchange.

fate: Taken private by founder Leo Ou Chen, 2020 ($20 per ADS)
dek: Jumei sold Chinese shoppers discounted makeup and skincare online, one limited-time deal at a time.
lede: Jumei sold lipstick the way other sites sold concert tickets: a few deals at a time, gone when the clock ran out. Leo Ou Chen and his co-founders built the Beijing company around flash sales of makeup and skincare for young Chinese women. By May 2014, when Jumei listed in New York, Chinese e-commerce was booming. Alibaba was months away from its own record listing, and investors wanted a piece of every kind of Chinese shopper.

sections.heading: A Beauty Deal a Day
sections.body: Chen and two co-founders, including Yusen Dai, formed the company in Beijing in August 2009 and opened the Jumei store in March 2010. It started with discounted beauty deals that lasted a short time, a group-buying format then popular across China. Shoppers came back each day for new offers. Jumei soon bought stock from brands and held it in its own warehouses, so it could promise real products and fast delivery. Chen kept control through a separate class of voting shares.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two Dollars Down to Twenty
sections.body: Jumei priced its IPO at $22 per American depositary share on May 16, 2014, and listed on the NYSE as JMEI. Growth slowed as Alibaba and JD.com pushed into cosmetics, and worries about fake products hung over the whole category. The stock slid far below its offer price. In 2020 a buyer group controlled by Chen offered $20 per American depositary share in cash. The offer closed that spring, and Jumei left the NYSE in April 2020.

dek: ONI built optical gear that moved data as light across a city's fiber, between offices and long-haul lines.
lede: ONI Systems went public in June 2000 having sold its first product for barely five months. It didn't matter. Optical networking was the hottest corner of the stock market, and ONI built the gear for the stretch everyone said was jammed: the fiber loops inside cities. Long-haul lines between cities had grown huge. The metro networks that fed them had not. ONI promised to carry many wavelengths of light around those loops at once.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Optivision
sections.body: Rohit Sharma founded ONI in a spin-out from Optivision, a Silicon Valley optics company. It was incorporated in California on October 20, 1997, as Optical Networks, Incorporated, and took the name ONI Systems in April 2000. The bet was that phone companies and carriers would rebuild their city networks around light instead of copper and old electronic switches. ONI's first product became generally available in January 2000, and carriers began testing it in their metro rings.

sections.heading: Peak Price, Then Ciena
sections.body: ONI priced its IPO at $25 a share on June 1, 2000, and sold more stock in a follow-on offering that October. Then the telecom boom broke, and the stock fell with the rest of the sector. Carriers stopped spending, and many of ONI's young customers went broke. In 2002 Ciena, a larger optical equipment maker, bought ONI in an all-stock deal. ONI deregistered its shares in June 2002.

cover.artwork: The actor Yamanaka Heikuro I as a demon

fate: Taken private by founder Germain Lamonde, 2021
dek: EXFO made the instruments that tell fiber-optic engineers whether their light is getting through.
lede: EXFO started in Quebec City in 1985 with two employees and a handheld box for testing fiber. Fifteen years later the world was laying fiber as fast as crews could dig, and every new strand needed checking. Carriers, equipment makers and research labs used EXFO's gear to measure how light behaved in the glass. When EXFO went public in June 2000, it sold shares on Nasdaq and the Toronto Stock Exchange at the height of the optical boom.

sections.heading: Two People, One Test Box
sections.body: Germain Lamonde founded EXFO in 1985 to build portable instruments that measured the physical traits of optical fiber. Fiber carries data as pulses of light, and a bad splice or a dirty connector can ruin a link. EXFO's tools found the problem. The company grew from handheld testers into a full line of test, measurement and monitoring products. Lamonde ran it as chairman, president and chief executive when it filed to go public.

sections.heading: Back to Its Founder
sections.body: EXFO priced its IPO at $26 a share on June 30, 2000. The optical bust arrived months later, and test-equipment orders fell with the rest of the industry. EXFO survived and kept selling to carriers as networks moved to faster speeds. In 2021 Lamonde took the company private through a buyout that paid public shareholders in cash. Its shares left Nasdaq in August 2021.

cover.theme: a rainbow over falls (light split into its colors)
cover.artwork: Freer Glen at Watkins Rainbow Falls and Triple Cascade 3rd Glen

dek: Qunar let Chinese travelers search every airline and hotel site at once and find the cheapest trip.
lede: Qunar's name asks a question in Chinese: where to go. In 2005 three founders launched it as a travel search engine on a domain registered in CC Zhuang's own name. By 2013 millions of Chinese were taking their first flights and hotel trips, and Qunar compared prices across hundreds of sellers. Baidu, China's biggest search company, owned most of it. Baidu founder Robin Li chaired its board when it listed in New York.

sections.heading: A Search Box for Trips
sections.body: Frederick Demopoulos, Chenchao (CC) Zhuang and Douglas Khoo launched Qunar.com in May 2005. Online travel agencies like Ctrip sold tickets and kept a cut. Qunar searched the agencies, airlines and hotels together and showed every price on one page. It made money from clicks and ads, and later took bookings itself. Zhuang became chief executive. In 2011 Baidu bought a majority stake, which gave Qunar a steady stream of searchers.

sections.heading: From Rival to Ctrip's Family
sections.body: Qunar priced its IPO at $15 per American depositary share on November 1, 2013, on Nasdaq. It spent heavily to win hotel bookings, and its fight with Ctrip cost both companies money. In 2015 Baidu swapped much of its Qunar stake for shares of Ctrip, and the rivals became partners. A buyer group then took Qunar private for $30.39 per American depositary share. Its shares left Nasdaq in early 2017.

fate: Bankrupt, 2003; assets sold to XO Communications, 2004
tagline: Taking On the Bells, City by City
dek: Allegiance sold phone lines, long distance and internet service to small businesses, competing with the old Bell companies.
lede: Allegiance Telecom went public just 15 months after it was founded. Its leaders had done this before. Royce Holland had co-founded MFS Communications, and Thomas Lord had been a telecom banker at Bear Stearns. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 let new carriers rent pieces of the Bell networks and sell service in their own name. Allegiance set out to do that in big cities, starting with small and midsize businesses.

sections.heading: A Team From MFS
sections.body: Holland and Lord founded Allegiance in Dallas in April 1997. They raised money from private equity firms and planned to enter many of the largest U.S. markets at once. The model was simple. Put switches in each city, lease the last stretch of copper from the local Bell, and sell a bundle of local calling, long distance, data and internet service. Small business owners would get one bill and one company to call, often at a lower price.

sections.heading: Bundles, Debt and XO
sections.body: Allegiance priced its IPO at $15 a share in July 1998 and sold more stock in 1999 and 2000. Building a network in each city took heavy borrowing. When the telecom bust hit, many rival carriers failed, and lenders lost patience with the rest. Allegiance and its subsidiaries filed for Chapter 11 in May 2003 in New York. XO Communications bought its operations out of bankruptcy in 2004.

cover.artwork: The Standard Bearer, Turned to Left

dek: USinternetworking ran big business software in its own data centers and rented it to companies by the month.
lede: USinternetworking filed to go public barely a year after it was founded, promising to run a company's software so the company did not have to. Its prospectus said it on the inside cover: "At last, running enterprise applications doesn't require you to run anything but your business." In 1999 big software meant big projects, with servers, consultants and months of setup. USi offered the same programs over a network for a monthly fee.

sections.heading: An Annapolis Data Center Bet
sections.body: USi was incorporated in Delaware in January 1998 and based in Annapolis, Maryland, with Christopher McCleary as chairman and chief executive. It called itself an application service provider. USi bought licenses for business software from large vendors, installed it in its own data centers and ran it for customers over its network. Customers paid a monthly fee for software, hardware and support together. The model needed huge spending up front, before the monthly fees added up.

sections.heading: Too Early, Too Much Debt
sections.body: USi priced its IPO at $21 a share in April 1999 and sold more stock in early 2000. Then the dot-com crash dried up funding for young internet companies, including many of its customers. Building data centers ahead of demand left USi with heavy debts. On January 7, 2002, USi and four subsidiaries filed for Chapter 11 in Maryland. USi deregistered its public shares that May.

cover.theme: a forge (the engine room behind the software)

fate: Taken private by GI Partners, 2021 ($11.50 a share)
dek: ORBCOMM used small low-orbit satellites to send short data messages from trucks, ships and machines anywhere on Earth.
lede: ORBCOMM's satellites never carried a phone call. They carried short bursts of data: a truck's location, a tank's fill level, a container's temperature in the middle of the ocean. A fleet of small satellites in low orbit picked up those messages and relayed them to the ground. When ORBCOMM went public in November 2006, connected machines were still a niche, and it was one of the few companies selling a global network built for them.

sections.heading: A Network for Machines
sections.body: An earlier company built the first ORBCOMM satellites in the 1990s and went bankrupt in 2000. A new ORBCOMM bought the network out of bankruptcy and rebuilt the business around it. Its customers were companies that tracked and monitored equipment, such as trucking fleets, heavy machinery makers, shipping lines and utilities. A small modem on each asset talked to the satellites. ORBCOMM charged for the messages and for the devices.

sections.heading: From Satellites to Buyout
sections.body: ORBCOMM priced its IPO at $11 a share on November 3, 2006, on Nasdaq. It launched new generations of satellites and bought companies that sold tracking hardware and software, so it could offer the whole system. Growth came slowly, and the stock spent long stretches below its offer price. In 2021 GI Partners agreed to buy ORBCOMM for $11.50 a share in cash. Its shares left Nasdaq that September.

fate: Taken private by Francisco Partners and Evergreen Coast Capital, 2020 ($86.05 a share)
dek: LogMeIn let people reach their own computers from anywhere, and let IT staff fix machines without a visit.
lede: LogMeIn went public in July 2009, when almost no tech company dared to. The financial crisis had shut the IPO window for more than a year. LogMeIn walked through anyway with a simple product: open a browser, log in, and control your computer at home or the office as if you sat in front of it. A free version pulled in users. Businesses and IT departments paid for more. Its engineers worked out of Budapest.

sections.heading: Born in Budapest
sections.body: Michael Simon founded LogMeIn in February 2003 with Marton Anka, who became its chief technology officer. Simon had founded Uproar, an online game show company, in 1995. Anka had run 3am Labs, a Hungarian software developer. Their bet was a freemium model. Give away basic remote access, win a crowd of users, and sell paid versions with more features to professionals and IT teams. Hungary supplied the engineers, and the company was based near Boston.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars to GoTo
sections.body: LogMeIn priced its IPO at $16 a share on July 1, 2009, on Nasdaq. It grew past remote access into password management with LastPass and, in 2017, merged with Citrix's GoTo business, which included GoToMeeting. In 2020 Francisco Partners and Evergreen Coast Capital took LogMeIn private for $86.05 a share in cash. Its shares left Nasdaq in August 2020. The company later renamed itself GoTo.

cover.theme: a figure at an open door (remote access)

tagline: The Home That Texts You Back
dek: Alarm.com connected home alarms, cameras, locks and thermostats to the cloud, so owners could check them from a phone.
lede: Alarm.com began as a side project inside MicroStrategy, a business software company better known today for buying bitcoin. In 2000 the unit set out to change a sleepy industry: home security, where alarms dialed a monitoring center over a landline and owners knew nothing. Alarm.com put the alarm on a wireless connection and the controls on the owner's phone. By its June 2015 IPO, it sold that service through local security dealers across the country.

sections.heading: Spun Out of MicroStrategy
sections.body: Alarm.com started in 2000 as a business unit of MicroStrategy and launched its first product in 2003. It became a majority-owned MicroStrategy subsidiary that year. MicroStrategy sold all of its interest in 2009, and Alarm.com Holdings was formed for the sale. The bet was to sell software through the dealers who already installed alarms. Dealers paid Alarm.com a monthly fee for each home, then added cameras, smart locks and thermostats to the same app.

sections.heading: A Steady Climb From $14
sections.body: Alarm.com priced its IPO at $14 a share on June 26, 2015, and listed on Nasdaq as ALRM. Its business ran on recurring fees, and dealers kept adding customers as smart-home devices spread. The company bought makers of video, energy and commercial security products to widen what its platform could control. As of October 2026, Alarm.com is still public on Nasdaq and based in Tysons, Virginia.

dek: Western Multiplex built radio systems that beamed broadband between buildings and towers without digging up streets.
lede: Laying fiber meant tearing up streets. Western Multiplex sold a shortcut: a pair of radios that beamed data from one rooftop or tower to another. The Sunnyvale company had made radio parts since 1979. By August 2000, when it went public, carriers and wireless companies were racing to build networks, and a radio link could go up in days instead of months. Two years later it took a new name, Proxim.

sections.heading: From Parts to Point-to-Point
sections.body: Western Multiplex started in Sunnyvale in 1979 as a vendor of radio components and services. In 1992 it changed course and began designing and making broadband wireless systems of its own. Its main products linked two fixed points, such as cell towers or office buildings, with a high-capacity radio beam. Phone companies, cellular carriers and businesses used them where fiber was too slow or too costly to install.

sections.heading: The Proxim Name, Then Terabeam
sections.body: Western Multiplex priced its IPO at $12 a share on August 1, 2000, raising $90 million. The telecom bust soon cut demand from carriers. In 2002 it merged with Proxim, a maker of wireless office networks, and took the Proxim name. Losses kept piling up. Proxim filed for Chapter 11 in 2005, and Terabeam Wireless bought nearly all of its assets that July for about $28 million.

cover.artwork: Beacon at Zandvoort, from Views in the Surroundings of Haarlem (Plaisante Plaetsen)

dek: Ashford.com sold luxury watches and jewelry online, at a time when people still bought them under glass.
lede: Ashford.com began life in March 1998 as the NewWatch Company. Its founders in Houston thought people would buy a fine watch online, if the price was right and the box arrived safely. Fine watches were sold in hushed stores, through dealers the brands picked. Ashford sold them on the web, then added jewelry, fragrances and leather goods. It went public in September 1999, in the last fat months of the dot-com boom.

sections.heading: The NewWatch Company
sections.body: J. Robert Shaw co-founded Ashford and became its chairman in April 1998. The company was incorporated in Texas that March as NewWatch and later took the Ashford.com name. Watches were a smart first product online. They were small, costly and easy to ship, and buyers knew the exact model they wanted. The hard part was supply. Many luxury brands did not want their watches sold at a discount on the internet.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars to GSI
sections.body: Ashford priced its IPO at $13 a share in September 1999, selling 6.25 million shares and raising $81 million on Nasdaq. Like many online retailers, it spent heavily on marketing and lost money as it grew. The dot-com crash cut its stock price far below the offer. In 2002 GSI Commerce, which ran online stores for other retailers, bought Ashford. Ashford deregistered its public shares in March 2002.

cover.theme: a still life of heirlooms (luxury goods)
cover.artwork: Still Life with Ostrich Egg Cup and the Whitfield Heirlooms

fate: Acquired by Analog Devices, 2014 ($78 a share)
tagline: An Ancient Name for Radio Chips
dek: Hittite designed the chips that send and receive high-frequency radio signals in radios, radar, satellites and test gear.
lede: Hittite Microwave took its name from an empire of ancient Anatolia, and its chips worked at frequencies most engineers found hard to tame. Yalcin Ayasli founded the company outside Boston in 1985. For twenty years it designed small, specialized chips that handled microwave and radio signals for cell towers, military radios, satellites and lab instruments. When Hittite went public in July 2005, Ayasli still controlled more than half the votes.

sections.heading: Ayasli's Microwave Workshop
sections.body: Ayasli founded Hittite in 1985 and served as its chief executive until December 2004, then stayed on as chairman. The company designed integrated circuits, modules and subsystems for radio frequency, microwave and millimeter-wave signals. These chips amplify, mix and switch signals before they reach a device's digital brain. Hittite sold them to equipment makers in telecom, defense, space, test and industrial markets.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars to Seventy-Eight
sections.body: Hittite priced its IPO at $17 a share on July 22, 2005, and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as HITT. It stayed profitable and kept adding product lines as wireless networks and defense systems pushed into higher frequencies. In June 2014 Analog Devices launched a tender offer for Hittite at $78 a share in cash. The deal closed that summer, and Hittite deregistered its shares in August 2014.

cover.theme: a chariot in the sky (an ancient empire of chariots)
cover.artwork: Phaeton Driving the Chariot of Phoebus

dek: Vipshop sold discounted brand-name clothes and goods in short online flash sales to Chinese shoppers.
lede: Vipshop's IPO in March 2012 raised money at $6.50 per American depositary share, a modest price for a Chinese retailer. The Guangzhou company ran online flash sales: each day it offered deep discounts on a brand's clothes, shoes or cosmetics for a short time, then moved on. Chinese brands had unsold stock to clear, and a growing middle class wanted labels at lower prices. Vipshop sat between them.

sections.heading: Clearing Stock for Brands
sections.body: Eric Ya Shen and Arthur Xiaobo Hong co-founded Vipshop in 2008, along with three other partners. The idea borrowed from the flash-sale sites then popular in Europe and the United States. Vipshop bought or took in excess stock from brands, photographed it and sold it in time-limited sales. Brands got rid of surplus goods without cutting prices in their own stores. Shoppers got a reason to check the site every morning.

sections.heading: A Long NYSE Run
sections.body: Vipshop priced its IPO at $6.50 per American depositary share on March 23, 2012, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as VIPS. It sold more shares the next year as sales climbed.
