The company built its own warehouses and delivery network to control the shopping experience. More than fourteen years after its listing, Vipshop is still public on the NYSE and based in Guangzhou.

dek: Aironet made wireless networking gear that let laptops and handheld scanners connect to a company network without cables.
lede: Before most people had heard of Wi-Fi, Aironet was already putting warehouse scanners on radio. Aironet, a unit of the Akron barcode-scanner maker Telxon, built wireless local area networks for factories, stores and hospitals. Its radios let handheld computers and laptops talk to a company network without a cable. In July 1999 it went public, and within months Cisco Systems decided it wanted wireless networking for itself.

sections.heading: Born Inside Telxon
sections.body: Aironet was incorporated in 1993 under the name Spider, Inc., and grew up as a subsidiary of Telxon, which sold handheld computers and scanners. It leased its Akron headquarters and assembly plant from its parent. Aironet sold access points, client cards and bridges that carried data by radio. Many early customers were in retail, logistics and health care, where workers moved around all day. Telxon remained its controlling shareholder.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars to Cisco
sections.body: Aironet priced its IPO at $11 a share on July 30, 1999. In late 1999 Cisco agreed to buy Aironet in an all-stock deal, giving 0.63734 of a Cisco share for each Aironet share. On February 4, 2000, Cisco stock closed at $121.13. Shareholders approved the merger, and Aironet deregistered in April 2000. Cisco kept the Aironet name on its wireless products.

cover.artwork: Kites of Fukuroi and Distant View of Akiba in Totomi Province, from the series "One Hundred Famous Views in the Various Provinces"

tagline: The Box That Brought DSL Home
dek: Efficient Networks made the DSL modems that turned ordinary phone lines into fast internet connections.
lede: In 1999 most Americans reached the internet through a screeching dial-up modem. Efficient Networks sold the small box that ended that. Its DSL modems sat in a home or office and turned the existing copper phone line into an always-on broadband link. Phone companies and new carriers such as Covad bought them in volume. When the Dallas company went public that July, broadband was the next great race in telecom.

sections.heading: Floyd's Copper Bet
sections.body: Mark Floyd co-founded Efficient in June 1993 and served as its president and chief executive. The company built customer premises equipment, the gear at the subscriber's end of a DSL line. Phone companies had miles of copper already in the ground. DSL let them sell fast internet over it without laying new cable. Efficient bought chipsets from suppliers like Alcatel, Analog Devices and Texas Instruments, and sold finished modems to carriers.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars to Siemens
sections.body: Efficient priced its IPO at $15 a share on July 15, 1999, and Covad's convertible debt turned into stock at that price. The shares rose with the broadband boom, and Efficient sold more stock in early 2000 and early 2001. Then many DSL carriers collapsed. In March 2001 Siemens launched a tender offer for Efficient at $23.50 a share in cash, and Efficient deregistered that April.

dek: Allaire made ColdFusion, which let web designers build database-driven websites without being expert programmers.
lede: Allaire started in May 1995 in Minnesota with one young programmer and one tricky problem: web pages were static, and businesses wanted them to talk to databases. JJ Allaire wrote ColdFusion, a simple tag language that pulled data into a page on the fly. Companies used it to build online stores, catalogs and intranets. By January 1999, when Allaire went public, it had moved to Cambridge, Massachusetts, with Lotus founder Mitch Kapor on its board.

sections.heading: Brothers and a Tag Language
sections.body: Joseph J. Allaire founded the company in May 1995 and ran it as chief executive until January 1997. His brother Jeremy joined him to build the business. ColdFusion's pitch was speed. A designer who knew HTML could learn a few extra tags and build a working web application in days. Allaire sold the server software and the tools to write for it. Customers listed in its prospectus included Hewlett-Packard, Intel, Lucent and UPS.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars to Macromedia
sections.body: Allaire priced its IPO at $20 a share on January 22, 1999, selling 2.5 million shares, and sold more stock that September. Microsoft, Sun and open-source tools crowded the market for web servers. In January 2001 Allaire agreed to merge with Macromedia, the maker of Flash and Dreamweaver. The deal closed in March 2001. ColdFusion lived on under Macromedia, and later Adobe.

dek: AMCC designed the high-speed chips that carriers' fiber-optic and networking gear used to move data.
lede: Applied Micro Circuits was eighteen years old when it went public, an old hand by internet standards. The San Diego chipmaker designed high-speed circuits for the gear that moved data across fiber-optic networks. In November 1997 the internet was swelling, and phone carriers were rebuilding their backbones to carry it. Every new optical switch and router needed chips that could keep up. AMCC sold to the companies that built them.

sections.heading: A San Diego Chip Shop
sections.body: AMCC was incorporated in California in 1979 and moved its legal home to Delaware in 1987. By its IPO it focused on communications. Its circuits handled the fastest signals inside networking equipment, turning streams of light-speed data into bits a system could read. AMCC's customers were equipment makers, so its fortunes rode on how much carriers spent on their networks.

sections.heading: Eight Dollars to MACOM
sections.body: AMCC priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 1997. The optical boom sent its stock soaring, and the 2001 bust cut it down. AMCC later bet on server processors built on ARM designs, sold under the X-Gene name. In December 2016 MACOM offered $3.25 in cash plus 0.1089 of a MACOM share for each AMCC share. The deal closed in January 2017, ending AMCC's run on Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: Plan of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, Railroad Circuits Diagram

tagline: Paid in Points to Read Ads
dek: MyPoints paid people in reward points for reading marketing emails and shopping online through its site.
lede: MyPoints paid people to open their email. Members agreed to get marketing messages, and each one they read, along with each purchase they made through the site, earned points toward rewards such as gift certificates. Advertisers paid MyPoints for the attention. In August 1999 email was the internet's busiest room, and marketers were desperate for a way to stand out. MyPoints went public promising them readers who had asked for their offers.

sections.heading: Intellipost's Reward Program
sections.body: MyPoints was founded in November 1996 as Intellipost Corporation in San Francisco. In May 1997 it launched its email direct marketing and rewards program. Members signed up and listed their interests. Marketers sent offers through MyPoints, which targeted them by those interests and tracked what each member read or bought. Members then traded their points for rewards from partner merchants. Every offer went only to people who had signed up to receive it.

sections.heading: From $8 to United Airlines
sections.body: MyPoints priced its IPO at $8 a share in August 1999 and sold more stock in February 2000. Then the online ad market collapsed, and its stock fell with it. In June 2001 a subsidiary of UAL, the parent of United Airlines, launched a tender offer for MyPoints at $2.60 a share in cash. MyPoints deregistered its shares in July 2001.

dek: Interactive Intelligence built software that ran a company's phone calls, email and contact center from one system.
lede: A doctor from Indiana built a phone system out of software. Donald Brown, who trained as a physician, had already sold one software company to IBM when he started Interactive Intelligence in 1994. His new product replaced racks of business phone hardware with one program running on standard servers. It routed calls, voicemail, faxes and email to the right person. In September 1999 the Indianapolis company went public on that idea.

sections.heading: Dr. Brown's Third Company
sections.body: Brown co-founded Interactive Intelligence in October 1994. It was his third software company. In 1988 he had co-founded Software Artistry, a customer support software maker that went public in 1995 and was bought by IBM in January 1998. His new bet was that contact centers would rather buy software than closed telephone switches. Interactive Intelligence sold its system to companies that took a lot of customer calls.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars to Genesys
sections.body: Interactive Intelligence priced its IPO at $13 a share on September 23, 1999, selling 2.67 million shares on Nasdaq under the ticker ININ. It survived the dot-com crash and later moved its contact center software into the cloud. Genesys, a larger contact center company, agreed to buy it in 2016. The deal closed in December 2016, and Interactive Intelligence's shares left Nasdaq.

dek: White Pine Software sold CU-SeeMe, which put live video calls on ordinary computers over the internet.
lede: In 1996 a video conference room cost tens of thousands of dollars. White Pine Software sold a program that did it on a desktop computer with a cheap camera and a 28.8 kbps modem. The software, CU-SeeMe, came out of Cornell University, and early internet users loved its grainy, jerky video. White Pine held the worldwide rights. It went public in October 1996 and later renamed itself after the product everyone knew.

sections.heading: A Cornell Experiment
sections.body: Researchers at Cornell developed CU-SeeMe in 1992 as free desktop video conferencing software. In June 1995 White Pine Software of Nashua, New Hampshire, secured the exclusive worldwide rights to license it, along with its multipoint conferencing server. In March 1996 it released Enhanced CU-SeeMe. The bet was that people would trade picture quality for price and convenience. White Pine also sold connectivity software that linked PCs to larger computers.

sections.heading: White Pine to First Virtual
sections.body: White Pine priced its IPO at $9 a share in October 1996. Video calling grew slowly over the dial-up internet, and the company struggled to turn its famous name into steady sales. It renamed itself CUseeMe Networks to match its best-known product. In March 2001 it agreed to merge with First Virtual Communications, a video networking company. CUseeMe deregistered its shares in June 2001.

cover.artwork: Pheasant on a Snow-Covered Pine Tree

dek: NetScout watched the traffic inside corporate networks, so IT teams could spot slowdowns and failures before users complained.
lede: NetScout was fifteen years old when it went public, and its two founders still ran it. Anil Singhal and Narendra Popat left Wang Laboratories in 1984 to start the company outside Boston. By August 1999 corporate networks had become the plumbing of every business. When an application slowed down, nobody could tell why. NetScout sold probes and software that watched the traffic and showed IT staff where the trouble was.

sections.heading: Two Engineers From Wang
sections.body: Singhal and Popat co-founded NetScout in June 1984. Singhal had been a project manager at Wang Laboratories, the Massachusetts computer maker. NetScout's products sat on a network and recorded the packets passing through it. Its software turned that data into reports on which applications were using the network and how well they performed. Large companies and government agencies used it to keep their networks running and plan for growth.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars and Still Watching
sections.body: NetScout priced its IPO at $11 a share in August 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as NTCT. It survived the dot-com crash by selling to big enterprises and, later, to phone carriers. In 2015 it agreed to take on Danaher's communications business in a large stock deal. More than 27 years after its IPO, NetScout is still public on Nasdaq and based in Westford, Massachusetts.

cover.artwork: Scouts and Guides to the Army of the Potomac

dek: MaxLinear made tiny radio chips that let TVs, set-top boxes and phones pick up broadcast and cable signals.
lede: Every television once needed a metal tuner can, a bulky box of parts that pulled one channel out of the air or the cable. MaxLinear shrank that job onto a single chip of standard silicon. Its radio-frequency chips went into TVs, set-top boxes, mobile TV devices and car receivers. When the Carlsbad company went public in March 2010, it was one of the few chip IPOs to brave the market after the financial crisis.

sections.heading: Radio in Plain Silicon
sections.body: Kishore Seendripu co-founded MaxLinear in September 2003 and served as chairman, president and chief executive. Kimihiko Imura joined as a co-founder and ran semiconductor technology and operations. The team bet that radio-frequency circuits, usually built with exotic processes, could be made in cheap, standard CMOS silicon. That made tuners smaller, cheaper and easier to put on a circuit board. Its first chips went into televisions and set-top boxes.

sections.heading: From the NYSE to Nasdaq
sections.body: MaxLinear priced its IPO at $14 a share on March 24, 2010, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MXL. It grew by buying other chip businesses and moved into broadband, Wi-Fi and data center connectivity. In 2021 it moved its listing from the NYSE to Nasdaq. MaxLinear is still public on Nasdaq and based in Carlsbad, California.

cover.theme: a railway bridge (straight lines and signals)

dek: Impinj makes the tiny RFID chips that let stores and warehouses count and track individual items by radio.
lede: Impinj wants every pair of jeans, box and pallet to answer when asked. Its tiny chips sit inside paper-thin RFID tags. A reader sends a radio signal, and each tag replies with its own identity, with no battery and no line of sight. Retailers use them to count stock in seconds. When the Seattle company went public in July 2016, it had spent years pushing a single radio standard, RAIN, across the industry.

sections.heading: Caltech Roots, Seattle Home
sections.body: Chris Diorio co-founded Impinj in 2000 with Carver Mead, the Caltech chip designer who had been his doctoral adviser. Diorio became chief executive. Their early technology stored data on chips in a new way, and the company soon aimed it at radio identification. Impinj led the work on the RAIN radio standard, lobbied governments for spectrum and co-founded the RAIN Industry Alliance with Google, Intel and Smartrac.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars and Counting
sections.body: Impinj priced its IPO at $14 a share on July 21, 2016, raising $67.2 million on Nasdaq. Clothing retailers adopted RFID tags to track stock, and other industries began to follow. Demand swung with retail spending and the chip cycle. More than ten years after its IPO, Impinj is still public on Nasdaq under the ticker PI and based in Seattle.

cover.theme: insect specimens (every item tagged and catalogued)
cover.artwork: Five Butterflies and a Moth, from Diversae Insectorum...Figurae

fate: Bought back by Tyco, 2001; the business lives on as SubCom
tagline: Eleven Ships and a Seafloor of Glass
dek: TyCom built, laid and fixed the fiber optic cables that carry the internet across the ocean floor.
lede: TyCom owned eleven ships, and their job was to lay glass on the bottom of the sea. The company had designed, made and installed more than 300,000 kilometers of undersea cable, a part in most of the world's big ocean networks. In the summer of 2000, with carriers racing to wire every ocean, Tyco International put its cable arm up for sale to the public. It planned to keep about 88 percent of the shares for itself.

sections.heading: AT&T's Cable Fleet Changes Hands
sections.body: TyCom grew out of two old businesses. Tyco bought Simplex Technologies, a cable factory in New Hampshire, in 1974. In July 1997 it bought AT&T's submarine systems business, with its labs in New Jersey and its fleet of cable ships. Simplex alone grew its yearly output from 22,000 to 60,000 kilometers of cable. The bet in the prospectus went further. TyCom planned to own its own network, the TyCom Global Network, and sell bandwidth on it.

sections.heading: Thirty-Two Dollars at the Top
sections.body: TyCom priced at $32 a share in July 2000 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as TCM. The timing was the peak of the telecom boom. Within months, carriers stopped buying and capacity on the ocean floor sat unused. Tyco bought back the public shares, and TyCom filed to end its registration in December 2001. The cable business stayed inside the Tyco family for years and now runs on its own as SubCom.

cover.theme: boats on a stormy sea (undersea cable fleet)

tagline: The Airline Computer Goes Public Again
dek: Sabre ran the booking system that travel agents, websites and airlines used to sell seats and rooms.
lede: Sabre went public in 2014 for the second time. The company began life as a division of American Airlines, building one of the first computer systems to book airline seats. AMR spun it off completely in 2000. Silver Lake and TPG took it private in 2007. Seven years later the owners brought it back to market. By then Sabre ran a giant travel marketplace, airline software and Travelocity, the consumer booking site.

sections.heading: A Seat Map in a Mainframe
sections.body: Sabre sat in the middle of the travel business. Travel agencies and websites searched it for fares and booked seats, hotels and cars. Airlines paid it to run their reservations, check-in and flight planning. Much of that still ran on IBM mainframes, and the prospectus warned that fewer programmers knew the old technology each year. The bet was that travel would keep growing, and every booking would pass through Sabre's pipes.

sections.heading: Back on the Board
sections.body: Sabre priced at $16 a share in April 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as SABR. The owners used the offering to cut a heavy debt load from the buyout. Sabre sold Travelocity to Expedia in 2015 and kept its focus on the business side of travel. The pandemic grounded flights in 2020 and hit bookings hard. Sabre is still public on Nasdaq, with its headquarters in Southlake, Texas.

cover.theme: a cavalry officer with a drawn saber (Sabre)
cover.artwork: Sketches of a Mounted Chasseru and a Cavalry Officer with Drawn Saber

fate: Taken private by DigitalBridge and IFM Investors, 2022 ($34.25 a share)
dek: Switch built huge, power-hungry data center campuses in the Nevada desert and rented the space to big companies.
lede: Every piece of technology inside Switch's data centers, the prospectus said, was designed by one man. Rob Roy, the founder, held more than 350 issued and pending patent claims on the cooling, power and building designs. His company ran giant campuses in Las Vegas and near Reno, plus one in Grand Rapids, Michigan. In 2017 Switch went public with a share structure that kept control with Roy.

sections.heading: Tier 5 in the Desert
sections.body: Switch called its biggest sites Primes: The Core Campus in Las Vegas, The Citadel Campus near Reno and The Pyramid Campus in Grand Rapids. Together they had room for up to 4 million square feet and 415 megawatts of power. Switch said it built to its own Tier 5 Platinum standard, above the industry's top Tier IV rating. The bet was that companies would pay more for a safe, connected home for their servers.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars, Then a Buyout
sections.body: Switch priced at $17 a share in October 2017, above its planned range of $14 to $16, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as SWCH. Roy's Class C shares carried 10 votes each, so the founder kept control. Demand for data center space kept growing as companies moved to the cloud. In 2022, funds tied to DigitalBridge and IFM Investors bought Switch for $34.25 a share in cash, and the stock left the exchange that December.

cover.theme: a power room full of switchgear (data center power)
cover.artwork: The Mines Today By Cables (Electric Driven). This Is The Power Room Of A Pennsylvania Coal Mine

dek: The RealReal let people sell their designer clothes, bags and watches, with experts checking each piece was real.
lede: The RealReal hired a horologist in its second year, because someone had to tell a real Rolex from a fake. Julie Wainwright launched the company in 2011 to resell the luxury goods that sat unworn in people's closets. By March 2019 it had sold 11.4 million items. That June it went public as what it called the world's largest online marketplace for authenticated, consigned luxury goods, with the resale boom just reaching the mainstream.

sections.heading: The Closet as Inventory
sections.body: The RealReal did not buy what it sold. Owners sent in handbags, jewelry, watches and dresses, and the company took a cut of each sale. Its staff photographed, priced and checked every item for authenticity. The mission line in the prospectus said the future of luxury was circular. Wainwright's bet was that buyers would trust a secondhand designer piece online if a company stood behind it.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars and a Long Slide
sections.body: The RealReal priced at $20 a share in June 2019 and listed on Nasdaq as REAL. The stock jumped on its first day. Losses and the cost of checking every item weighed on it over the next three years, and the shares fell far below the IPO price. Wainwright stepped down as CEO in June 2022. The company cut costs, closed stores and is still public on Nasdaq.

tagline: Storage You Plug In Like Power
dek: StorageNetworks stored and backed up companies' data in its own data centers and charged for it like a utility.
lede: StorageNetworks wanted companies to plug into data storage the way they plugged into the electric grid. It said it was the first company to offer storage purely as a service. Two years after it started work in October 1998, it ran 37 data centers in 11 American cities and one in London. Its timing was the edge of the dot-com crash, and its pitch was close to what the cloud sells today.

sections.heading: An EMC Salesman's Idea
sections.body: Peter Bell spent nearly ten years selling storage at EMC before he co-founded StorageNetworks with William Miller in 1998. The company opened its first storage data center in Houston in May 1999. It kept customers' main data, backed it up to tape, and copied it to remote sites in case of disaster. Its customers ran banks, phone companies, retailers and fast-growing web businesses. The bet was that storage would grow so fast that companies would rather rent it.

sections.heading: Cash in the Bank, Then Goodbye
sections.body: StorageNetworks priced at $27 a share on June 30, 2000, and listed on Nasdaq as STOR. Within months the dot-com crash hit its web customers, and big companies cut their spending. In 2003 the board weighed a sale, acquisitions and going it alone, and chose none of them. Shareholders voted that October on a plan to dissolve the company. With about $201 million in cash, StorageNetworks expected to pay out roughly $1.60 to $1.70 a share.

fate: Taken private by Rizvi Traverse, 2016 ($11 a share)
dek: RealD put 3D on movie theater screens and handed audiences the glasses to see it.
lede: When Avatar opened in December 2009, about 4,200 of its screens ran on RealD. Four years earlier the company's system had played Disney's Chicken Little on roughly 100 screens, the first commercial 3D shown with digital projection. By 2010 the big chains, AMC, Cinemark and Regal, had RealD in their theaters. That summer, riding the biggest 3D wave Hollywood had ever seen, RealD sold its shares to the public.

sections.heading: Two Founders and a Silver Screen
sections.body: Michael V. Lewis and Joshua Greer founded RealD in 2003 to bring 3D to audiences everywhere. In 2005 they bought Stereographics, a 3D company founded in 1980. RealD licensed its cinema system to theater owners, who paid for its use, and sold the glasses. Its system threw a bright image that worked on larger screens than most rivals. The bet was that 3D would stop being a gimmick and become a premium ticket for every big film.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars a Pair
sections.body: RealD priced at $16 a share in July 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as RLD. The company had hopes for 3D televisions at home as well. Those sets never caught on, and audiences grew tired of paying extra for 3D tickets. In 2016 the investment firm Rizvi Traverse took RealD private for $11 a share in cash. Its stock left the exchange that March.

cover.artwork: Mirror View of Cathedral Rocks. Yo Semite Val, Cal.

fate: Taken private by John Hui, 2001 ($1.06 a share); sold to Gateway, 2004
dek: eMachines sold cheap home PCs to first-time buyers and hoped to earn more from ads than from hardware.
lede: eMachines put the first branded PC under $400 on American store shelves in November 1998, two months after the company was formed. Within about a year it had sold more than two million of them. About half its buyers had never owned a computer. When eMachines filed to go public in early 2000, it pitched itself as more than a box maker. It wanted to earn money from ads shown to all those new users.

sections.heading: Korean Factories, Cheap Towers
sections.body: Two Korean companies stood behind eMachines. TriGem Computer built all of its eTower PCs, and Korea Data Systems was another major backer. Stephen Dukker ran the company as chief executive. In 1999 eMachines sold the third-largest number of desktop PCs through American retailers. It bought FreePC, an idealab! startup that gave away computers in exchange for ads. The bet was that a cheap PC could open a door to the buyer for years.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars, Then One
sections.body: eMachines priced at $9 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as EEEE. The timing could hardly have been worse. Ad money dried up as the dot-com bubble burst, and price wars squeezed every PC maker. In November 2001 Lap Shun (John) Hui, a major shareholder, offered $1.06 a share to buy out the public holders, and eMachines went private. Gateway bought the company in 2004.

cover.theme: a rider and his machine (a cheap home computer)

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2013 ($14.50 a share)
tagline: Sign Up for the Marathon Here
dek: Active Network ran the online sign-ups for races, campsites, sports leagues, fishing licenses and conferences.
lede: If you booked a campsite, signed up for a 10K or bought a fishing license online in 2011, Active Network probably took your money. The San Diego company began in 1998 as Racegate, a site for race registrations. By its IPO it served more than 47,000 organizations and handled over 70 million sign-ups a year. Its pitch was simple: the people who ran events were drowning in paper forms.

sections.heading: From Racegate to ActiveWorks
sections.body: Active Network launched its platform in 1999. Organizers used its software to take registrations, collect payments and manage their events. Consumers found those events on Active.com. Over time the company added park reservations through ReserveAmerica and corporate conference sign-ups through RegOnline. David Alberga served as chairman and chief executive. The bet was that one network could serve a local swim league and a state park system at the same time.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars and a Tender Offer
sections.body: Active Network priced at $15 a share in May 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ACTV. The offering raised $165 million, part of it for selling shareholders. Two years later Vista Equity Partners made a tender offer of $14.50 a share in cash, a deal worth about $1.05 billion. That was just under the IPO price. Vista took Active private, and the stock left the exchange in November 2013.

cover.theme: a campfire in the woods (campsites and outdoor events)

dek: OpenTV wrote the software that let digital cable and satellite boxes run games, guides and interactive shows.
lede: OpenTV's software ran on more than 4.5 million set-top boxes when it went public, most of them outside the United States. Twenty-two TV operators in 17 countries had picked it to make their channels interactive. Right before the IPO, America Online, News Corporation, Time Warner, General Instrument, Liberty Digital and Sun Microsystems all bought in. In November 1999, the company was a bet that television would become the next internet.

sections.heading: Born at Thomson and Sun
sections.body: OpenTV began in July 1996 as Thomson Sun Interactive, a venture of the French electronics maker Thomson and Sun Microsystems. The South African media group MIH later took a controlling stake. OpenTV's software sat in two places: at the broadcaster, where it streamed data, and inside the viewer's box, where it ran the apps. The bet was that every TV operator would need an operating system for its boxes, and OpenTV would be it.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars in Two Markets
sections.body: OpenTV priced at $20 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq and in Amsterdam as OPTV. Interactive television grew slower than the hype. Liberty Media bought control from MIH in 2002, and OpenTV absorbed rivals along the way. In 2009 the Swiss security company Kudelski offered $1.55 a share for the stock it did not already own. OpenTV left Nasdaq in 2010.

cover.theme: an audience in a theater box (watching a show)

tagline: Every Solar Panel Gets a Brain
dek: SolarEdge made the electronics that squeeze more power out of each rooftop solar panel and track it online.
lede: A single shaded panel can drag down a whole row of solar panels, and SolarEdge built a business on fixing that. The Israeli company put a small power optimizer on each panel and paired it with its own inverter and a cloud monitoring service. By early 2015 it had shipped about 1.3 gigawatts of systems to 73 countries. Rooftop solar was booming in America, and SolarEdge wanted to ride it to Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Five Founders in Herzliya
sections.body: SolarEdge was founded in 2006 in Israel and began shipping in 2010. Older solar systems linked panels in long strings, so the weakest panel set the pace for the rest. Microinverters fixed part of that problem, at a cost. SolarEdge split the job. Optimizers on each panel tuned the power, and one central inverter turned it into household current. The bet was that this design would beat both rivals on price, safety and monitoring.

sections.heading: Eighteen Dollars in the Sun
sections.body: SolarEdge priced at $18 a share in March 2015 and listed on Nasdaq as SEDG. Over the next several years it became one of the largest inverter makers in the world and moved into batteries and electric-vehicle parts. Co-founder and chief executive Guy Sella died in 2019. When high interest rates slowed rooftop solar in 2023, SolarEdge's sales fell hard. It is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: the sun rising over the sea (solar power)
cover.artwork: Sunrise on New Year's Day at Susaki (Susaki hatsu hinode no zu), from the series "Famous Places in the Eastern Capital (Toto meisho)"

tagline: The Norwegian Browser That Wouldn't Quit
dek: Opera made fast web browsers for phones and computers, used by hundreds of millions of people outside the big names.
lede: Opera had been making web browsers for 22 years when it listed in New York, and by then its owners were Chinese. The company traced its roots to a Norwegian startup formed in June 1995. Its first browser came out in September 1996. In 2016 a consortium led by Yahui Zhou bought the business. By early 2018 Opera served about 322 million people a month, many of them on phones in emerging markets.

sections.heading: A Third Choice Since 1996
sections.body: Opera never ruled the desktop. It survived by being fast and lean, and its mobile browsers did well where data was slow or costly. By 2018 the company also pitched itself as a news and content business, with recommendations driven by artificial intelligence. About 239 million of its monthly users were on phones and PCs. The bet was that a browser people trusted could also choose what they read, and sell ads around it.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars an ADS
sections.body: Opera priced its American depositary shares at $12 each in July 2018 and listed on Nasdaq as OPRA. Bitmain, the bitcoin mining company, and IDG Capital bought shares in private deals alongside the offering. Opera later launched Opera GX, a browser for gamers, and added AI tools to its products. The company is still public on Nasdaq, with its headquarters in Oslo.

cover.artwork: Rehearsal of the Pasdeloup Orchestra at the Cirque d'Hiver

dek: Varonis showed companies who could see and touch their files, and flagged it when someone touched the wrong ones.
lede: Varonis made a business out of the files nobody thinks about: the spreadsheets, slide decks, emails and memos that pile up on company servers. Those files hold plans, finances and secrets, and most companies could not say who had access to them. Varonis built software that tracked every touch. It went public in early 2014, just as a string of big data breaches made that question urgent.

sections.heading: Data About the Data
sections.body: Yakov Faitelson and Ohad Korkus started Varonis, incorporated in Delaware in November 2004. Faitelson ran the company and Korkus led its technology. Their Metadata Framework pulled data about data from a company's systems. It mapped which employees used which files, and how. Customers used it for security, archiving and cleanup. Varonis sold mostly through resellers and distributors. The bet was that the fastest-growing data in any company was the kind people made themselves.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two Dollars, Then Up
sections.body: Varonis priced at $22 a share in late February 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as VRNS. The stock jumped in its first day of trading. Over the next decade the company kept selling data security as breaches and ransomware attacks made headlines. It later moved its customers from installed software to a cloud subscription. Faitelson still runs Varonis, and it is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a sentinel rock standing guard (data security)
cover.artwork: The Sentinel, 3270 feet, Yosemite Valley, Mariposa County, Cal., from the series "Watkins' Pacific Coast"

fate: Bought out by USA Interactive, 2003; Ticketmaster merged with Live Nation, 2010
tagline: Concert Tickets Meet the City Guide
dek: Ticketmaster Online-CitySearch sold event tickets on the web and ran local city guides in one company.
lede: Ticketmaster Online-CitySearch was two web businesses glued together three months before its IPO. One sold concert and game tickets online. The other ran CitySearch, a set of local city guides that Bill Gross had co-founded in 1995. Barry Diller's USA Networks owned Ticketmaster and held about 68 percent of the new company. In December 1998, at the height of the web stock frenzy, the combination went public on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: A Guide Plus a Box Office
sections.body: CitySearch launched its first city guide in May 1996, with listings for restaurants, shops and events. Ticketmaster Online sold tickets for the live events that Ticketmaster's clients put on. In September 1998 the two merged. The plan was to use Ticketmaster's reach in cities at home and abroad to spread CitySearch into new places. Charles Conn ran the combined company as chief executive from Pasadena.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars, Then Folded In
sections.body: The company priced at $14 a share in December 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as TMCS. In 2001 it combined with the rest of Ticketmaster and took the Ticketmaster name. USA Interactive bought out the public shareholders, and the company ended its public registration in January 2003. IAC spun Ticketmaster off again in 2008. In 2010 Ticketmaster merged with Live Nation and left the market for good.

dek: Xunlei made the download accelerator that most Chinese internet users relied on to fetch movies, games and files.
lede: Xunlei means swift thunder, and for a decade it was how China downloaded things. Its free Xunlei Accelerator had about 142 million monthly users in March 2014 and an 84.1 percent share of its market. The Shenzhen company first filed to go public in the United States in 2011, then waited. When it finally listed in June 2014, it was selling paid speed to a country hungry for video.

sections.heading: Shenzhen, January 2003
sections.body: Sean Shenglong Zou and Hao Cheng started Xunlei in Shenzhen in January 2003. Its software split big downloads into pieces and pulled them from many sources at once. The core product was free. Xunlei made money from subscribers who paid for faster cloud downloads, and from ads. It struck deals to preinstall its mobile apps on phones, including those from Xiaomi. The bet was that Chinese users would pay to skip the wait.

sections.heading: Three Years Late, Twelve Dollars
sections.body: Xunlei priced its American depositary shares at $12 each in June 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as XNET, raising about $88 million. Faster home connections and streaming apps slowly made download tools less vital. Xunlei shifted toward cloud computing and other services, and its shares traded far below the IPO price for most of the years that followed. It is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: The Actor Nakamura Nakazo I as the Thunder God, an Incarnation of Kan Shojo, in the Play Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami, Performed at the Morita Theater in the Third Month, 1780

dek: Compellent sold smart, easy storage networks that let midsize companies keep and protect huge amounts of data.
lede: Compellent's three founders had built a storage company once before, and in 2002 they did it again in the Minneapolis suburbs. Their Storage Center was a storage area network that paired clever software with standard hardware. By August 2007 more than 600 companies ran it, in fields from education and government to insurance and media. That October Compellent went public, pitching itself as the simpler, cheaper way to store a lot of data.

sections.heading: Second Time in Eden Prairie
sections.body: Philip Soran, John Guider and Lawrence Aszmann incorporated Compellent in Minnesota in March 2002. They had earlier founded Xiotech, another storage maker. Compellent's software moved data between fast and cheap disks on its own, so customers paid less for the same capacity. It sold only through channel partners, which kept its own sales force small. The bet was that midsize companies wanted big-company storage without big-company bills.

sections.heading: Dell Pays Double
sections.body: Compellent priced at $13.50 a share in October 2007 and listed on NYSE Arca as CML. It later moved to the New York Stock Exchange. In December 2010 Dell agreed to buy the company for $27.75 a share in cash, a few months after Dell lost a bidding war with HP for 3PAR, another storage maker. The deal closed in February 2011, and Compellent became part of Dell's storage business.

fate: Acquired by Liberty Media, 2002 ($3.00 a share)
tagline: Click the Remote, Buy the Ad
dek: Wink let TV viewers press a button during a commercial to order a product, get a coupon or play along.
lede: Wink wanted the remote control to work like a mouse. During a Wink-enhanced ad, a viewer could press one button to order a product, ask for a sample or grab a coupon. During a show, the same button pulled up scores, weather or a poll. By 1999 the Alameda company had backing from Microsoft, General Instrument, Scientific Atlanta, Toshiba, GE Capital, DIRECTV's parent and Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures.

sections.heading: A Toll Booth on Every Click
sections.body: Brian Dougherty co-founded Wink in October 1994 and ran it as chief executive until late 1996. Maggie Wilderotter led the company by the time it went public. Wink began rolling out its service in the United States in June 1998. It licensed its software to 60 partners across the TV business. The plan was to earn most of its money from fees charged to advertisers and merchants each time a viewer clicked to buy or ask for more.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars to Three
sections.body: Wink priced at $16 a share in August 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as WINK. Interactive TV grew far slower than its backers hoped, and the transaction fees never added up to a big business. In June 2002 Wink agreed to sell itself to a unit of Liberty Media for $3.00 a share in cash. The company ended its public registration that August.

fate: Acquired by Keysight Technologies, 2017 ($19.65 a share)
dek: Ixia built machines that flood network gear with simulated traffic, so makers could test it before customers did.
lede: Before a router maker ships a box, someone has to pound it with more traffic than the real world will send. Ixia built the machines that did the pounding. Each system held cards that pretended to be a large network, sending and measuring streams of data over fiber and copper. In October 2000, as the telecom boom crested, the Calabasas company went public selling test gear to the companies building the internet.

sections.heading: A Chassis Full of Imaginary Users
sections.body: Ixia was incorporated in California in May 1997. Errol Ginsberg, a networking engineer, ran it as president. Jean-Claude Asscher, who had founded the French electronics company Tekelec-Airtronic in 1961, served as chairman and principal shareholder. Ixia's systems tested gear for fast optical networks and Gigabit Ethernet. The bet was that every jump in network speed would send equipment makers back to buy faster testers.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Keysight
sections.body: Ixia priced at $13 a share in October 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as XXIA. The telecom crash that followed hit its customers hard, but Ixia stayed in business and kept growing. Over the years it bought other testing and network visibility companies. In January 2017 Keysight Technologies agreed to buy Ixia for $19.65 a share in cash. The deal closed that April, and Ixia's name lives on as a Keysight brand.

cover.theme: a lily in bloom (the ixia flower)
cover.artwork: The Superb Lily, from The Temple of Flora

fate: Merged with Media Metrix, 2000; Jupiter Media Metrix sold off its businesses, 2002
dek: Jupiter sold research and forecasts on internet commerce to executives trying to figure out the web.
lede: Jupiter Communications made its living telling companies how big the internet economy would get. The New York firm sold subscriptions to its research, forecasts and analysts, and ran conferences where executives came to hear them. It had 145 subscription contracts at the end of 1997 and 654 by June 1999. That October, at the peak of the boom it studied, Jupiter went public.

sections.heading: Research for the New Economy
sections.body: Jupiter was formed in New York on December 1, 1994. Gene DeRose was chief executive, and Kurt Abrahamson was president. Its main product was Strategic Planning Services, a subscription that bundled written analysis, data and access to analysts. Revenue grew from $8.5 million in 1997 to $14.8 million in 1998. The bet was that every company going online would pay for a guide to a market that changed every quarter.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Dollars and a Merger
sections.body: Jupiter priced at $21 a share in October 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as JPTR. In 2000 it merged with Media Metrix, the web audience measurement firm, to form Jupiter Media Metrix. The dot-com bust then wiped out many of the young internet companies that bought its research. In 2002 Jupiter Media Metrix sold off its pieces, with Media Metrix going to comScore, and wound down.

cover.artwork: View of the Temple of Jupiter Tonans [Jupiter the Thunderer], from Views of Rome

fate: Renamed LiveWorld, 2001; went dark in 2008 and now trades over the counter
dek: Talk City ran moderated online chat rooms, message boards and live events, and built communities for other brands.
lede: Talk City had 270 paid staff and 1,800 volunteers whose job was to keep online chat civil. In 1999 it was one of the stickiest sites on the web, ranked 16th of the top 500 by time spent per day. Three former Apple people had founded it in 1996 to build online communities that felt safe. That July, with chat rooms at the center of web culture, Talk City went public.

sections.heading: Apple Alumni Build a Town
sections.body: Peter Friedman, Jenna Woodul and Bernard Bernstein co-founded the company in March 1996, straight out of Apple. Woodul had run the online community for Apple's eWorld service. Talk City hosted chats, events, home pages and message boards, all watched over by hosts. It also built co-branded versions of its community for partner sites. The bet was that people would gather, and advertisers would follow, where the conversation stayed friendly.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars, Then a New Name
sections.body: Talk City priced at $12 a share in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as TCTY. Ad money vanished in the dot-com bust, and the company shifted to running communities for other businesses. It renamed itself LiveWorld in 2001. LiveWorld stopped filing reports with the SEC in 2008. It kept working as a social media and moderation agency, with shares trading over the counter.

dek: FriendFinder ran dozens of paid dating and adult sites, plus Penthouse, and went public carrying heavy debt.
lede: FriendFinder Networks claimed more than 445 million registrations across a network of over 38,000 websites. Its biggest sites ranged from FriendFinder.com and Amigos.com to BigChurch.com, and to adult services it did not hide. It also owned Penthouse. In 2010 it booked $346 million in revenue and $71.7 million in operating income, yet still lost $43.2 million. The reason was debt, and in May 2011 it went public to start paying it down.

sections.heading: Penthouse Buys the Dating Web
sections.body: FriendFinder.com began in 1996 as one of the first online dating sites, started by Andrew Conru. In December 2007 the company that owned Penthouse bought Various, the parent of FriendFinder, and took the FriendFinder Networks name. The deal left the company with a large debt load. The combined company earned most of its revenue from subscriptions and pay-per-use video. The bet was that a huge paying audience could carry the debt.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars to Chapter 11
sections.body: FriendFinder priced at $10 a share in May 2011 and listed on Nasdaq as FFN. The stock soon fell below its offering price, and the debt stayed heavy. Paid subscriptions faced growing competition from free sites and apps. In September 2013 the company filed for Chapter 11 to restructure what it owed. Its shares left Nasdaq that November, and FriendFinder emerged from bankruptcy as a private company.

cover.theme: cats meeting on a rooftop (a rendezvous)

dek: Trusted Information Systems built the Gauntlet firewall, which kept company networks safe from strangers on the internet.
lede: Before he started a company, Stephen Walker spent 20 years on computer security inside the National Security Agency, ARPA and the Pentagon. In 1983 he founded Trusted Information Systems in Maryland. By 1996 its Gauntlet firewall was one of the best-known ways to wall a corporate network off from the open internet. That October, as businesses rushed online and worried about who might follow them in, TIS went public.

sections.heading: From Toolkit to Gauntlet
sections.body: TIS built its name on security research, with a strong reputation among government security experts. Then the internet arrived. The company released an Internet Firewall Toolkit, and in 1994 it turned that work into the Gauntlet Internet Firewall. Gauntlet let companies wall off a trusted network from an untrusted one. It also built encrypted links, called virtual private networks, across the open internet. The bet was that every company going online would need a guard at the gate.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then McAfee's Parent
sections.body: TIS priced at $13 a share in October 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as TISX. Its directors and officers still held about 41 percent of the stock. The firewall market grew crowded fast, with Check Point and others selling their own boxes. In 1998 Network Associates, the company formed by McAfee's merger with Network General, bought TIS. Gauntlet became part of its security lineup.

cover.artwork: Gauntlet from a Tournament Garniture of a Hapsburg Prince

fate: Merged with Interwoven, 2003; iManage bought itself back from HP in 2015 and is private
tagline: Where Law Firms Keep Their Files
dek: iManage gave big law firms one place to store, find and share every document and email on a case.
lede: Forty-nine of iManage's 50 biggest customers were law and professional service firms. Its client list read like a who's who of the legal world: Cravath, Swaine & Moore, Sidley & Austin, Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher and Paul, Weiss. The company sold software that kept a firm's documents in order and let lawyers find them fast. In November 1999 it went public pitching that same tool to every company doing business on the web.

sections.heading: NetRight, Then iManage
sections.body: The company was founded in Illinois in October 1995 as NetRight Technologies and shipped its first product a year later. Mahmood Panjwani ran it as chief executive, and Rafiq Mohammadi was chief technology officer. Its software pulled text, graphics, audio and data into one managed library on the web. By September 1999, 81 percent of its customers were law or professional service firms. The bet was that lawyers' document problem was every company's problem.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars and a Long Way Home
sections.body: iManage priced at $11 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as IMAN. In 2003 it merged with Interwoven, a content management company. Autonomy bought Interwoven in 2009, and HP bought Autonomy in 2011. In 2015 iManage's leaders bought the business back from HP. It runs today as a private company focused on documents for law firms and other professionals.

cover.artwork: A defence lawyer at the Court of Arbitration discussing business at his usual office premises, plate 27 from Les Gens De Justice

dek: NEON sold software that let a company's separate computer systems pass data to each other without custom wiring.
lede: Big companies in the 1990s ran dozens of computer systems that could not talk to each other. A bank's trading system, its accounting system and its customer records all spoke different languages. New Era of Networks, called NEON, sold the translator. Its NEONet software sat in the middle and moved messages between them. In June 1997 the Colorado company went public on a fresh idea with a dull name: application integration.

sections.heading: Built on Wall Street Plumbing
sections.body: Rick Adam founded NEON in June 1993 and began operations in January 1994. He served as chairman, chief executive and president. NEON first built its software for financial firms, a demanding market where errors cost money. It leaned on its founders' experience in that industry and on early customers who worked with it on the product. The plan was to move from finance into health care, telecommunications and other industries with the same tangle of systems.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars, Then Sybase
sections.body: NEON priced at $12 a share in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as NEON. It sold more stock in 1998 and 1999 and used its shares to buy other software companies. Integration software turned into a crowded field as rivals and big vendors joined in. In March 2001 the database maker Sybase launched an offer to buy NEON. The deal closed that year, and NEON ended its public registration in June 2001.

cover.artwork: Women watching fireworks at Sumida River

tagline: The Software That Served the Banner Ads
dek: NetGravity made AdServer, the software early websites used to schedule, target and count their banner ads.
lede: Early websites had a problem: they sold banner ads but had no good way to run them. NetGravity's AdServer let a publisher schedule each campaign, show it to the right visitors and count the results. It also forecast how much ad space a site had left to sell. In June 1998, when online advertising was still small and banners were the whole business, the San Mateo company went public.

sections.heading: Selling Software, Not Space
sections.body: John Danner and Thomas Shields co-founded NetGravity in 1995. Danner ran the company as chief executive. Rival DoubleClick ran ads for publishers as a network. NetGravity sold publishers the software to run their own ad sales. It opened a European subsidiary in 1997 and a Japanese one in 1998. The bet was that big websites would want to keep control of their ad inventory and their data.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars, Then DoubleClick
sections.body: NetGravity priced at $9 a share in June 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as NETG. Online advertising grew fast, and NetGravity sold more shares in March 1999. It now had offices in Europe and Japan as well as California. That year DoubleClick, its biggest rival, agreed to buy NetGravity in a stock deal. The merger closed in the fall of 1999, and NetGravity's software became part of DoubleClick's tools for publishers.

dek: Xylan made network switches that let companies speed up their office networks without ripping out what they had.
lede: Xylan priced its IPO at $26 a share in March 1996, and its stock never closed below $51 in the weeks that followed. Eleven weeks later, holders sold more stock at $59.50, and that second sale is the filing in this book. The Calabasas startup made switches that sped up crowded office networks, just as the World Wide Web, desktop video and faster PCs were choking the old hubs.

sections.heading: OmniSwitch and PizzaSwitch
sections.body: Xylan was incorporated in California in July 1993. Steve Kim served as chairman, president and chief executive. Its OmniSwitch could link every popular kind of office network and translate between them. Its smaller PizzaSwitch, launched in March 1996, brought in about 10 percent of revenue in its first quarter. Alcatel, Digital Equipment and Hitachi resold Xylan's gear. Revenue in the first quarter of 1996 reached $23.4 million, up 51 percent in three months.

sections.heading: Wall Street's Favorite Switch
sections.body: Xylan listed on Nasdaq as XYLN on March 12, 1996, and more than doubled from its offering price right away. The May follow-on sold 4 million shares at $59.50, raising $238 million, most of it for selling shareholders. Xylan kept selling through partners as office networks moved to switching. Alcatel, its longtime partner, bought the company in 1999, and Xylan's switches became part of Alcatel's enterprise line.

cover.theme: a woodcutter in the forest (xylan, from wood)

fate: Still public (NYSE: GDOT); sale to CommerceOne Financial approved by shareholders in 2026, pending close
tagline: A Bank Account on a Drugstore Rack
dek: Green Dot sold prepaid debit cards at Walmart and drugstores to people who did not have, or want, a bank.
lede: You could buy a Green Dot card off a rack at Walmart, Walgreens, CVS or 7-Eleven and load your paycheck onto it. For millions of Americans without a bank account, that card was the bank. By March 2010 Green Dot counted 3.4 million active cards, the most of any prepaid provider in the country. That July, with the financial crisis still fresh and banks out of favor, it went public.

sections.heading: Founded on the Unbanked
sections.body: Steve Streit founded the company in October 1999 to sell and service prepaid debit cards. A general-purpose reloadable card worked like a debit card, but anyone could get one without a credit check. Green Dot's real asset was the checkout aisle. Walmart, Walgreens, CVS, Rite Aid, Kroger and others sold its cards and took reloads at the register. The bet was that prepaid cards would grow into a mainstream way to bank.

sections.heading: Thirty-Six Dollars and a Bank
sections.body: Green Dot priced at $36 a share in July 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as GDOT. Class B shares carried ten votes each. It bought a small Utah bank, which let it issue its own cards and run banking for partners such as Apple Pay Cash. Streit stepped down as chief executive in 2020. In November 2025 Green Dot agreed to sell itself to CommerceOne Financial, with its payments business going to Smith Ventures. Shareholders approved in June 2026.

cover.theme: a color wheel of dots (Green Dot)

dek: MOGU sold everyday fashion to young Chinese shoppers through influencers, live video and its Mogujie app.
lede: MOGU's app is called Mogujie, which means mushroom street, and it sold clothes through people rather than shelves. Fashion influencers on the platform posted live video, short clips and photos, and viewers bought straight from the stream. Tencent, owner of WeChat, was one of its principal shareholders and steered its users to MOGU's store inside the messaging app. In December 2018 the Hangzhou company went public in New York.

sections.heading: Two Fashion Apps Become One
sections.body: MOGU's holding company was set up in June 2011. Its co-founder, Qi Chen, served as chairman and chief executive. In February 2016 it bought Meilishuo, another big online fashion platform in China. MOGU stated its mission as making fashion accessible to everyone. It worked with influencers who got actual products from brands and merchants and turned them into content. The bet was that young shoppers would buy what people they followed wore on camera.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars an ADS
sections.body: MOGU priced its American depositary shares at $14 each in December 2018 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MOGU, raising $66.5 million. Qi Chen kept about 79 percent of the voting power. Bigger rivals such as Alibaba and Pinduoduo, along with short-video apps, crowded into live-stream selling. MOGU's sales shrank and its shares fell far below the offering price. It is still listed in New York.

fate: Left the NYSE, 2019; still public in Hong Kong and Shanghai
tagline: A Chip Foundry Built in Three Years
dek: SMIC made chips to order for designers around the world, from factories in Shanghai.
lede: SMIC went from a company on paper to a working chip factory in Shanghai in about three years. Richard Chang, a veteran of Taiwan's chip industry, founded it in April 2000. It built wafer plants in the Zhangjiang High-Tech Park and made chips that other companies designed. By early 2004 it offered copper wiring, a leading-edge process. When it filed to sell shares in New York and Hong Kong, it asked investors to back a chipmaker not yet four years old.

sections.heading: Other People's Designs
sections.body: SMIC is a foundry. It does not sell chips under its own name. Chip designers send it their plans, and SMIC turns them into finished silicon wafers. Chang set up the company in the Cayman Islands in April 2000. He raised money from venture investors and others to pay for its plants. The company ran all of its fabs from one headquarters in the Pudong New Area of Shanghai.

sections.heading: Two Listings, Then One
sections.body: SMIC priced its offering in March 2004 at $17.50 per American depositary share. Each ADS stood for 50 ordinary shares. The stock listed in New York and Hong Kong at the same time. The start was rough: the shares fell more than 10 percent from their opening price as investors worried about spending and a trade fight over chip taxes. SMIC pulled its shares from the NYSE in 2019. In 2020 it added a listing on Shanghai's STAR Market, and it still trades in Hong Kong and Shanghai.

fate: Taken private by Golden Gate Capital, 2017 ($2.9B); sold to TransUnion, 2021 ($3.1B)
dek: Neustar kept your phone number working when you switched carriers, as the neutral referee between rival networks.
lede: Neustar began inside Lockheed Martin, the defense contractor, as the group that ran the plumbing behind American phone numbers. It sat between rival carriers as a neutral party. When a customer switched carriers and kept the same number, Neustar's database told every network where calls to that number should go. By the time it filed to go public in 2005, cell phones were everywhere, and each switch passed through a company most callers had never heard of.

sections.heading: Born at Lockheed Martin
sections.body: The business started in 1996 as a Lockheed Martin division called the Communications Industry Services group. Managers and an investor group led by Warburg Pincus later bought it out, and it became Neustar. Its value came from neutrality. Carriers that fought each other for customers all trusted Neustar to run shared systems, such as the clearinghouse for telephone number portability. The company was based in Sterling, Virginia, near Washington's Dulles airport.

sections.heading: Twenty-Two Dollars, Then Private
sections.body: Neustar priced its IPO at $22 a share in June 2005 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker NSR. The offering raised about $605 million. Over the next decade it added internet address, marketing data and security businesses. In 2017 the private equity firm Golden Gate Capital took Neustar private in a deal worth about $2.9 billion. In December 2021 TransUnion, the credit bureau, bought most of Neustar for $3.1 billion.

cover.theme: a guiding star (the new star of the phone network)

tagline: Anyone Can Teach, Anyone Can Learn
dek: Udemy let anyone teach an online course and sell it to learners anywhere in the world.
lede: More than 44 million people in over 180 countries had signed up to learn on Udemy by mid-2021, and the company employed almost none of the teachers. Independent instructors filmed the courses. Anyone could record a class on Python, guitar or Excel and sell it on the site. The pandemic had pushed work and school online. When Udemy filed to go public in 2021, it bet that people would keep paying to learn new skills after offices reopened.

sections.heading: A Marketplace for Lessons
sections.body: Eren Bali, Oktay Caglar and Gagan Biyani started Udemy in 2010. They built a marketplace. Instructors made courses and set prices, and Udemy handled the hosting, the payments and the customers. Free courses brought new learners in. Later the company sold Udemy Business, a plan that gave employers a library of courses for their staff. By June 2021 it had more than 8,600 business customers, and learners had made 594 million course enrollments.

sections.heading: A Debut Below the Offer
sections.body: Udemy priced its IPO at $29 a share and began trading on Nasdaq as UDMY on October 29, 2021. The stock opened at $27 and closed its first day at $27.50, below the offer price. In December 2025 Udemy agreed to combine with Coursera in an all-stock deal. Udemy holders got 0.8 Coursera shares for each share they owned. The merger closed on May 11, 2026, and Udemy now runs as part of Coursera.

fate: Still public (NYSE: CPAY); renamed from FleetCor, 2024
tagline: The Card in Every Fleet Truck
dek: FleetCor, now Corpay, gave trucking and delivery fleets fuel cards that let managers control what drivers spent.
lede: FleetCor had about 2.5 million cards in drivers' hands in December 2009, and most people had never heard of it. The Georgia company sold fuel cards to businesses that ran fleets of trucks and vans. The cards let managers set limits and see every gallon bought. In 2009 its networks handled about $14 billion in purchases across 18 countries. When it filed to go public in 2010, the economy was still climbing out of recession, and FleetCor offered a payments business built on fuel.

sections.heading: Closed Loops at the Pump
sections.body: FleetCor served more than 530,000 business accounts. It owned six closed-loop networks, which tied its cards directly to about 83,000 fuel stations and other merchants. That gave it data a general credit card could not match: which driver, which vehicle, how many gallons. Ronald F. Clarke had run the company as chief executive since 2000. At the time of its IPO, FleetCor was based in Norcross, Georgia.

sections.heading: From FleetCor to Corpay
sections.body: FleetCor priced its IPO at $23 a share and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as FLT on December 15, 2010. The shares closed the first day at $27.25, up about 18 percent. Over the next decade the company moved past fuel into lodging, tolls and corporate payments. In 2024 it changed its name to Corpay and its ticker to CPAY. It is still public on the NYSE and is based in Atlanta.

cover.artwork: Fleet of Ships Anchored at Sea
cover.artist: Imitator of Willem van de Velde, II

dek: Fusion-io put flash memory right inside servers, so busy websites stopped waiting on spinning disks.
lede: Fusion-io's chief scientist was Steve Wozniak, the man who co-founded Apple. The Salt Lake City company made cards packed with flash memory that plugged straight into a server, skipping the slow trip out to spinning hard drives. Facebook was among its biggest buyers. Revenue jumped from $0.6 million in fiscal 2008 to $36.2 million in fiscal 2010. When it filed to go public in 2011, data centers strained under social networks and cloud apps, and Fusion-io sold speed.

sections.heading: Canvas Becomes Fusion
sections.body: The company was incorporated in December 2005 as Canvas Technologies. David Flynn, its chief executive, and Rick White started it in Utah. It sold its first products in April 2007. Its ioMemory cards used NAND flash, the same kind of chip found in a USB stick, and its software made that flash act like a fast extension of the server's memory. Dell, HP and IBM resold the cards inside their own machines. Headcount grew from 262 to 395 in nine months.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars to Eleven
sections.body: Fusion-io priced its IPO at $19 a share and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as FIO on June 9, 2011. The stock opened at $25, touched $33 and closed its first day at $22.50. The offering raised about $234 million. Rivals soon crowded into flash storage. In June 2014 SanDisk agreed to buy Fusion-io for $11.25 a share in cash, about $1.1 billion, and the deal closed that summer.

cover.artwork: Looking out of Boat Cave, a flash light picture, No. 1132

dek: Switch & Data rented space where rival networks plugged into each other, without taking sides.
lede: Switch & Data owned one of the first commercial internet exchanges in the world, a building in Palo Alto where networks met to swap traffic. The Tampa company owned no network of its own. That was the point. Carriers, internet providers and content companies rented space and power in its buildings and connected straight to each other. By the time it filed to go public in 2006, it ran 34 sites in 23 markets, with about 17,000 connections between customers.

sections.heading: Owning No Wires
sections.body: Switch & Data called itself network neutral. Because it did not sell bandwidth, it never competed with its own tenants. Each new customer made a building more useful to the next one, since there were more networks to reach. The company grew by buying others. In March 2003 it bought the assets of PAIX, the Palo Alto exchange. In 2004 it added MeridianTelesis and the RACO Group.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars, Then Equinix
sections.body: Switch & Data priced its IPO at $17 a share in February 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as SDXC. The offering raised about $198 million, split between the company and selling stockholders. Demand for data center space kept rising. In 2010 Equinix, a larger rival in the same business, bought Switch & Data for about $689 million in cash and stock. The deal closed that spring, and Switch & Data left Nasdaq in May 2010.

cover.theme: a railway station (traffic switching between lines)

dek: UTStarcom sold phone and internet gear to China's carriers while the country built out its phone network.
lede: UTStarcom was a California company that made nearly all of its money in China. Its founders, Hong Lu and Ying Wu, set up shop in 1991 and aimed straight at China's phone network. They sold access equipment, wireless systems and handsets to the country's service providers. SoftBank, the Japanese investor, bought in early. When UTStarcom filed to go public at the end of 1999, the internet boom was near its peak.

sections.heading: Built for China First
sections.body: The company was incorporated in Delaware in 1991 as Unitech Industries. It shipped its first network access products in 1993. In 1995 it bought StarCom Network Systems and took the name UTStarcom. Its wireless product, called PAS, gave city customers a low-cost phone they could carry around town. Nearly all of its revenue came from service providers in China. Its gear followed international telecom standards, so carriers could plug it into the networks they already ran.

sections.heading: SoftBank's Majority Stake
sections.body: UTStarcom priced its IPO at $18 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as UTSI. After the offering, SoftBank and its related companies owned 52.3 percent of the stock. The company grew fast in the early 2000s on PAS phones in China, then shrank as mobile carriers won those customers. It later moved its headquarters to Hangzhou, China. UTStarcom is still listed on Nasdaq, as a much smaller company.

cover.theme: portraits of China's people (phones for China)

dek: Arlo made wire-free security cameras you could mount anywhere and check from your phone.
lede: Arlo shipped its first camera in December 2014, and three and a half years later it had sold more than 7.5 million smart devices. The cameras ran on batteries and Wi-Fi, so people could mount them on a fence or a porch with no cord. An app showed the video live. Arlo began as a product line inside Netgear, the router maker. When it filed to go public in 2018, Netgear was spinning it off as its own company.

sections.heading: A Brand Inside Netgear
sections.body: Arlo was incorporated in January 2018 to separate from Netgear. Its line included Wi-Fi and LTE cameras, baby monitors and security lights. By April 2018 its platform had more than 1.9 million registered users in over 100 countries. The plan was to sell paid subscription services on top of the hardware, so each camera kept earning money long after the sale.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars and a Spinoff
sections.body: Arlo priced its IPO at $16 a share in August 2018 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ARLO. It sold about 10.2 million new shares, and Netgear kept a large majority stake. At the end of 2018 Netgear handed its remaining Arlo shares to its own stockholders, and Arlo stood alone. The company later moved its headquarters to Carlsbad, California. It is still public on the NYSE.

cover.artwork: Banditti on the Lookout, from Fifteen etchings dedicated to Sir Joshua Reynolds

tagline: One Shoe Store, Then Brazil Online
dek: Netshoes sold sneakers, jerseys and sports gear online to millions of shoppers across Brazil.
lede: Netshoes started as a single shoe store in São Paulo, and in 2007 it closed its shops to sell only online. Founders Marcio Kumruian and Hagop Chabab bet that Brazilians would buy sports gear on the internet. By 2017 the company had sold to more than 12.8 million customers in Brazil, Argentina and Mexico. When it filed to list in New York that year, it called itself the leading online sports and lifestyle retailer in Latin America.

sections.heading: Closing the Stores
sections.body: Kumruian and Chabab opened their store in January 2000. Seven years later they shut their physical stores and launched Netshoes.com. The site sold brands such as Nike, Adidas and Mizuno, and the company ran its own distribution centers to ship orders across Brazil. In December 2014 it launched Zattini, a site for fashion and beauty. It also began building private label brands of its own.

sections.heading: Eighteen Dollars and an Exit
sections.body: Netshoes priced its IPO at $18 a share in April 2017 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as NETS. The shares fell in the months that followed as the losses continued. In 2019 Magazine Luiza, one of Brazil's biggest retailers, bought Netshoes after a bidding contest with the sporting goods chain Centauro. Netshoes left the NYSE in June 2019 and now runs as part of Magazine Luiza.

cover.theme: a shoe (a shoe store gone online)

tagline: The Brain of the Budget Phone
dek: Spreadtrum designed the main chips for low-cost mobile phones, many of them built in China.
lede: Within 15 months of starting up, Spreadtrum had designed its first full family of phone chips. The Shanghai company made baseband processors, the part of a handset that encodes and decodes every call and runs the phone's software. It packed in music, video and TV-out features at a low price. It also backed TD-SCDMA, China's own 3G standard. When it filed to list on Nasdaq in 2007, it was a chip designer barely six years old.

sections.heading: Fabless in Shanghai
sections.body: Ping Wu, Datong Chen and Renyong Fan were among the founders who started Spreadtrum in April 2001. The company was fabless: it designed chips and paid others to make them. It began earning revenue in 2003. Its chips supported GSM and GPRS phones, and its open platform let handset makers add their own features quickly. Wu served as president, chief executive and chairman from the start.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars an ADS
sections.body: Spreadtrum priced its IPO at $14 per American depositary share in June 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as SPRD. The stock struggled at first, then recovered as its chips won orders for low-cost smartphones. In 2013 Tsinghua Unigroup, a state-backed Chinese tech group, bought Spreadtrum for about $1.78 billion. The company left Nasdaq that December. Its business later became part of UNISOC.

cover.theme: a kite on the wind (wireless signals)

dek: Guidewire sold insurers modern software to write policies, pay claims and send bills, replacing their aging core systems.
lede: Guidewire asked insurance companies to replace the systems at the center of their business. Property and casualty insurers ran underwriting, claims and billing on old software that was hard to change. Guidewire's products let them change rules, workflows and screens without rewriting code. Its customers made those changes through a web browser. When Guidewire filed to go public in 2011, it was a ten-year-old San Mateo company selling to one of the most careful industries in the world.

sections.heading: Policy, Claims and Billing
sections.body: Guidewire was incorporated in Delaware in 2001. Its chief executive at the IPO, Marcus Ryu, was one of its founders. The company built three main products: PolicyCenter for underwriting, ClaimCenter for claims and BillingCenter for billing. Insurers could buy them together as Guidewire InsuranceSuite. The software could run in a customer's own data center or in the cloud, and the insurer could configure it without touching the underlying code.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars in January
sections.body: Guidewire priced its IPO at $13 a share in January 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as GWRE. Over the next decade it moved its customers toward a hosted version of its products, called Guidewire Cloud. Mike Rosenbaum took over from Ryu as chief executive in 2019. Guidewire is still public on the NYSE, and it is still based in San Mateo, California.

cover.artwork: Young Man Holding Umbrella Beside a Fence

tagline: Cheap Radios for the Unwired World
dek: Ubiquiti sold low-cost wireless gear that let small operators bring broadband to places big carriers skipped.
lede: Ubiquiti sold its radios to people building internet service where the big carriers would not go. Its customers were small operators in emerging markets and rural areas, plus businesses that wanted fast networks for less. Founder Robert Pera kept costs low and prices lower. When Ubiquiti filed to go public in 2011, it told investors that larger rivals could not match its prices, because their business models cost too much to run.

sections.heading: From Pera Networks
sections.body: The company was incorporated in California in 2003 as Pera Networks. It sat mostly idle until 2005, when it began its current business and took a new name. Pera, a former Apple engineer, served as chief executive. Ubiquiti made radios, antennas and management software for long-range wireless links. It sold through distributors and relied on an online community of users for support and product ideas.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars, One Big Owner
sections.body: Ubiquiti priced its IPO at $15 a share in October 2011 and listed on Nasdaq as UBNT. Pera kept most of the stock. The company later expanded into networking gear for homes and offices under the UniFi brand. It moved its listing to the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker UI and its headquarters to New York City. Ubiquiti is still public, and Pera still runs it.

cover.theme: a lone tower on a hill (rural wireless)

fate: Became MaxWorldwide, 2002; sold its businesses and planned to dissolve, 2003
dek: L90 sold banner ads on other companies' websites and tracked how well those ads worked.
lede: L90 went public at the peak of the dot-com boom, and two years later it had to restate its financial results. The Santa Monica company sold online ads for web publishers, mostly banners priced per thousand views. It also charged advertisers for adMonitor, its tool for tracking campaigns. In the first nine months of 1999, ad sales made up 93.6 percent of its revenue. When L90 filed to go public that year, it was betting that every website would need someone to sell its ad space.

sections.heading: Latitude 90
sections.body: John Bohan and Mark Roah co-founded the company in January 1997. Both had worked at Screaming Media. The company took the name Latitude 90 in December 1998 and became L90 in September 1999. It earned commissions for selling ad space on publishers' sites. It also sold direct marketing programs priced per action, such as each new user registration. Bohan served as chief executive from the start.

sections.heading: From L90 to MaxWorldwide
sections.body: L90 priced its IPO at $15 a share in January 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The online ad market crashed soon after. An internal investigation led L90 to restate its results for 2000 and most of 2001. In 2002 it reorganized as MaxWorldwide and took over DoubleClick's media business in exchange for stock. In February 2003 it sold its MaxDirect division, and it planned to liquidate and dissolve the company.

cover.theme: a man pasting posters (selling ad space)
cover.artwork: The Poster Man, plate 17 from Bohémiens de Paris

dek: Vimicro designed the processors inside PC webcams, from a base in Beijing.
lede: By 2004, more PC webcams shipped with Vimicro's processors inside than with any other company's, Vimicro said. Logitech was among the camera makers that used them. Zhonghan Deng and Xiaodong Yang were among its co-founders in 1999, a year after they co-founded Pixim, an imaging startup.
