The Beijing company sold whole systems: chips, firmware, software and reference designs. When it filed to list on Nasdaq in 2005, it hoped to repeat its webcam win inside mobile phones.

sections.heading: Webcams First, Phones Next
sections.body: Vimicro was fabless. It designed mixed-signal system-on-chip products and paid foundries to make them. Most of its operations were in China, where it found skilled design engineers, lower costs and a growing electronics industry close by. Its PC camera processors sold to the big camera brands. The next target was multimedia processors for mobile phones. Deng served as chairman, chief executive and president.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars an ADS
sections.body: Vimicro priced its IPO at $10 per American depositary share in November 2005 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as VIMC. Each ADS stood for four ordinary shares. Competition in camera and phone chips grew in the years that followed. In 2015 a group that included Deng and Yang took the company private for $3.375 a share in cash, or $13.50 per ADS. Vimicro left Nasdaq in December 2015.

cover.theme: a camera on a tripod (webcam chips)
cover.artwork: Self-Portrait with camera, tripod and pistol

dek: Chordiant gave big companies one view of each customer, whether that customer came by web, phone or branch.
lede: Chordiant spent six years as a consulting shop before it shipped a product. In September 1997 it released its Customer Communications Solution, software that pulled a customer's details from many systems into one place. A bank teller, a call center agent and a website could then treat the same person the same way. When Chordiant filed to go public in late 1999, every big company wanted an e-business plan, and Chordiant sold the plumbing behind one.

sections.heading: Consultants Turn Product Makers
sections.body: Chordiant was incorporated in California in March 1991 and moved to Delaware in October 1997. Before 1997 it did custom consulting work. Its CCS suite combined customer data from different sources and automated the steps behind each request. It kept service the same across the internet, telephone, e-mail and branch offices. Customers bought perpetual licenses, plus services to install and fit the software to their business.

sections.heading: Eighteen Dollars, Then Pegasystems
sections.body: Chordiant priced its IPO at $18 a share in February 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The timing was close to the top of the tech market, and the stock fell hard when the bubble burst. Chordiant stayed public for another decade. In 2010 Pegasystems, a business software maker, made a tender offer of $5 a share in cash. The deal went through, and Chordiant left Nasdaq in April 2010.

cover.theme: a harp (Chordiant, many strings in one chord)
cover.artwork: Lélio: The Aeolian Harp, from Hector Berlioz, sa vie et ses oeuvres

fate: Acquired by Nortel Networks, 2000 (about $7.8B in stock)
dek: Alteon built switches that spread web traffic across many servers, so busy sites stayed up under heavy load.
lede: Alteon sold a box that sat in front of a website's servers and decided which one should answer each visitor. It called the idea Web-working. Its switches balanced load across servers, steered traffic to caches and firewalls, and kept sessions running when a machine failed. E-commerce shops, portals and hosting companies were its buyers. When Alteon filed to go public in 1999, the web was growing faster than any one server could keep up with.

sections.heading: Research First, Then Switches
sections.body: Alteon was incorporated in Delaware on March 18, 1996. Through April 1997 it did mostly research and development. Its products combined switches, server adapters and software. One Alteon Web switch could do the work of a regular switch plus several traffic management appliances, at a lower cost. Customers included web portals, content publishers, internet service providers and large companies running their own data centers.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars, One Year Public
sections.body: Alteon priced its IPO at $19 a share in September 1999 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as ATON. It sold 4 million shares. Demand for web gear was near its peak. In 2000 Nortel Networks, the Canadian telecom equipment maker, agreed to buy Alteon in a stock deal valued at about $7.8 billion. The merger closed that fall, and Alteon stopped reporting as a public company in October 2000.

cover.theme: a river pilot steering through rapids (directing web traffic)
cover.artwork: The Pilot, from the series "The Camera's Story of Raftman's Life on the Wisconsin"

tagline: The Brains Inside the Thumb Drive
dek: Silicon Motion designed the controller chips that make flash memory cards and USB drives work.
lede: Every flash memory card needs a small chip to manage it, and in 2005 many of those chips came from Silicon Motion. Its controllers went into storage products sold by Lexar, Samsung, SanDisk and Sony. It also made chips for MP3 players and PC cameras. The company had roots in both Taiwan and California. When it filed to list on Nasdaq in 2005, cameras and music players were all moving their memory onto flash.

sections.heading: Controllers Behind the Brands
sections.body: Silicon Motion was fabless. It designed chips and paid foundries to make them. The company combined two predecessors: Silicon Motion, Inc. in California, and Feiya Technology in Taiwan, later renamed Silicon Motion, Inc. Its customers were the device makers and their contract manufacturers, which put Silicon Motion chips inside products under their own brands. Wallace Kou served as president and chief executive.

sections.heading: Ten Fifty an ADS
sections.body: Silicon Motion priced its IPO at $10.50 per American depositary share in June 2005 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as SIMO. The offering raised about $70 million. The company later became a major supplier of controllers for solid-state drives. In 2022 MaxLinear agreed to buy it, then walked away from the deal in 2023. Silicon Motion is still public on Nasdaq.

tagline: Racks and Bandwidth Above the Valley
dek: AboveNet rented server space and fast internet connections to websites that could not afford to go down.
lede: AboveNet made most of its money selling bandwidth, by the month, to websites that kept their servers in its buildings. It opened its first facility in San Jose in July 1996, four months after its founding. Content providers moved in first. Then internet service providers came, and AboveNet built what it called an ISX, a place where customers could connect to many networks at once. When it filed to go public in 1998, online stores needed somewhere safe to plug in.

sections.heading: San Jose to Vienna
sections.body: AboveNet was founded in March 1996, with Sherman Tuan as chief executive. In August 1997 it began serving ISPs as well as content providers, which led to its ISX model. In July 1998 it opened a second ISX facility in Vienna, Virginia, and added about 7,000 square feet in San Jose. Customers paid monthly for bandwidth and space, plus one-time installation fees.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then a Merger
sections.body: AboveNet priced its IPO at $13 a share in December 1998 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as ABOV. Less than a year later, in 1999, Metromedia Fiber Network bought AboveNet in an all-stock deal. Metromedia Fiber went bankrupt in 2002. It came out of bankruptcy in 2003 under the AboveNet name. That second AboveNet was sold to Zayo Group in 2012.

fate: Acquired by Cable & Wireless, 2001 ($3.40 a share)
tagline: A Private Road Across the Internet
dek: Digital Island ran a global network that let companies deliver web applications fast and reliably worldwide.
lede: Digital Island started life doing something else entirely, and only in January 1997 did it begin selling the global network that made its name. The San Francisco company offered businesses the reach of the public internet with the reliability of a private network. Customers got speed guarantees, custom billing and security services. When Digital Island filed to go public in 1999, companies were putting their key applications online and worrying about the public internet's slow, unreliable stretches.

sections.heading: From California to the World
sections.body: Digital Island was incorporated in California on February 10, 1994. It took the name Digital Island on August 15, 1996. Its Global IP Applications Network carried customer traffic across the United States, Asia and Europe. The company planned to grow by hiring direct sales staff and adding agents and resellers in all three regions. Its targets were corporations deploying business applications worldwide.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars and a Takeover
sections.body: Digital Island priced its IPO at $10 a share in June 1999 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as ISLD. Later that year it bought Sandpiper Networks, a content delivery company, to speed up websites. The bust hit hard. In May 2001 Cable & Wireless, the British telecom group, launched a cash tender offer of $3.40 a share for Digital Island. The deal went through, and Digital Island stopped reporting as a public company in September 2001.

dek: SPS Commerce connected suppliers to the retailers they sold to, so orders, invoices and shipping notices flowed automatically.
lede: SPS Commerce started in 1987 as St. Paul Software, more than two decades before it went public. A supplier that sold to big retailers had to swap orders, invoices and shipping notices in each retailer's exact format. SPS built those connections once and rented them out over the internet. By the end of 2009 it had over 11,000 customers paying monthly fees. When it filed to go public in 2010, it was selling software as a monthly service to the long tail of retail suppliers.

sections.heading: St. Paul Software
sections.body: The company was incorporated in Minnesota on January 28, 1987, as St. Paul Software. In May 2001 it reincorporated in Delaware as SPS Commerce. It delivered its service, SPSCommerce.net, as software over the internet. Pre-built links to retailers let suppliers shorten supply cycles, hold less inventory and meet each retailer's rules. Each new connection made the network more useful, and about 24,000 more organizations had used SPS for other services.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars in April
sections.body: SPS Commerce priced its IPO at $12 a share in April 2010 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as SPSC. The offering came less than two years after the financial crisis. Retailers kept tightening their rules for suppliers, and the company kept adding retailers, suppliers and data services in the years that followed. SPS Commerce is still public on Nasdaq and still based in Minneapolis, Minnesota.

dek: Bottomline let companies pay their bills, first by printing checks in-house, then by sending payments electronically.
lede: Bottomline's first product let companies print their own checks on laser printers, with no pre-printed check stock to steal. LaserCheck for DOS came out in 1989. By the time the New Hampshire company filed to go public in 1998, it had become one of the largest resellers of Xerox magnetic ink products. It had also bought its way into electronic payments. Corporate finance departments were moving off paper, and Bottomline wanted to handle the payments whichever way they went.

sections.heading: Checks Without Check Stock
sections.body: Daniel M. McGurl co-founded Bottomline in May 1989 and served as chairman, president and chief executive. In 1992 it struck a deal with Xerox to sell an advanced laser printer and new magnetic ink toners. It moved LaserCheck to Windows and added software to fight check fraud. In 1996 it bought CertiSoft Solutions, which made software for secure electronic payments. That gave Bottomline a path from paper to electronic payments.

sections.heading: EPAY at Thirteen Dollars
sections.body: Bottomline priced its IPO at $13 a share in February 1999 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the fitting ticker EPAY. The offering raised $44.2 million. Over the next two decades it added banking software and payment networks for businesses in the United States and Britain. In 2022 the private equity firm Thoma Bravo took Bottomline private, and its shares left Nasdaq that May.

cover.theme: a ship at anchor (the bottom line)

dek: NetIQ watched over company servers running Windows NT and fixed problems before users noticed them.
lede: NetIQ's revenue grew from $0.4 million in fiscal 1997 to $7.1 million in fiscal 1998, and it kept climbing. The Santa Clara company sold software that watched Windows NT servers and the applications running on them. It spotted problems, fixed many of them automatically, and showed everything on one console. Microsoft's server software was spreading through big companies. When NetIQ filed to go public in 1999, those companies needed tools to keep it running.

sections.heading: Managing the NT Server Room
sections.body: Ching-Fa Hwang co-founded NetIQ in California in June 1995 and served as president and chief executive from the start. Its AppManager software managed the performance and availability of distributed Windows NT systems from one place. NetIQ sold through its own field sales force, with offices in Chicago, Dallas, Denver, New York and Washington, D.C. Revenue reached $15.1 million in the nine months ended March 31, 1999.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Attachmate
sections.body: NetIQ priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as NTIQ. In 2000 it merged with Mission Critical Software, a maker of Windows management tools, and grew into a broader systems management company. In 2006 Attachmate, a privately held software company, bought NetIQ. NetIQ stopped reporting as a public company in July 2006. The NetIQ name stayed in use under its new owner.

dek: Actuate let big companies pull data out of their systems and publish clean reports to everyone who needed them.
lede: Actuate's software did for business data what a printing house did for books: it turned raw material into pages people could read. Companies had data spread across many systems. Actuate's Reporting System extracted it, formatted it and pushed the reports to employees and customers. The company first shipped its product in January 1996. When it filed to go public in 1998, it was still losing money, and it was growing through direct sales and partners who built Actuate into their own applications.

sections.heading: A Reporting System, Shipped
sections.body: Actuate was founded in November 1993 as Actuate Software Corporation. Nicolas C. Nierenberg served as president, chief executive and chairman. Version 3.1 of its Reporting System began shipping in May 1998. The company lost $6.1 million in 1996 and $7.2 million in 1997. It sold directly to large customers and through enterprise application vendors, resellers and distributors, which bundled its reporting tools into their own products.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars, Then OpenText
sections.body: Actuate priced its IPO at $11 a share in July 1998 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as ACTU. It later shortened its name to Actuate Corporation. The company backed BIRT, an open-source reporting project, and stayed independent for more than fifteen years. In December 2014 OpenText, the Canadian software company, offered $6.60 a share in cash. The deal closed in January 2015, and Actuate left Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: Interior of the Lemercier Lithographic Printing House

dek: GeoTel's software sent each incoming call to the best agent across a company's call centers, wherever they were.
lede: GeoTel became profitable in the first quarter of 1996, less than a year after its first customer installed its product. That product was the Intelligent CallRouter. It looked at every incoming call to a company's call centers and sent it to the best place to answer it, even across different cities and phone systems. Big companies ran call centers in many locations. When GeoTel filed to go public in 1996, it had licensed its software to more than 20 companies.

sections.heading: One Product, One Job
sections.body: GeoTel was incorporated in Delaware in June 1993 to build software for call centers. Through the first half of 1995 it worked mostly on research and development. Its first customer installed the Intelligent CallRouter in May 1995, and revenue followed in the fourth quarter of that year. The company expected that one product to bring in almost all of its revenue. It was based in Littleton, Massachusetts.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars, Then Cisco
sections.body: GeoTel priced its IPO at $12 a share in November 1996 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as GEOC. Call routing grew more valuable as phone calls and data networks came together. In 1999 Cisco Systems agreed to buy GeoTel in a stock deal worth about $2 billion. The merger closed in mid-1999, and GeoTel stopped reporting as a public company in June 1999.

cover.theme: a map of the globe (routing calls by geography)
cover.artwork: The Map of the Globe, Terminal Page of the set of eight Pictures of Foreign Ships

dek: Nextlink built its own local phone networks to sell calling and data service to small and mid-sized businesses.
lede: Nextlink was Craig McCaw's next move after he sold McCaw Cellular to AT&T. He founded it in 1994 to compete with the regional Bell companies for local phone customers. The Telecom Act of 1996 had opened local markets to new carriers. Nextlink built its own networks instead of reselling the Bells' lines. By the fall of 1997 it ran 14 networks serving 23 markets in seven states. When it went public that September, McCaw was its main owner.

sections.heading: Facilities, Not Resale
sections.body: Nextlink aimed at small and mid-sized businesses. It sold switched local and long distance service over networks it owned, which meant laying fiber and buying switches city by city. That cost a great deal of money, so Nextlink raised it through stock and debt offerings. Its rules for connecting to the Bell companies' networks depended on regulators and the courts. In July 1997 a federal appeals court threw out many of the FCC's rules for those connections.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars, Then XO
sections.body: Nextlink priced its IPO at $17 a share in September 1997 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market as NXLK. It sold 15.2 million Class A shares, some of them from a selling shareholder. The company spent heavily to build fiber networks and bought Concentric Network in 2000. That year it renamed itself XO Communications. When the telecom bubble burst, XO could not carry its debt, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2002.

dek: IntraLinks gave bankers and lawyers secure online rooms to share confidential deal documents.
lede: IntraLinks went public at $13 a share and was bought, seven years later, for exactly $13 a share. In between, it ran the secure online rooms where bankers, lawyers and buyers read confidential documents during loans and mergers. Before IntraLinks, those papers moved by fax, courier and email, or sat in a physical data room. When IntraLinks filed to go public in 2010, it wanted to sell the same locked-down sharing to every kind of company.

sections.heading: From Loans to Mergers
sections.body: IntraLinks was incorporated in Delaware in June 1996. At its founding it offered online collaboration for the debt capital markets, where banks share loan documents with lenders. Soon after, it moved into merger and acquisition deals, where its virtual data rooms let bidders review a company's files. In June 2007 a merger made IntraLinks part of a new holding company. It was based in New York City.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Both Ways
sections.body: IntraLinks priced its IPO at $13 a share in August 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as IL. It sold 11 million shares and used much of the money to pay down debt. In December 2016 Synchronoss Technologies launched a tender offer to buy IntraLinks for $13 a share in cash. The deal closed in January 2017, and IntraLinks left the NYSE.

cover.theme: chains and a locked pier (a secure data room)
cover.artwork: The Pier with Chains, plate 16 from Imaginary Prisons

dek: ZEEKR built premium electric cars for Chinese drivers, backed by the factories and supply chain of Geely.
lede: ZEEKR delivered its first car in October 2021, and by the end of 2023 it had delivered 196,633 of them. In October 2022 its ZEEKR 001 became the first premium pure-electric model from a Chinese brand to sell more than 10,000 units in one month. The company was the high-end electric brand of Geely, the Chinese car group that also owns Volvo Cars. When ZEEKR filed to list in New York, China's electric car market was crowded and in a price war.

sections.heading: A Brand Built Inside Geely
sections.body: ZEEKR was set up in 2021, led by An Conghui, who had already built the Geely and Lynk & Co brands. It leaned on Geely's factories and supply chain to ramp up production fast. The ZEEKR 001, a fast electric shooting brake, came first, and more models followed. Almost all of its deliveries were in China. Its headquarters sat in the Beilun District of Ningbo, in Zhejiang province.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Dollars an ADS
sections.body: ZEEKR priced its IPO at $21 per American depositary share in May 2024 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ZK. Geely Auto bought about 12.9 million of the ADSs itself, and Mobileye and CATL also bought in. The stock closed its first day well above the offer price. In 2025 Geely Auto agreed to buy out the other shareholders. ZEEKR left the NYSE in December 2025.

cover.theme: a chariot race (a fast electric car)
cover.artwork: The Chariot Races at Santa Maria, from The Caprices

tagline: A Network Owned by Phone Companies
dek: Infonet ran one private data network that big companies could reach from more than 180 countries.
lede: Infonet went public owned by six of the world's biggest phone companies, from Japan's KDD to Australia's Telstra. The El Segundo company ran The World Network, a private data network that clients could reach from more than 180 countries. Multinationals used it to link offices on different continents without stitching together a dozen local carriers. When Infonet filed in late 1999, every telecom stock seemed to be climbing, and its owners saw a chance to sell part of their stake.

sections.heading: Born Inside Computer Sciences
sections.body: Infonet began operations in 1969 as part of Computer Sciences Corporation. Between 1988 and 1992, CSC sold the business to a group of telecom companies. That gave Infonet an odd and useful position. Its owners included KDD, KPN, Swisscom, Telefonica, Telia and Telstra, and it kept close ties with carriers such as Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom. It had local representatives in more than 60 countries. The bet was that global companies wanted one network and one bill, everywhere they did business.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Dollars to Two
sections.body: Infonet priced its IPO at $21 a share in December 1999 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker IN. The timing was close to the top of the telecom bubble. As the market for network capacity collapsed, the stock fell with it. In November 2004, BT agreed to buy Infonet for $2.06 a share in cash, about $965 million in total. The deal closed in early 2005, and BT renamed the business BT Infonet inside BT Global Services.

cover.theme: the Houses of Parliament in fog (a London future with BT)

dek: Clearwire sold fast wireless internet to homes and laptops before 4G phones made it ordinary.
lede: Craig McCaw made a fortune selling McCaw Cellular to AT&T, and in 2003 he started over with Clearwire. The Kirkland, Washington company sold wireless broadband: a small modem that pulled fast internet from the air, with no cable or phone line. In 2007 the iPhone was months away, and most people still got online through a wire at home. Clearwire filed to go public with McCaw holding 34 percent of the equity and 49 percent of the votes.

sections.heading: Internet Without the Wire
sections.body: Clearwire's idea was simple to say and costly to build. It gathered radio spectrum and put up towers, city by city, so customers could plug in a modem and get broadband with no installer. It aimed at towns and households where cable and DSL were weak or overpriced. The plan needed billions in spectrum and network spending before it could pay off. McCaw had done this before with cellular phones, and investors were willing to bet he could do it again.

sections.heading: Six Hundred Million, Then Sprint
sections.body: Clearwire sold 24 million shares at $25 each in March 2007, raising $600 million, and began trading on Nasdaq as CLWR. In 2008 it merged with Sprint's WiMAX business, Xohm, to form a new Clearwire with Sprint as the largest owner. The network became the backbone of Sprint's early 4G service. In July 2013, Sprint bought the shares it did not already own and became the sole owner of Clearwire.

cover.theme: a wide open sky over a beach (clear air, signals through it)

dek: Virgin Mobile USA sold no-contract cell phone plans to young people, using Sprint's network and Richard Branson's brand.
lede: Virgin Mobile USA owned no cell towers. It rented space on Sprint's network and put Richard Branson's red brand on top, selling prepaid plans to young people who did not want a two-year contract. The Warren, New Jersey company began as a joint venture between the Virgin Group and Sprint. By 2007 it was a big name in prepaid wireless, and it filed to go public just as the iPhone was turning phones into the year's hottest product.

sections.heading: A Brand Without Towers
sections.body: Virgin Mobile USA was what the industry calls a mobile virtual network operator. Sprint carried the calls. Virgin did the marketing, the phones and the customer service. The target was teenagers and young adults with no credit history or no wish to sign a long contract. They paid in advance, with no commitment. Service launched nationally in July 2002, and the company reached one million customers in November 2003, eighteen months later.

sections.heading: Priced at the Low End
sections.body: Virgin Mobile USA sold 27.5 million shares at $15 in October 2007, at the bottom of its $15 to $17 range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock slid fast. By mid-November it traded near $9. In July 2009, Sprint Nextel agreed to buy the company in a stock deal valued at about $5.50 a share. The deal closed in late 2009, and Virgin Mobile became a prepaid brand inside Sprint.

cover.theme: a young woman in black (the brand's young customers)

dek: trivago let travelers compare hotel prices from many booking sites in one search.
lede: trivago's IPO marketed shares at $13 to $15, then priced at $11, and the stock still rose on day one. The Düsseldorf company ran a hotel search engine that pulled prices from many booking sites into one list, and its TV ads had made the name familiar in dozens of countries. Expedia had bought a majority stake in 2013. trivago listed in December 2016, one of the final IPOs of the year.

sections.heading: Four Founders in Düsseldorf
sections.body: Rolf Schrömgens, Peter Vinnemeier, Stephan Stubner and Malte Siewert started trivago in 2005. Booking sites often showed the same hotel room at different prices. trivago gathered those prices and showed them side by side, then sent the traveler to the booking site to pay. The site earned money for each click it sent. To win travelers, trivago spent heavily on television ads, which made it one of the best known travel names in Europe and beyond.

sections.heading: Below the Range, Then Up
sections.body: trivago sold 26.1 million American depositary shares at $11 and began trading on Nasdaq as TRVG on December 16, 2016. The stock closed its first day at $11.85, up about 8 percent. Expedia kept a majority of the shares after the offering. The years after were harder, as Google and the big booking sites spent more on their own hotel search. trivago is still public on Nasdaq, with Expedia as its largest owner.

cover.theme: a grand hotel's long porch (hotel search)
cover.artwork: Rear Piazza, Grand Union Hotel, Saratoga, N.Y.

fate: Taken private by Silver Lake and P2 Capital, 2018 ($3.5B)
tagline: The Gift Card Rack at Checkout
dek: Blackhawk Network put gift cards for hundreds of brands on the racks of grocery and drug stores.
lede: The rack of gift cards near a supermarket checkout lane was Blackhawk Network's business. The Pleasanton, California company started inside the grocery chain Safeway and grew into the network that let stores sell cards for other brands, then moved the money between them. A shopper could buy a card for a restaurant, an app store or a phone plan while picking up milk. In 2013, Safeway took Blackhawk public on Nasdaq under the ticker HAWK.

sections.heading: Born in a Grocery Chain
sections.body: Blackhawk began in 2001 as a Safeway project. The insight was that grocery stores had foot traffic and checkout space, and brands wanted to sell prepaid cards to the people walking past. Blackhawk built the system in the middle. It signed up the brands, stocked the racks across many retailers, and handled activation at the register so a card had value only after a customer paid for it. Each sale earned a fee, and the network grew with every new store.

sections.heading: A Hawk Goes Private
sections.body: Blackhawk priced its IPO at $23 a share in April 2013, raising $230 million, with Safeway still holding most of the company. Over the next five years it added corporate rewards and incentive programs to its gift card business. In January 2018, Silver Lake and P2 Capital Partners agreed to buy Blackhawk for $45.25 a share in cash, about $3.5 billion including debt. The deal closed on June 15, 2018, and the stock left Nasdaq that day.

cover.theme: a hawk seizing a crane in flight
cover.artwork: A Hawk Capturing a Crane in Flight

dek: GDS built and ran the big, power-hungry data centers that China's cloud and internet companies rent.
lede: By the fall of 2016, GDS held about a quarter of China's market for high-performance, carrier-neutral data centers, the largest share of anyone. The Shanghai company builds the halls where servers live: big floors, heavy power, cooling and links to every phone carrier. Its customers were cloud providers, internet giants and banks that needed more capacity every year. GDS filed to list in New York as China's cloud companies raced to keep up with demand.

sections.heading: Huang's Long Build
sections.body: William Wei Huang founded GDS in 2001 and still ran it as chairman and CEO at the IPO. The company placed its data centers in China's main economic hubs, close to the customers who needed them most. Being carrier-neutral meant a client could connect to any telecom network inside a GDS building. The bet was about scale. Each new hall cost a great deal up front, then earned rent for many years once the racks filled.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars in New York
sections.body: GDS sold American depositary shares at $10 in November 2016 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker GDS. Huang held all of the Class B shares, which carried extra votes. The company kept borrowing and building, and later added a second listing in Hong Kong. It also built data centers outside China through a separate international business. GDS is still public on Nasdaq.

dek: Castlight showed employees what doctors and procedures would cost before they got care.
lede: Castlight Health went public having made its first customer sale only four years earlier. The San Francisco company sold software to large employers that showed their workers the price and quality of doctors, scans and procedures before they booked them. American health care hid its prices, and companies paying the bills wanted their staff to shop. In March 2014, investors were hungry for health tech and for cloud software, and Castlight was both.

sections.heading: A Doctor and a Price Tag
sections.body: Giovanni Colella co-founded Castlight in 2008 after running RelayHealth, and he became its CEO. Bryan Roberts, a venture investor, co-founded it and chaired the board. Todd Park was the third co-founder. The company built its first product, Castlight Medical, in 2009 and closed its first sale in 2010. The bet was that big self-insured employers would pay for software that steered workers toward cheaper, better care and cut their health bills.

sections.heading: A Pop, Then a Long Slide
sections.body: Castlight priced at $16 a share on March 14, 2014, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under CSLT. The shares more than doubled on the first day. Growth then slowed, and the stock spent years far below its offer price. In 2017 Castlight bought the health app maker Jiff. In early 2022, Vera Whole Health bought Castlight through a tender offer, and the stock was delisted in February 2022.

cover.theme: an old castle on the water (Castlight)

dek: Violin Memory sold all-flash storage arrays that made databases run much faster than spinning disks.
lede: Violin Memory's IPO fell on its first day, and the company spent its short public life trying to recover. The Santa Clara company built storage arrays made entirely of flash memory chips, at a time when most corporate data still sat on spinning hard drives. Flash cost more but answered requests far faster, which mattered for big databases. In September 2013, all-flash storage was the hot new corner of the data center, and Violin was one of the first to sell it.

sections.heading: Chips Instead of Disks
sections.body: Violin was incorporated in March 2005 and recapitalized in 2009, when Donald Basile arrived as CEO. It shipped its Flash Memory Arrays in May 2010 and added PCIe flash cards in March 2013. The pitch was raw speed. A bank or retailer could swap racks of hard drives for a few Violin boxes and run its databases in a fraction of the time. The risk was that much bigger storage vendors would build or buy their own flash products.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars, Then Court
sections.body: Violin priced at $9 a share in late September 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as VMEM. The stock dropped on day one, and within weeks the board replaced Basile as CEO. Rivals such as Pure Storage, EMC and NetApp crowded the flash market. Violin never turned a profit. Its shares were delisted in November 2016, and it filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in December 2016.

cover.theme: an old violin hung on a door

tagline: Closing the Books in the Cloud
dek: BlackLine gave finance teams cloud software to close the books each month without endless spreadsheets.
lede: Every month, accountants at big companies spend days matching numbers across spreadsheets so the books can close. BlackLine sold cloud software to automate that grind. Therese Tucker started it in 2001 and was still CEO when it filed, a founder-led company in a part of software usually run by giants such as SAP and Oracle. In October 2016, cloud software IPOs were coming back after a slow year, and BlackLine was one of the first in line.

sections.heading: Therese Tucker's Spreadsheet Problem
sections.body: Tucker had spent years building accounting software before she founded BlackLine. Her idea was narrow and deep. The month-end close ran on spreadsheets, email and checklists, and mistakes were easy to miss. BlackLine moved account reconciliations, journal entries and task lists into one cloud system that auditors could follow. Silver Lake Sumeru invested before the IPO. At the offering, Tucker and Mario Spanicciati, the chief marketing officer, owned 12.9 percent and 9.0 percent of the company.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars in Woodland Hills
sections.body: BlackLine priced its IPO at $17 a share on October 28, 2016, and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker BL. Its investors sold more shares in follow-on offerings over the next two years. The company also built a close partnership with SAP, which resold BlackLine to its own customers. That gave a small Los Angeles company a sales channel into SAP's large customer base. BlackLine is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: dark lines of railroad track (a black line)

dek: MatrixOne let manufacturers and their suppliers work on the same product designs and parts lists over the web.
lede: MatrixOne began in 1983 as Adra Systems, a maker of engineering software, and reinvented itself for the internet just in time for the 2000 IPO window. The Chelmsford, Massachusetts company sold collaboration software for manufacturers. Engineers, buyers and outside suppliers could all work from the same designs, part lists and change orders. In March 2000, the Nasdaq was at its peak, and any company with an internet story could find buyers for its shares.

sections.heading: From Adra to eMatrix
sections.body: Adra Systems was incorporated in Delaware in July 1983. It shipped the first version of its business collaboration software in November 1993 and released an internet version in March 1997. The company later took the name MatrixOne and launched its eMatrix suite in June 1999. The bet was that big manufacturers would stop passing drawings by fax and email. They would manage a product's whole life, from first sketch to retirement, in one shared system.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Dollars to Seven
sections.body: MatrixOne priced its IPO at $25 a share on March 1, 2000, days before the Nasdaq peaked. The crash that followed hit software companies hard, and MatrixOne moved its headquarters to nearby Westford. In March 2006, Dassault Systèmes, the French maker of CATIA design software, agreed to buy MatrixOne for $7.25 a share in cash. The deal closed in May 2006, and MatrixOne became part of Dassault's ENOVIA product line.

fate: Merged with GENBAND to form Ribbon Communications, 2017
dek: Sonus built switches that let phone companies carry ordinary voice calls over internet-style data networks.
lede: Sonus had not recorded any product revenue when it filed to go public. The Westford, Massachusetts company was barely two years old. It built switching gear that let phone carriers move voice calls over packet networks, the same kind of network that carried the internet, instead of the old circuit-switched phone system. In May 2000, telecom spending was near its peak, and carriers were buying anything that promised cheaper, faster networks.

sections.heading: Two Founders, One Switch
sections.body: Rubin Gruber and Michael Hluchyj founded Sonus in August 1997, and operations started that November after its first funding. Hassan Ahmed became CEO. Its products included the GSX9000 Open Services Switch and the PSX6000 SoftSwitch. Earlier voice-over-internet gear had fallen short on quality and reliability. Sonus aimed to match the toll quality of the phone network, then beat it on cost. Its pitch to carriers was an open system that could add new services fast.

sections.heading: From Bubble to Ribbon
sections.body: Sonus priced its IPO at $23 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Weeks later, the telecom market began to collapse, and carriers cut their spending. Sonus survived the bust and kept selling to phone companies and large enterprises for nearly two decades. In 2017, Sonus merged with GENBAND, another network equipment company. The combined business took the name Ribbon Communications, and Sonus stock was delisted in October 2017.

cover.theme: a baker sounding his horn (sound carried far)

dek: Ticketmaster sold seats to concerts, games and shows by phone, at outlets and on the early web.
lede: Ticketmaster started life selling ticketing machines to arenas, not tickets to fans. Organized in 1976, it switched in 1982 to running the ticket sales itself, and the fees made it the dominant name at box offices across America. By its 1996 IPO, Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen sat on the board, and insiders would still own 68.4 percent of the shares after the offering. Fans grumbled about the service charges. Investors saw a toll booth on live entertainment.

sections.heading: From Machines to Seats
sections.body: Ticketmaster Corporation was organized in 1976 to build stand-alone automated ticketing systems for individual venues. For its first years it earned money from equipment sales, royalties and service fees, and it did not sell tickets to the public. In the fall of 1982 it began to change into a service provider. It linked one ticket inventory system to phone centers and retail outlets, so a fan could buy seats for many venues in one place. Fredric Rosen became CEO in 1993.

sections.heading: Fourteen Fifty a Share
sections.body: Ticketmaster Group priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in November 1996 and listed on Nasdaq under TKTM. Allen & Company led the deal. Its public life was short. Barry Diller's USA Networks bought a large stake in 1997 and the rest of the company in 1998, and Ticketmaster deregistered its stock in June 1998. The brand lived on, and today Ticketmaster is part of Live Nation Entertainment.

cover.theme: a packed kabuki theater (a full house)
cover.artwork: Perspective Picture of a Kabuki Theater (Uki-e Kabuki shibai)

tagline: The Tiny Package Inside Billions of Chips
dek: Tessera invented ways to package chips smaller and licensed them to the companies that made memory and processors.
lede: By 2003, Tessera's packaging technology sat inside more than 2.5 billion chips, and Tessera made almost none of them. The San Jose company licensed its designs for chip-scale packages, the tiny casings that connect a silicon chip to a circuit board. Forty-four companies paid to use them in memory, DSP and Flash chips. Tessera filed in the fall of 2003, as the chip market climbed out of the dot-com bust, with a rare thing among tech IPOs: profits.

sections.heading: Selling Ideas, Not Chips
sections.body: Tessera was incorporated in Delaware in May 1990. From 1990 through 1995 it did mostly research into chip-scale and multi-chip packages. It started earning license revenue in 1994. The pitch to chipmakers was size, speed, reliability and cost. Smaller packages meant smaller phones and denser memory modules. Tessera collected royalties on each chip that used its patents, so it grew when its licensees shipped more. In 2002 it earned $6.5 million on revenue of $28.3 million.

sections.heading: Royalties and Courtrooms
sections.body: Tessera priced at $13 a share in November 2003 and listed on Nasdaq as TSRA. Its patents became its main asset, and it spent years suing and settling with big chipmakers over royalties. In December 2016 it merged with the audio company DTS, and in 2017 the combined company took the name Xperi. In 2022, Xperi split off its product business, and the patent licensing company that began as Tessera renamed itself Adeia.

cover.theme: a Byzantine mosaic made of tesserae
cover.artwork: Mosaic Fragment with a Man Leading a Giraffe

dek: Apigee gave companies the tools to open their data and services to outside apps through managed APIs.
lede: Apigee started in 2004 as Nexgen Machines, became Sonoa Systems that fall, and only took the Apigee name in 2010. By then its business was APIs, the plugs that let one piece of software talk to another. Retailers, banks and phone companies were opening their systems to mobile apps and partners. Apigee sold the gatekeeper: software to publish those APIs, secure them and track who used them. It filed in the spring of 2015, as every big company tried to become a software company.

sections.heading: Chet Kapoor's Pivot
sections.body: Chet Kapoor joined as CEO in January 2007 after leading content management and search products at IBM. Under him the company turned toward API management. The bet was that APIs would become the main way businesses connected to customers and partners. Each company would need one place to control access, set traffic limits and measure use. Apigee told investors in its prospectus that this market was new and unproven, and it was spending heavily to win it early.

sections.heading: Google Comes Calling
sections.body: Apigee priced at $17 a share in April 2015 and listed on Nasdaq as APIC. The stock traded below its offer price for much of the next year. In June 2016 its shares closed at $12.62. That September, Google agreed to buy Apigee for $17.40 a share in cash, about $625 million. The deal closed in November 2016, and Apigee became part of Google Cloud, where it still runs under its own name.

cover.theme: a gentleman studying bees too closely (Apigee, apis)
cover.artwork: A Gentleman Who Wanted to Study the Habits of Bees too Closely

fate: Still public as Ziff Davis (NASDAQ: ZD)
tagline: Faxes That Landed in Your Inbox
dek: JFAX gave people one phone number that turned their faxes and voicemails into email.
lede: The company that owns Mashable and IGN today went public in 1999 as JFAX.COM, a service that sent your faxes to your email. JFAX was founded in December 1995 to let people get faxes and voice messages over the internet. A subscriber got a phone number, and anything sent to it arrived in their inbox. Its co-chairman, Jaye Muller, was 26 at the IPO. In July 1999, an internet company with recurring subscription fees was an easy sell.

sections.heading: One Number, Every Message
sections.body: Jaye Muller and John Rieley founded JFAX in 1995. Business travelers then carried laptops but could not carry their fax machines. JFAX solved that with a local number in many cities and a server that turned each fax or voicemail into an email attachment. Richard Ressler became CEO and co-chairman in 1997. The bet was that millions of small offices would pay a few dollars a month for a fax line without a machine.

sections.heading: From JFAX to Ziff Davis
sections.body: JFAX.COM priced at $9.50 a share in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. It soon renamed itself j2 Global and bought rivals such as eFax, building a large online fax business. j2 later used that cash to buy media and software brands, including the publisher Ziff Davis. In 2021 it spun off the fax business as Consensus Cloud Solutions and took the Ziff Davis name. The same company still trades on Nasdaq as ZD.

cover.theme: a woman reading a love letter (messages delivered)

tagline: Office Phones on the Data Network
dek: ShoreTel sold business phone systems that ran over a company's computer network instead of old phone wiring.
lede: ShoreTel began in 1996 as Shoreline Communications and kept the name until 2004. The Sunnyvale company sold office phone systems built on internet protocol, so calls ran over the same network as a company's computers. Its customers were mid-sized businesses with offices in more than one place, which could run every site's phones as one system. In July 2007, the old office PBX was dying, and Cisco and Avaya were chasing the same customers.

sections.heading: Edwin Basart's Simpler PBX
sections.body: Edwin Basart founded the company and was still its chief technology officer at the IPO. John Combs ran it as chairman and CEO. The pitch was ease. A ShoreTel system arrived as hardware and software that a company's own IT staff could install and manage, without a phone specialist. Firms with many branch offices could add a site and have it join the system. The bet was that buyers cared more about simple setup and low running costs than about the biggest brand.

sections.heading: A Small Price, a Long Run
sections.body: ShoreTel priced at $9.50 a share in July 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as SHOR. It stayed public for ten years, adding cloud phone services as businesses moved their systems online. Competition and slow growth weighed on the stock. In 2017, the Canadian company Mitel bought ShoreTel through a tender offer at $7.50 a share in cash, about $530 million. ShoreTel's shares came off Nasdaq in September 2017.

fate: Taken private by Insight Venture Partners, 2015
dek: E2open connected big manufacturers with their suppliers, shippers and contract factories on one cloud network.
lede: E2open started in 2000 as a venture backed by a group of corporate investors, at the peak of the B2B exchange craze, and it outlived nearly all of that craze's companies. By its 2012 IPO, the Foster City company ran a cloud network where manufacturers and their trading partners shared orders, forecasts and inventory. Customers included Boeing, Cisco, Dell, IBM, Motorola and Vodafone. Dell and RIM each made up more than 10 percent of its revenue.

sections.heading: Twelve Years to Market
sections.body: E2open began operations in 2000 as a venture between strategic corporate investors, financial investors and advisors. In 2003 it was incorporated in Delaware and merged with the original E2open, LLC. The idea was a network effect. Every new supplier or shipper that joined made the network more useful for the next customer. Big electronics makers outsourced most of their manufacturing, so they needed to see orders and stock across dozens of outside partners.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars, Then Insight
sections.body: E2open priced at $15 a share in July 2012 and listed on Nasdaq as EOPN. It sold more stock in a second offering in January 2014. Losses continued, and the shares fell. In early 2015, Insight Venture Partners bought E2open through a tender offer at $8.60 a share in cash, and the stock left Nasdaq in March 2015. Insight then built E2open into a larger supply chain software company through acquisitions.

cover.theme: a harbor at sunrise (goods moving between partners)

fate: Taken private by a Chinese investor group, 2016
tagline: A Camera on a Single Chip
dek: OmniVision made the tiny image sensor chips that let phones, laptops and toys take pictures and video.
lede: The cover of OmniVision's prospectus showed its image sensor beside a quarter, to prove how small a camera could get. The Sunnyvale company made single-chip CMOS image sensors, the part that turns light into a digital picture. Older sensors needed several chips and more power. OmniVision squeezed the job onto one cheap chip. When it went public in July 2000, webcams and digital toys were its market, and camera phones were still a few years off.

sections.heading: Shaw Hong's Single Chip
sections.body: OmniVision was incorporated in California in May 1995, with Shaw Hong as CEO and Raymond Wu among its top executives. The bet was on CMOS, the same cheap process used to make most computer chips. CCD sensors gave better pictures but cost more and drew more power. OmniVision wagered that CMOS sensors would get good enough, and that low cost and small size would then win. That would put a camera into products that had never had one.

sections.heading: Into Every Phone
sections.body: OmniVision priced at $13 a share in July 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as OVTI, just as the tech market turned down. Camera phones then made image sensors a mass product, and OmniVision became one of the biggest suppliers. In 2015 a group of Chinese investors agreed to buy the company for $29.75 a share in cash, about $1.9 billion. The deal closed in January 2016. OmniVision later became part of China's Will Semiconductor.

cover.theme: a camera obscura (the first image sensor)

tagline: Traffic Cops for the Office Network
dek: Packeteer's PacketShaper boxes let companies decide which network traffic got through first.
lede: Packeteer's last chapter was a bidding fight: a hedge fund offered $5.50 a share, and a rival paid $7.10. That came nine years after its IPO. In 1999 the Cupertino company sold PacketShaper, a box that sat on a company's internet link and set priorities. Business apps went first. Music downloads and web surfing waited. Corporate networks were filling up with new kinds of traffic, and Packeteer gave IT managers a way to see it and control it.

sections.heading: Shaping Every Packet
sections.body: Robert Packer and Brett Galloway co-founded Packeteer, which was incorporated in January 1996 and began shipping products in February 1997. Its PacketWise software classified the traffic on a network, measured it, controlled the flows and reported on performance. Installing a PacketShaper required no changes to the rest of the network. Partners such as Lucent resold the technology under their own names. The bet was that bandwidth would stay costly enough that companies would pay to manage it.

sections.heading: Two Bids for One Company
sections.body: Packeteer priced at $15 a share in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as PKTR. It rode the dot-com boom, then the bust, and stayed in business selling to large enterprises. In March 2008, the hedge fund Elliott Associates launched a hostile tender offer at $5.50 a share. Blue Coat Systems topped it with an offer of $7.10 a share in cash in May 2008. Blue Coat completed the deal, and Packeteer left Nasdaq in June 2008.

cover.theme: a shepherd guiding his flock (directing traffic)
cover.artwork: Arcadian Shepherd Boy and His Flock of Sheep

tagline: DSL Chips From a Paradyne Lab
dek: GlobeSpan designed the chips inside DSL modems that brought fast internet over ordinary phone lines.
lede: GlobeSpan began as a research group inside AT&T Paradyne and became its own company when Lucent sold Paradyne in 1996. The Red Bank, New Jersey company designed chip sets for DSL, the technology that pushed fast internet over the copper phone lines already in people's homes. By its 1999 IPO it had shipped more than one million DSL chip sets to makers such as Cisco, NEC and Westell. Phone companies were racing cable to sell broadband, and GlobeSpan's chips powered the phone side.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Paradyne
sections.body: GlobeSpan was formed as an independent company in July 1996 as part of Lucent's divestiture of AT&T Paradyne, and it began operations that August. Before that, its business ran as Paradyne's Advanced Transmission Technologies group. Texas Pacific Group was a key backer, and its partner James Coulter sat on the board. The company sold chip sets to the equipment makers who built DSL modems and phone-company gear. Its pitch was long experience with DSL and an active seat in setting its standards.

sections.heading: Merger After Merger
sections.body: GlobeSpan priced at $15 a share in June 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. Broadband demand pushed its stock up during the boom, then the telecom crash cut it down. In December 2001, GlobeSpan merged with the British chip company Virata and took the name GlobespanVirata. In early 2004, Conexant Systems bought GlobespanVirata in a stock deal, and the company deregistered its shares in March 2004.

dek: Informatica moved and cleaned data between a company's systems so its reports and warehouses told the truth.
lede: Informatica went public, was bought out, went public again, and was then sold to Salesforce. The first IPO came in April 1999. Back then the Palo Alto company sold software for data warehouses: tools that pulled numbers out of sales, finance and supply systems, cleaned them up and loaded them into one place for analysis. Every big company was building a warehouse, and most were writing that plumbing by hand. Informatica offered to sell it off the shelf.

sections.heading: Dhillon and Nesamoney
sections.body: Informatica was incorporated in California in February 1993. Gaurav Dhillon was CEO and Diaz Nesamoney was president when it filed. The two built the company around what the industry calls ETL: extract, transform and load. A retailer could pull orders from one database and customers from another, match them, and load the result into a warehouse on a schedule. The bet was that data integration would grow into its own market, separate from the databases themselves.

sections.heading: Three Lives on Wall Street
sections.body: Informatica priced at $16 a share in April 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as INFA. It survived the dot-com crash and grew into a large data management company. In 2015, Permira and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board took it private for $48.75 a share in cash. Informatica returned to the public market in October 2021 on the New York Stock Exchange. In 2025, Salesforce bought it for about $8 billion.

cover.theme: shelves of a great library (organized data)

tagline: Two Brothers and the Cable Modem
dek: Terayon built cable modem systems that turned TV cable networks into fast internet lines.
lede: Terayon was run by two brothers: Zaki Rakib was CEO and CFO, and Shlomo Rakib was chairman, president and chief technical officer. The Santa Clara company built cable modem systems that let cable TV operators sell internet service over the coaxial cable already wired into homes. Its S-CDMA technology was meant to handle the noisy, shared lines of real cable networks. In August 1998, broadband at home was new, and cable and phone companies were racing to sell it.

sections.heading: A Noisy Line, Tamed
sections.body: Terayon was incorporated in California in January 1993. It began shipping products commercially in June 1997 and only shipped in volume from early 1998. The Rakib brothers bet on S-CDMA, a way of sending data that held up on the noisy upstream path of old cable systems. Customers included Shaw Communications and TCA Cable. The risk was standards. The cable industry was settling on a common modem standard called DOCSIS, and Terayon's own technology sat outside it.

sections.heading: From Boom to a Buck Eighty
sections.body: Terayon priced at $13 a share in August 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as TERN. Cable broadband made it one of the hot stocks of the boom, and it spent heavily on acquisitions. The bust and the shift to DOCSIS left it struggling. Terayon moved into digital video gear for cable operators. In April 2007, Motorola agreed to buy the company for $1.80 a share in cash, and Terayon deregistered its stock in July 2007.

cover.theme: rays of sunlight through a window (Terayon)

dek: Syntel wrote and maintained software for big American companies, using engineering teams in the US and India.
lede: Syntel was founded by a married couple, and at its 1997 IPO they still owned almost all of it. Bharat Desai and Neerja Sethi started the company in 1980 in Troy, Michigan. Syntel built and maintained software for Fortune 1000 companies in banking, manufacturing, retail and transportation. Much of the work happened at its Global Development Center in Mumbai. The Year 2000 bug was on every CIO's mind, and companies needed programmers to fix old code before the deadline.

sections.heading: A Couple and a Time Zone
sections.body: Desai earned an MBA at the University of Michigan and an engineering degree at IIT Bombay. He became Syntel's president and CEO at its formation in 1980. Sethi ran corporate affairs. The model was a blend of staff at client sites in the US and teams in India working while America slept. Syntel was expanding its Mumbai center and opening a new one in Chennai when it filed. The bet was that clients would accept distance for lower cost and around-the-clock work.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars to Forty-One
sections.body: Syntel priced at $11 a share in August 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as SYNT. It came through the Y2K rush and the dot-com bust and kept growing as Indian IT outsourcing became mainstream. Desai and Sethi remained major owners for two decades. In 2018 the French IT company Atos agreed to buy Syntel for $41 a share in cash. The deal closed in October 2018, and Syntel's stock left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: the Trojan horse entering Troy (Troy, Michigan)
cover.artwork: The Trojan Horse Being Dragged into the City of Troy

dek: Marchex sold search ads for merchants, then built software that analyzes the phone calls those ads produce.
lede: Marchex was barely a year old when it went public. Its five founding officers, led by Russell Horowitz, had already built and sold one internet company: Go2Net, which merged into InfoSpace in 2000. They formed Marchex in Seattle in January 2003, put up the first money themselves, and bought two search marketing firms that same year. By its March 2004 IPO, Google's own offering was months away, and paid search ads were the hottest part of the web.

sections.heading: Buying Its Way In
sections.body: Marchex grew by acquisition from day one. It bought Enhance Interactive, formerly ah-ha.com, in February 2003 and TrafficLeader in October 2003. Both helped merchants buy and manage search ads and pay-per-click listings. The founders still owned 71 percent of the company in late 2003. Horowitz had been chairman, CEO and CFO of Go2Net. The bet was that a team that had already ridden one internet wave could buy small search firms cheaply and stitch them together.

sections.heading: From Clicks to Calls
sections.body: Marchex priced at $6.50 a share on March 31, 2004, and listed on Nasdaq as MCHX. It kept buying, including a large portfolio of web domain names. Over time it moved away from search ads toward call analytics, software that listens to and scores the sales calls that ads bring in. In 2026 it agreed to buy Archenia, Inc. Marchex is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: an allegory of the month of March (Marchex)

dek: Amkor packaged and tested chips for semiconductor companies that did not want to run their own factories.
lede: When Amkor went public in 1998, it called itself the world's largest independent provider of chip packaging and test services. Most of its work happened in Korean factories owned by a separate company, Anam, run by its CEO's family. James Kim had founded Amkor's predecessor in 1968. Chip companies designed the silicon. Amkor wrapped each chip in a protective package, wired it to the outside world and tested it. Asia was in a financial crisis, and Korea was hit hard.

sections.heading: A Family Business in Two Countries
sections.body: James Kim founded Amkor Electronics in 1968 and served as its chairman from 1970. His father, H. S. Kim, had founded Anam Industrial in Korea in 1956. The two companies worked hand in hand. In 1996 and 1997, most of Amkor's revenue came from packaging done in four Anam factories in Korea, with Amkor running three more plants in the Philippines. The bet was that chipmakers would hand off packaging and testing to a specialist, the same way many already handed off manufacturing.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars a Share
sections.body: Amkor priced its IPO at $11 a share on May 1, 1998, alongside an offering of convertible notes, and listed on Nasdaq as AMKR. Over the following years it bought the Anam factories it had relied on. It grew into one of the biggest outsourced chip packaging companies in the world, with plants across Asia. Its headquarters moved to Arizona. Amkor is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a pair of carp in Korean ink (Amkor's Korean roots)

fate: Taken private by a Tencent-led group, 2020
dek: Bitauto let Chinese car buyers research new cars online and gave dealers software to reach them.
lede: Bitauto went public just as China became the world's biggest car market. The Beijing company ran bitauto.com, a website where Chinese families researched new cars, and Easypass, software that let dealers post prices and inventory online. Its Easypass subscribers grew from 981 dealers in 2007 to 2,783 by September 2010. Automakers paid it for digital ads. In November 2010, investors were eager for Chinese internet stocks, and Bitauto rode that demand to the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: Dealers on the Internet
sections.body: Bin Li and Weihai Qu controlled Bitauto's main operating companies, one formed in 2002 and one in 2005. Li later founded the electric carmaker NIO. Bitauto had three businesses: the consumer website, the Easypass platform for dealers, and digital marketing for automakers. The bet was that tens of millions of first-time Chinese car buyers would start their search online, and that dealers would pay to meet them there. Bitauto planned custom Easypass editions for dealer groups and automakers.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and Tencent
sections.body: Bitauto sold 10.6 million American depositary shares at $12 each in November 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as BITA. It sold more shares in 2013. Tencent and JD.com later became major shareholders, and Bitauto added an auto finance business. In 2020, a buyer group led by Tencent took the company private. Bitauto's shares came off the New York Stock Exchange in November 2020.

cover.theme: a grand triumphal car (cars and showrooms)
cover.artwork: The Triumphal Car of Prince Hendrik of Orange

dek: Galaxy Digital offered trading, lending, asset management and data centers for crypto and AI customers.
lede: Galaxy Digital had been public for years before this offering, just not in the United States. Michael Novogratz's crypto firm traded in Toronto. In May 2025 it moved its home listing to Nasdaq under the ticker GLXY, and two weeks later it sold $600.4 million of stock to American investors. Galaxy traded and lent digital assets, managed funds, and was building data centers to rent to AI companies. Bitcoin was near record highs, and Washington had turned friendly to crypto.

sections.heading: A Macro Trader Goes Digital
sections.body: Novogratz founded Galaxy Digital in 2018 and runs it as CEO. He had been a well known macro investor before he turned to crypto. Galaxy built a business that looked like a small investment bank for digital assets: trading desks, lending, asset management and advice on deals. It also mined bitcoin, then began turning its Texas mining site into data centers for AI computing. The bet was that crypto would become part of mainstream finance, with Galaxy as a trusted firm in the middle.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: Galaxy's Class A shares began trading on Nasdaq in May 2025, while also staying listed in Toronto. On May 29, 2025, the stock closed at $19.60. The next day Galaxy priced an offering at $19.00 a share, raising $600.4 million in total, part for the company and part for selling stockholders. Novogratz kept a large economic interest through Galaxy's operating partnership. Galaxy is still public on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Urania, muse of astronomy, among the stars (Galaxy)
cover.artwork: Urania, The Muse of Astronomy, from The Nine Muses

fate: Taken private by a Chinese investor group, 2015 (about $1.9B)
tagline: The Legend of Mir Goes Solo
dek: Shanda Games ran online fantasy worlds that Chinese players logged into for years, starting with Legend of Mir II.
lede: The biggest American IPO of 2009 came from a company that built online worlds of swords and sorcery. Shanda Games raised about $1 billion in September, in a year when few companies dared to go public at all. Its parent, Shanda Interactive, had grown into a Shanghai giant on Legend of Mir II, a fantasy game licensed from Korea's Actoz Soft. Now the games arm would trade on its own, with its own ticker: GAME.

sections.heading: A Game Licensed From Korea
sections.body: Shanda Interactive launched Legend of Mir II in China in November 2001, under a license from Actoz Soft. It followed with Woool, its own game, in October 2003. The parent went public in May 2004 and then spread into other kinds of entertainment. In July 2008 it moved the game business into a separate company, Shanda Games. The bet was simple: investors would pay more for a pure game maker than for a sprawling holding company.

sections.heading: A $1 Billion Debut, Then a Slide
sections.body: Shanda Games priced at $12.50 per ADS and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The first day went badly. The stock opened at $10.75, about 14 percent under the offer, and it never found firm footing. In April 2015 a Chinese buyer group agreed to take the company private at $7.10 per ADS, a deal worth about $1.9 billion. It closed in November 2015, and Shanda Games left Nasdaq.

dek: Sogou let Chinese phone users search the web and type Chinese faster, with a search engine and a keyboard app.
lede: Sogou's name means "search dog," and its most loved product was the one people typed with. The Beijing company ran the second largest search engine in China by mobile queries, according to iResearch. Its Sogou Input Method turned typed pinyin into Chinese characters on phones and computers. When it filed in 2017, Sogou was a child of the portal Sohu, with Tencent as a major owner, and it was chasing Baidu in the toughest race on the Chinese internet.

sections.heading: Sohu's Spinoff, Tencent's Partner
sections.body: Sogou began in 2004 as the search engine inside Sohu, one of China's first big web portals. Tencent invested in 2013 and folded its own search service, Soso, into Sogou. That deal put Sogou search inside Tencent's apps, the busiest doors on the Chinese internet. The company also bet on artificial intelligence, from voice typing to machine translation. After the IPO, Sohu, Tencent and management together held about 97.1 percent of the votes.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Tencent
sections.body: Sogou priced at $13 per ADS and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on November 9, 2017, under the symbol SOGO. The offering raised about $585 million. The shares soon slid well below the offer price. In July 2020 Tencent proposed to buy the rest of the company for $9 per ADS. The deal, valued at about $3.5 billion, closed in September 2021, and Sogou became a wholly owned unit of Tencent.

cover.theme: a dog in a landscape (the 'search dog')

dek: LG.Philips LCD made the thin glass panels inside the monitors, laptops and TVs that replaced bulky tube screens.
lede: In 2003, about one in five large flat panels sold worldwide came out of LG.Philips LCD. The Korean maker held roughly 22 percent of the market by revenue, according to DisplaySearch, and ran five fabs in Gumi, Korea. Its panels went into computer monitors, notebooks and a fast-growing crop of flat televisions. In July 2004 it listed in New York and Seoul at the same time, betting that the world was ready to throw out its tube TVs.

sections.heading: A Korean-Dutch Marriage
sections.body: LG.Philips LCD was formed in September 1999 as a 50-50 joint venture between LG Electronics and Philips of the Netherlands. The pairing joined a Korean manufacturer with a European electronics giant. The bet was scale. LCD panels are cut from huge sheets of glass, and each new generation of fab cuts bigger sheets and cheaper screens. The company that built the next fab first could sell panels to the whole industry.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars in Two Markets
sections.body: The ADSs priced at $15 each, the bottom of the range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol LPL. The shares also listed on the Korea Stock Exchange. The deal was the first concurrent dual-listed IPO by a Korean company. Philips sold down its stake over the following years, and in 2008 the company changed its name to LG Display. It still trades in New York under LPL.

dek: Syniverse passed calls, texts and roaming bills between rival mobile carriers, so phones worked across networks.
lede: When a text crossed from one mobile carrier to another, a company in Tampa was often working in between. Syniverse sat between the operators, linking their networks, routing their messages and sorting out roaming charges. Almost no phone user had heard of it. In February 2005 it went public anyway, a plumbing company for the wireless age, owned by managers and the buyout firm GTCR.

sections.heading: Born Inside GTE
sections.body: The business began in 1987 as GTE Telecommunication Services, a unit of the phone company GTE. When GTE and Bell Atlantic merged in 2000 to form Verizon, it became a Verizon subsidiary. In February 2002 a group of managers and investors led by GTCR bought it, and in 2004 it took the name Syniverse. The bet was that every carrier would rather pay one neutral party than wire itself to every rival.

sections.heading: From the Big Board to Carlyle
sections.body: Syniverse sold 17.6 million shares at $16 each and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol SVR. Lehman Brothers and Goldman Sachs led the offering. Six years later the Carlyle Group agreed to buy the company for $31 a share in cash, a deal valued at about $2.6 billion. It closed in January 2011. Syniverse left the exchange and has stayed private, still based in Tampa.

cover.artwork: The Courier Kantan dreaming of Himself as a Daimyo (Hikyaku Kantan: yume no daimyo), no. 8 from a series of 12 prints depicting parodies of plays

dek: Uxin let Chinese buyers find, finance and buy secondhand cars online, from dealers and from each other.
lede: Kun Dai launched one of China's first online used-car sites, CarResume.com, in 2005. Six years later he founded Uxin in Beijing to take the idea much further. By its 2018 filing, Uxin ran online markets where consumers and dealers bought secondhand cars, with loans arranged on the same platform. China had become a nation of new drivers, and millions of their cars would one day need second owners.

sections.heading: From CarResume to Uxin
sections.body: Dai spent 2007 to 2011 at BitAuto, a listed car information company, rising to vice president. Then he left to build Uxin. The company ran two businesses: a consumer site for buying used cars, and an online auction where dealers traded cars with each other. The bet was trust. In a market full of hidden accident histories, a platform that inspected cars and arranged loans could win nervous buyers.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars and a Long Road
sections.body: Uxin priced at $9 per ADS in June 2018 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol UXIN. The stock soon fell far below the offer. Uxin sold its dealer auction business and shifted to selling cars from its own large used-car superstores. In 2025 it signed up $50 million in new funding from NIO Capital and a partner. Uxin still trades on Nasdaq.

fate: Taken private by founder Chi Yufeng, 2015 (about $1B)
tagline: A Game Engine Built in Beijing
dek: Perfect World built its own 3D game engine and online fantasy games, then sold them in China and abroad.
lede: Perfect World spent nearly two years building before it earned any revenue. Its predecessor started in Beijing in March 2004 and used that time to write a home-grown 3D game engine and a first online role-playing game, also called Perfect World. Many Chinese game companies licensed their hits from Korean studios. Perfect World wrote its own. In the first quarter of 2007 it earned 40 million yuan, and that July it brought the bet to Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Writing the Engine First
sections.body: From its founding through 2005, the company was still building its engine, its development platform and its first game. Owning that technology let the studio turn out new titles faster. Players paid nothing to start and bought virtual items inside the games. By 2007 it was also licensing its games to operators overseas, including in Japan and Taiwan. Founder Michael Yufeng Chi, known in China as Chi Yufeng, was chairman and chief executive.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then Home
sections.body: Perfect World sold 11.8 million ADSs at $16 each and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market under the symbol PWRD. The stock hit a record high of $50.49 in 2009. By late 2014 it was back near its offer price. On the last day of that year, Chi offered to buy out public holders. His company took Perfect World private in 2015 in a deal worth about $1 billion, and it left Nasdaq that summer.

cover.theme: a garden of paradise (a perfect world)

fate: Taken private by Blackstone and Vista Equity Partners, 2025 (about $8.4B)
tagline: The Spreadsheet That Learned to Manage
dek: Smartsheet turned the familiar spreadsheet grid into a shared place to plan projects and track work.
lede: Smartsheet's big idea looked like something every office already had: rows and columns. The Bellevue, Washington company took the spreadsheet grid and made it a place where teams planned projects, assigned tasks and tracked work together online. Customers paid by subscription, and use often started with one team before spreading through a company. When Smartsheet went public in April 2018, the stock jumped 30 percent on its first day.

sections.heading: A Grid Everyone Already Knew
sections.body: Brent Frei co-founded Smartsheet in 2005, after an earlier run building the business software company Onyx. Mark Mader joined as chief executive the next year. The bet was that people who already lived in spreadsheets would adopt a work tool that looked like one. Smartsheet piled Gantt charts, forms, reports and automation on top of the grid. Users never had to learn a new way to see their work.

sections.heading: A 30 Percent Pop, Then Private
sections.body: Smartsheet priced at $15 a share, above a raised range of $12 to $14, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol SMAR on April 27, 2018. The offering raised $175 million. The stock opened near $18.40 and closed its first day at $19.50. In January 2025 Blackstone and Vista Equity Partners took the company private for $56.50 a share, a deal valued at about $8.4 billion.

cover.theme: a grid of colored blocks (a spreadsheet)
cover.artwork: Lozenge Composition with Yellow, Black, Blue, Red, and Gray

tagline: A Social Network Behind the Firewall
dek: Jive gave big companies their own private social networks, where employees shared ideas and found each other's work.
lede: Before Slack, big companies paid Jive to make work feel more like Facebook. Its software gave employees profiles, discussion threads, blogs and shared documents inside a private network. Jive started in 2001 as a small software shop and later moved its headquarters to Palo Alto. By its December 2011 IPO, social networking was the hottest idea in tech, and Jive was the business version investors could buy.

sections.heading: From Forums to the Whole Office
sections.body: Co-founders Bill Lynch and Matt Tucker incorporated Jive in Delaware in February 2001. Its early products included online community software such as discussion forums. In 2007 the company launched the Jive Engage Platform and began selling it by subscription. The bet was that the tools people used to talk online at home could also fix how they worked together on the job. Customers used it inside their companies and on public sites.

sections.heading: A Fast Start, a Discount Exit
sections.body: Jive priced at $12 a share and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol JIVE. Shares soon ran into the mid-$20s. Growth slowed as Microsoft and newer chat tools crowded the market. In May 2017 ESW Capital agreed to buy Jive for $5.25 a share, or $462 million in cash, through its affiliate Wave Systems. The deal closed in June, and Jive joined ESW's Aurea software group.

tagline: From the i-opener to Intrusion Prevention
dek: Netpliance sold a simple web appliance called the i-opener, then rebuilt itself as TippingPoint, a network security company.
lede: An Austin startup with $25,716 in lifetime revenue raised $144 million from the public in March 2000. The company was Netpliance, and its product was the i-opener, a small device that put email and the web on a kitchen counter with no PC required. Customers paid a monthly fee for the service. Netpliance had been incorporated in January 1999 and began offering the i-opener service that November. It was a pure bet on the dot-com dream.

sections.heading: A Web Box for the Kitchen
