sections.body: Co-founders John McHale and Kent Savage built Netpliance around one idea: plenty of people wanted the internet but did not want a computer. The i-opener came with its own screen and keyboard and dialed in over a phone line. The company sold the hardware cheap and planned to earn its money from the service. Through 1999 it had lost $43.5 million while waiting for subscribers to arrive.

sections.heading: Reborn as TippingPoint
sections.body: Netpliance priced at $18 a share and listed on Nasdaq under the symbol NPLI. The dot-com crash began within weeks, and the i-opener business was soon shut down. The company kept its cash and its Austin base and changed course. As TippingPoint Technologies, it built hardware that blocked network attacks as they happened. In January 2005 3Com bought it for $47 a share in cash, about $430 million.

cover.theme: the edge of a great waterfall (a tipping point)
cover.artwork: Sunset, Horseshoe Fall - Niagara, No. 292 from the series "Niagara Falls"

dek: SouFun ran China's leading real estate website, where home buyers searched listings and developers paid to reach them.
lede: By page views and visitors, SouFun ran the leading real estate website in China in 2009, according to the research firm DCCI. Vincent Mo started it in Beijing in 1999, as a private housing market took shape in Chinese cities. Buyers came to search listings, read property news and compare new projects. Developers and agents paid to reach them. In September 2010 SouFun brought that market to the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: Listings for a New Market
sections.body: SouFun earned money from marketing services for property developers, listing fees from real estate agents and other paid services on its sites. It covered new homes and resales across many Chinese cities. Mo kept control as founder and executive chairman, while Richard Jiangong Dai ran the company as president and chief executive. The bet was that as Chinese families bought homes, the search for those homes would move online.

sections.heading: From SouFun to Fang
sections.body: SouFun priced its ADSs at $42.50 each and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol SFUN. The offering totaled about $125 million, including shares from selling holders. The company later pushed into running its own brokerage and changed its name to Fang Holdings. The stock lost most of its value over the following decade. Its shares were delisted from the NYSE in 2022.

dek: MACOM designs analog chips that move radio, microwave and fiber-optic signals through networks, radars and satellites.
lede: MACOM's roots reach back more than 60 years, to an engineering company called Microwave Associates. By the time it filed in 2012, the brand had passed through several corporate owners and landed in Lowell, Massachusetts. Its chips handled the high-frequency signals that cell towers, fiber links, radars and cable networks depend on. Smartphones and data traffic were exploding, and every new wireless bit had to pass through analog parts like these.

sections.heading: Bought Back From Cobham
sections.body: In March 2009 a new company bought the M/A-COM technology business and brand from Cobham, the British defense group. The buyers were led by John Ocampo, who became chairman, alongside Summit Partners. They added Mimix, a maker of gallium arsenide chips, in 2010 and the fiber-optic chip designer Optomai in 2011. The bet was that an independent MACOM, focused on analog parts, could grow faster than it had as a unit of a defense contractor.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars in Lowell
sections.body: M/A-COM Technology Solutions priced at $19 a share in March 2012 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol MTSI. The offering totaled $114 million. At that price, the shares going to Ocampo and his affiliates were worth about $497.8 million. The company later shortened its name to MACOM and kept buying chip businesses. It still trades on Nasdaq and is based in Lowell.

cover.artwork: Jove Casts His Thunderbolts at the Rebellious Giants

tagline: The Storage Startup Two Giants Wanted
dek: 3PAR built storage arrays that let big companies and web firms share disk space flexibly, like a utility.
lede: Three years after its IPO, 3PAR set off one of the loudest bidding wars in tech. Dell and HP traded offers for the Fremont, California storage maker through the late summer of 2010, and the price more than doubled. The prize was an idea 3PAR called utility storage: arrays that handed out disk space as it was needed, the way a power company hands out electricity. Cloud computing made that idea suddenly valuable.

sections.heading: Storage Sold Like Power
sections.body: 3PAR began operations in May 1999. Its co-founders, Jeffrey Price and Ashok Singhal, built the InServ Storage Server arrays, run by the InForm software suite, for large companies, service providers, government agencies and fast-growing web firms. The pitch was simplicity and efficiency. Customers could carve one shared pool of storage into many virtual pieces, instead of buying dedicated disks for every application.

sections.heading: From $14 to a Bidding War
sections.body: 3PAR sold 7.5 million shares at $14 each in November 2007 and listed on NYSE Arca under the symbol PAR. Goldman Sachs led the offering. In August 2010 Dell agreed to buy the company. HP jumped in with a higher bid, and the two companies raised their offers again and again. HP won at $33 a share in cash, about $2.35 billion, and closed the deal that September.

cover.artwork: Medieval Granary in the Roman Campagna

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2019 ($1.94B); sold to IBM, 2023
dek: Apptio showed chief information officers what their technology cost and where the money went, line by line.
lede: Every department in a big company had a system for its numbers except the one that ran the computers. Apptio set out to fix that. The Bellevue, Washington company sold software that pulled together data on servers, software licenses, cloud bills and staff, then showed chief information officers what each service cost. It called the field Technology Business Management. When Apptio filed in 2016, cloud spending was rising fast and getting harder to track.

sections.heading: Accounting for the CIO
sections.body: Sunny Gupta co-founded Apptio and became chief executive in October 2007. He had just sold his previous startup, iConclude, to Opsware. Apptio built a set of cloud applications for IT cost transparency, benchmarking, planning and a Bill of IT that charged costs back to business units. The bet was that technology chiefs wanted to run their departments like a business, with the same hard numbers a finance chief used.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then Vista
sections.body: Apptio priced at $16 a share in September 2016 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market under the symbol APTI. Two years later Vista Equity Partners agreed to buy it for $38 a share in cash, a deal valued at about $1.94 billion. Apptio left Nasdaq in January 2019. In 2023 Vista sold the company to IBM for about $4.6 billion, and Apptio became part of IBM's software business.

tagline: Factory Software From a Beach Town
dek: QAD sold MFG/PRO, software that ran planning, inventory and accounting for manufacturers in more than 70 countries.
lede: A software company in the beach town of Carpinteria, California ran the factory floors of Colgate-Palmolive, Johnson & Johnson and Philips. QAD sold MFG/PRO, an enterprise system that tied together manufacturing, distribution and finance. By April 1997 it had licensed the software at about 3,200 sites for 1,880 customers in over 70 countries. When it went public that August, enterprise software was booming as companies rushed to replace old systems before the year 2000.

sections.heading: A Founder and Her Husband
sections.body: Pamela Lopker founded QAD in 1979 and served as its president. Her husband, Karl Lopker, joined in 1981 and became chief executive; he had earlier founded Deckers Outdoor. The company incorporated as qad.inc in 1986 and became QAD Inc. in February 1997. The bet was focus. QAD built only for manufacturers, from Cargill and Unilever to St. Jude Medical, and sold the same software around the world.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars, Then Thoma Bravo
sections.body: QAD sold 5.75 million shares at $15 each in August 1997 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol QADI. After the offering, its directors and officers still owned about 71 percent of the company. QAD stayed public for 24 years and moved its software to the cloud. In November 2021 Thoma Bravo took it private for $87.50 a share, a deal worth about $2 billion.

tagline: Selling on eBay, Amazon and Everywhere
dek: ChannelAdvisor let retailers and brands list and sell their products on Amazon, eBay, Google and hundreds of other channels.
lede: ChannelAdvisor's chief executive wrote one of the most-read blogs about selling on eBay. Scot Wingo's eBay Strategies became a widely followed source of e-commerce data. His North Carolina company sold the tools behind that advice: software that pushed a retailer's products onto eBay, Amazon, Newegg, Google and Bing from one place. By its May 2013 filing, online marketplaces had become as important to many merchants as their own websites.

sections.heading: Born on eBay
sections.body: ChannelAdvisor began operations in July 2001, in the years when eBay was the main online marketplace for small sellers. Scot Wingo and his co-founders built software to manage listings, prices and orders across many sites at once. As Amazon opened its marketplace and search ads grew, the company followed its customers there. The bet was that merchants would sell everywhere, and needed one control panel to do it.

sections.heading: Fourteen Dollars to CommerceHub
sections.body: ChannelAdvisor sold 5.75 million shares at $14 each and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol ECOM, a fitting ticker for an e-commerce company. It grew as a subscription business serving retailers and brands. In 2022 CommerceHub, owned by private equity firms, agreed to buy it for $23.10 a share in cash. The deal, worth about $680 million, closed that November and ChannelAdvisor left the NYSE.

tagline: The Virus Clinic in Your Browser
dek: McAfee.com let home users scan and repair their PCs for viruses through a website, paying a yearly subscription.
lede: McAfee.com started charging for its online virus clinic on September 2, 1999. By late November it had more than 135,000 paid subscribers. The idea was that a website could guard your computer, scanning it for viruses and tuning it up through a browser instead of a box of disks. Network Associates owned the business and the McAfee name, and in December 1999 it sold a slice to a public hungry for anything ending in .com.

sections.heading: A Spinoff From Network Associates
sections.body: Network Associates, the security software maker, formed McAfee.com as a subsidiary in December 1998. On January 1, 1999 it moved its consumer online business into the new company. McAfee.com offered the McAfee Clinic, VirusScan and a PC tune-up called Oil Change, and it earned money from subscriptions, banner ads and sponsorships. The bet was that consumers would rent their security online year after year, long before most software worked that way.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars, Then Home Again
sections.body: McAfee.com sold 6.25 million Class A shares at $12 each and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol MCAF. Network Associates kept control of the company. In March 2002 the parent launched an exchange offer to buy the shares it did not own. The deal closed later that year, McAfee.com stopped reporting as a public company in September 2002, and its business folded back into the parent.

cover.artwork: The Battle around the Shield and Lance

tagline: Live Voices on the Early Web
dek: Mpath, later HearMe, ran live online communities where people played games and talked by voice over the internet.
lede: In 1999 more than 3 million people had signed up to play games and talk live on Mpath's websites. Its Mplayer.com let gamers meet online, and HearMe.com let people speak to each other over the internet with voice and music. Most of the web was still pages you read alone. Mpath was betting on real-time crowds, and in April 1999 it brought that bet to Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Mplayer and a Microphone
sections.body: Mpath Interactive began operations in January 1995 in the Bay Area, with Brian Apgar as founder. It built technology that let thousands of users share one live session through graphics, text and sound. Mpath ran its own sites and licensed the technology to partners including Yahoo!, Excite, Intel and Sega. By March 1999 visitors spent an average of more than 300 minutes a month on its communities.

sections.heading: Eighteen Dollars to Liquidation
sections.body: Mpath priced at $18 a share and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol MPTH. Soon after, it renamed itself HearMe after its voice service. The dot-com crash cut off advertising and investor money. In 2001 the board proposed a plan of liquidation and dissolution, including the sale of substantially all of HearMe's assets. Shareholders met to vote in September 2001, and the company wound down.

tagline: The Home Phone Without the Phone Bill
dek: Ooma sold a small device that gave homes and small businesses phone service over the internet, with low monthly costs.
lede: Ooma's pitch to American households fit in a small box: stop paying the phone company for a landline. Its Ooma Telo plugged into a home internet connection and turned it into phone service with HD voice and extra features. Readers of a leading consumer research magazine ranked it the number one home phone service for satisfaction and value. When it filed in 2015, Ooma was also selling the same idea to small businesses.

sections.heading: A Box Against the Landline
sections.body: Ooma was founded in late 2003 to build new kinds of home communications. It launched its first device, the Ooma Hub, in the U.S. in 2007. Customers bought the hardware once and paid little or nothing each month for basic calling. Ooma made money from premium features and its business service. Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder and early Facebook president, sat on its board.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars on the NYSE
sections.body: Ooma priced at $13 a share in July 2015 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol OOMA. Over the next decade it kept adding products, from home security sensors to phone systems for small businesses. Customers still bought a device once and paid for premium features as they went. Ooma stayed independent. It still trades on the NYSE and is based in Sunnyvale, California.

cover.theme: two people in conversation (a phone call)

tagline: Live From the Middle of the Ocean
dek: Quokka Sports turned live data from races, climbs and sailing voyages into interactive sports coverage online.
lede: Quokka Sports put cameras and sensors on yachts racing around the world and streamed the story to the web. It covered the Whitbread and America's Cup sailing races, CART car racing, desert ultramarathons and mountain climbs. A small Australian software team had moved to San Francisco to build what it called digital sports entertainment. By July 1999 the dot-com market was ready to buy the dream that fans would follow sports live, online.

sections.heading: From Ozware to Quokka
sections.body: Alan Ramadan ran an Australian software developer called Ozware Development from 1990. In August 1996 he adopted a new business model and incorporated in Delaware as Quokka Productions, renaming it Quokka Sports a month later. The company named itself after a small Australian marsupial. The bet was that sports full of data, like sailing and car racing, made better interactive shows than television could deliver.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and a Fast Fall
sections.body: Quokka sold 5 million shares at $12 each in July 1999 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol QKKA. It kept adding events and channels, and in 2000 it agreed to buy Golf.com for about 3.9 million Quokka shares. Then online advertising dried up as the dot-com bubble burst, and investors stopped funding money-losing media companies. Quokka filed for bankruptcy in April 2001, and its sites went dark.

dek: Unica sold software that let marketers plan, target and measure their campaigns, from direct mail to email.
lede: Capital One, Comcast, Nordstrom and Vodafone all ran marketing campaigns on software from a company in Waltham, Massachusetts. Unica sold what it called enterprise marketing management: tools to pick the right customers, send the right offer and measure what came back. About 300 companies used it by 2005. Marketing was shifting from gut feel to data, and Unica wanted to be the system of record for that change.

sections.heading: Consulting to Pay for Code
sections.body: Unica was incorporated in December 1992, and co-founder Yuchun Lee became its chief executive. In its early years the company took on consulting work to fund development of data-mining and analytics software. That work grew into the Affinium suite for campaign management, marketing resource management and web analytics. The bet was that marketers would want the same rigor finance teams had, with every dollar traced to a result.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars, Then IBM
sections.body: Unica priced at $10 a share in August 2005 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol UNCA. Lee owned about 27.8 percent of the stock after the offering. Five years later IBM agreed to buy Unica for $21 a share in cash, about $480 million. The deal closed in October 2010, and Unica became part of IBM's software group.

dek: TubeMogul gave brands self-serve software to buy, place and measure video ads across websites, apps and TV.
lede: TubeMogul began by counting views. Its first tools sent online videos out to many sites and tracked how they performed. That data showed where audiences watched, and advertisers wanted to follow them. By its July 2014 IPO the Emeryville, California company sold software that let brands buy video ads automatically, in real time, across websites, apps and connected TVs, while blocking fraud and ugly placements.

sections.heading: From View Counts to Ad Buying
sections.body: Brett Wilson and John Hughes started TubeMogul, which was incorporated in March 2007. Wilson became chief executive and Hughes ran products. The company rebuilt itself as a buying platform for brands and agencies. Advertisers could run campaigns themselves through Platform Direct, or hand their goals to TubeMogul's team through Platform Services. The bet was that video ads would be bought by software, the way search ads already were.

sections.heading: Seven Dollars to Adobe
sections.body: TubeMogul priced at $7 a share in July 2014 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol TUBE. It kept its headquarters in Emeryville and kept growing its platform. In November 2016 Adobe agreed to buy TubeMogul for $14 a share in cash, about $540 million, to add video ad buying to its marketing tools. The deal closed in December 2016, and the business became part of Adobe Advertising Cloud.

cover.theme: an actor greeting the theater audience (video reaching viewers)
cover.artwork: The Actor Nakamura Kumetaro II Greeting the Audience on His Arrival from Osaka at the Nakamura Theater in the Eleventh Month, 1790

dek: MMC Networks designed network processors, programmable chips that let switch and router makers move data at full speed.
lede: MMC Networks explained itself to investors with a time-lapse photo of a busy freeway interchange at night. Its chips were the interchange. The Sunnyvale company designed network processors, programmable chips that moved packets through switches and routers at wire speed. By its October 1997 IPO it had more than 35 design wins with 27 equipment makers, including Cisco, NEC, Fujitsu and Toshiba. Internet traffic was surging, and every box on the network needed faster silicon.

sections.heading: Programmable Silicon for Networks
sections.body: MMC Networks was incorporated in California in September 1992 and did not ship products in volume until late 1995. It left chip manufacturing to outside foundries and spent its money on design. The bet was programmability. Equipment makers could load their own software onto MMC's processors and reach the market faster than if they built custom chips. Kleiner Perkins, Institutional Venture Partners and U.S. Venture Partners backed the company.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars to $4.5 Billion
sections.body: MMC Networks priced at $11 a share and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol MMCN, with Prabhat Dubey as chief executive. Network processors became one of the hottest corners of the chip business during the telecom boom. In 2000 Applied Micro Circuits agreed to buy MMC in a stock deal valued at about $4.5 billion. It closed that October, and MMC stopped reporting as a public company.

cover.artwork: Wakasa Province: Fishing Boat Netting Flatfish (Wakasa, gyosen karei ami), from the series "Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces (Rokujuyoshu meisho zue)"

fate: Taken private by a Hellman & Friedman group, 2019 (about $11B)
dek: Ultimate Software sold UltiPro, payroll and HR software that let mid-sized companies pay and manage their workers.
lede: Ultimate Software sold software about people, and it lived by a slogan to match: People First. Its UltiPro product handled payroll, benefits and human resources records for mid-sized employers. The South Florida company began in 1990 as a partnership and listed on Nasdaq in June 1998 at $10 a share. Two decades later, an investor group paid about $11 billion for it, one of the biggest software buyouts on record.

sections.heading: From Partnership to UltiPro
sections.body: Scott Scherr organized The Ultimate Software Group as a Florida limited partnership in August 1990. The company incorporated in April 1996 to take over the partnership's business. Scherr served as chairman, president and chief executive, with Alan Goldstein, a medical doctor, as executive vice president and technology chief. The bet was that mid-sized employers wanted one system for payroll and HR instead of a patchwork of vendors and paper files.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars to $11 Billion
sections.body: Ultimate sold 3.25 million shares at $10 each and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol ULTI. It later moved UltiPro to the cloud and sold it by subscription, and the stock climbed for years. In May 2019 an investor group led by Hellman & Friedman bought the company for $331.50 a share in cash, about $11 billion. In 2020 it merged with Kronos to form UKG.

cover.theme: a worker high on a skyscraper (people at work)
cover.artwork: Derrick Worker on the Empire State Building

tagline: An Auction House Open Every Day
dek: uBid ran live online auctions where shoppers bid on surplus and refurbished computers, electronics and other goods.
lede: uBid called itself a live internet auction house, and it closed a sale every day of the week. Businesses and consumers bid against each other for excess, refurbished and limited merchandise, mostly computers and electronics. The company was barely a year old, a spinoff of the catalog seller Creative Computers. In December 1998, a few months after eBay's public debut, uBid offered its own shares to a market hungry for online auctions.

sections.heading: A Catalog Seller Goes Live
sections.body: Creative Computers began funding uBid in April 1997. The company incorporated that September and ran its first internet auctions in December 1997, from Elk Grove Village, Illinois. uBid sold the goods itself, from brands such as Sony, Toshiba and Uniden. The bet was that bargain hunters would enjoy the thrill of bidding, and that suppliers would welcome a quick way to clear surplus stock without slashing prices in stores.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars, Then CMGI
sections.body: uBid sold 1.58 million shares at $15 each and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol UBID. Creative Computers kept most of the stock and handed its remaining stake to its own shareholders in 1999. In 2000 the internet holding company CMGI bought uBid, and uBid stopped reporting as a public company that spring. The brand changed hands several more times in the years that followed.

fate: Still public as ASE Technology Holding (NYSE: ASX)
tagline: Wrapping the World's Chips in Kaohsiung
dek: ASE packaged and tested chips for semiconductor companies around the world, from factories in Taiwan and across Asia.
lede: A chip that leaves the fab still has work ahead. Someone has to cut it, seal it in a protective package, wire it to the outside world and test that it works. Advanced Semiconductor Engineering did that job for chip companies around the globe from its base in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Already listed in Taipei, it sold American depositary shares on the New York Stock Exchange in September 2000, as the chip boom peaked.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and a Back End
sections.body: Brothers Jason C.S. Chang and Richard H.P. Chang led ASE as chairman and as vice chairman and chief executive. The company described itself as one of the world's largest independent providers of chip packaging. Its subsidiary ASE Test, quoted on Nasdaq since 1996, ran testing plants in Taiwan, the United States, Hong Kong and Singapore. The bet was that chip companies would hand off more of the back end of manufacturing to specialists.

sections.heading: Seven Dollars, Then a Merger
sections.body: ASE sold 20 million ADSs at $7 each and listed them on the NYSE under the symbol ASX. Just before pricing, its Taipei shares had closed at the equivalent of $7.62 per ADS. ASE kept growing through acquisitions. In 2018 it combined with its rival Siliconware Precision Industries under a new holding company, ASE Technology Holding. That company still trades on the NYSE under ASX.

cover.theme: glass workers at a bench (precise handwork)

fate: Merged with HomeAdvisor to form ANGI Homeservices, 2017
dek: Angie's List sold memberships that let homeowners read trusted reviews of plumbers, roofers, doctors and other local services.
lede: Angie's List charged people to read reviews while Yelp gave them away. The Indianapolis company had more than 1 million paid memberships by its November 2011 IPO. Members rated local plumbers, roofers, dentists and auto shops, and only members could read the results. Highly rated providers could pay to offer members discounts. The pitch was trust: real names on every review, and no company could buy a better grade.

sections.heading: Door to Door for Members
sections.body: Bill Oesterle and Angie Hicks started the business in 1995. Hicks went door to door signing up the first members and became the company's spokeswoman, her name on every ad. It was organized in Indiana as Brownstone Publishing and took the name Angie's List in 2010. The bet was that homeowners would pay for advice on what the company called high cost of failure services, where one bad contractor costs thousands.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then IAC
sections.body: Angie's List sold 8.8 million shares at $13 each and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market under the symbol ANGI. It spent heavily on advertising to win members and lost money for years. In 2016 it opened up a free tier and dropped its paywall. In 2017 it merged with IAC's HomeAdvisor to form ANGI Homeservices, which kept the ANGI ticker. The combined business now runs under the Angi name.

tagline: A Red Koi and a Web Empire
dek: divine interVentures backed and ran a network of business internet startups, then tried to remake itself as a software company.
lede: Divine interVentures put a red Japanese koi on the cover of its prospectus and a family of startups behind it. Andrew "Flip" Filipowski, who had built Platinum Technology before Computer Associates bought it, founded the Chicago-area company in May 1999. Within a year it had 265 employees and stakes in a web of business-to-business internet companies. In July 2000 it asked the public for money to feed them all, just as the dot-com market began to crack.

sections.heading: Platinum Veterans Build a Family
sections.body: Filipowski brought Platinum colleagues Michael Cullinane and Paul Humenansky with him as top executives. They called their model the divine family. Associated companies were grouped as infrastructure service providers, market makers and other businesses, and they shared services, staff and customers. Divine took stakes in each one. The bet was that a network of linked startups, run by experienced operators, would grow faster together than any could alone.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars to Bankruptcy
sections.body: Divine sold 14.3 million Class A shares at $9 each in July 2000 and listed on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol DVIN. The stock sank as the dot-com bust wiped out many of its associated companies. The company shortened its name to divine and bought struggling software and services firms, trying to rebuild as an enterprise technology company. It filed for bankruptcy in February 2003 and sold off its pieces.

tagline: The Market Maker Who Coded First
dek: Interactive Brokers gave traders cheap, automated access to more than 60 exchanges around the world.
lede: Interactive Brokers sold its IPO the way it ran its business: by machine. In May 2007 the Greenwich, Connecticut firm skipped the usual bank-run book and held an online auction, where anyone could bid and every winner paid the same price. The auction settled at $30.01 a share and raised $1.2 billion. Even then, the public bought only about 10 percent of the business. Founder Thomas Peterffy and his team kept the rest.

sections.heading: A Lone Trader on the Amex
sections.body: Thomas Peterffy started in 1977 as a lone market maker on the American Stock Exchange. His market making firm, Timber Hill, formed in 1982 and leaned on computers to price trades. A brokerage arm, Interactive Brokers, followed and sold the same machinery to outside traders. By the time it filed, the company called itself an automated global electronic market maker and broker. It was a member of more than 60 electronic exchanges and trading venues, handling stocks, futures and foreign exchange.

sections.heading: Forty Million Shares by Auction
sections.body: The OpenIPO auction, run by W.R. Hambrecht + Co., closed in early May 2007. Interactive Brokers sold 40 million shares at $30.01 each and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as IBKR. The new public company owned about 10 percent of IBG LLC, the holding company for the whole business. Peterffy and the other insiders held the other 90 percent through a holding company of their own. Interactive Brokers still trades on Nasdaq under IBKR.

tagline: Cash Back for the Grocery Run
dek: Ibotta paid shoppers cash back on groceries and everyday buys, and brands paid only when a sale happened.
lede: By the spring of 2024, Ibotta had handed American shoppers more than $1.8 billion in cash back on everyday purchases. The Denver company ran a network that pushed digital offers from consumer brands to over 200 million people. Some came through its own rewards app. Many more came through retailers like Walmart and Dollar General, which ran Ibotta offers inside their own loyalty programs. Brands paid Ibotta only when a promotion turned into a sale.

sections.heading: Zing Enterprises Becomes Ibotta
sections.body: Bryan Leach incorporated the company in 2011 as Zing Enterprises and renamed it Ibotta in 2012. The idea was simple. Brands that make groceries and household goods spend heavily on promotions they cannot measure. Ibotta offered them a deal tied to results: it got paid only when a shopper bought the item. Over time it built the Ibotta Performance Network, which sent one brand offer to Ibotta's own app and to retailer apps at the same moment.

sections.heading: A Walmart-Powered Debut
sections.body: Ibotta priced its IPO at $88 a share in April 2024 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as IBTA. The offering raised about $197.8 million for the company, and some existing holders sold shares too. Leach kept about 70 percent of the voting power through high-vote Class B stock. The Walmart deal sat at the center of the pitch, since Walmart ran Ibotta's offers under its own name. Ibotta still trades on the NYSE as IBTA.

cover.theme: a girl with a shopping basket (everyday purchases)

fate: Bought out by NBC and liquidated, 2001 ($2.19 a share)
dek: NBCi bundled Snap, Xoom.com and NBC's websites into one portal, promoted by a national TV network.
lede: NBCi sold new stock at $81.375 a share in February 2000, three months after it was born. The company was a merger of web properties: the Snap.com portal, the Xoom.com community site, and NBC's own sites, including NBC.com and VideoSeeker. NBC added its TV network and its brand. In December 1999 the combined sites ranked in the top ten on the web, with 14.9 million unique visitors. Investors paid a high price for a TV network with a portal attached.

sections.heading: Snap, Xoom and a Peacock
sections.body: NBC Internet launched in November 1999 as a separate public company based in San Francisco. It folded together Xoom.com, founded in April 1996, the Snap.com portal, launched in September 1997, and the internet businesses NBC contributed, from NBC.com to NBC-IN.com. The plan was to mix portal search, online communities and e-commerce with NBC's shows and on-air promotion. None of the pieces had reached positive yearly operating cash flow, and the company expected losses ahead.

sections.heading: From $81 to $2.19
sections.body: The February 2000 offering sold 4.6 million shares at $81.375, worth about $374 million, split between the company and some selling holders. NBCi already traded on Nasdaq as NBCI, so this was a follow-on sale. Within weeks the dot-com crash began, and ad-supported portals lost their buyers. In 2001 NBC offered $2.19 in cash for each Class A share it did not own. Shareholders approved, NBCi left the market that August, and the company was liquidated into NBC.

tagline: Selling Ads Through the Living Room
dek: Vizio sold affordable smart TVs, then made money from the ads and streaming on their screens.
lede: Vizio told IPO investors that the money was in what happened on its TVs after people bought them. Its SmartCast software put streaming apps, free channels like WatchFree, and targeted ads in front of every viewer. Founder William Wang had started the Irvine, California company in 2002 to make home entertainment affordable for everyone. By March 2021, when it went public, Vizio sold Smart TVs and sound bars and pitched advertisers an audience drifting away from cable.

sections.heading: V, Inc. in Irvine
sections.body: Wang incorporated the company in California in October 2002 as V, Inc. It began operating in January 2003 and took the name VIZIO in 2007. The first bet was plain: shoppers wanted big flat-screen TVs at friendly prices. The second bet came later with SmartCast, Vizio's own operating system. Every set sold became a small channel for streaming services and advertisers, which gave Vizio a platform business that grew beside the hardware.

sections.heading: Walmart Buys the Screen
sections.body: Vizio priced its IPO at $21 a share in March 2021 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as VZIO. The offering brought the company about $144 million, and Wang kept control through Class B shares. The stock later traded well below its offer price. In December 2024 Walmart completed its purchase of Vizio for $11.50 a share in cash, about $2.3 billion in all. Vizio's shares left the NYSE that month.

cover.theme: a figure at a glowing window (the screen)

fate: Still public as Hello Group (NASDAQ: MOMO)
dek: Momo let people in China find and chat with strangers nearby, based on where they were and what they liked.
lede: Momo reached 60.2 million monthly users in about three years by helping people in China talk to strangers. The Beijing app used a phone's location to show who was nearby, then let users chat, join groups and meet in person. It launched in August 2011, just as smartphones spread across the country. By its December 2014 IPO, Momo had 180.3 million registered users and was learning to turn that crowd into revenue.

sections.heading: Location as the Hook
sections.body: Yan Tang founded Momo in 2011, with Yong Li as a co-founder. The bet was that the phone in every pocket could do more than message old friends. Momo built a mobile social platform around location and interests, so users could find people nearby and move from online chats to real meetings. Growth came fast. By September 2014, Momo counted 25.5 million average daily active users, up from about half that a year earlier.

sections.heading: From Momo to Hello Group
sections.body: Momo priced its IPO at $13.50 per American depositary share in December 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as MOMO. The sale came with a concurrent private placement. In 2021 the parent company changed its name from Momo Inc. to Hello Group Inc., and the Momo app kept its name. Hello Group still files with the SEC from China and still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker MOMO.

dek: Proxicom built websites and internet systems for big companies learning to do business online.
lede: Proxicom's stock quadrupled in six months, so the company went back and sold more at $52.38 a share. It had gone public in April 1999 at $13. The Reston, Virginia firm built internet systems for Global 1000 companies, and by the end of 1998 it had finished more than 600 client projects. For the October 1999 sale, Intel planned to buy 100,000 of the new shares.

sections.heading: Internet Only, Since 1994
sections.body: Raul Fernandez founded Proxicom in 1991 and ran it as chief executive. Before that he directed emerging technologies at Digicon, a government contractor. From 1994 on, Proxicom worked only on the internet. It sold a four-step method, the Proxicom Process, that mixed strategy, technology and creative design. Teams were organized by industry: energy and telecom, financial services, retail and manufacturing, and service businesses. At the end of 1998 it had about 150 projects underway.

sections.heading: From $13 to Compaq
sections.body: Proxicom priced its IPO at $13 a share in April 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as PXCM. The October follow-on at $52.38 raised money for the company and for selling shareholders. Then the dot-com bust hit internet consulting firms hard. In 2001 Compaq Computer agreed to buy Proxicom through a tender offer at $5.75 a share in cash. The deal closed that summer, and Proxicom's shares left the public market in June 2001.

cover.theme: a monument under construction (building the web)
cover.artwork: Nelson's Column under Construction, Trafalgar Square, London

fate: Merged with Youku, 2012; Youku Tudou later bought by Alibaba
dek: Tudou let Chinese internet users upload, share and watch videos on one of the country's first video sites.
lede: Tudou went public with a divorce in its risk factors. The ex-wife of founder Gary Wang had sued him for a share of the company that held Tudou's operating license, seeking to divide 76 percent of his stake. The prospectus warned that the case clouded Tudou's control of its own business. The Shanghai video site, whose name means potato, had launched in April 2005. By 2011 it was fighting crowded rivals for viewers and advertisers.

sections.heading: First to Share Video
sections.body: Gary Wang launched Tudou.com in April 2005. A 2010 Gartner report named it the first user-generated video sharing site launched in China. The bet was that Chinese internet users would want to post their own clips and watch everyone else's. Tudou grew into a broad online video platform paid for by advertising. By 2011 it also streamed to phones, offering mobile video channels on China Unicom's wireless video platform from April of that year.

sections.heading: Merged Within a Year
sections.body: Tudou priced its IPO at $29 per American depositary share in August 2011 and listed on Nasdaq as TUDO. Its largest rival, Youku, already traded in New York. In March 2012 the two agreed to merge, and the deal closed that August. Tudou became a subsidiary of the renamed Youku Tudou Inc., and each Tudou share was swapped for 7.177 Youku Class A shares. Alibaba bought Youku Tudou outright in 2016.

tagline: The Back Office Behind Wall Street
dek: SS&C sold software and services that ran the trading, accounting and reporting behind investment firms.
lede: More than 4,500 financial firms ran their unseen work on SS&C: fund accounting, reconciliation, performance reports and trade clearing. Bill Stone had started the Windsor, Connecticut company in 1986. In 2005 a holding company backed by the Carlyle Group bought it. When SS&C Technologies Holdings priced its IPO at $15 a share in March 2010, Carlyle funds still owned about 62.8 percent, and Stone owned about 25.2 percent.

sections.heading: Bill Stone's Connecticut Shop
sections.body: William C. Stone organized SS&C as a Connecticut corporation in March 1986. The bet was that banks, insurers and money managers would pay for software that handled the exact, tedious work behind every investment. SS&C covered the front office, with trading and modeling, the middle office, with portfolio management, and the back office, with accounting and clearing. It also ran that software for clients as a service. In November 2005, the Carlyle-backed holding company completed its purchase of SS&C.

sections.heading: Carlyle Brings It to Nasdaq
sections.body: SS&C priced its IPO at $15 a share in March 2010 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as SSNC. The company sold 8,225,000 shares for about $112.3 million in net proceeds and planned to use most of it to pay down debt. Selling shareholders sold more shares alongside. Carlyle and Stone kept control of the company. SS&C still trades on Nasdaq as SSNC and is still based in Windsor, Connecticut.

cover.theme: a woman at her counting counter (fund accounting)

fate: Acquired by Software AG, 2007 ($9.15 a share)
dek: webMethods sold software that let companies link their systems with suppliers and partners over the internet.
lede: SAP was webMethods' biggest customer, paying for about 31 percent of its revenue in the nine months before its IPO. The Fairfax, Virginia startup made software that let companies swap information and transactions with suppliers and partners in real time over the internet. It had grown from 17 employees in March 1998 to 197 by the end of 1999. In February 2000, at the height of the business-to-business boom, it sold shares at $35.

sections.heading: Seventeen People and SAP
sections.body: webMethods was founded in June 1996. From then through March 1997, its revenue was $12,000. It shipped its main product, webMethods B2B, in June 1998. The bet was that every big company would need to connect its software to everyone it bought from and sold to. SAP licensed the technology and became a major customer. Dell and Eastman Chemical bought shares in a private sale that closed alongside the IPO.

sections.heading: From the Bubble to Software AG
sections.body: webMethods priced its IPO at $35 a share in February 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as WEBM. It sold 4.1 million shares, raising $143.5 million before fees. Weeks later the dot-com market began to fall. webMethods kept selling integration software from Fairfax for seven more years. In 2007 Software AG of Germany bought it through a tender offer at $9.15 a share in cash, and the stock left Nasdaq that June.

fate: Taken private by Thoma Bravo, 2009 ($1.85 a share)
dek: Entrust sold software that issued and managed digital certificates, so companies knew who was on the other end.
lede: Entrust explained its product with one image: digital certificates work like electronic passports. Its software proved who sent an email or signed a transaction, and kept the contents private. Entrust began in 1994 as the Secure Networks group inside Nortel, the Canadian telecom giant. When it went public in August 1998, it was based in Richardson, Texas, with its research lab in Ottawa. Nortel still owned about 55.3 percent once the shares sold.

sections.heading: Born Inside Nortel
sections.body: Nortel's team built public key infrastructure, or PKI, the system that creates and tracks digital certificates. In December 1996 Nortel set the group up as its own company, Entrust Technologies, and moved the business into it. The bet was that companies moving email, forms and commerce onto networks would need one trusted way to manage keys and identities. Entrust sold a software framework that ran across many platforms, browsers and applications.

sections.heading: From $16 to $1.85
sections.body: Entrust priced its IPO at $16 a share in August 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as ENTU. Later it dropped Technologies from its name and moved its headquarters to Plano, Texas. Its shares ended up far below the IPO price. In 2009 a company controlled by a Thoma Bravo fund bought Entrust for $1.85 a share in cash. Shareholders voted that June, and the stock left Nasdaq in July 2009.

cover.artwork: The Guard Gate, Gatun Lock, Panama

dek: Wipro wrote software and ran IT projects for companies worldwide from its base in India.
lede: Wipro was incorporated in 1945 as Western India Vegetable Products Limited. By October 2000 it was one of India's leading IT services companies, selling software design and development to firms around the world. It still sold soaps, toiletries, lighting and cooking oils at home. That fall it listed American depositary shares on the New York Stock Exchange at $41.375 each. Its chairman, Azim Premji, controlled the company.

sections.heading: Western India Vegetable Products
sections.body: The company became Wipro Products in 1977 and Wipro Limited in 1984. Its consumer care business had run since 1945, and its lighting business since 1992. The big bet was software. Through its Wipro Technologies division, Wipro did research and development for hardware and telecom makers and built applications for large companies. A separate unit sold IT services and products inside India. Consumer care and lighting made up 14 percent of revenue.

sections.heading: Bangalore on the Big Board
sections.body: Wipro sold 2,750,000 American depositary shares at $41.375 each in October 2000, with each share backed by one equity share in India. They listed on the New York Stock Exchange as WIT, months after the dot-com peak. The offering gave American investors a direct way to own one of India's software exporters. Wipro still trades on the NYSE as WIT and files its reports with the SEC from Bengaluru.

cover.theme: sunflowers (vegetable oil roots, the Wipro sunflower)

fate: Chapter 11, 2025; reorganized under new owners and public shares canceled
tagline: One Screen for Every Ad Dollar
dek: Marin gave advertisers and agencies one place to manage, measure and tune their search, social and display ads.
lede: Marin Software ended in a Delaware bankruptcy court. It began as a bet on the ad budget. The San Francisco company sold cloud software that let advertisers and agencies run campaigns across search, display, social and mobile from one screen, then measure what each dollar earned. When it listed on the New York Stock Exchange in March 2013 at $14 a share, marketers were spreading their money across more ad channels every year.

sections.heading: Three Co-Founders, One Dashboard
sections.body: Chris Lien founded Marin in 2006 and soon brought in Wister Walcott and Joseph Chang as co-founders. Lien had been chief operating officer of Adteractive, an online performance marketing company. Marin called its product a Revenue Acquisition Management platform. It handled reporting, ad creation and bidding across many publishers, sold as a subscription service. The pitch was plain: big ad buyers needed one tool to see which ads paid off.

sections.heading: From the NYSE to Chapter 11
sections.body: Marin priced its IPO at $14 a share in March 2013 and listed on the NYSE as MRIN. The business shrank over the following decade. By early 2025 Marin had about 80 employees, and in March it cut 22 of them. On July 1, 2025, it filed for Chapter 11. Under a plan confirmed that August, Kaxxa Holdings and lender 5Y took ownership. The old public shares were canceled in September 2025.

tagline: From a Dictionary App to Class
dek: Youdao turned China's most popular dictionary app into a business selling online courses and learning tools.
lede: Youdao Dictionary had 51.2 million average monthly users in the first half of 2019, more than any other language app in China. Its owner, Youdao, started inside the internet company NetEase in 2006 and launched the dictionary a year later. Then it used that audience to sell something bigger: online courses and smart learning devices. When Youdao listed in New York in October 2019, NetEase still controlled it.

sections.heading: Born Inside NetEase
sections.body: Youdao began operating in March 2006 as part of NetEase, the Chinese internet company. Its first products were search and reference tools. In 2007 it launched Youdao Dictionary, which became the habit that brought millions of students and workers back every day. In 2014 the company shifted its focus to what it called the intelligent learning industry. The bet was that people who looked up words would also pay to learn.

sections.heading: A NetEase Spin-Off on the NYSE
sections.body: Youdao priced its IPO at $17 per American depositary share in October 2019 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as DAO. Alongside the IPO, the investment firm Orbis bought shares in a private placement at the same price. NetEase and chief executive Feng Zhou held the high-vote Class B shares. Youdao still trades on the NYSE as DAO and is based in Hangzhou.

cover.theme: a reader with a book (the dictionary)

tagline: Guarding the Keys to the Kingdom
dek: CyberArk protected the powerful admin accounts that attackers hunt for once they get inside a network.
lede: CyberArk called privileged accounts the keys to the IT kingdom. These are the admin logins that control servers, factory systems and the most sensitive data. An attacker who steals one can take over a company from the inside. In September 2014 the Israeli company went public with a simple pitch: firewalls fail, so guard the keys. It sold 5.36 million shares at $16, raising about $85.8 million.

sections.heading: Assume the Attacker Is In
sections.body: CyberArk started in 1999 in Israel. Udi Mokady, a founder, was chief operating officer from 1999 and became chief executive in 2005. Most security companies tried to keep attackers out. CyberArk built a new layer for attacks that had already gotten past the network perimeter. Its software locked away privileged accounts, watched how they were used, and flagged misuse. It ran headquarters in Petach Tikva, Israel, and a U.S. base in Newton, Massachusetts.

sections.heading: Palo Alto Networks Buys the Vault
sections.body: CyberArk priced its IPO at $16 a share in September 2014 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as CYBR. Identity security grew into a large market, and CyberArk grew with it. In July 2025 Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy the company. The deal closed on February 11, 2026. Each CyberArk share became $45 in cash plus 2.2005 Palo Alto Networks shares, and CyberArk left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Noah building the ark (CyberArk, a safe vessel)
cover.artwork: God Commanding Noah to Build the Ark

dek: GetThere let companies book employee travel on the web, inside their own travel rules and supplier deals.
lede: Boeing, Nike, Chevron and Hewlett-Packard all booked business trips through GetThere.com before it went public. The Menlo Park, California company sold web tools that let employees reserve flights, hotels and cars themselves while the company kept control of policy and costs. It had started in 1995 as Internet Travel Network, selling travel to consumers. In November 1999 it sold 5 million shares at $16 to bet on business travel instead.

sections.heading: Internet Travel Network Turns
sections.body: Daniel Whaley was one of the founders of Internet Travel Network, incorporated in California in August 1995. At first it sold trips to consumers through its itn.net website. In 1996 it turned to businesses and travel suppliers. It launched ITN Global Manager for corporate travel that year and ITN FlightRez for airlines in 1997. In July 1999 it renamed itself GetThere.com, and by October it had 61 business customers.

sections.heading: Sabre Buys Within a Year
sections.body: GetThere priced its IPO at $16 a share in November 1999 and raised $80 million. Gadi Maier, a former Oracle executive, ran it as chief executive. Less than a year later, Sabre Holdings, the airline reservation giant, made a tender offer of $17.75 a share in cash. The deal closed in October 2000, and GetThere became part of Sabre's travel business.

fate: Acquired by Hewlett Packard Enterprise, 2016 ($7.75 a share)
dek: Rackable built dense, cool-running servers for giant data centers, then bought Silicon Graphics and took its name.
lede: Rackable Systems sold to Microsoft, Yahoo, Oracle and Nvidia as they filled buildings with computers. The Milpitas, California company packed servers into tight racks and solved the heat and power problems that came with them. Its quarterly revenue swung hard, from $18.1 million to $34.8 million in one quarter of 2004, then back down to $23.0 million. It went public in June 2005 at $12 a share.

sections.heading: Built for the Server Farm
sections.body: Rackable was founded in 1999 by a team that included Giovanni Coglitore, Nikolai Gallo and Jack Randall. They saw that big data centers ran thousands of servers and fought the same limits: floor space, power use, heat and repair time. Rackable's answer was its Foundation Series, high-density rack servers built for scale-out data centers. By its IPO it had sold to more than 100 customers in internet, government, finance, energy and biotech.

sections.heading: From Rackable to SGI to HPE
sections.body: Rackable priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2005 and listed on Nasdaq as RACK. In 2009 it bought the assets of Silicon Graphics, the famous workstation and supercomputer maker, and renamed itself Silicon Graphics International. It sold high-performance computers as SGI for seven more years. In November 2016 Hewlett Packard Enterprise bought SGI for $7.75 a share in cash.

cover.theme: objects lined up on shelves (server racks)
cover.artwork: Articles of Glass on Three Shelves

dek: Cardlytics put cash-back offers inside online banking, using card purchase data to show who bought what.
lede: Cardlytics saw one in five debit and credit card swipes in the United States. In 2016 its platform analyzed more than 18 billion purchases across 94 million accounts, drawn from over 2,000 banks and credit unions. The Atlanta company used that data to place cash-back offers inside online banking, where customers already checked their balances. Bank of America alone supplied about half of its users when it went public in February 2018.

sections.heading: Purchase Data, Put to Work
sections.body: Scott Grimes and Lynne Laube co-founded Cardlytics in 2008. Their first product, Cardlytics Direct, turned a bank's website and app into an ad channel. A shopper saw an offer from a retailer, paid with a card, and got cash back. Marketers liked it because Cardlytics could show which offers led to real sales. Banks liked it because they shared in the revenue. By September 2017, Cardlytics worked with 2,041 financial institutions.

sections.heading: One Big Bank Partner
sections.body: Cardlytics priced its IPO at $13 a share in February 2018 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as CDLX. The prospectus flagged its dependence on Bank of America, which supplied about 51 percent of its bank users in the first nine months of 2017. Lloyds, its largest partner in Britain, supplied about 9 percent. Cardlytics is still based in Atlanta and still trades on Nasdaq as CDLX.

fate: Acquired by Royal Ahold, 2001 ($2.15 a share)
tagline: Shopping the Aisles From a Keyboard
dek: Peapod let shoppers buy groceries from their computers and have them delivered from local supermarkets.
lede: Peapod took its first online grocery orders in 1990, in a suburban Chicago test market served by a single warehouse. By its June 1997 IPO, members could browse virtual aisles of more than 20,000 grocery, drug and household items, shop from saved lists, clip electronic coupons and get orders delivered from partner supermarkets. The Evanston, Illinois company called itself the leading online grocery shopping and delivery company. It had never turned a profit.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and a Test Market
sections.body: Andrew and Thomas Parkinson ran Peapod, which began in 1989 and operated as an Illinois partnership from 1992. The model served three customers at once. Shoppers got home delivery. Grocery chains got a new sales channel without building one themselves. Consumer goods companies got targeted ads, promotions and research drawn from members' buying habits. After the IPO, the Parkinsons and an affiliated company would still own about 19.8 percent of the stock.

sections.heading: Ahold Takes the Basket
sections.body: Peapod priced its IPO at $16 a share in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as PPOD. It sold 4 million shares. Picking, packing and delivering groceries proved expensive, and the losses kept growing. Dutch grocer Royal Ahold invested and gained control of the company. In 2001 Ahold bought out the remaining public shareholders at $2.15 a share in cash, and Peapod became an Ahold subsidiary that August.

fate: Taken private by an investor group, 2010 ($7.65 a share)
dek: Airvana built the software and gear that let cell networks carry fast internet to phones and laptops.
lede: Almost all of Airvana's revenue came through one customer: Nortel Networks. The Chelmsford, Massachusetts company built internet-based equipment that let wireless carriers deliver broadband over the EV-DO standard, and Nortel resold it under an OEM deal. Through Nortel, Airvana's products reached more than 30 operators, including Verizon Wireless, Sprint Nextel, Alltel and Telus. In July 2007, weeks after the first iPhone went on sale, Airvana went public at $7 a share.

sections.heading: Built on Internet Protocol
sections.body: Airvana was incorporated in Delaware in March 2000. Its bet was that cell networks would run on internet technology and carry far more than voice calls. Airvana combined wireless communications, IP and broadband networking into products that brought internet access, email, music, video and gaming to mobile devices. By 2007 it was also working on UMTS networks and on small in-building systems for better indoor coverage.

sections.heading: Taken Private at $7.65
sections.body: Airvana priced its IPO at $7 a share in July 2007 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as AIRV. It sold 8.3 million shares. In December 2009 it agreed to sell itself to a new company owned by affiliates of S.A.C. Private Capital, GSO Capital Partners and ZelnickMedia, with some existing holders rolling over their stakes. Shareholders received $7.65 a share in cash, and the stock left Nasdaq in April 2010.

cover.theme: a gust of wind (signals through the air)

tagline: Turning TV Cable Into a Network
dek: Entropic made chips that sent video between rooms over the coaxial cable already inside homes.
lede: Verizon's FiOS boxes talked to each other over the TV cable in the walls, and Entropic made the chips that let them. The San Diego company was a founding member of the Multimedia over Coax Alliance, or MoCA, and in 2007 it was the only high-volume supplier of MoCA chipsets. That meant a family could watch a DVR recording in any room. Entropic's revenue jumped from about $3.7 million in 2005 to $41.5 million in 2006.

sections.heading: Video Over Wires You Own
sections.body: Entropic worked on MoCA technology from 2001 and shipped its home networking products in volume from 2006. The idea was simple. Most homes already had coaxial cable in several rooms, so nobody had to pull new wires. Entropic sold MoCA chipsets, broadband access chips, satellite TV chips and silicon TV tuners. In 2007 it bought RF Magic. Customers included Actiontec, Jabil and Motorola.

sections.heading: From $6 to MaxLinear
sections.body: Entropic priced its IPO at $6 a share in December 2007 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as ENTR. It sold 8 million shares as the financial crisis began. Neither Entropic nor RF Magic had ever earned an annual profit. Entropic kept selling chips for cable and satellite boxes for seven more years. In April 2015 MaxLinear completed its purchase of Entropic, and Entropic's shares left Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: The Whirlpools in Naruto Strait, Awa Province (Awa Naruto no fukei)

tagline: Soft Skills, Taught Through a Browser
dek: SkillSoft sold web-based courses that taught workers business and people skills right at their desks.
lede: SkillSoft went public while its founders' old employer sued it for $400 million. NETg, a training software company, said founder Charles Moran and other former employees took its trade secrets, including the business plan for teaching soft skills on the web. The Nashua, New Hampshire company had started operating in January 1998 and released its first product in March 1999. In February 2000 it priced its IPO at $14 a share anyway.

sections.heading: Courses Built for the Web
sections.body: SkillSoft was incorporated in Delaware in October 1997 and opened for business in January 1998 with its first round of funding. Warburg, Pincus Ventures was its largest investor. The company sold courses on professional effectiveness and business topics, the subjects trainers call soft skills. Every course ran in a standard web browser, so employees could learn anytime, at any desk. One customer made up 29 percent of its early revenue.

sections.heading: Merged With SmartForce
sections.body: SkillSoft priced its IPO at $14 a share in February 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as SKIL. It sold 3.1 million shares weeks before the dot-com peak. In 2002 it agreed to merge with SmartForce, a larger e-learning company based in Ireland. Each SkillSoft share became 2.3674 SmartForce American depositary shares, and the combined company was run by executives from both sides. SkillSoft stopped filing as a separate public company in September 2002.

tagline: Watching Every Alarm on the Network
dek: Micromuse sold Netcool, software that pulled alarms from across a network and showed operators what was breaking.
lede: Micromuse paid for its first product by reselling other people's computers. Founded in London in 1989, it ran a systems integration and consulting business for network managers, then used that cash to build Netcool/OMNIbus, which shipped in January 1995. Netcool pulled alarms from every corner of a network into one live database and showed operators which business services were at risk. In 1997 the company moved its headquarters to San Francisco.

sections.heading: From London to San Francisco
sections.body: In March 1997 Micromuse reorganized as a Delaware company and moved from London to San Francisco, raising $4.9 million and arranging a $3 million credit line. Its customers were the builders of the commercial internet, including GTE Internetworking, MindSpring, Netcom, PSINet, Pacific Bell and WorldCom's UUNet, plus banks such as Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley. The bet was that bigger networks would need one clear view of what was failing.

sections.heading: IBM Pays $10 a Share
sections.body: Micromuse priced its IPO at $12 a share in February 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as MUSE. It sold 3.1 million shares, then returned to the market for more stock offerings in 1998, 2000 and 2001. Netcool stayed its core product. In 2006 IBM bought Micromuse for $10 a share in cash, a deal worth about $840 million, and Micromuse stopped trading that February.

cover.theme: Urania, the muse who watches the heavens
cover.artwork: Urania, plate twelve from Apollo and the Muses

dek: Power Integrations made chips that turned wall current into steady power for phones, PCs and set-top boxes.
lede: Power Integrations spent its first five years making chips that worked but did not sell. From 1988 through 1993 the Sunnyvale, California company built products for many markets, and none was cheap enough to beat the loose parts engineers already used. Then it narrowed its aim. Its TOPSwitch chips put a power controller, a MOSFET switch and other parts on one piece of silicon. By its December 1997 IPO, they were selling into phone chargers and PCs.

sections.heading: One Chip Instead of Many
sections.body: The company was incorporated in California in March 1988, with Steven J. Sharp among its founders. It designed high-voltage analog chips for AC to DC power conversion, the job done by the adapter between a wall socket and a device. Early products had strong technology and weak sales. The fix was a focus on cost. Power Integrations also signed partnerships with Matsushita Electronics and OKI Electric to reach high-volume manufacturing and earn royalties.

sections.heading: Still Switching on Nasdaq
sections.body: Power Integrations priced its IPO at $8 a share in December 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as POWI. It sold 2.1 million shares. Revenue had grown from $7.1 million in 1994 to $23.9 million in 1996, led by the TOPSwitch family. The company later moved its headquarters to San Jose. Nearly three decades after its IPO, Power Integrations is still independent and still trades on Nasdaq as POWI.

cover.artwork: Women Inside a Mosquito Net During a Thunderstorm

tagline: A Fiber Ring Around the World
dek: 360networks laid fiber optic cable across North America, Europe and the oceans, and sold capacity to carriers.
lede: 360networks raised $647.85 million in its April 2000 IPO, and it needed every dollar. The Vancouver company planned a 56,300-mile fiber network by the end of 2001, spanning North America and Europe and running under two oceans. Investors including Comcast and Tyco had agreed to buy about $510 million more in stock. Its new chief executive, Gregory Maffei, had just left the chief financial officer job at Microsoft. Fourteen months later, 360networks was bankrupt.

sections.heading: Worldwide Fiber Goes Global
sections.body: The company began as Worldwide Fiber, and the Canadian construction group Ledcor was a major shareholder. Its bet was that the internet would need far more long-haul capacity than existed. By early 2000 it had built more than 12,200 route miles in North America and 4,900 in Europe. It planned undersea cables of 7,600 route miles between North America and Europe and 14,000 between South America and North America.

sections.heading: Fourteen Months to Bankruptcy
sections.body: 360networks priced its IPO at $14 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as TSIX and on the Toronto Stock Exchange. It sold 46.275 million shares, weeks after the dot-com market peaked. Then carriers stopped buying capacity, and fiber builders ran short of cash. On June 27, 2001, 360networks cut 800 jobs. The next day it filed for creditor protection in Canada, and its main U.S. unit filed for Chapter 11.

cover.theme: tracks running to the horizon (fiber routes)

tagline: A Bank Card Without a Bank
dek: NetSpend sold reloadable prepaid debit cards to people who lived without a regular bank account.
lede: NetSpend built its business around an estimated 60 million Americans who had no regular bank account or leaned on check cashers and other alternatives. The Austin, Texas company sold general-purpose reloadable prepaid debit cards. Customers put money on a card and used it like any other debit card. By mid-2010 NetSpend had about 2 million active cards and $8.8 billion in yearly card volume. Its October 2010 IPO priced at $11 a share.

sections.heading: Banking for the Underbanked
sections.body: NetSpend Corporation was incorporated in Texas in 1999. The bet was that people outside the banking system still needed a card to pay bills, shop and manage money, and that traditional banks were not serving them well. NetSpend called these customers underbanked and built its products around them. Check-cashing chain ACE became one of its biggest sales channels. In May 2004, Oak Investment Partners took a controlling stake through a recapitalization.

sections.heading: TSYS Pays $16
sections.body: NetSpend priced its IPO at $11 a share in October 2010 and listed on Nasdaq as NTSP. In early 2013 the payment processor TSYS made a run at the company. Its offers rose from $15.25 to $15.40 a share as the two sides bargained over terms. The final deal paid $16 a share in cash. It closed in July 2013, and NetSpend became part of TSYS.

fate: Acquired by Voya Financial, 2023 ($10.50 a share)
dek: Benefitfocus ran cloud software where employees, employers and insurers shopped for, signed up for and managed benefits.
lede: Benefitfocus took on one of the dullest problems in American business: getting people signed up for health, dental, life and disability insurance at work. The Charleston, South Carolina company built a cloud platform where employers, insurance carriers and their members could shop, enroll and manage benefits in one place. It went public in September 2013, weeks before the Affordable Care Act's insurance exchanges opened. It had about 862 employees.

sections.heading: A Charleston Startup
sections.body: Shawn Jenkins and Mason Holland founded Benefitfocus in June 2000. Jenkins ran it as chief executive, and Holland served as executive chairman. The bet was that benefits administration, a tangle of rules, forms and money moving between employers and insurers, belonged on the web. Benefitfocus sold to both sides. Employers used it to run their plans, and carriers used it to sell and manage coverage, including extras like critical illness and wellness programs.

sections.heading: Voya Buys at $10.50
sections.body: Benefitfocus priced its IPO at $26.50 a share in September 2013 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as BNFT. It entered the market as a controlled company. The shares later fell well below the offer price. In November 2022 Voya Financial agreed to buy Benefitfocus for $10.50 a share in cash, a 49 percent premium to the last close before the news. The deal closed in January 2023.

cover.artwork: Sharing an Umbrella - A Set of Three (Aigasa sanpukutsui)

fate: Acquired by Dassault Systèmes, 2019 ($92.25 a share)
dek: Medidata ran clinical trials in the cloud, replacing the paper forms drug companies used to collect patient data.
lede: Medidata sold drug companies a way to run clinical trials without paper. Its Medidata Rave platform captured patient data electronically and managed it in one hosted system, replacing the binders and forms that slowed trials down. Johnson & Johnson, AstraZeneca, Amgen, Astellas and Takeda were its biggest customers in early 2009. That June, in the depths of the financial crisis, the New York company went public at $14 a share.

sections.heading: Three Founders on Fifth Avenue
sections.body: Medidata was organized as a New York corporation in June 1999 and kept its offices on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. Tarek Sherif became chief executive in 2001. Glen de Vries served as chief technology officer before becoming president in 2008. Edward Ikeguchi, a physician, sat on the board. The bet was that testing new medicines would move to the web, from protocol design and investigator contracts to data capture and analysis.

sections.heading: Dassault Pays $92.25
sections.body: Medidata priced its IPO at $14 a share in June 2009 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Market as MDSO. It sold 6.3 million shares. Over the next decade it grew into one of the largest cloud software companies serving drug and device makers. In 2019 France's Dassault Systèmes agreed to buy Medidata for $92.25 a share in cash, about $5.8 billion in all. The deal closed that October.

cover.artwork: Flying Raven: ex libris, from The Raven (Le Corbeau)

fate: Taken private by Shi Yuzhu, Baring Private Equity Asia and Hony Capital, 2014 (about $3B)
dek: Giant Interactive gave Chinese gamers a vast online war for free, then sold them the weapons to win it.
lede: Shi Yuzhu had already lost one fortune before he made his second in video games. His Shanghai company, Giant Interactive, ran ZT Online, a sprawling fantasy war game that cost nothing to join. Players paid for the gear, potions and status that helped them win. Millions of them did. When Giant listed on the New York Stock Exchange in November 2007, it raised $887 million, the largest US listing by a private Chinese company up to then.

sections.heading: Free to Enter, Paid to Win
sections.body: Most online games of the era charged players by the hour or the month. ZT Online, known in Chinese as Zhengtu, let anyone in for free. Giant made its money selling virtual items inside the game, from stronger armor to faster mounts. The model fit China, where many players gamed in internet cafes and few wanted a monthly bill. It turned a Shanghai studio founded in 2004 into one of China's biggest online game companies by 2007.

sections.heading: Fifteen Fifty, Then Twelve
sections.body: Giant priced its shares at $15.50, above the $12 to $14 range it had marketed, and sold them as American Depositary Shares under the ticker GA. The stock closed its first day 17.6 percent higher, at $18.23. The glow faded as newer games competed for the same players and growth slowed. In 2014, Shi teamed up with Baring Private Equity Asia and Hony Capital to buy out the public holders at $12 a share, a deal worth about $3 billion.

cover.artwork: Dancing Giant, from Disparates, published as plate 4 in Los Proverbios
cover.artist: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes

dek: Pivotal taught big, old companies to build and run software the way Silicon Valley startups did.
lede: Pivotal was born in 2013 as a corporate spinout, assembled from pieces of EMC and VMware and a San Francisco consulting shop famous for pair programming. Its pitch was simple. Banks, carmakers and insurers needed to ship software fast, and Pivotal would teach them how, then sell them the platform to run it on. General Electric was an early backer. By the time it filed to go public in 2018, Pivotal sold Cloud Foundry software to many of the largest companies in the world.

sections.heading: Two Programmers, One Keyboard
sections.body: The heart of the company was Pivotal Labs, a consultancy where engineers worked in pairs at a single machine and shipped code every day. Clients sent their own developers to sit beside Pivotal's and learn the habits. Pivotal paired that teaching with Pivotal Cloud Foundry, a platform that let a company's programmers push an app live without waiting on the IT department. The bet was that every big company would become a software company, and would pay well to learn how.

sections.heading: Back Where It Started
sections.body: Pivotal priced its offering at $15 a share, the middle of its range, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on April 20, 2018, as PVTL. The stock opened at $16.75 and closed the day at $15.73. Growth slowed as rivals like Kubernetes changed how companies ran cloud apps. In August 2019, VMware, its own former parent, agreed to buy Pivotal back. The merger closed on December 30, 2019, and Pivotal's products became part of VMware Tanzu.

cover.theme: a weathervane turning on its pivot

fate: Acquired by PeopleSoft, 2003; now part of Oracle
dek: J.D. Edwards ran the books, warehouses and factories of midsize companies from a Denver software house.
lede: Three partners started J.D. Edwards in Denver in 1977, a long way from Silicon Valley, and spent twenty years building it before they sold a single share to the public. The company wrote the software that ran a business's ledgers, payroll, inventory and factory floors, mostly on IBM's sturdy midrange computers. By 1997 thousands of companies used it. That September, J.D. Edwards went public into a market hungry for enterprise software and nervous about the year 2000.

sections.heading: Accountants Who Wrote Code
sections.body: Jack Thompson, Dan Gregory and Ed McVaney had worked on business systems for clients, so they wrote software that matched how companies kept their books. They built it for IBM's System/38 and later the AS/400, machines that midsize manufacturers and distributors trusted for decades. The initials came from the founders' first names. J.D. Edwards stayed private for twenty years, adding offices around the world and a new client/server product called OneWorld.

sections.heading: A Prize in a Software War
sections.body: J.D. Edwards priced its offering at $23 a share in September 1997, above the $15 to $17 range first filed, and raised $417.9 million on Nasdaq as JDEC. Morgan Stanley led the deal. The company stayed independent for six more years. In 2003 PeopleSoft agreed to buy it, just as Oracle launched a hostile bid for PeopleSoft. The merger closed that year. Oracle won PeopleSoft in 2005, and J.D. Edwards lives on as an Oracle product line.

tagline: The Scanner Named for a Centaur
dek: Tenable shows companies every weak spot in their networks before an attacker finds it.
lede: Before Tenable was a company, it was Nessus, a free security scanner that a young French programmer, Renaud Deraison, released in 1998. System administrators everywhere used it to probe their own networks for holes. In 2002 Deraison joined Ron Gula and Jack Huffard in Maryland to build a business around it. By its 2018 public offering, Tenable sold to governments and large companies and pitched a bigger idea it called Cyber Exposure.

sections.heading: Open Source, Then a Business
sections.body: Nessus checked computers for known weaknesses: unpatched software, open ports, default passwords. Because it was free and open, it spread across the security world. Tenable sold tools on top of it for large networks, then in 2005 made new versions of Nessus closed source so it could fund the research behind its checks. The company grew into a full platform for vulnerability management, selling to banks, governments and thousands of mid-sized firms near its home in Columbia, Maryland.

sections.heading: Thirty-Two Percent on Day One
sections.body: Tenable priced its shares at $23, above its expected range of $20 to $22, and began trading on Nasdaq on July 26, 2018, under TENB. The stock closed its first day up nearly 32 percent. The company sold 12,535,000 shares once the underwriters took their full option. Tenable has since expanded into cloud security and attack-surface tools through acquisitions, and it remains an independent public company on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Hercules and the centaur Nessus (the Nessus scanner)
cover.artwork: Hercules and Nessus, from The Labors of Hercules

fate: Merged with Bookham to form Oclaro, 2009
dek: Avanex made the optical parts that let one strand of fiber carry far more internet traffic.
lede: On February 4, 2000, Avanex shares more than quadrupled in a single afternoon.
