The Fremont company had sold just $10.9 million of products in the prior six months, and its biggest buyer, MCI WorldCom, also owned a piece of it. None of that mattered. Avanex made photonic processors, small devices that sorted and steered beams of light inside fiber optic networks, and in early 2000 anything that promised more bandwidth looked priceless.

sections.heading: More Colors in the Glass
sections.body: Simon Cao founded Avanex in 1997 around a simple promise: squeeze more data down the fiber that carriers had already buried. Long-haul networks sent many colors of light down one strand, each color carrying its own stream. Avanex built parts that packed those colors closer together and kept them clean over long distances. Carriers were racing to add capacity for the internet boom, and every extra channel per fiber saved them from digging new trenches.

sections.heading: From $172 to a Merger
sections.body: Avanex priced its offering at $36 a share and raised about $216 million on Nasdaq under AVNX. By the close of its first day the stock traded near $172. The telecom bust hit within a year, as carriers stopped buying and the company's market value collapsed. Avanex spent the next decade cutting costs and buying rivals' optical units. In April 2009 it merged with Bookham in an all-stock deal, and the combined company took the name Oclaro.

cover.artwork: Landscape with Sun Breaking Through Clouds

dek: Chegg saved college students money on textbooks, then sold them homework help by the month.
lede: Chegg's name mashes together "chicken" and "egg," after the old trap every graduate knows: you need experience to get a job, and a job to get experience. The company started with a smaller student problem, the $200 textbook. Chegg rented books by mail for a fraction of the price and shipped them back and forth across the country. By its 2013 offering, it was trying to turn those renters into subscribers for online study help.

sections.heading: Renting the Required Reading
sections.body: Aayush Phumbhra, Osman Rashid and Josh Carlson started Chegg in 2005 as a campus classifieds site, then found their business in textbook rentals. Students hated paying full price for books they used for one semester. Chegg bought the books, rented them out, and took them back at the end of term. The model drew millions of students, but it tied up cash in warehouses full of paper. The real bet was Chegg Study, a subscription of step-by-step homework answers.

sections.heading: Down on Day One
sections.body: Chegg priced its offering at $12.50 a share, above its $9.50 to $11.50 range, and raised $188 million on the New York Stock Exchange in November 2013. The stock fell 22.6 percent on its first day. Chegg handed its print rentals to a partner and leaned into digital study help, which boomed during the pandemic. Then AI chatbots began answering homework questions for free. In October 2025 Chegg ended a sale review, chose to stay public, and cut about 45 percent of its staff.

fate: Taken private by a Jason Jiang and Carlyle-led group, 2013; later relisted in Shenzhen
dek: Focus Media put flat-screen ads beside the elevators of China's office towers, where bored workers had nothing else to watch.
lede: Jason Jiang noticed that office workers in Shanghai spent a few idle minutes every day waiting for elevators, staring at nothing. He filled that gap with flat-panel screens running ads on a loop. Focus Media signed up building after building and sold the audience to advertisers chasing China's new white-collar class. When it listed on Nasdaq in July 2005, it was one of the first Chinese media companies to raise money in New York.

sections.heading: A Captive Audience in the Lobby
sections.body: Jiang had run an ad agency before he started Focus Media in 2003. His idea needed no new technology. He leased small LCD screens, mounted them in the lobbies of office towers, and paid landlords a fee. The audience was young, employed, and stuck in place for a minute or two. Advertisers paid for that attention. Focus Media grew by adding thousands of buildings across China's big cities, then by buying rival networks in supermarkets, residential complexes and online advertising.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Shenzhen
sections.body: Focus Media sold American Depositary Shares at $17 each on Nasdaq under the ticker FMCN, raising about $171 million. Its acquisitions made it China's largest out-of-home ad network, but they also brought losses and scrutiny. In 2011 the short seller Muddy Waters attacked its disclosures, and the stock fell hard. In 2013 a group led by Jiang and the Carlyle Group took the company private in a deal worth about $3.7 billion. Focus Media later relisted on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange.

cover.artwork: Elevator Grille from the Chicago Stock Exchange, Chicago, Illinois

fate: Acquired by VoiceStream Wireless, 2001; now part of T-Mobile US
tagline: The First GSM Calls in New York
dek: Omnipoint built New York's first GSM cell network, years before most Americans owned a mobile phone.
lede: Omnipoint won the right to build a wireless network in New York City without bidding a dollar for it. The Federal Communications Commission handed the small company a pioneer's preference license, a reward for its work on new radio technology. Omnipoint then had to raise the money to build. When it went public in January 1996, it was a company with a license, big plans, and almost no revenue.

sections.heading: A License as a Prize
sections.body: Douglas Smith founded Omnipoint in Colorado Springs in 1987 to work on spread-spectrum radio, a way of spreading a signal across many frequencies. That research earned the license for the New York area, the richest phone market in the country. Omnipoint chose GSM, the digital standard already common in Europe, and launched service in late 1996. Its customers got clear calls, text messages and phones with SIM cards, all new to most Americans.

sections.heading: Folded Into T-Mobile
sections.body: Omnipoint priced its offering at $16 a share, above its first range of $13 to $15, and began trading on Nasdaq on January 26, 1996. The stock was near $20 by the end of its first day. Building a network cost far more than the offering raised, and Omnipoint borrowed heavily and lost money for years. In 2000 VoiceStream Wireless agreed to buy it, and the deal closed in early 2001. Deutsche Telekom bought VoiceStream later that year and renamed it T-Mobile USA.

cover.theme: a winter night in New York (the first market)

tagline: A CEO's Social Security Number on Billboards
dek: LifeLock watched for signs that someone was using your name and credit, and promised to fix it if they did.
lede: LifeLock's chief executive printed his own Social Security number in the company's ads, daring thieves to try. Todd Davis meant it as proof that LifeLock's identity protection worked. Thieves took the dare, and his identity was stolen more than once. The stunt still made LifeLock famous. By the fall of 2012, the Arizona company had millions of paying members and was ready to sell shares to the public.

sections.heading: Selling Peace of Mind
sections.body: Todd Davis and Robert Maynard Jr. started LifeLock in Tempe in 2005. Identity theft was in the news, and most people had no idea what to do about it. LifeLock charged a monthly fee to place fraud alerts, watch for new accounts opened in a member's name, and help clean up the damage. The pitch landed. The promises in its ads also drew the Federal Trade Commission, which in 2010 made LifeLock pay $12 million to settle charges of deceptive advertising.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars, Then Symantec
sections.body: LifeLock priced its offering at $9 a share, below its $10 to $12 range, and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as LOCK on October 3, 2012. The company kept growing its members, though regulators returned. In 2015 it paid $100 million to settle FTC claims that it broke the 2010 order. In 2016 Symantec agreed to buy LifeLock for $24 a share in cash, about $2.3 billion. The deal closed in February 2017.

cover.theme: an angel holding the key (lock and key)
cover.artwork: The Angel with the Key of the Bottomless Pit, from The Apocalypse

tagline: Card Swipes for Main Street Diners
dek: Heartland processed card payments for restaurants and small shops, and promised them fair, plain pricing.
lede: Heartland Payment Systems made its money on the card swipe at the corner diner. Every time a customer paid with plastic, a processor took a small cut, and many small merchants had no idea how much. Robert Carr built Heartland around a sales force that knocked on restaurant doors and offered simpler deals. By its 2005 offering, the Princeton company handled card payments for tens of thousands of small businesses across the country.

sections.heading: Selling Door to Door
sections.body: Robert Carr founded Heartland in 1997 after years in the payments business. He saw a market of small and midsize merchants that big banks treated as an afterthought. Heartland paid its salespeople well, kept them for the long run, and focused on restaurants, a business that runs on cards. It later published a Merchant Bill of Rights, a pledge to show merchants every fee they paid. The company grew quickly in an industry known for hidden charges.

sections.heading: A Breach, Then a Buyer
sections.body: Heartland priced its offering at $18 a share in August 2005 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as HPY. In early 2009 it disclosed that hackers had broken into its systems and stolen card data, one of the largest breaches in history. The hacker Albert Gonzalez later went to prison for it. Heartland paid heavy settlements and pushed the industry toward end-to-end encryption. In 2016 Global Payments bought Heartland for about $4.3 billion.

cover.theme: harvesters in a wheat field (the heartland)

dek: Avenue A bought and tracked online ads for big brands, then grew into a $6 billion Microsoft purchase.
lede: Microsoft paid $6 billion for this Seattle ad company in 2007, and five years later wrote off almost all of it. The story began much smaller. Avenue A opened for business in July 1997, buying banner ads for marketers and measuring which ones made people click and buy. It worked out of the old Smith Tower downtown. In February 2000, with web advertising in a frenzy, it sold shares on Nasdaq under the ticker AVEA.

sections.heading: Counting Every Click
sections.body: Nick Hanauer and Scott Lipsky started Avenue A to bring discipline to online ad spending. Most marketers bought web ads the way they bought magazine pages, on hope. Avenue A placed ads across many sites, tracked each one with its own technology, and moved money toward what worked. In September 1999 it bought iballs, a New York internet media firm, to widen its client list. The company sold both the media buying and the measurement tools behind it.

sections.heading: A Write-Off in Redmond
sections.body: Avenue A priced its offering at $24 a share on February 29, 2000, and raised money just before the dot-com crash. Online ad budgets shrank and its stock collapsed. The company survived, renamed itself aQuantive in 2003, and grew again through Razorfish, its ad server Atlas, and an ad network. In 2007 Microsoft bought aQuantive for $66.50 a share, about $6 billion in cash, to fight Google in advertising. In 2012 Microsoft wrote down $6.2 billion tied to the deal.

cover.theme: a wet day on a city avenue (Avenue A)
cover.artwork: A Wet Day on the Boulevard, Paris

dek: Viatel sold cheaper international phone calls to businesses in Europe, routing them around the old national phone monopolies.
lede: In 1996, a phone call from Madrid to Milan could cost a small business a fortune, because each country's state monopoly set its own prices. Viatel lived in that gap. The New York company ran switches in London, Paris, Frankfurt, Rome and four other European cities, linked by leased fiber. It sold businesses long distance service at lower rates, often through callback, where a customer dialed in, hung up, and got a cheap line back.

sections.heading: An Argentine in New York
sections.body: Martin Varsavsky, an Argentine entrepreneur who had already started a real estate firm and a biotech company, founded Viatel in 1991. The company began with callback service and grew a switched network across Western Europe, with a hub in Omaha, Nebraska linked to London. Most of its customers were small and midsize businesses. The bet was that Europe's phone markets would open to competition, and that a nimble carrier already in place would win when they did.

sections.heading: Fiber, Then Chapter 11
sections.body: Viatel priced its offering at $12 a share on October 17, 1996, and listed on Nasdaq as VYTL, with Salomon Brothers leading the deal. Europe's markets did open, and Viatel borrowed heavily to build its own fiber network across the continent. The telecom boom turned to bust in 2000, and prices for long distance capacity collapsed. Viatel could not carry its debt. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in May 2001.

cover.theme: an ancient Roman road (via, a route across Europe)
cover.artwork: Part of the ancient Appian Way about three miles outside Porta San Sebastiano

dek: SpeechWorks let callers talk to automated phone systems in plain words instead of punching buttons.
lede: "Say the name of the person or department you want to reach." SpeechWorks printed that line inside the cover of its prospectus, with a caller's one-word answer: "Sales." It sounds ordinary now. In 2000 it was a leap past press-one-for-billing menus. The Boston company sold software that let airlines, brokers and banks answer the phone with a computer that understood spoken words, so callers could book tickets or trade funds just by talking.

sections.heading: Teaching Phones to Listen
sections.body: SpeechWorks was incorporated in Massachusetts in May 1994, with Michael Phillips as co-founder and chief technology officer. Its SpeechWorks 6 platform gave companies the recognition engine, tools and design help to build voice services in several languages. Phone lines were noisy and callers mumbled, so the company paired its software with teams that wrote and tuned each conversation. The bet was that businesses would trade expensive call-center staff for software that never put anyone on hold.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Nuance
sections.body: SpeechWorks priced its offering at $20 a share on August 1, 2000, and listed on Nasdaq as SPWX. It arrived as the dot-com crash was spreading, and buyers of new software pulled back. Revenue kept growing, but losses persisted. In 2003 ScanSoft, the company behind the old Xerox scanning software, bought SpeechWorks in an all-stock deal. ScanSoft later took the name Nuance Communications, and Microsoft bought Nuance in 2022.

cover.theme: a parrot (a machine that talks back)

dek: BladeLogic automated the chores of running thousands of data center servers, from setup to patches to audits.
lede: Two entrepreneurs-in-residence at rival venture firms teamed up in 2001 to fix a dull, costly problem. Big companies ran thousands of servers, and armies of administrators configured, patched and checked them one machine at a time. Mistakes caused outages and failed audits. Dev Ittycheria and Vijay Manwani founded BladeLogic to do that work with software. By its 2007 offering, banks and telecom carriers used it to run some of the largest data centers in the world.

sections.heading: Two Founders, Two VC Firms
sections.body: Ittycheria had been at Bessemer Venture Partners and Manwani at Battery Ventures before they started BladeLogic in Lexington, Massachusetts. Their product handled the full life of a server: provisioning it, rolling out changes, enforcing settings and proving compliance to auditors. It worked across Windows, Linux and Unix machines from one console. The timing helped. New rules like Sarbanes-Oxley forced companies to prove who changed what, and BladeLogic kept the record.

sections.heading: Seventeen Dollars, Then BMC
sections.body: BladeLogic priced its offering at $17 a share in July 2007 and listed on Nasdaq under BLOG. It was one of the last enterprise software offerings before the financial crisis. Less than a year later, BMC Software agreed to buy the company for $28 a share in cash, about $800 million, and closed the deal in April 2008. Ittycheria later became chief executive of MongoDB.

cover.artwork: The Swordsmith Munechika and the God of Inari

dek: Marimba pushed software updates to thousands of company computers at once, so IT staff never had to touch each machine.
lede: Four members of the team that launched Java at Sun Microsystems left in 1996 to start a company named after a musical instrument. Kim Polese had been Java's product manager. Arthur van Hoff, Sami Shaio and Jonathan Payne had written its code. Their company, Marimba, first promised to push live content to desktops over the internet. By its April 1999 offering, it had found steadier work: keeping software up to date on every computer a big company owned.

sections.heading: Push, Then Pivot
sections.body: Marimba's product was Castanet, named, like the company, for an instrument. Early on it was hyped as "push" technology that would beam channels of content to users. That craze faded fast. Marimba turned Castanet toward corporate IT, where it could deliver and update applications on thousands of machines automatically. Customers named in its prospectus included Bear Stearns, Charles Schwab, Home Depot, Intuit and Sun Microsystems. Polese ran the company as chief executive, a rare woman leading a hot startup.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars in April
sections.body: Marimba priced its offering at $20 a share on April 30, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as MRBA, at the height of the internet boom. When the bubble burst, spending on corporate software slowed and the stock sank far below its offer price. Marimba kept selling systems management software to large companies for five more years. In 2004 BMC Software bought it, folding Castanet into its own tools for running data centers.

tagline: Selling the Web's Leftover Ad Space
dek: Flycast bundled unsold ad space from hundreds of websites and sold it cheaply to advertisers who paid for results.
lede: Most websites in 1999 had more ad space than they could sell. Flycast bought the leftovers. The San Francisco company pooled unsold banner slots from more than 780 sites and resold them, unbranded, to direct marketers and online stores that cared about clicks and sales, not prestige. Sites earned money on space that would have sat empty. Advertisers got a big audience at a low price. In May 1999 Flycast took that idea to Nasdaq.

sections.heading: A Market Maker for Banners
sections.body: Flycast began operations in April 1996, when the web ad business was a few years old. It called itself a market maker for response-oriented advertising. Advertisers could buy across the whole network or pick categories, and Flycast's software reported what each campaign returned. Because the ads ran without the site's name attached, publishers could sell remnant space without undercutting their own sales teams. The bet was that web advertising would be judged like direct mail, by measurable response.

sections.heading: Swept Into CMGI
sections.body: Flycast priced its offering at $25 a share in May 1999 and listed on Nasdaq under FCST, in the thick of the dot-com boom. A few months later CMGI, the Massachusetts internet holding company, agreed to buy it in an all-stock deal. The purchase closed in early 2000, and CMGI folded Flycast into its Engage advertising business. When the bubble burst that year, the value of that stock fell with it.

dek: SimpleTech made memory modules and flash cards, then rebuilt itself as STEC to sell fast solid-state drives to data centers.
lede: SimpleTech's most prized idea was a way to stack memory chips on top of each other. Its patented IC Tower packed several chips into the footprint of one, a trick that mattered in crowded servers and routers. The Santa Ana company, run by the Moshayedi brothers, sold more than 2,500 memory, storage and connectivity products when it filed in 2000. Its CompactFlash cards went into early digital cameras and handhelds.

sections.heading: Brothers in Orange County
sections.body: Manouch and Mike Moshayedi co-founded Simple Technology in California in March 1990. The company bought standard memory chips and built them into modules and cards, some custom-made for equipment makers in networking, telecom and industrial gear. Memory was a brutal, cyclical business, where prices could halve in months. SimpleTech's edge was engineering: denser modules, stacked chips and rugged flash storage that bigger, cheaper rivals did not bother to make.

sections.heading: From Flash Cards to SSDs
sections.body: SimpleTech priced its offering at $11 a share in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq under STEC, just as the tech market turned down. Years later it sold its consumer products line, renamed itself STEC, and bet on solid-state drives for enterprise storage systems. Its ZeusIOPS drives sold well to large storage makers for a time. Competition grew fierce, and in 2013 Western Digital bought STEC for about $340 million in cash.

cover.artwork: The Pagoda at Zojo Temple and Akabane

tagline: A Radio Tuner on a Chip
dek: Microtune shrank the bulky radio tuner inside TVs and cable modems down to a single chip.
lede: Every cable modem, set-top box and digital TV needs a tuner, the part that picks one channel out of the crowded airwaves. For decades that meant a metal can full of hand-tuned parts. Microtune, a Texas startup, set out to put the whole thing on silicon. By its August 2000 offering, it sold radio frequency tuners and transceivers to makers of broadband gear, betting that every new device would need one.

sections.heading: Two Founders in Plano
sections.body: Douglas Bartek and John Norsworthy founded Microtune in Texas in May 1996 and started work that August. Norsworthy served as chief technology officer. Their idea was a radio frequency integrated circuit that did the job of a traditional can tuner, smaller, cheaper and easier to build into a product. The timing looked ideal. Cable modems and digital set-top boxes were spreading fast, and each one needed at least one tuner to receive video, data or voice.

sections.heading: Tuned Out in 2010
sections.body: Microtune priced its offering at $16 a share in August 2000 and listed on Nasdaq under TUNE. The telecom and tech slump hit soon after, and demand for broadband gear fell. Microtune kept selling tuner chips into TVs, cable boxes and car radios for the rest of the decade, as tuners moved onto silicon across the industry it had targeted. In 2010 Zoran, a California maker of digital TV and imaging chips, bought the company.

dek: Pixelworks made the chips that turn video and computer signals into sharp pictures on screens and projectors.
lede: While the rest of tech fought over the "last mile" of broadband, Pixelworks said it cared about the last meter: the short trip from the cable into the screen. The Oregon startup designed chips that took video, computer graphics and web pages and made them look right on flat panel monitors and projectors. It went public in May 2000, three years after it was founded, with its ImageProcessor chip already inside high-end displays.

sections.heading: Founded in Tualatin
sections.body: Pixelworks was incorporated in Oregon in January 1997, with Allen Alley as president, chief executive and chairman. The company bundled a whole display system onto one chip, with software that made it easy for manufacturers to use. It started with demanding products like high-resolution flat panels and multimedia projectors, where image quality sold the device. In December 1998 it launched its ImageProcessor chip.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars and Still Trading
sections.body: Pixelworks priced its offering at $10 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as PXLW. The stock rode the boom, then fell with the market. Over the next two decades the company kept adapting: projectors, then TVs, then image processors for smartphones, with much of its work centered in Shanghai. More than twenty-five years after its offering, Pixelworks still trades on Nasdaq and still files quarterly reports.

dek: SilverStream sold application servers, the software companies used to build and run their first serious web applications.
lede: In 1999 every large company wanted its own e-business, and most had no idea how to build one. Their data sat in old databases. Their programmers knew client/server tools, not the web. SilverStream sold the plumbing in between: an application server and tools for building web apps that took orders, handled supply chains and let employees serve themselves. The Massachusetts company went public that August, at the peak of the rush.

sections.heading: One Platform for E-Business
sections.body: David Skok founded SilverStream in 1996 and served as its chairman from the start. The company bet that businesses would move their core software onto the web, and would want one platform to build, deploy and manage those apps. Its rivals included BEA, IBM and a crowd of startups, all racing to own the application server, a new category. SilverStream pitched speed: developers could build working web applications fast without stitching together tools from many vendors.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then Novell
sections.body: SilverStream priced its offering at $16 a share in August 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as SSSW. The stock soared with the internet boom, then fell hard when it ended. Application servers became a standard feature, and BEA and IBM took most of the market. In 2002 Novell bought SilverStream for about $212 million, using its technology in Novell's web services products.

cover.theme: a silvery morning by the water (SilverStream)

dek: NetCreations rented lists of people who had agreed to get marketing email, in an age of spam.
lede: NetCreations had just 19 employees in June 1999, and five months later it was a public company. The New York firm ran a simple, timely business. Web users signed up to hear about topics they cared about, from cooking to computers, and NetCreations rented those opt-in lists to marketers. In a year when inboxes were filling with junk mail, permission was the selling point. NetCreations went public on Nasdaq that November.

sections.heading: Permission as a Product
sections.body: Rosalind Resnick and Ryan Scott Druckenmiller founded NetCreations in March 1995. In February 1996 they moved into opt-in email direct marketing and found a business that grew fast with very few staff. Partner websites invited visitors to check a box and pick their interests. NetCreations pooled those addresses into lists by subject and charged marketers for each message sent. Advertisers got readers who had asked to hear from them. Sites shared in the revenue.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Italy
sections.body: NetCreations priced its offering at $13 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq under NTCR, with Resnick as chief executive. The company was profitable, earning $1.3 million in the first half of 1999, a rarity among internet listings that year. When the dot-com market collapsed in 2000, its shares fell with everything else on the web. In 2001 Seat Pagine Gialle, the Italian yellow pages publisher, bought NetCreations in a cash deal.

cover.theme: a reader lost in the page (mail people chose to read)

fate: Renamed Authorize.Net Holdings; acquired by CyberSource, 2007
tagline: Signing Up the Cell Phone Boom
dek: Lightbridge helped wireless carriers sign up new customers fast and screen out the ones who would never pay.
lede: When a new cell phone customer walked into a store in 1996, the carrier had minutes to decide whether to trust them with a phone and a monthly bill. Lightbridge made that call. The Massachusetts company sold software and services that checked credit, flagged fraud and activated new subscribers. Nine of the 12 largest US cellular carriers were clients when it went public. A decade later it would turn itself into a different company entirely.

sections.heading: Credit Checks at the Counter
sections.body: Lightbridge began in June 1989 as Credit Technologies, founded by Torrence Harder and Michael Perfit, and took its new name in 1994. Pamela Reeve ran it as chief executive. Cellular carriers were adding subscribers as fast as they could, and bad debt and fraud ate into every new account. Lightbridge built systems to qualify, activate and keep customers. By its offering it served 34 wireless carriers, including the only two then running new digital PCS networks.

sections.heading: From Phones to Payments
sections.body: Lightbridge priced its offering at $10 a share in September 1996 and listed on Nasdaq under LTBG. Its business followed the wireless industry through mergers and consolidation, which shrank its customer list. In 2004 it bought Authorize.Net, a gateway that let small online merchants accept cards. The payments arm became the whole company: Lightbridge sold its telecom units and renamed itself Authorize.Net Holdings. CyberSource bought it in 2007, and Visa bought CyberSource in 2010.

cover.theme: lanterns crossing a bridge at night (Lightbridge)
cover.artwork: No. 37: Miyanokoshi, from the series "Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaido"

fate: Acquired by Hyperion Solutions, 2003; now part of Oracle
dek: Brio let office workers query and chart company data themselves, without filing a request with IT.
lede: Two former Arthur Young consultants started Brio in 1989 to fix a daily annoyance. Business people had questions about sales, costs and customers, and the answers sat in databases only programmers could reach. Every report meant a ticket and a wait. Brio's software let users ask the questions themselves, pull the data, and turn it into tables and charts. By its 1998 offering, the Palo Alto company sold to large enterprises across the country.

sections.heading: Pointing and Clicking at Data
sections.body: Yorgen Edholm and Katherine Glassey worked at Arthur Young in New York, where they co-founded a group that used personal computers to help managers make decisions from corporate data. At Brio, Edholm served as president and Glassey as an executive vice president. Their product, BrioQuery, put a friendly front end on corporate databases and ran within the systems companies already owned. Later versions reached users through the web and email. The pitch was freedom for business users and less work for the IT department.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars, Then Hyperion
sections.body: Brio priced its offering at $11 a share in May 1998 and listed on Nasdaq. The business intelligence market grew crowded, with Business Objects, Cognos and others chasing the same buyers. Brio grew through the boom, then struggled as tech budgets were cut after 2000. In 2003 Hyperion Solutions bought Brio to add reporting tools to its planning software. Oracle bought Hyperion in 2007.

dek: CoStar built the database every commercial real estate broker checks, then grew into Apartments.com and Homes.com.
lede: CoStar's researchers drove city streets photographing office buildings and phoning landlords to ask what space was empty. Nobody else bothered to collect it all. Andrew Florance started the company in 1987 to build that record of commercial real estate, and brokers came to depend on it. When it filed to go public in 1998, it was still called Realty Information Group, a Bethesda firm selling data to brokers, owners and lenders.

sections.heading: Knocking on Every Door
sections.body: Florance founded the company with backing from Michael Klein, who became chairman. Commercial real estate ran on scattered, private knowledge: who owned a building, what rent it asked, which floors stood vacant. The company paid researchers to gather it street by street and kept it current. Brokers paid subscriptions to search it. The bet was that one complete database, expensive to build and hard to copy, would become the industry's standard.

sections.heading: A Nine-Dollar Start
sections.body: The company priced its offering at $9 a share in July 1998 and listed on Nasdaq, later trading as CoStar Group under CSGP. It spent the next decades buying rivals and moving into rentals and homes, adding LoopNet, Apartments.com and Homes.com. It became one of the largest real estate data companies in the world. CoStar remains a public company on Nasdaq.

dek: EVERTEC runs the ATM and debit network and card processing behind much of Puerto Rico's daily spending.
lede: In Puerto Rico, paying with a debit card usually means using ATH, the island's own network, and EVERTEC runs it. The company grew up inside Popular, Puerto Rico's largest bank, processing card swipes, ATM withdrawals and bank systems. In 2010 the private equity firm Apollo bought a majority of it. When EVERTEC went public in April 2013, it was the largest merchant acquirer and payment processor in the Caribbean and Central America.

sections.heading: Spun Out of a Bank
sections.body: EVERTEC was organized in 1988 as Popular's technology and processing arm, serving the bank and many of its competitors. Apollo's purchase turned it into a standalone company, with Popular keeping a large stake and a long contract as its biggest customer. The business had three parts: merchant acquiring, which let stores take cards; payment processing, including the ATH network; and running core systems for banks and governments. Its home market was small, but EVERTEC owned much of it.

sections.heading: Twenty Dollars on the NYSE
sections.body: EVERTEC priced its offering at $20 a share in April 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as EVTC, raising about $505 million with selling holders. Apollo and Popular sold down their stakes in the years that followed. The company expanded across Latin America, buying payment businesses in Chile, Brazil and other markets. EVERTEC remains public on the NYSE, still headquartered in San Juan.

cover.artwork: View on the River Roseau, Dominica

dek: A10 Networks makes the gear that spreads web traffic across servers so busy apps stay fast and online.
lede: Lee Chen had already helped build one networking company, Foundry Networks, when he started another in 2004. His new firm, A10 Networks, made application delivery controllers, the boxes that sit in front of a data center and spread incoming traffic across many servers. They keep sites fast, fend off attacks and stop one overloaded machine from taking down an app. By its March 2014 offering, A10 sold to large web companies, carriers and enterprises around the world.

sections.heading: A Second Act for Lee Chen
sections.body: Chen founded A10 in San Jose to take on F5 Networks, the leader in load balancing. A10 built its Thunder line on its own operating system, aiming for more performance per dollar. It won customers among big internet firms and phone carriers, which ran enormous traffic and were sensitive to price. A10 also sold carrier-grade tools to help operators stretch their dwindling supply of old internet addresses.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars on the NYSE
sections.body: A10 priced its offering at $15 a share on March 21, 2014, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ATEN, raising $187.5 million with selling holders. Growth slowed after the offering, and the stock spent years below its debut price. A10 cut costs, focused on profit, and added security features to its products. It remains an independent public company on the NYSE.

dek: Calix sells small and rural internet providers the equipment and software to bring fiber broadband to homes.
lede: Calix shipped its first product in December 2001, more than two years after its founding and in the middle of the telecom crash. The Petaluma company built access equipment, the gear that links a phone company's network to homes and businesses over copper and fiber. Its best customers were small and regional providers, not the giants. When Calix went public in March 2010, many of those providers were using federal stimulus money to run fiber into rural towns.

sections.heading: Built in a Downturn
sections.body: Calix was founded in August 1999 and spent its early years building the C-Series, a platform that could deliver voice, data and video over either copper or fiber. Then the telecom bubble burst and carriers stopped spending. Calix survived by focusing on hundreds of independent and rural telephone companies across the United States. They needed to replace aging copper lines with fiber and wanted a supplier that would treat them as more than an afterthought.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Software
sections.body: Calix priced its offering at $13 a share in March 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under CALX, raising about $82 million with selling holders. In 2011 it bought Occam Networks, a rival in the same market. Hardware margins stayed thin. Under chief executive Carl Russo, Calix moved toward cloud software and services that help broadband providers market to and support their subscribers. It remains public on the NYSE.

dek: Galileo let travel agents book seats on hundreds of airlines from one screen.
lede: Before Galileo International sold a single share, it belonged to 11 airlines. United Airlines, British Airways, KLM, Swissair and US Airways were among the owners of this Illinois company. It ran the computer systems travel agents used to find a fare and book a seat, sold under the Galileo and Apollo names. In July 1997 the airlines took it public, and a piece of the plumbing behind every plane ticket went on the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: United's Apollo Meets Europe
sections.body: Galileo's roots go back to 1971, when United Airlines built Apollo as its own internal reservation system. United later rented Apollo terminals to travel agents. In Europe, a group of airlines built a rival system called Galileo. In September 1993 the two combined into one partnership, with headquarters in Rosemont, Illinois, near O'Hare. The business earned a booking fee each time an agent reserved a seat, a room or a rental car, and its screens sat in about 13,000 agency locations by 1997.

sections.heading: From Airlines to Cendant
sections.body: Galileo priced its offering at $24.50 a share in July 1997 and listed on the NYSE under the ticker GLC. The airline owners sold part of their stakes, and United stayed the largest holder. The internet soon pushed fares onto websites, yet those sites still needed systems like Galileo underneath. In June 2001 Cendant agreed to buy the company. The deal closed that October for about $1.8 billion in stock and cash, and Cendant also took on about $550 million of debt.

cover.theme: planets watching the sky (Galileo, the astronomer)
cover.artwork: Even the Planets are Watching with Interest the Arrival of the Famous Comet, plate 9 from La Comète De 1857

fate: Taken private by Silver Lake and TPG, 2007; public again since 2014 (NASDAQ: SABR)
dek: Sabre ran the reservation computer that travel agents, airlines and websites used to sell flights.
lede: Sabre started as American Airlines' answer to a mess of index cards. The airline and IBM built a computer system around 1960 to track who sat in which seat. By 1996 that system had grown into a business of its own, serving travel agents around the world and running a new website called Travelocity. That October, American's parent AMR sold a slice of Sabre to the public and kept the rest.

sections.heading: A Seat Map in a Mainframe
sections.body: American Airlines and IBM designed Sabre to replace clerks who tracked bookings by hand. It worked so well that American put Sabre terminals in travel agencies, where agents could book flights on many airlines. Every booking earned a fee. Sabre also ran American's own computer operations from its base in Fort Worth, Texas. By the mid-1990s Sabre was among the largest private computer systems in the world, with terminals in travel agencies on every continent.

sections.heading: Twice Through the Door
sections.body: Sabre priced its offering at $27 a share in October 1996. AMR kept about 82 percent of the shares and almost all of the votes. In 2000 AMR spun off its remaining stake to its own shareholders. Silver Lake and TPG took Sabre private in 2007, in a deal worth about $5 billion including debt. Sabre came back to the public market in April 2014 and still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker SABR.

fate: Taken private by HNA Group, 2016 (about $6B); public again since 2024 (NYSE: INGM)
dek: Ingram Micro bought computers and software by the truckload and resold them to the shops that served everyone else.
lede: Most people never heard of Ingram Micro, yet the PC on their desk had likely passed through one of its warehouses. The Santa Ana, California company sat between the makers of computers, printers and software and the thousands of resellers who sold them. In 1996 it was still owned by Ingram Industries, a Nashville family company. That November it went public as the world's largest wholesale distributor of computer products.

sections.heading: Boxes In, Boxes Out
sections.body: The business began in 1979 as Micro D, started in California by two schoolteachers, Geza Czige and Lorraine Mecca. Ingram Industries bought it in 1989 and merged it with its own distributor. The model was simple and hard to copy. Buy huge volumes from makers at a discount. Store them in giant warehouses. Ship them overnight to resellers who could never stock everything themselves. Margins were thin, so scale was everything. By 1996 Ingram Micro sold to customers in countries around the world.

sections.heading: Three Owners, Two Listings
sections.body: Ingram Micro priced its IPO at $18 a share in November 1996 and listed on the NYSE as IM. Ingram Industries then split the company off from the family business. Ingram Micro stayed public for 20 years. China's HNA Group bought it in 2016 for about $6 billion, and Platinum Equity bought it from HNA in 2021 for about $7.2 billion. In October 2024 Ingram Micro listed again on the NYSE at $22 a share, under the ticker INGM.

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: CRTO); moved its legal home to Luxembourg, 2026
tagline: The Shoes That Follow You Home
dek: Criteo showed shoppers ads for the exact products they had looked at and left behind.
lede: You look at a pair of shoes online, close the tab, and the same shoes follow you across the internet. Criteo, a Paris company, built a business on that trick, called retargeting. Its software watched what shoppers browsed on a retailer's site and bid to show them those products elsewhere. Advertisers paid only when someone clicked. In October 2013 Criteo became one of the few French tech startups to list on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: From Film Picks to Ads
sections.body: Jean-Baptiste Rudelle, Franck Le Ouay and Romain Niccoli founded Criteo in Paris in 2005. The company started as a movie recommendation engine. The founders found a better use for the same math: predicting which product a shopper would buy and when. Criteo charged retailers per click, so a store paid for results instead of views. That model won online retailers in Europe and the United States, and Criteo grew into one of the largest ad tech companies outside Silicon Valley.

sections.heading: Thirty-One Dollars on Nasdaq
sections.body: Criteo sold 8.1 million American Depositary Shares at $31 each on October 29, 2013, above a range it had already raised. It collected about $251 million. The stock closed its first day at $35.39, about 14 percent higher. Later threats came from browsers and phones that limited the tracking cookies retargeting depended on, and Criteo pushed into ads on retailers' own sites. It moved its legal home from France to Luxembourg in July 2026 and still trades on Nasdaq as CRTO.

cover.theme: a figure looking back (ads that follow you after you leave)
cover.artwork: Courtesan Looking Back at Shadows on the Shoji

fate: Sold its Russian business and was delisted from Nasdaq, 2024; renamed NanduQ
tagline: Paying Bills in Cash at the Kiosk
dek: Qiwi let Russians pay phone bills, loans and online purchases in cash at a kiosk on the corner.
lede: In 2013 most Russians still paid for things in cash, so Qiwi put a cash machine on almost every corner. Its bright kiosks stood in train stations and next to convenience stores. Feed in rubles and you could top up a phone, pay a loan or fund an online wallet. Qiwi counted over 169,000 kiosks and terminals and over 65 million monthly users when it listed on Nasdaq that May.

sections.heading: A Kiosk for Every Bill
sections.body: Qiwi formed in 2007 from Russian payment businesses led by Sergey Solonin. Its kiosks were built to Qiwi's design by outside makers and bought by over 9,300 independent agents, who placed and ran them and set the fees. The network linked cash-paying customers to over 40,000 merchants. Qiwi also ran Visa Qiwi Wallet, an online account people could load at a kiosk and spend on the web. The holding company sat in Cyprus, and the business ran from Moscow.

sections.heading: Sanctions and a Sale
sections.body: Qiwi priced its American Depositary Shares at $17 in May 2013 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker QIWI. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 brought sanctions and pressure on Russian listings. Nasdaq moved to delist the company in 2023. In January 2024 Qiwi agreed to sell its Russian business for 23.75 billion rubles. Nasdaq delisted the shares in September 2024, and shareholders renamed the company NanduQ.

cover.theme: Moscow from the Kremlin (a Russian payments network)
cover.artwork: View of the Stone Bridge from the Kremlin, from Views of Moscow

tagline: TV Ads Sold Like Search Ads
dek: MNTN let small and midsize brands buy streaming TV ads and see what sales they brought in.
lede: MNTN's chief creative officer is Ryan Reynolds, the actor behind Deadpool. He joined when MNTN bought Maximum Effort, his marketing studio. The Austin company sells software that puts ads on streaming TV and tracks whether viewers then visit a site or buy something. TV had been a medium for giant brands with giant budgets. MNTN pitched it to smaller companies as a channel they could measure, like search ads. It went public in May 2025.

sections.heading: SteelHouse Changes the Channel
sections.body: Mark Douglas founded the company in 2009 as Steel House, Inc. It began by helping marketers aim display ads at households across desktops and phones. In 2018 the team saw a shift coming in connected TV, the streaming apps on smart TVs and devices. They began building tools to buy those ads and link them to sales. The company took the name MNTN, said "mountain," and called its product Performance TV. It later added the QuickFrame creative marketplace along with Maximum Effort.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then Twenty-One
sections.body: MNTN priced 11.7 million shares at $16 on May 21, 2025, the top of its range, and raised $187.2 million. The stock opened on the New York Stock Exchange the next day at $21, about 31 percent higher, under the ticker MNTN. In the second quarter of 2026 revenue grew 21 percent from a year earlier. The company guided to $347 million to $357 million in revenue for 2026, and it still trades on the NYSE.

fate: Bought out by WorldCom (MCI), 2003; later part of Verizon
dek: Digex ran the servers behind big companies' websites so they did not have to build data centers themselves.
lede: When Microsoft, Cisco and Sun needed someone else to run their web servers, they called a company in Beltsville, Maryland. Digex built data centers, filled them with servers, and kept its customers' sites up around the clock. By mid-1999 it served over 500 customers, from big corporations to internet startups. Its parent, the phone company Intermedia Communications, had bought Digex two years earlier. That summer Intermedia sold part of it to a public that wanted every slice of the web it could get.

sections.heading: Renting Out the Server Room
sections.body: Running a busy website in 1999 meant buying servers, wiring them to fast lines and hiring people to watch them all night. Digex offered to do all of it. A customer's site lived on servers Digex managed in its own data centers, with its staff handling the networking, the security and the late-night failures. Intermedia Communications, a Tampa phone company, acquired Digex in July 1997.

sections.heading: Passed From Owner to Owner
sections.body: Digex sold 11.5 million shares at $17 each in the summer of 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as DIGX. Intermedia kept control. Then the owners kept changing. WorldCom agreed to buy Intermedia in September 2000 and closed the deal in July 2001, taking voting control of Digex with it. In 2003 WorldCom, which renamed itself MCI, bought out the remaining public shareholders. Verizon acquired MCI in 2006 and folded the hosting business into Verizon Business.

cover.theme: a corridor of rented rooms (web hosting)
cover.artwork: Interior of an Inn (The Corridor of an Inn)

dek: Altair let engineers test cars, planes and parts in software before anyone built a physical prototype.
lede: Altair spent 32 years as a private company before it sold a single share. Three engineers started it in 1985 near Detroit, the home of the car industry. Their software let designers bend, crash and heat-test a part on a screen before they built it. Carmakers, aircraft makers and electronics companies used it to cut the costly cycle of build, break and rebuild. Altair listed on Nasdaq in November 2017.

sections.heading: Three Engineers Near Detroit
sections.body: James Scapa, George Christ and Mark Kistner founded Altair in Michigan in 1985 as an engineering consulting firm. Their work for automakers turned into software, and the software became the business. Its tools model how a part behaves under stress, heat or a crash, and they help designers strip out weight while keeping a part strong. Altair, based in Troy, Michigan, sold licenses as a pool of units that customers could spend across its whole catalog.

sections.heading: Up 41 Percent, Then Siemens
sections.body: Altair priced its offering at $13 a share and raised about $156 million. The stock started trading on Nasdaq as ALTR on November 1, 2017, and closed its first day at $18.31, up 41 percent. Altair grew into data analytics and high-performance computing as simulation work moved to bigger machines. Siemens agreed to buy the company in 2024. It closed the deal in March 2025 at an enterprise value of about $10 billion.

cover.theme: an eagle (Altair, the brightest star in the Eagle constellation)

dek: Corio let midsize companies rent big business software over the internet instead of installing it themselves.
lede: In 2000 a company that wanted PeopleSoft or SAP had to buy servers, licenses and a team of consultants to make it run. Corio, of San Carlos, California, offered to rent it to them instead. It ran the software in its own data centers and customers reached it over the network for a recurring fee. The idea had a name, application service provider, and in the spring of 2000 Wall Street was eager to back it.

sections.heading: Big Software, Small Budgets
sections.body: Corio started in 1998. It hosted applications from PeopleSoft and SAP for human resources, finance and manufacturing, and from Siebel Systems for sales. A midsize company could get the same systems as a giant without building an IT department to run them. Corio set up the software, kept it running and charged a recurring fee. The pitch sounds like today's cloud software. The hard part was that each customer still needed its own setup, which made the work slow and costly.

sections.heading: A Dot-Com Price, an IBM Ending
sections.body: Corio priced its offering at $14 a share in July 2000, just after the dot-com peak, and listed on Nasdaq as CRIO. The timing was rough. Many young customers ran short of cash in the downturn, and the stock sank as the market for application service providers shrank. Corio kept going under chief executive George Kadifa. In January 2005 IBM agreed to buy the company for $182 million in cash, or $2.82 a share, to build out its own hosted software business.

cover.theme: a row of houses (software you rent instead of own)

dek: CacheFlow sold boxes that stored copies of popular web pages near users so the internet felt faster.
lede: On November 19, 1999, CacheFlow's stock rose about 426 percent in a single day. It was one of the biggest first-day jumps of the dot-com era. The Sunnyvale company sold caching appliances, boxes that kept copies of popular web pages close to users so they loaded faster and saved bandwidth. The founder behind it, Michael Malcolm, had already started Network Appliance. Wall Street wanted anything that promised to make the crowded web less slow.

sections.heading: A Copy Closer to Home
sections.body: Michael Malcolm enlisted Joe Pruskowski and Doug Crow, and CacheFlow was incorporated in March 1996. The idea was simple. Each time someone fetched a popular page from across the world, the trip cost time and money. A CacheFlow box sat in a company or internet provider's network, kept a nearby copy and served it to the next person who asked. Internet providers bought them to cut bandwidth bills. Companies bought them to speed up the web for their staff.

sections.heading: From Cache to Blue Coat
sections.body: CacheFlow priced its IPO at $24 a share and listed on Nasdaq as CFLO. The stock closed its first day near $126. When the bubble burst, demand for caching boxes fell hard. The company turned its boxes into security gateways that watched and filtered web traffic, and on August 21, 2002, it renamed itself Blue Coat Systems. Thoma Bravo took Blue Coat private in 2012. Bain Capital bought it in 2015, and Symantec acquired it in 2016 for $4.65 billion.

cover.theme: a gentleman in a blue coat (Blue Coat)
cover.artwork: Portrait of a Gentleman in Blue Coat

fate: Taken private by Veritas Capital and Elliott Management, 2019 ($5.7B)
tagline: Getting Doctors Paid Over the Web
dek: athenahealth took over the billing headaches of doctors' offices and got their insurance claims paid faster.
lede: athenahealth began as a women's health practice near San Diego that could not get insurers to pay its bills. Its founders, Jonathan Bush and Todd Park, built software to fix that, and the software became the company. By 2007 athenahealth ran billing for medical practices across the country from its base outside Boston. It did the work over the web, for a cut of what it collected. Its stock nearly doubled on its first day of trading.

sections.heading: The Clinic That Couldn't Collect
sections.body: Bush and Park incorporated the company in August 1997. Running their own practice taught them how much money doctors lost to denied and delayed insurance claims. Their answer was athenaCollector, a service that handled a practice's billing through software and a team that knew each insurer's rules. Doctors paid a percentage of what came in, so athenahealth only did well when they did. The company moved to Watertown, Massachusetts, and later added medical records and patient messaging services.

sections.heading: Ninety-Seven Percent on Day One
sections.body: athenahealth priced 6.3 million shares at $18 on September 19, 2007, above its $14 to $16 range. The stock opened on Nasdaq the next day at $30 under the ticker ATHN and closed at $35.50, up 97 percent. Shares kept climbing for years. In 2018 the activist investor Elliott Management pushed for change, and Bush stepped down that June. Veritas Capital and Elliott agreed in November 2018 to buy the company for $5.7 billion, taking it private.

dek: Tiger Brokers gave Chinese investors a phone app to buy US and Hong Kong stocks.
lede: Tiger Brokers counted Interactive Brokers and the phone maker Xiaomi among its backers. Its app let Chinese investors buy shares listed in New York and Hong Kong, markets that were hard for them to reach. The Beijing company began building in June 2014 under its founder, Wu Tianhua. In March 2019 it listed on Nasdaq itself, under its formal name, UP Fintech Holding.

sections.heading: An App for Overseas Markets
sections.body: Wu Tianhua started the business to serve a growing class of Chinese investors who wanted to own stocks like Apple or Alibaba directly. Tiger built the app, the research and the account tools in Beijing. The app charged low commissions and offered news and data in Chinese. Wu and his family held all of the Class B shares, which gave them voting control.

sections.heading: Eight Dollars, Then a Pop
sections.body: UP Fintech sold 13 million American Depositary Shares at $8 on March 19, 2019, above its range of $5 to $7, and raised about $104 million. The stock closed its first day at $10.92, up 36.5 percent, under the ticker TIGR. The company kept growing outside China as rules there tightened. In the second quarter of 2026 it reported record revenue of $182.3 million, 1.3 million funded accounts and $60.7 billion in client assets.

fate: Taken private by Thoma Bravo, 2021 ($2.4B); merged into Qlik, 2023
dek: Talend gave away software to move and clean company data, then sold the version big teams needed.
lede: Talend's free software had been downloaded more than two million times before the company sold a single share to the public. That was the plan. Developers found the open-source tools, used them to move data between systems, and brought them into their companies. Then Talend sold those companies a paid version with more power and support. The French startup, with offices near Paris and in Redwood City, California, listed on Nasdaq in July 2016.

sections.heading: Open Source as a Sales Team
sections.body: Bertrand Diard and Fabrice Bonan founded Talend in France in 2005. It launched its first product in 2006 and began selling subscriptions in 2007. The work it did was unglamorous and vital: pulling data out of one system, cleaning it and loading it into another. Talend's free version did the job for small projects and found its own users. The paid platform, Talend Data Fabric, was priced mostly by the number of users.

sections.heading: A 54 Percent Opening
sections.body: Talend priced 5.25 million American Depositary Shares at $18 on July 28, 2016, and raised about $94.5 million. The stock opened on Nasdaq the next day at $27.66 under the ticker TLND, 54 percent above the offer, and closed at $25.50. Talend moved its products to the cloud in the years that followed. Thoma Bravo agreed to buy it in March 2021 for $66 a share, about $2.4 billion. Thoma Bravo then combined it with Qlik, another company it owned, in 2023.

cover.theme: an old footbridge joining two banks (data integration)
cover.artwork: The Old Footbridge, Banks of the Petit Morin

tagline: Seagate's Old Plant, Reborn for Light
dek: Fabrinet builds the precise optical parts that move data through the fiber networks other companies design.
lede: Fabrinet filed to go public in 2007 and did not price its shares until June 2010. In between, the financial crisis shut the door on new listings. The company makes optical components on contract in Thailand: lasers, lenses and modules that turn electrical signals into light for fiber networks. Its founder, Tom Mitchell, had co-founded the disk drive maker Seagate. Fabrinet began life in a former Seagate factory outside Bangkok.

sections.heading: A Disk Drive Plant Turns to Optics
sections.body: Mitchell set up Fabrinet in the Cayman Islands in 1999. On January 2, 2000, it bought Seagate's Chokchai campus in Thailand and began building parts for Seagate's hard drives. He believed the same precision skills could serve the booming market for optical networking. Fabrinet shifted toward optics as the Seagate work wound down. Companies that designed lasers and fiber modules sent it their hardest jobs, and it also made its own glass, crystals, prisms and lenses.

sections.heading: A Cut Price, a Long Climb
sections.body: Fabrinet priced 8.5 million shares at $10 in June 2010, below its range of $12 to $14, and raised $85 million. It listed on the NYSE under the ticker FN. The discount aged well. Demand for fast links inside data centers grew, and then the artificial intelligence boom made optical parts scarce. In fiscal 2026 Cisco supplied 19.9 percent of Fabrinet's revenue and Nvidia 16.3 percent. The company employs more than 20,000 people and still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: fishermen hauling a net (Fabrinet, fabric and net)

fate: ID business sold to L-1 Identity Solutions, 2008; watermarking unit spun off, still public (NASDAQ: DMRC)
tagline: A Signature Hidden in the Picture
dek: Digimarc hid invisible codes inside images, money and packaging so machines could identify them.
lede: Digimarc's product was a mark you could not see. The Oregon company hid digital watermarks inside photos, printed pages and video, small changes to the pixels or ink that software could read and people never noticed. A watermark could prove who owned an image or link a magazine ad to a website. Geoffrey Rhoads founded the company in 1995. It went public in December 1999, at the height of the dot-com rush.

sections.heading: Invisible Ink for the Digital Age
sections.body: Rhoads incorporated Digimarc in Oregon on January 3, 1995, and built a pile of patents around one idea. Any picture could carry a hidden code that survived printing, copying and scanning. Photographers and stock-image libraries could track their work online. Publishers could let readers hold a printed page up to a webcam and jump to a website. Banks and governments wanted the same trick to fight counterfeit money and fake documents.

sections.heading: Split in Two, 2008
sections.body: Digimarc priced its offering at $20 a share in December 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as DMRC. Over the next years its largest business became secure ID systems, such as driver's licenses. In 2008 L-1 Identity Solutions bought that business. Before the sale closed, Digimarc spun its watermarking unit off to shareholders as a new company on August 1, 2008. The new Digimarc kept the name and the DMRC ticker, and still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a still mill pond (a watermark, hidden in plain sight)

tagline: Long Distance by Way of the Internet
dek: ITXC carried phone calls for other carriers over the internet, cutting the cost of calling overseas.
lede: In the spring of 1998 ITXC carried 47,000 minutes of phone calls in a quarter. A year later it carried over 11 million. The Princeton, New Jersey company ran a wholesale network that moved voice calls over the internet instead of costly international phone lines. Phone companies handed it their traffic and paid less to reach far-off countries. Tom and Mary Evslin had founded it only two years before it went public in September 1999.

sections.heading: A Couple and a Network
sections.body: Tom Evslin and his wife, Mary, started ITXC in July 1997 with seed money from AT&T and the Israeli internet phone company VocalTec. Their network, ITXC.net, linked gateways around the world that turned voice into data packets and back again. A carrier in one country passed a call to ITXC, which delivered it to a local partner at the other end. Calls to places with high international rates were where the savings were biggest.

sections.heading: Wholesale Voice, Sold Again
sections.body: ITXC priced its offering at $12 a share in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq under the ticker ITXC. Traffic kept growing as internet calling moved from novelty to normal, while prices per minute kept falling. In November 2003 ITXC agreed to merge with Teleglobe, an international carrier, and Tom Evslin was named non-executive chairman of the combined company. The deal closed in 2004.

cover.theme: a voice crying out (calls carried across the world)

tagline: A Cambridge Lab Wires Up DSL
dek: Virata designed the chips and software inside DSL modems that brought fast internet over ordinary phone lines.
lede: Virata started life in a university town, as a spin-out from the Olivetti Research Laboratory in Cambridge, England. By 1999 it ran its business from Santa Clara, California, and sold the chips and software inside DSL modems. DSL squeezed fast internet out of the copper phone lines already running into homes. Phone companies were racing to sell it. Virata went public that November, and its stock nearly doubled on day one.

sections.heading: From Olivetti's Lab
sections.body: Virata was incorporated in June 1993 in Cambridge as a spin-out from the Olivetti Research Laboratory, which later became part of AT&T. It spent its first two years developing technology. The company found its market in DSL, the service that let a phone line carry data and a voice call at once. Virata sold modem makers a chip together with the software to run it, so they could ship faster. It kept engineering teams in Cambridge and Raleigh, North Carolina.

sections.heading: Fourteen to Twenty-Seven
sections.body: Virata sold 5 million shares at $14 in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as VRTA. The stock rose to about $27 on its first day. The DSL rush lifted it higher, then the telecom crash cut orders. In 2001 Virata merged with GlobeSpan, a rival chipmaker, in an all-stock deal, with each Virata share swapped for 1.02 GlobeSpan shares. The combined company, GlobeSpanVirata, called itself the world's largest supplier of DSL chips and software.

cover.artwork: King's College Chapel, Cambridge, South Entrance

fate: Acquired by SnapAV, 2019 ($680M); now part of Resideo
tagline: One Remote for the Whole House
dek: Control4 let homeowners run their lights, music, TVs, locks and thermostats from one remote or phone.
lede: Control4 sold through custom installers who wired the system into a house room by room. Once it was in, one remote or phone app ran the lights, the music, the TVs, the thermostat and the door locks. The Salt Lake City company wanted to bring the smart home to ordinary buyers, well before voice assistants made it common. Its 2013 listing was arguably the first IPO of a pure home automation company.

sections.heading: The Home's Operating System
sections.body: William West co-founded Control4 in March 2003 with a goal of making home automation affordable for the mainstream. It began shipping products in 2005. Its controllers acted as the operating system of a home, tying together devices from many brands. Control4 sold mostly through a network of independent dealers who designed and installed each system. A feature called 4Sight let owners check on their homes from a phone or laptop while away.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars to Snap One
sections.body: Control4 priced its IPO at $16 a share in August 2013 and listed on Nasdaq as CTRL. The stock closed its first day at $20.05, valuing the company above $500 million. In 2019 SnapAV, a supplier to the same installers, bought Control4 for about $680 million, or $23.91 a share in cash. The combined company took the name Snap One and went public in 2021. Resideo bought Snap One in June 2024 for about $1.4 billion including debt.

cover.theme: a puppeteer working the strings (one controller for the whole home)

tagline: The Hidden Switch Behind New Phones
dek: Synchronoss ran the software that signed up and switched on customers for phone and cable companies.
lede: When Synchronoss went public in 2006, one customer, Cingular Wireless, made up about 75 percent of its revenue. The New Jersey company ran the back-office software that turned an online order for a phone or a service plan into a working account. Its ActivationNow platform handled the steps between clicking buy and getting a signal. Phone carriers and cable companies were pushing more sales online, and every sale needed that plumbing.

sections.heading: Orders In, Phones On
sections.body: Stephen Waldis founded Synchronoss in 2000 in Bridgewater, New Jersey. The company took orders from a carrier's website or store, checked them, and pushed them through billing, shipping and network systems until a customer's service was live. Its customers included Cingular Wireless, Vonage and Cablevision. Synchronoss charged per transaction, so it earned more as its customers sold more. Its reliance on Cingular was both its biggest strength and its biggest risk.

sections.heading: Eight Dollars, Then Lumine
sections.body: Synchronoss priced its IPO at $8 a share in June 2006 and listed on Nasdaq as SNCR. It later moved into cloud storage and messaging for carriers. In 2023 Lumine Group, a software buyer, purchased its messaging and NetworkX units. Lumine then agreed in December 2025 to buy the rest of the company for $9 a share in cash, about $116 million in equity value. The deal closed on February 13, 2026, and Synchronoss left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a clock tower (keeping systems in sync)

dek: Great Plains sold accounting software that helped small and midsize businesses keep their books.
lede: Doug Burgum mortgaged $250,000 of farmland to fund a small accounting software company in Fargo, North Dakota. He joined in 1983, when it had eleven employees, and became its president the next year. By 1997 Great Plains Software sold its Dynamics accounting products to small and midsize businesses through a network of resellers. That June it went public, a software company far from Silicon Valley with a sun-and-wheat logo.

sections.heading: Seed Money From the Farm
sections.body: Great Plains was founded in 1981 and built accounting software for personal computers when most businesses still kept books on paper or on costly minicomputers. Burgum's farmland stake put him at the center of it. His family group bought out the other owners in 1984. The company sold through local partners who installed and supported the software. Its Dynamics product lines ran general ledger, payables and payroll for growing firms.

sections.heading: Fargo Sells to Redmond
sections.body: Great Plains priced its IPO at $16 a share in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq. It grew to more than 2,000 employees. In December 2000 Microsoft agreed to buy the company for about $1.1 billion in stock, and the deal closed in April 2001. Burgum became a senior vice president running Microsoft Business Solutions. Its main product lives on as Microsoft Dynamics GP. Burgum later served as governor of North Dakota and became US Secretary of the Interior in 2025.

cover.theme: a grain harvest (the Great Plains, the sun-and-wheat logo)

tagline: Counting Every Visitor at the Door
dek: WebSideStory told website owners who was visiting, where they came from and what they did once there.
lede: WebSideStory filed to go public in 2000 and did not sell a share until September 2004. The dot-com crash came in between. The San Diego company sold web analytics, the tools that count a site's visitors and track where they click. Its HitBox service started as a free visitor counter for small sites. By 2004 it sold hosted analytics to businesses that wanted to know what their web traffic was worth.

sections.heading: A Hit Counter Grows Up
sections.body: Blaise Barrelet founded WebSideStory in San Diego in 1996. Its first hit was HitBox, a small piece of code that counted visits and showed site owners where traffic came from. The free version spread across the early web. The company then sold a paid version, and later HBX, to businesses that wanted detailed reports on what visitors read, clicked and bought. It ran the service from its own servers, so customers had no software to install.

sections.heading: From WebSideStory to Visual Sciences
sections.body: WebSideStory priced its IPO at $8.50 a share in September 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as WSSI. In 2006 it bought Visual Sciences, a maker of data analysis software, for $57 million, and a year later it took the Visual Sciences name. Omniture, a larger rival, agreed in October 2007 to buy the company for about $394 million in stock and cash. The deal closed in January 2008. Adobe bought Omniture in 2009.

cover.theme: a spectator watching the show (counting a site's visitors)

dek: Veritone let media companies and police search their audio and video using AI tools from many vendors at once.
lede: Veritone did not build one artificial intelligence. It built a switchboard for dozens of them. Its platform sent audio and video files to more than 40 engines from Google, IBM, Microsoft, Nuance and others, picked the best one for each job, and merged the results. Broadcasters used it to find every mention of a brand. Police used it to search body-camera footage. The Costa Mesa company went public in May 2017, years before AI became a household word.

sections.heading: Brothers Who Sold Radio Ads
sections.body: Chad and Ryan Steelberg founded Veritone in 2014. The brothers had built ad tech companies before, including a radio advertising startup they sold to Google. Their new idea was that no single AI engine was best at everything. One might transcribe speech well, another might spot faces or logos. Veritone's platform, later called aiWARE, chose among them and charged customers through a software subscription. It also ran an advertising agency business that placed ads for brands on radio and podcasts.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars and a Hard Road
sections.body: Veritone priced its IPO at $15 a share in May 2017 and listed on Nasdaq as VERI. The stock swung hard in the years that followed. The company sold its Veritone One advertising unit in October 2024 for up to $104 million. In June 2026 it began cutting at least a quarter of its workforce, and its shares traded near $1. Veritone still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a figure listening (AI that listens to audio and video)
cover.artwork: Saint Jerome Listening to the Trumpet of the Last Judgment

dek: Deltek sold accounting software built for companies that bill the federal government by the project.
lede: Deltek's name is short for deLaski Technologies, after the father and son who started it. Donald and Kenneth deLaski built software for a niche most vendors ignored: companies that work on government contracts. Those firms must track every hour and dollar by project, under strict federal rules. Deltek, based in McLean, Virginia, near Washington, did that bookkeeping. It went public in February 1997.

sections.heading: A Father, a Son, a Niche
sections.body: Donald and Kenneth deLaski founded Deltek in Virginia in 1983. Their customers were engineering firms, defense contractors and consultants that billed clients project by project, often under federal government contracts. Generic accounting packages could not handle the way those contracts required costs to be tracked and reported. Deltek's software could. At the IPO, Kenneth deLaski was chief executive and Donald deLaski was chairman, and together they kept a large stake in the company.

sections.heading: Four Owners in Twenty Years
sections.body: Deltek priced its IPO at $11 a share in February 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as DLTK. It left the public market in 2002. In 2005 New Mountain Capital bought 75 percent of the company, and Deltek went public again in 2007, raising $162 million. Thoma Bravo bought it in 2012 for about $1.1 billion. Roper Technologies bought it in late 2016 for $2.8 billion in cash.

fate: Acquired by Dicom Group, 1999 (about $75M); later renamed Tungsten Automation
dek: Kofax made the boards and software that let scanners turn stacks of paper into clean digital images.
lede: Every insurance form or bank check that went into a high-speed scanner in the 1990s had to come out as a clean, readable image. Kofax made that happen. The Irvine, California company sold image processing boards and software that sat between scanners and computers, cleaning up and compressing each page as it flew past. Its founders came from FileNet, an early document imaging company. Kofax went public in October 1997.

sections.heading: Two Engineers From FileNet
sections.body: David Silver and Dean Hough had worked together at FileNet before they started Kofax in 1985. Silver had helped develop the FileNet imaging system, and he became Kofax's chief executive. As scanners got faster, the computers behind them struggled to keep up. Kofax built accelerator boards that did the heavy lifting, plus scanner enhancement products that straightened and cleaned images. It sold through value-added resellers, system integrators and equipment makers who built document imaging systems.

sections.heading: Small Listing, Long Afterlife
sections.body: Kofax priced its IPO at $11 a share in October 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as KOFX. It was a small company, with fiscal 1997 sales of about $29.3 million. In July 1999 Dicom Group, a British imaging company, agreed to buy it for about $75 million in cash. Dicom later took the Kofax name for itself. The business moved its headquarters to Denver and now operates as Tungsten Automation.

cover.theme: a scribe copying a page (document capture)

dek: RetailMeNot found shoppers a working coupon code before they paid, and charged stores a cut of the sale.
lede: RetailMeNot traded under the ticker SALE, and it earned that name. The Austin company ran the largest digital coupon websites in the United States. Shoppers looked up a store, copied a code and saved money at checkout. Retailers paid RetailMeNot a commission on the sale. In 2012 its sites drew about 450 million visits, and more than 10,000 retailers paid to be on them. It went public in July 2013.

sections.heading: WhaleShark Buys a Brand
sections.body: Cotter Cunningham founded the company as WhaleShark Media, entered the coupon business in 2009 and set out to buy coupon sites. In 2010 it acquired RetailMeNot.com, a site that let anyone post and rate coupon codes. It bought others too, including VoucherCodes.co.uk in Britain and sites in France, Germany and the Netherlands. In 2013 the company renamed itself after its best-known brand. Over 90 percent of its 2012 traffic came from unpaid sources, such as search results.

sections.heading: Thirty-Two Percent, Then a Sale
sections.body: RetailMeNot sold 9.1 million shares at $21 on July 18, 2013. The stock began trading on Nasdaq the next day as SALE and gained about 32 percent on its first day. Growth slowed, and the stock drifted far below its offer price. In April 2017 Harland Clarke agreed to buy the company for $11.60 a share in cash, about $630 million, and folded it into its Valassis coupon business. Cunningham stayed on as chief executive.

dek: Globant built websites, apps and software for big companies using engineers across Latin America.
lede: In July 2014 Globant became the first Latin American software company to list on the New York Stock Exchange. Four friends had started it in Buenos Aires in 2003, just after Argentina's economic collapse. They saw that the country had skilled engineers who cost less than their American peers and worked in nearby time zones. Globant sold their work to global brands that needed apps, websites and games built well and fast.

sections.heading: Four Founders After the Crash
sections.body: Martín Migoya, Guibert Englebienne, Martín Umaran and Néstor Nocetti founded Globant in 2003. Migoya became chief executive. The company pitched itself as more than a cheap outsourcer. It organized engineers and designers into studios focused on areas such as games, mobile and user experience.
