It hired across Argentina and then in other Latin American countries, putting teams in the same working hours as clients in the United States.

sections.heading: Below the Range, Above It Later
sections.body: Globant cut its IPO price to $10 a share, below its $11 to $13 range, and sold 5.85 million shares. The stock began trading on the NYSE on July 18, 2014, under the ticker GLOB, and closed its first day at $11.25. The company grew for years through hiring and acquisitions. Growth flattened in 2026, and second-quarter revenue held at $614.4 million. Globant still trades on the NYSE.

cover.theme: a philosopher resting his hand on a globe (Globant)

dek: AutoNavi drew the digital maps of China that car navigation systems and phone apps used to find their way.
lede: China was building roads faster than anyone could map them, and AutoNavi set out to keep up. The Beijing company built a digital map of the country and sold it to carmakers for in-dash navigation, to makers of portable navigation devices and to internet companies. It had even made 3-D maps of key areas in 19 major cities. In July 2010 AutoNavi listed on Nasdaq under the ticker AMAP.

sections.heading: Survey Teams and Licenses
sections.body: Jun Hou, Congwu Cheng and Jun Xiao started AutoNavi in 2002, with a focus on map data for in-dash car navigation. Mapping in China required government licenses, which kept many foreign rivals out. AutoNavi kept updating its database as cities grew. It licensed the data to international and Chinese carmakers. It also offered location services for websites and phones.

sections.heading: Alibaba Takes the Wheel
sections.body: AutoNavi priced its American Depositary Shares at $12.50 in July 2010 and raised about $107.8 million. Alibaba bought about 28 percent of the company in 2013. In April 2014 it agreed to buy the rest for $21 an ADS, valuing AutoNavi at about $1.5 billion. Its app, Amap, became one of China's main navigation apps. Amap claimed 150 million average daily users in March 2023.

cover.theme: a winding road through the land (navigation)

tagline: A Cable Wrapped Around the Globe
dek: FLAG laid fiber-optic cable along the ocean floor so calls and data could cross continents.
lede: The company's name was its mission statement: Fiberoptic Link Around the Globe. FLAG Telecom owned undersea cable that ran from Britain through the Mediterranean and the Middle East to Asia. It sold that capacity to phone companies and internet carriers who needed to move traffic between continents. When it went public in February 2000, traffic on the internet was doubling fast, and investors were paying almost any price for the pipes that carried it.

sections.heading: Selling Space on the Seabed
sections.body: FLAG's business was simple to explain and expensive to build. Lay glass fiber across the ocean, then sell long-term rights to use it. Its first system linked Europe and Asia by way of the Middle East. The company was incorporated in Bermuda and sold to carriers on every stretch of the route. Its bet was that demand for bandwidth would keep rising faster than anyone could lay new cable.

sections.heading: Too Much Glass, Too Soon
sections.body: FLAG priced its offering at $24 a share in February 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as FTHL and in London as FTL. It sold more than 36 million shares. The bet on demand proved right, but so many rivals laid cable that prices for capacity collapsed. FLAG filed for Chapter 11 in April 2002 and emerged that October. In 2004 India's Reliance group bought the company for $207 million.

cover.theme: ships under flags (a sea route around the world)

fate: Renamed Worldpay, 2018; acquired by FIS, 2019; sold to Global Payments, 2026 ($24.25B)
tagline: The Bank's Card Machine Walks Out
dek: Vantiv moved the money every time a shopper swiped a card at a store, a gas pump or a website.
lede: Vantiv began life inside a Cincinnati bank as Fifth Third Processing Solutions. It sat between the card in a shopper's hand and the money landing in a merchant's account. Every swipe at a grocery store or gas station needed someone to approve it, route it and settle it, and Vantiv did that billions of times a year. In 2009 the private equity firm Advent International bought a majority stake and gave the unit its own name.

sections.heading: A Bank Sells Its Plumbing
sections.body: Fifth Third had built a payments business that worked for thousands of merchants and for other banks. Advent saw a company that could grow faster on its own than as a division. Vantiv's pitch was scale. Processing is a business of tiny fees on huge volume, and the biggest processors run the cheapest. Vantiv set out to win more small and midsize merchants, often through software companies that sold to them.

sections.heading: Three Owners in Seven Years
sections.body: Vantiv priced its IPO at $17 a share in March 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as VNTV. It raised about $500 million and rose nearly 15 percent on its first day. In 2018 it bought Britain's Worldpay and took that name. FIS bought the combined company in 2019 for about $43 billion. Global Payments bought Worldpay for $24.25 billion, closing in January 2026.

cover.theme: a shopper at the market (every purchase)

dek: Rent the Runway let women wear designer dresses for a night, or a month, without buying them.
lede: Rent the Runway started with a sister and a dress she could not afford. Jennifer Hyman watched her sister spend money she did not have on an outfit for a wedding. Hyman and her Harvard Business School classmate Jennifer Fleiss decided she should have been able to rent it instead. By the time the company filed to go public in 2021, it ran a subscription closet, shipped garments across the country and cleaned them in its own warehouses.

sections.heading: Two Jennifers and a Dry Cleaner
sections.body: The founders launched in 2009 by renting designer gowns for single events. They soon learned the hard part was logistics. Every dress had to go out, come back, get cleaned, get repaired and go out again, fast. Rent the Runway built one of the largest dry-cleaning operations in America to make that loop work. Later it added a monthly subscription, so a customer could treat its warehouse as her own closet.

sections.heading: A Pandemic, Then the Bell
sections.body: The pandemic emptied the calendar of weddings and office days, and the company cut deep. It came back to price its IPO at $21 a share in October 2021, listing on Nasdaq as RENT. The stock opened at $23 and closed its first day at $19.29. Losses and debt weighed on the shares for years. In October 2025 a recapitalization cut its debt to $120 million, and the stock still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a woman in a grand gown (the dress for the night)

fate: Renamed Moatable, 2023; moved from the NYSE to OTC, 2024
dek: Renren gave Chinese college students one place to post photos, share news and find their friends.
lede: Renren raised $743 million when it went public in May 2011, a big bet on a site whose name means "everyone." The site began as Xiaonei, a social network for college students started by Wang Xing, who later founded Meituan. Joseph Chen's company bought it in 2006 and renamed it Renren in 2009. By its IPO, tens of millions of young Chinese used it to keep in touch.

sections.heading: Everyone, on One Site
sections.body: Facebook was blocked in China, and Renren filled the gap. Students signed up with their real names and schools, then added classmates. Chen's bet was that the habits of a college network would follow users into work and adult life. Renren added games, a group-buying site called Nuomi and ads. The company argued it owned the social graph of China's most educated young people.

sections.heading: From Social Network to Software
sections.body: Renren priced at $14 a share for its ADSs in May 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as RENN. The stock touched about $24 and closed its first day at $18.01. Then mobile apps, led by Tencent's WeChat, pulled users away, and the shares slid for years. The company sold its Chinese social network and renamed itself Moatable in 2023. In 2024 its shares left the NYSE for the OTC market.

cover.artwork: Crowd Visiting Benzaiten Shrine at Enoshima in Sagami Province (Soshu Enoshima Benzaiten kaicho sankei gunshu no zu)

dek: Dangdang sold books to Chinese readers online, then grew into a general store shipped to the door.
lede: Dangdang's shares jumped 87 percent on their first day of trading in December 2010. China's biggest online bookseller had been started in 1999 by a married couple, Peggy Yu and Li Guoqing. They bet that Chinese readers would order books online, even if few of them had a credit card, and pay the courier in cash at the door. When Dangdang filed to go public, it had grown well past books into a broad online store.

sections.heading: Cash on Delivery
sections.body: Few Chinese shoppers had credit cards in 1999, and many did not trust paying online. Dangdang let them pay when the package arrived, so the risk sat with the company instead of the customer. It built its own warehouses and delivery network in cities across China. Books came first because they were cheap to ship, hard to break and easy to search. Over time the company added clothes, electronics and home goods to compete with a general store.

sections.heading: From Wall Street Back Home
sections.body: Dangdang priced its ADSs at $16 in December 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as DANG. The shares closed the first day up 87 percent. Then Alibaba's Tmall and JD.com spent heavily to win the same shoppers, and Dangdang's growth slowed. Its stock fell for years. In 2016 Yu and Li took the company private at $6.70 per ADS, less than half the IPO price.

dek: Longtop sold software and IT services to Chinese banks, until its auditor said the books were false.
lede: Longtop's auditor quit in May 2011 and said the company's financial records were false. Four years earlier, the Xiamen software maker had been one of the hottest Chinese listings in New York. It wrote the systems that Chinese banks used to run branches, process transactions and manage risk. China's banks were spending heavily to modernize, and Longtop pitched itself as the local supplier best placed to ride that wave.

sections.heading: Software for China's Banks
sections.body: Longtop was founded in 1996 in Xiamen, a port city on China's southeast coast. It sold banking software, plus the people to install and maintain it. Its pitch was that foreign vendors did not understand Chinese banks and local rivals were too small. Longtop reported fast growth and high profit margins, numbers that later drew hard questions. Goldman Sachs and Deutsche Bank led its offering.

sections.heading: Halted on the Big Board
sections.body: Longtop priced its ADSs at $17.50 in October 2007, above a range that had already been raised, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as LFT. The shares jumped on the first day. In 2011 short sellers questioned its numbers. That May its auditor, Deloitte, resigned, citing the falsity of the company's records. The NYSE halted trading when Longtop was valued at about $1.08 billion, and the stock never traded on the exchange again.

cover.theme: a Noh mask (a face that hides another)

tagline: Five Weeks From Bell to Buyout
dek: ArrowPoint built switches that sent each web request to the server best placed to answer it.
lede: ArrowPoint went public on the last day of March 2000, and five weeks later Cisco agreed to buy it for about $5.7 billion. The Massachusetts company made content switches. These boxes sat in front of a website's servers and read each incoming request, then sent it to the machine that could answer fastest. In the spring of 2000, every big site was straining under traffic, and that kind of gear was in hot demand.

sections.heading: Reading the Request
sections.body: Chin-Cheng Wu founded ArrowPoint in April 1997. Ordinary network switches looked only at addresses. ArrowPoint's switches looked at what a visitor was asking for, such as a page, a picture or a shopping cart, and routed it to match. That let a busy site spread its load, keep a shopper on one server and survive a failed machine. Wu had earlier co-founded Arris Communications and run engineering at Cascade Communications.

sections.heading: Cisco Pays in Stock
sections.body: ArrowPoint priced its IPO at $34 a share and began trading on Nasdaq as ARPT on March 31, 2000. In early May its stock jumped 27 percent in a day on rumors of a deal. On May 5 Cisco announced it would pay 2.1218 of its own shares for each ArrowPoint share. The deal was worth about $5.7 billion, Cisco's second-largest purchase after Cerent, and it closed later in 2000.

cover.artwork: A Young Man with an Arrow

dek: Finisar made the small modules that turn electrical signals into laser light for fiber-optic networks.
lede: Finisar's stock touched $106 on its first day of trading, more than five times its $19 offering price. It closed at $89. That November 1999 debut was among the biggest first-day gains in American market history. The Sunnyvale company made optical transceivers, small modules that convert electrical data into pulses of laser light and back again. Every data center and fiber network needed them, and the bubble made them look like gold.

sections.heading: A Small Part Everyone Needs
sections.body: Frank Levinson founded Finisar in April 1987, and Jerry Rawls joined him to run the business. They focused on the parts that connect computers and storage systems over fiber. The bet was that as data volumes grew, copper wires would run out of room and light would take over. Finisar made its modules in volume and sold them to the companies that built switches, routers and storage gear.

sections.heading: Boom, Bust and Back
sections.body: Finisar priced at $19 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as FNSR. Rawls later said the first-day jump ranked seventh in the history of American exchanges. The telecom crash in 2001 crushed demand, and the stock fell below $1. Finisar survived, bought rivals and grew with cloud data centers. In 2019 II-VI bought it for about $3.2 billion, and II-VI later took the name Coherent.

tagline: More Channels Down the Same Wire
dek: BigBand sold cable companies the gear to squeeze more TV channels and faster internet through their networks.
lede: A cable network has room for only so many channels, and in 2007 every operator wanted more of them in high definition. BigBand Networks sold the equipment that made the room. Its gear sent a channel down the wire only when someone in a neighborhood was actually watching it. That freed space for more HD channels and faster internet. Founded by Amir Bassan-Eskenazi and Ran Oz, the company had engineering roots in Israel.

sections.heading: Only the Channels You Watch
sections.body: The old cable model broadcast every channel to every home all the time. BigBand's switched digital video turned that around. When a viewer tuned in, the system sent that channel to that part of the network. When nobody watched, the space went to something else. Cable operators facing satellite rivals and phone companies bought it to add HD without rebuilding their plant.

sections.heading: A Sale for Its Cash
sections.body: BigBand priced its IPO at $13 a share in March 2007 and raised $139 million on Nasdaq as BBND. Sales depended on a handful of big cable customers, and orders swung from quarter to quarter. The stock sank well below its offering price. In October 2011 ARRIS agreed to buy BigBand for $2.24 a share in cash, about $172 million. Net of BigBand's cash, the price was about $53 million.

dek: Prodigy brought millions of American families online, first as a walled garden and later as a dial-up provider.
lede: Prodigy was online before most Americans had heard the word. IBM and Sears started it in 1984, with CBS as an early partner, to sell news, shopping and email to families with a home computer and a modem. It peaked early and lost ground to AOL. By the time it went public in February 1999, Prodigy had remade itself as a plain internet service provider, with Mexico's Telmex as a major shareholder.

sections.heading: IBM and Sears Dial In
sections.body: The first Prodigy was a closed service with its own screens, banner ads and catalogs. Users paid a monthly fee for news, weather, banking and messages. It signed up more than a million homes but cost its owners a fortune. In 1996 a new investor group bought it and shifted to the open web. The new Prodigy sold dial-up access and bet on its old brand to win customers.

sections.heading: Telmex Takes a Seat
sections.body: Prodigy priced its IPO at $15 a share in February 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as PRGY. Telmex, run by Carlos Slim's group, bought 2 million shares directly and owned about 19 percent of the company. Prodigy also advised Telmex on its own internet service in Mexico. In 2001 SBC Communications bought out the rest of Prodigy, paying $6.60 a share after raising its first offer.

dek: Qlik let ordinary business people click through their company's data and find answers without waiting on IT.
lede: Qlik was born in Lund, a Swedish university town, and grew up in suburban Philadelphia. Its product, QlikView, loaded a company's data into memory so a manager could click on a region or a product and see every related number change at once. Older business intelligence tools needed specialists to build each report. When Qlik went public in July 2010, the market was still shaky from the financial crisis, and tech IPOs were rare.

sections.heading: Click, and the Numbers Follow
sections.body: Björn Berg and Staffan Gestrelius founded the company in Sweden in 1993. Its software kept data in a computer's memory and linked every field to every other, so a user could explore instead of asking a fixed question. Qlik sold to the department first, often to a sales or finance team, and then spread across the company. It moved its headquarters to Radnor, Pennsylvania, to chase the American market.

sections.heading: A Bright Week in a Gray Year
sections.body: Qlik priced at $10 a share in July 2010, above its expected range, and listed on Nasdaq as QLIK. It raised $112 million, and the shares rose about 28 percent on the first day. CEO Lars Björk rang the opening bell. Qlik grew for years but faced Tableau and cheaper cloud tools. In 2016 Thoma Bravo took it private for about $3 billion, and Qlik remains privately held.

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: NCTY); now a bitcoin miner
dek: The9 ran online games for Chinese players, most famously World of Warcraft, before turning to bitcoin mining.
lede: For four years, millions of Chinese gamers entered World of Warcraft through a Shanghai company called The9. Jun Zhu founded it in 1999, when online games were becoming the main way young Chinese spent time on the internet. The9 licensed big foreign titles and ran the servers, billing and customer service inside China. It went public in December 2004, just as it was preparing to launch Blizzard's new game.

sections.heading: Renting Out Other People's Worlds
sections.body: The9's model was to operate games that others had made. Foreign studios needed a local partner to deal with Chinese rules, payments and players. The9 paid for the license and earned its money from players' time cards and fees. World of Warcraft launched in China in 2005 and became its main business. The bet was that the best games would keep coming to the best operator.

sections.heading: From Azeroth to Bitcoin
sections.body: The9 priced its ADSs at $17 in December 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as NCTY. In 2009 Blizzard moved World of Warcraft to NetEase, and The9 lost most of its revenue. It spent years trying new games without a hit. In 2021 it turned to crypto mining, and the stock jumped. As of July 2026 it held 285 bitcoin, and Jun Zhu still runs the company.

cover.artwork: Snake (Mi): Nitan Shiro, from the series "Heroes for the Twelve Animals of the Zodiac (Buyu mitate junishi)"

dek: Taleo gave big employers web software to post jobs, sort applicants and manage hiring from one place.
lede: Taleo started as a French-language job board in Quebec City. In 1996 Martin Ouellet launched Viasite to match candidates and employers in Quebec. The company became Recruitsoft, moved its base to California and sold software that let large companies run their whole hiring process on the web. It filed to go public in 2004 under its new name, Taleo, and listed the following year, a slow road to the market.

sections.heading: From Quebec Job Board
sections.body: Louis Têtu co-founded the business and led it as CEO from 1999. The idea was to rent software over the internet instead of selling it to be installed. Big employers received thousands of applications for each opening. Taleo's system let recruiters post jobs, screen applicants and track every candidate. Customers paid a subscription, an early version of what later came to be called software as a service.

sections.heading: Oracle Comes Calling
sections.body: Taleo priced its IPO at $14 a share in September 2005 and listed on Nasdaq as TLEO. It added tools to manage performance and pay, and bought rivals to grow. Its subscription model put it in the sights of the big software houses. In February 2012 Oracle agreed to buy Taleo for $1.9 billion, and Taleo became part of Oracle's cloud suite.

cover.theme: workers in the field (talent at work)

dek: Uproar ran free web games and online game shows, paid for by ads and prizes.
lede: Uproar put Family Feud on the web. The New York company licensed classic TV game shows and ran them as free online games, along with bingo, trivia and puzzles. In December 1999, 3.6 million people visited its sites in a single month. Its shares already traded in Europe on EASDAQ. In March 2000, at the top of the dot-com market, Uproar sold stock to American investors at $33.88 a share.

sections.heading: Game Shows Without a Studio
sections.body: Uproar was founded in February 1995 and launched uproar.com in September 1997. Its pitch was time on site. People who played games stayed longer than people who read news, and advertisers paid for that attention. Uproar ran sites in 14 languages and offered PrizePoints, a currency players earned and spent on drawings and prizes. Its operations stretched from the United States to Hungary, Germany and Britain.

sections.heading: Thirty-Three Dollars to Three
sections.body: Uproar priced its American offering at $33.88 a share in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as UPRO. It bought iwin.com that October, and revenue rose to $33.7 million for 2000. Losses were larger, and online ad spending collapsed. The stock fell below $1. In 2001 Vivendi Universal's Flipside unit bought Uproar for $3 a share, about $140 million. Kenneth Cron, Uproar's CEO, took charge of the combined company.

cover.artwork: At the Circus: Trained Pony and Baboon

dek: Responsys let big brands send millions of personal marketing emails and texts, and track who responded.
lede: Responsys chose MKTG as its ticker, which told investors exactly what it sold. The San Bruno company ran email campaigns for big consumer brands. Its software sent millions of messages, tailored each one to the reader and tracked every open and click. By its 2011 IPO, marketers were moving budgets from print and TV to the inbox and the phone, and they wanted one system to run it all.

sections.heading: Email at Industrial Scale
sections.body: Responsys was founded in 1998, early in the age of email marketing. Most companies then blasted the same message to everyone. Responsys bet that marketers would pay for tools to target and time each message, and to coordinate email with texts, social posts and display ads. It sold its software as a hosted service. In 2010 it booked $94 million in sales.

sections.heading: Priced High, Sold Higher
sections.body: Responsys priced its IPO at $12 a share in April 2011, above its expected range of $8.50 to $10. It listed on Nasdaq as MKTG and rose about 28 percent on its first day. Large software makers were racing to build marketing clouds. In December 2013 Oracle agreed to buy Responsys for about $1.5 billion, and the deal closed in early 2014.

cover.theme: a letter being read (the marketing message)
cover.artwork: The Letter, or The Spanish Conversation

dek: Official Payments let Americans pay taxes, fines and government fees with a credit card, by phone or online.
lede: In 1999 the IRS started letting Americans pay their income taxes with a credit card, and Official Payments ran the system. The California company charged a convenience fee on each payment, so the government paid nothing. It handled property taxes, parking tickets and court fines for state and local governments too. When it went public that November, it was a small company with one giant customer and a bank as its majority owner.

sections.heading: A Phone Line Finds a New Job
sections.body: The business grew out of a company founded in 1986 to run phone systems for classified advertising. In 1996 it dropped that work to focus on government payments. Imperial Bank, its majority owner, gave it access to the card networks. The bet was that millions of citizens would pay a small fee for the convenience of a card, and that governments would welcome payments that cost them nothing to accept.

sections.heading: Sold for Three Dollars
sections.body: Official Payments priced its IPO at $15 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as OPAY. Revenue swung with tax season and leaned on a few big contracts. Its shares sank with the rest of the dot-com market. In 2002 Tier Technologies bought it for $3 a share in cash, about $74.5 million, gaining more than 1,200 government clients and the IRS contract.

cover.theme: a satire of the income tax (paying the taxman)

tagline: The Linux Company That Sued Linux
dek: Caldera sold a business-friendly version of Linux, then became SCO and sued IBM over the code.
lede: The company that sold Linux to businesses later spent years suing over it. Caldera Systems of Orem, Utah, packaged the free Linux operating system for companies and backed it with support. It went public in March 2000, one of a run of hot Linux IPOs after Red Hat and VA Linux. Two years later it had renamed itself SCO Group, and in 2003 it sued IBM, claiming Linux contained its Unix code.

sections.heading: Linux in a Box
sections.body: Ransom Love and Bryan Sparks founded Caldera in 1994 with backing from Ray Noorda, the former Novell chief. They saw Linux as a cheap, open rival to Windows and Unix for business servers and desktops. Caldera sold its own version, OpenLinux, with installation tools and support contracts. The bet was that companies would trust free software once a real company stood behind it.

sections.heading: From Open Source to Courtroom
sections.body: Caldera priced its IPO at $14 a share, above its first range of $7 to $9, and listed on Nasdaq as CALD. The stock opened at $26 and closed at $29.44, more than double. Sales never matched the hype. Caldera bought SCO's Unix business and took the SCO name in 2002. Its lawsuits against IBM and Linux users went badly, and SCO Group filed for bankruptcy in 2007.

dek: Endava built and ran software for banks, payment firms and media companies, using engineers across Central and Eastern Europe.
lede: A London company with most of its engineers in Romania, Moldova and the Balkans chose New York for its IPO. Endava wrote and maintained software for banks, payment companies, telecoms and media firms. Its engineers worked in delivery centers close to Western Europe in time zone and culture. In July 2018, when it listed, every big company was trying to rebuild itself around software, and good engineers were scarce and expensive in London and New York.

sections.heading: A Short Flight Away
sections.body: John Cotterell led Endava from its start in 2000. Indian outsourcers sent work across many time zones. Endava kept its engineers a short flight from its clients, so teams could work the same hours and meet in person. It focused on newer work, such as mobile apps, cloud systems and data, instead of keeping old systems running. Payments and banking clients made up a large share of its revenue.

sections.heading: A Strong Start, Then a Slide
sections.body: Endava priced its ADSs at $20 in July 2018, above its expected range, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as DAVA. The shares rose 26 percent on the first day. Demand for digital projects boomed through the pandemic, and the stock climbed for three years. Then clients cut spending, and the shares fell hard. By August 2026 they traded near $3, and Endava remains public.

dek: Novatel Wireless made modems that put laptops on cell networks, then the MiFi hotspot that shared that connection.
lede: Novatel Wireless later made the MiFi, the pocket hotspot that turned a cell signal into Wi-Fi for anyone nearby. In November 2000, when it went public, that was years away. The San Diego company sold wireless modems that let laptops and handheld computers reach the internet over cell networks. Those networks were slow and mobile data was costly, but carriers were promising faster service soon.

sections.heading: Modems for the Road
sections.body: Novatel Wireless was formed in 1996 to build wireless data devices. Its early products were modem cards that slid into a laptop and connected to a cellular network. The bet was that business travelers would pay to stay online away from the office. The company sold through carriers and device makers, so its fortunes rose and fell with each new generation of cell networks.

sections.heading: Hotspots, Then Inseego
sections.body: Novatel Wireless priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as NVTL, just as the tech crash began. It survived on carrier deals and launched the MiFi hotspot with Verizon in 2009. In 2016 it reorganized as Inseego and focused on 5G hotspots and fixed wireless gear for businesses. It still trades on Nasdaq as INSG and has agreed to buy Nokia's fixed wireless access business.

tagline: Consultants for the Web Gold Rush
dek: Viant built websites and online strategies for big companies racing to get onto the internet.
lede: Viant started in San Francisco as Silicon Valley Internet Partners and moved to Boston within months. It was one of the internet consultancies that big companies hired in a hurry as the web arrived. Viant sent teams of strategists, designers and engineers to plan and build online stores and services. When it went public in June 1999, clients were lining up, and firms like it were among the stock market's favorites.

sections.heading: Strategy, Design and Code
sections.body: Viant was founded in 1996. In mid-1996 Robert Gett became CEO and moved the headquarters to Boston. The firm's pitch was that one team could handle the business plan, the look of the site and the technology behind it. It opened offices in San Francisco, New York, Chicago, Dallas and Los Angeles. Its bet was that every large company would need help moving its business online.

sections.heading: When the Clients Stopped Calling
sections.body: Viant priced its IPO at $16 a share in June 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as VIAN. Much of the demand for firms like Viant came from dot-com startups and from older companies spending to fight them. When the bubble burst in 2000, those budgets vanished. Viant cut staff in several rounds between 2000 and 2002. In 2002 divine bought it in a stock deal worth about $96 million.

cover.theme: figures crossing a bridge (the passage online)
cover.artwork: Landscape with Figures Crossing a Bridge

fate: Taken private by Thoma Cressey Bravo, 2007; part of Idera since 2015
tagline: Tools for the People Who Guard the Database
dek: Embarcadero sold database administrators software to design, tune and manage the databases companies ran on.
lede: Embarcadero took its name from the San Francisco waterfront and sold tools to some of the least glamorous people in tech. Database administrators kept a company's orders, customers and accounts alive. Embarcadero gave them software to design databases, move changes safely and find slow queries. It went public in April 2000, weeks after the Nasdaq peak, selling the kind of plain, useful software that outlasts a bubble.

sections.heading: One Tool for Every Database
sections.body: Stephen Wong, Stuart Browning and Nigel Myers founded Embarcadero in October 1993. Big companies ran databases from Oracle, Microsoft, IBM and Sybase side by side, each with its own tools. Embarcadero's bet was that administrators would pay for one set of tools that worked across all of them. Products like DBArtisan and ER/Studio became standard kit in many corporate IT departments.

sections.heading: Private Hands, Then Delphi
sections.body: Embarcadero priced its IPO at $10 a share in April 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as EMBT. It rode out the crash as a small public company. In 2007 the private equity firm Thoma Cressey Bravo bought the company and took it private. A year later Embarcadero bought CodeGear, the Borland unit behind the Delphi programming tools. In 2015 it became part of Idera.

cover.theme: a ferry at the landing (embarcadero means a boat landing)
cover.artwork: Ferry boat on the Yodo River

dek: Yesmail sent marketing emails only to people who had signed up to get them.
lede: Yesmail built a business on one word: yes. In 1999, inboxes were filling with spam, and marketers wanted a way to reach people without making them angry. The suburban Chicago company sent offers by email only to people who had opted in to hear about a topic, such as travel or computers. Advertisers paid for each message. It went public that September, and three months later CMGI agreed to buy it.

sections.heading: From WebPromote to Yes
sections.body: The company was founded in 1995 as a supplier of internet marketing services, and later ran under the name WebPromote. In April 1999 it renamed itself yesmail.com to match its new focus. The idea was permission email. Users picked subjects they cared about, and Yesmail matched them with advertisers. Marketers got better response rates, and readers got fewer messages they did not want.

sections.heading: Three Months to a Buyer
sections.body: Yesmail priced its IPO at $11 a share in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as YESM. In December, CMGI, the Massachusetts internet holding company, agreed to buy it in a stock deal. The purchase closed in March 2000 at about $520 million. infoUSA bought Yesmail in 2003. In 2006 the company paid $50,717 to settle FTC charges under the CAN-SPAM Act.

fate: Sold its website to Salon.com LLC, 2019 ($5M)
tagline: A Magazine Born on the Web
dek: Salon published sharp political and cultural writing online, years before most print magazines took the web seriously.
lede: Salon sold itself for $5 million in 2019, twenty years after investors valued it far higher at its IPO. In 1995 David Talbot, an editor at the San Francisco Examiner, started one of the first serious magazines made only for the web. It published essays, criticism, politics and long interviews, free to read and paid for by ads. When it went public in June 1999, investors were betting that great writing would draw great ad money online.

sections.heading: A Newsroom Without Paper
sections.body: Talbot and a small group of journalists launched Salon in November 1995. Their bet was that the web could carry the writing of a good magazine without the cost of printing and mailing it. Salon built a loyal audience and a reputation for scoops and voice. It also learned early that web ads paid far less than print ads for the same readers.

sections.heading: Twenty Years of Hard Math
sections.body: Salon priced its IPO at $10.50 a share on June 22, 1999, with W.R. Hambrecht as lead underwriter, and listed on Nasdaq as SALN. The dot-com ad crash hit it hard, and the company lost money for years. It tried paid subscriptions and cut staff again and again. In 2019 Salon Media Group sold the website and its other assets to Salon.com LLC for $5 million.

cover.theme: a crowded Paris salon (a salon of ideas)
cover.artwork: View of the Salon in the Louvre in the Year 1753

fate: Became Rovi, 2009; TiVo, 2016; merged with Xperi, 2020
tagline: The Signal That Ruined Your Copy
dek: Macrovision put a hidden signal on rented videotapes that made home copies roll, flicker and fade.
lede: If you ever tried to copy a rented movie and got a picture that rolled and faded, you met Macrovision. The Sunnyvale company added a hidden signal to videotapes that a TV ignored but a VCR could not record cleanly. Hollywood studios paid a small fee per tape to protect their releases. When Macrovision went public in March 1997, the DVD was just arriving, and the studios needed the same protection for a new format.

sections.heading: The Cotton Club Goes First
sections.body: John O. Ryan and Victor Farrow founded Macrovision in 1983 to build video security. The first tape to carry its signal was The Cotton Club, released on video in 1985. The bet was that studios would pay a few cents a copy to stop casual piracy. They did, and Macrovision licensed its system to tape duplicators and, later, to the makers of DVD players and set-top boxes.

sections.heading: A Name That Kept Changing
sections.body: Macrovision priced its IPO at $9 a share in March 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as MVSN. Over the next decade it spread from copy protection into software licensing and digital rights. In 2008 it bought Gemstar-TV Guide and renamed itself Rovi in 2009. Rovi bought TiVo in 2016 for about $1.1 billion and took its name. TiVo then merged with Xperi in 2020.

cover.theme: a painted curtain hiding the picture (copy protection)
cover.artwork: Trompe-l'Oeil Still Life with a Flower Garland and a Curtain

tagline: Millions of Small Websites, One Landlord
dek: Endurance hosted websites for millions of small businesses under brands like Bluehost and HostGator.
lede: If you built a small business website in the 2010s, there was a good chance Endurance International hosted it, even if you never heard the name. The Massachusetts company owned dozens of hosting brands, including Bluehost and HostGator. It bought rivals, moved their customers onto shared systems and sold them add-ons like domains, email and security. When it went public in October 2013, it was one of the largest web hosts in the world.

sections.heading: A Roll-Up of the Web
sections.body: Hari Ravichandran founded Endurance in 1997. The company grew by buying other hosting companies, often with backing from private equity owners. The bet was scale. Hosting a small website earns a few dollars a month, so the winner is the company that serves the most sites at the lowest cost. Endurance kept each brand's name and storefront while it merged what ran underneath.

sections.heading: Subscribers Under Scrutiny
sections.body: Endurance priced its IPO at $12 a share in October 2013 and listed on Nasdaq as EIGI. It raised about $252 million. Growth slowed in the years after the offering. In 2018 the company paid an $8 million penalty to settle SEC charges that it had overstated subscriber numbers. In 2021 Clearlake Capital took it private for about $3 billion and combined it with Web.com to form Newfold Digital.

cover.theme: a ship in Arctic ice (Shackleton's Endurance)

dek: Workiva gave finance teams one cloud tool to write, check and file their reports with regulators.
lede: The software many public companies use to file their SEC reports came out of Ames, Iowa. Workiva, first called WebFilings, sold cloud software for the reports public companies must file with the SEC. Finance teams used it to pull numbers from many spreadsheets into one document, update them everywhere at once and tag the data for the regulator. Several of its founders had already taken a software company public in the 1990s.

sections.heading: Second Time Around in Iowa
sections.body: WebFilings was formed in 2008. Matt Rizai, Marty Vanderploeg and Jeff Trom were among its founders, and members of the team had earlier built Engineering Animation. The SEC was about to require companies to tag their financial data in a format called XBRL. WebFilings bet that finance teams would want one shared, online workspace to handle it instead of emailing files back and forth before every deadline.

sections.heading: A Quiet Debut
sections.body: The company renamed itself Workiva in 2014. It priced its IPO at $14 a share in December 2014, the middle of its range, and raised about $101 million on the New York Stock Exchange as WK. The stock slipped 1.8 percent on its first day. Workiva later added tools for audit, risk and sustainability reporting. It remains public on the NYSE.

dek: RealPage sold landlords software to run apartment buildings, from screening tenants to setting rents.
lede: RealPage started in 1998 by buying a company called Rent Roll. It grew into the software that ran millions of American apartments. Landlords used it to market units, screen applicants, collect rent, pay bills and, most controversially, set prices. When it went public in August 2010, the housing crash had pushed millions of families from owning to renting, and apartment owners wanted every tool that could fill units and raise income.

sections.heading: Every Task a Landlord Has
sections.body: Steve Winn formed the company in 1998 to acquire Rent Roll and led it as chairman and CEO. RealPage's bet was that property managers would buy one suite for the whole job instead of a dozen separate tools. It sold its software on demand over the web and kept adding products by acquisition. Its revenue management tools used data from many buildings to recommend what each unit should rent for.

sections.heading: From IPO to Antitrust
sections.body: RealPage priced its IPO at $11 a share in August 2010 and listed on Nasdaq as RP. The shares rose about 32 percent on the first day. The company kept growing for a decade. In 2021 Thoma Bravo took it private for $10.2 billion. In 2024 the Justice Department sued RealPage, claiming its pricing software let landlords push rents up together.

dek: Rambus designed a faster road between processors and memory, then charged chipmakers a royalty to use it.
lede: Every Nintendo 64 sold paid a little money to a company that made no chips at all. Rambus, from Mountain View, designed a fast way for processors to talk to memory and licensed the design to the companies that built the parts. When it went public in May 1997, PCs had a problem: processors kept getting faster, and memory could not feed them. Rambus said it had the answer, and it planned to collect rent on it.

sections.heading: A Toll Road for Memory
sections.body: Mike Farmwald and Mark Horowitz started Rambus in 1990. Their idea was a narrow, high-speed channel between a processor and its memory chips. Rambus decided early to stay out of manufacturing. It licensed the design to memory makers and chip companies and took royalties on what they shipped. That kept the company small and its margins high. It also meant Rambus depended on two things: its patents and the partners who chose its design. Before the IPO, Intel picked Rambus memory for future PCs.

sections.heading: Years in the Courtroom
sections.body: Rambus priced its IPO at $12 a share in May 1997. Rambus memory shipped in the first Pentium 4 computers, but the industry soon moved to cheaper rival designs. Rambus then spent years in court with memory makers over its patents, and those fights defined the company for a decade. It later added its own chips for server memory modules. Rambus is now based in San Jose and still trades on Nasdaq under RMBS.

tagline: Games That Paid for a Mall
dek: Sea turned a Southeast Asian gaming business into the region's biggest online shopping app and a digital bank.
lede: Sea paid for its shopping mall with video games. The Singapore company started as Garena, a platform for online games across Southeast Asia, and used that cash to build Shopee, a mobile marketplace, and a payments arm. When it listed in New York in October 2017, the region had hundreds of millions of people buying their first smartphones. Few of them had ever shopped online or held a credit card. Sea wanted to be where they did both for the first time.

sections.heading: From Garena to Shopee
sections.body: Forrest Li founded Garena in Singapore in 2009 with Gang Ye and David Chen. Garena licensed popular online games and ran them for players across Southeast Asia and Taiwan. The games made money, and Li used it to start Shopee in 2015. Shopee was built for phones from day one, and it spent heavily on free shipping to win buyers. A payments business followed. Just before the IPO, the company renamed itself Sea to reflect the three businesses under one roof.

sections.heading: Free Fire and the Long Climb
sections.body: Sea priced its American depositary shares at $15 each in October 2017 on the New York Stock Exchange. The same year, Garena released Free Fire, a mobile battle game built for cheap phones, and it became one of the most downloaded games in the world. That money kept funding Shopee as it fought rivals across the region and in Latin America. The payments arm grew into a digital bank. Sea still trades on the NYSE under the ticker SE.

cover.theme: merchant ships along a coast (trade across Southeast Asia)

fate: Bought by USA Interactive, 2003; spun off 2005; still public (NASDAQ: EXPE)
dek: Expedia let anyone search fares, book flights and reserve hotels on the web without calling a travel agent.
lede: Expedia started as a project inside Microsoft. Rich Barton, a young Microsoft manager, argued that travel agents' booking systems belonged on the web, where anyone could search fares themselves. Microsoft launched Expedia in October 1996 and soon had sites in Canada, Britain and Germany. In November 1999 Microsoft split the business out and sold a slice to the public. Online travel was one of the few web businesses with real revenue, and Expedia was one of its biggest names.

sections.heading: A Startup Inside Redmond
sections.body: Barton ran Expedia as a small business unit inside Microsoft. Expedia let people compare flights, book hotels and rent cars from one page, around the clock. It earned commissions and fees on each booking. Microsoft's money and its MSN portal brought traffic that a small startup could not buy. By the time of the offering, Expedia had sites in four countries, and Microsoft still held most of the company.

sections.heading: Diller Takes the Wheel
sections.body: Expedia priced its IPO at $14 a share in November 1999 on Nasdaq. Two years later Barry Diller's USA Networks bought control from Microsoft, and by 2003 it owned the whole company. In 2005 Diller spun Expedia back out as its own public company. It grew into Expedia Group, owner of Hotels.com and Vrbo. Barton went on to found Zillow. Expedia Group still trades on Nasdaq under EXPE.

cover.artwork: Mountain transportation. Pack mule, Pack and Packers, No. 7

dek: Siebel gave sales teams one system to track every customer, lead and deal, and made it a software category.
lede: Tom Siebel learned to sell software at Oracle, then left to build software for the people who sell. Siebel Systems made programs that tracked every customer, call and open deal so a sales team could see its whole pipeline in one place. When the San Mateo company went public in June 1996, most salespeople still kept their accounts in notebooks, card files and spreadsheets. Siebel was three years old and selling to some of the largest sales forces in the country.

sections.heading: An Oracle Salesman's Fix
sections.body: Tom Siebel and Pat House founded the company in 1993. Siebel had run sales teams at Oracle and knew how little managers could see about their own deals. Their product gave every rep, manager and executive the same view of each customer. Siebel sold to large companies with big sales forces, and it charged big license fees. The category later got a name, customer relationship management, and Siebel led it for most of a decade.

sections.heading: Back to Oracle
sections.body: Siebel priced its IPO at $17 a share in June 1996. Revenue grew fast through the dot-com years and passed $1 billion a year. Then the bubble burst, corporate budgets shrank, and lighter web-based rivals such as Salesforce went after its customers. In January 2006 Oracle, Tom Siebel's old employer, closed its purchase of Siebel for about $5.85 billion. Tom Siebel later founded C3.ai.

cover.theme: Mercury, god of merchants (the art of the sale)

tagline: Build It Yourself, Drag by Drag
dek: Wix let anyone build a website by dragging boxes around a page, with no code and no web designer.
lede: Wix started because its founders found building their own website too hard. Avishai Abrahami, Nadav Abrahami and Giora Kaplan built a tool in Tel Aviv where you drag text, photos and buttons onto a page and hit publish. Small businesses, photographers and bands signed up by the millions, most for free, and some paid for premium plans. When Wix listed on Nasdaq in November 2013, it had already rebuilt its product once, moving off Flash as phones took over the web.

sections.heading: Websites Without Code
sections.body: The three founders started Wix in 2006. The first version ran on Adobe Flash, which made rich pages easy but did not work on the iPhone. In 2012 Wix moved to HTML5 so its sites would load on any device. The business model was freemium: build a site for free, then pay to use your own domain, remove Wix ads or run a store. The bet was that a small share of a huge free audience would pay.

sections.heading: A Newer Kind of Builder
sections.body: Wix priced its IPO at $16.50 a share in November 2013. It added online stores, bookings and payments, and its paid subscribers kept growing. In 2025 Wix bought Base44, a startup that builds apps from plain-language prompts. In the first half of 2026 its shares fell 56 percent as investors worried that AI tools could replace drag-and-drop builders. Wix responded with a $2 billion buyback. It still trades on Nasdaq under WIX.

cover.artwork: Noah Supervising Construction of the Ark

fate: Merged with Juno Online to form United Online, 2001
dek: NetZero gave people free dial-up internet access and paid the bills by showing them ads while they surfed.
lede: NetZero's price was right there in the name. While AOL charged about $20 a month, this Southern California company gave away dial-up internet access to anyone who would put up with a small ad window that stayed on screen while they browsed. NetZero launched its service in October 1998 and went public less than a year later. In 1999 most American homes still reached the web by modem, and the monthly bill was the thing that kept millions offline.

sections.heading: Ads Pay the Phone Bill
sections.body: NetZero was incorporated in California in July 1997 and launched its free service in October 1998. Users downloaded software, dialed in and got online at no charge. In return they filled out a profile and saw targeted ads in a window that NetZero kept on screen. Advertisers paid to reach specific kinds of users. The bet was that ad revenue per user could cover the cost of modems, phone lines and support.

sections.heading: Free Meets the Crash
sections.body: NetZero priced its IPO at $16 a share in September 1999. Millions signed up, and the free model worked as long as the ad market boomed. When the dot-com crash hit in 2000, online ad prices fell, and NetZero began capping free hours and selling paid plans. In 2001 it merged with Juno Online, another free dial-up provider, to form United Online. The NetZero brand lived on inside the combined company.

cover.artwork: Wakasa Province: Fishing Boat Netting Flatfish

fate: Still public (NASDAQ: LI; also listed in Hong Kong)
tagline: An Electric Car With a Backup Engine
dek: Li Auto sold big electric family SUVs in China with a small gas engine that recharged the battery.
lede: Li Auto's first car carried a gasoline engine that never turned the wheels. The engine only charged the battery, so a family in the Li ONE could drive across China without hunting for a charger. That hedge set the Beijing company apart from rivals selling pure battery cars. When Li Auto listed on Nasdaq in July 2020, it had been selling its only model for less than a year, and China's crowded electric car market was in the middle of a shakeout.

sections.heading: Built for the Family Road Trip
sections.body: Li Xiang founded the company in 2015, after building Autohome, one of China's biggest car websites. He aimed at a buyer he knew well: the parent who wanted a large SUV, electric for the city, with no fear of running out of charge on a holiday drive. The Li ONE, a six-seat SUV, used an extended-range design. A battery drove the car, and a small engine topped it up. Deliveries began in late 2019.

sections.heading: Two Listings, One Model at First
sections.body: Li Auto priced its American depositary shares at $11.50 each in July 2020, raising about $1.1 billion. It added a listing in Hong Kong in August 2021. A wider lineup of family SUVs followed, and the company became one of China's best-selling new electric car makers. It later added pure battery models to the range. Li Auto still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker LI.

cover.theme: a family riding together (a car built for families)

tagline: A Wolf Spider on the Web
dek: Lycos sent software spiders crawling across the early web so people could search millions of pages from one box.
lede: Lycos took its name from the wolf spider, a hunter that runs down its prey instead of waiting in a web. Michael Mauldin, a researcher at Carnegie Mellon, built the search engine in 1994 to do the same thing to web pages. A year later CMG, a Massachusetts direct-marketing company, bought the rights and turned it into a business. When Lycos went public in April 1996, the web was small enough to index on a few servers, and search was a land grab.

sections.heading: Out of Carnegie Mellon
sections.body: Mauldin's crawler fetched pages, followed their links and built a catalog that users could search. Carnegie Mellon licensed the technology, and CMG's venture arm, CMG@Ventures, formed Lycos as a company in 1995 with Bob Davis as chief executive. Lycos made its money from banner ads on its search results. It soon added guides, directories and other features to keep visitors on its pages longer than a single search.

sections.heading: Twelve Billion Dollars, Then Less
sections.body: Lycos sold 3 million shares at $16 each in April 1996 and traded on Nasdaq as LCOS. It grew into one of the busiest portals of the dot-com years by buying sites such as Tripod and Angelfire. In 2000 Terra Networks, the Spanish internet company, bought Lycos in a deal valued at about $12.5 billion. The bubble burst months later. Terra sold Lycos to South Korea's Daum in 2004 for a small fraction of that price.

dek: @Home sold fast, always-on internet through cable TV lines years before most homes had heard the word broadband.
lede: @Home bet that the coaxial cable already running into American living rooms could carry the internet many times faster than a phone modem. The Redwood City company was founded in March 1995 with backing from the cable operator TCI and the venture firm Kleiner Perkins. It built a national network and sold service through local cable companies. When it went public in July 1997, nearly everyone online still dialed in, and @Home was asking them to switch.

sections.heading: Cable Companies Go Online
sections.body: @Home's partners owned the wires. @Home supplied the rest: the national backbone, the servers, the email and the home page that greeted every customer. The cable operators sold the service and split the money. The pitch was speed and a connection that never hung up. The risk was that @Home depended on cable companies that held big stakes in it and could one day decide to run the business themselves.

sections.heading: The Excite Merger and the Fall
sections.body: @Home priced its IPO at $10.50 a share in July 1997 on Nasdaq, under the ticker ATHM. In 1999 it bought Excite, the web portal, for about $6.7 billion and renamed itself Excite@Home. The merger never worked. The ad business sank with the dot-com crash, and AT&T, which had bought TCI, controlled the board. Excite@Home filed for bankruptcy in September 2001, and its network went dark within months.

cover.artwork: Wooded Landscape with Cottage and Horseman

dek: SiRF made the cheap, low-power GPS chips that put turn-by-turn navigation into cars, handhelds and phones.
lede: GPS was a military system that SiRF set out to fit into a dashboard gadget. The San Jose chipmaker designed receivers that found satellites fast, used little power and cost little enough for consumer devices. Its chips went into car navigation units and the handheld navigators that were selling fast in 2004. When SiRF went public that April, phones were starting to add location features too. SiRF wanted its chip inside every device that needed to know where it was.

sections.heading: Shrinking the GPS Receiver
sections.body: Sanjai Kohli, Dado Banatao and Kanwar Chadha founded SiRF in 1995. GPS receivers then were bulky, slow to get a fix and power hungry. SiRF designed chipsets and software that worked with weak signals, such as those in cities and under tree cover. It sold the chips to device makers, who built navigators, car systems and tracking gear around them. SiRF became the largest independent maker of consumer GPS chips.

sections.heading: Squeezed by the Smartphone
sections.body: SiRF priced its IPO at $12 a share in April 2004 on Nasdaq. Sales grew with the boom in personal navigation devices. Then the market shifted. Phones began to do navigation for free, and the big phone chipmakers built GPS into their own chips. Dedicated navigators sold fewer units, and SiRF's prices fell. In 2009 SiRF merged with CSR, the British Bluetooth chipmaker, in an all-stock deal.

cover.artwork: Diana Presiding over Navigation and Fishing, from Seven Planetary Gods

fate: Merged with Sirius to form Sirius XM, 2008
dek: XM sold car radio by subscription, sending about a hundred channels coast to coast from satellites with no static.
lede: XM went public with no satellites in space and no paying customers. The Washington company had won one of two federal licenses to broadcast radio from orbit, and it planned to sell drivers more than a hundred channels for a monthly fee. In October 1999 American radio was free, local and full of ads, and nobody had ever paid for it. XM was asking investors to fund rockets, satellites and new car radios on the bet that people would.

sections.heading: Two Satellites Named Rock and Roll
sections.body: XM began in 1992 inside American Mobile Satellite and won its broadcast license in a 1997 federal auction. The plan needed huge sums up front: satellites, ground repeaters in cities and chips for a new kind of receiver. Automakers were the key partners, since most listening happens in cars. In 2001 XM launched two satellites, named Rock and Roll, and turned on its service that fall.

sections.heading: Rivals Become One
sections.body: XM priced its IPO at $12 a share in October 1999 on Nasdaq. Its only rival, Sirius Satellite Radio, raced it for subscribers, and both spent heavily on talent and car deals. XM signed up millions of listeners but lost money for years. In 2007 the two companies agreed to merge, and regulators approved the deal in July 2008. The combined company, Sirius XM, still broadcasts today.

cover.theme: a bird singing against the moon (radio from the sky)

tagline: An Ad Agency Born in an Apartment
dek: Organic built websites and online campaigns for big brands when most companies barely knew the web.
lede: Organic started in Jonathan Nelson's San Francisco apartment in 1993, before most companies had a website or knew why they might need one. Nelson and his co-founders built sites and online campaigns for brands that wanted to look modern on the new web. One of them, Brian Behlendorf, was also a co-founder of the Apache web server project. When Organic went public in February 2000, at the peak of the dot-com boom, web agencies were some of the hottest stocks on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Websites for Hire
sections.body: Jonathan Nelson, Brian Behlendorf, Cliff Skolnick and Matthew Nelson founded Organic in 1993. They put designers, writers and engineers in one shop. Organic designed websites, built the software behind them and ran online ads for its clients. Omnicom, the advertising giant, became its first outside investor in 1997. The business grew as fast as big companies rushed to get online.

sections.heading: Forty Dollars, Then Pennies
sections.body: Organic priced its IPO at $20 a share in February 2000, and the stock closed above $40 on its first day. Within weeks the dot-com crash began. Clients cut their web budgets. Within a year the shares traded for pennies. Seneca, a holding company set up by Omnicom, already owned most of Organic and bought out the rest at 33 cents a share in 2001.

tagline: Selling Ad Space by the Millisecond
dek: Rubicon Project ran instant auctions that let websites sell each ad slot to the highest bidder.
lede: Every time a page loads, an auction can happen before the ad appears, and Rubicon Project ran those auctions for websites. The Los Angeles company built software that let publishers offer each ad slot to many buyers at once and sell it to the highest bid in a fraction of a second. When it went public in April 2014, most ad tech companies worked for advertisers. Rubicon worked for the sellers.

sections.heading: Working for the Publisher
sections.body: Frank Addante and Craig Roah founded Rubicon Project in 2007. Addante had founded ad companies before, including L90. Their idea was an automated exchange that let a publisher put each ad impression up for auction to many demand sources at once. Rubicon took a cut of each sale. The bet was that as ad buying moved to machines, publishers would need their own machine to get a fair price.

sections.heading: From Rubicon to Magnite
sections.body: Rubicon Project priced its IPO at $15 a share in April 2014 on the New York Stock Exchange. Growth stalled a few years later as fees fell across the industry and Google's tools grew stronger. In 2020 Rubicon merged with Telaria, a video ad company, and renamed itself Magnite. It then bought SpotX and SpringServe to build a large business in streaming TV ads. Magnite trades on Nasdaq under MGNI.

fate: Delisted from Nasdaq, 2015; deregistered with the SEC, 2017
tagline: A Web Directory Built by Hand
dek: LookSmart organized the web into a directory picked by human editors and sold that directory to the big portals.
lede: LookSmart was started by a husband-and-wife pair of McKinsey consultants in Melbourne, with money from Reader's Digest. Evan Thornley and Tracey Ellery built a web directory where human editors sorted sites into neat categories, so people could browse to an answer. The San Francisco company licensed its directory to portals, most importantly Microsoft's MSN. When it listed on Nasdaq in August 1999, search engines still returned messy results, and a hand-built map of the web looked like a lasting advantage.

sections.heading: Reader's Digest for the Web
sections.body: Thornley and Ellery began the business in Melbourne as Homebase, with Reader's Digest as the majority owner. When Reader's Digest wanted to shut it down, the founders arranged a cheaper buyout, and Reader's Digest kept a small stake. LookSmart's editors reviewed sites and filed them under topics. The company earned money from ads and from licensing the directory to other sites. Its deal with MSN put LookSmart results in front of millions of people.

sections.heading: Losing Microsoft
sections.body: LookSmart priced its IPO at $12 a share in August 1999 and raised $92.4 million. The stock climbed above $70 in early 2000. Then the crash hit, and Google's automated search made hand-built directories look slow. Thornley stepped down as chief executive in 2002 and later entered politics in Australia. Microsoft ended its MSN contract in 2003, and LookSmart lost much of its revenue. It left Nasdaq in 2015 and stopped filing with the SEC in 2017.

cover.artwork: Looking out of Bass Cove, No. 238

dek: ChinaCache stored copies of websites and videos on servers across China so pages loaded fast for users everywhere.
lede: China's internet in 2010 was split between rival telecom networks that did not connect well, and a page hosted on one could crawl for users on the other. ChinaCache, founded in Beijing in 1998, fixed that by keeping copies of its customers' content on servers spread across the country and across those networks. Portals, game companies and video sites paid it to make their pages load fast. When ChinaCache listed on Nasdaq in October 2010, online video in China was taking off.

sections.heading: A Network of Copies
sections.body: Song Wang founded ChinaCache in 1998. The company built a content delivery network: servers placed inside data centers run by different Chinese carriers. When a user requested a page or a video, ChinaCache served it from a nearby copy. Customers paid for the traffic it carried. The bet was that as China's internet grew, every large website would need a service like this, and that ChinaCache's head start would be hard to copy.

sections.heading: Undercut by the Clouds
sections.body: ChinaCache priced its American depositary shares at $13.90 each in October 2010. The giants of Chinese tech later built their own cloud and delivery services and cut prices hard. ChinaCache lost money and customers. In 2019 its former chief executive was arrested, and the company fell behind on its filings. Nasdaq removed its shares from listing in November 2019, and the company said they would trade over the counter.

cover.artwork: Landscape with Daoist Immortals Playing Weiqi

tagline: Ads for the Rest of the Web
dek: Fastclick placed ads across thousands of small and mid-size websites and paid the site owners a share.
lede: Fastclick lasted less than six months as a public company. The Santa Barbara ad network matched advertisers with thousands of smaller websites that were too small to sell their own ad space. Site owners pasted in Fastclick's code and got a share of every dollar. When Fastclick went public in April 2005, online advertising had recovered from the dot-com crash, and Google's AdSense had shown how much money sat in the long tail of the web.

sections.heading: The Long Tail of Websites
sections.body: Fastclick built its business on sites that big ad sales teams ignored. Advertisers bought campaigns, often paying by the click or by the action a user took. Fastclick's software decided which ad to show on which site to get the best result. Publishers earned a cut without hiring anyone to sell ads. The model depended on volume: many small sites, many ads and a small margin on each.

sections.heading: Bought Within Months
sections.body: Fastclick priced its IPO at $12 a share in April 2005 on Nasdaq. Four months later ValueClick, a larger online ad company from Southern California, agreed to buy it in an all-stock deal. Press reports valued the deal at about $214 million, based on ValueClick's share price when it was announced. The acquisition closed in September 2005, and Fastclick became part of ValueClick's ad network.

cover.artwork: Two Horses Walked by a Jockey

dek: About.com hired real people to curate the web topic by topic, from knitting to tax law, and write about it.
lede: About.com went public under a different name: The Mining Company. Scott Kurnit's New York startup hired hundreds of part-time experts, called guides, and gave each one a topic to cover, from gardening to tax law. Each guide ran a small site that pointed readers to the best of the web and added original articles. When the company sold shares in March 1999, search engines still struggled to tell good pages from bad. A human who knew the subject looked like the answer.

sections.heading: Mining the Web by Hand
sections.body: Kurnit, a veteran of online services, founded the company in 1996. By its IPO it ran more than 600 GuideSites. The guides were independent contractors spread across more than 40 states and 18 countries, and each went through a 16-week training program. The company sold ads across the network. More guides meant more topics, and more topics meant more readers arriving from search engines and staying to browse.

sections.heading: A New Name and New Owners
sections.body: MiningCo.com priced its IPO at $25 a share in March 1999 on Nasdaq under the ticker MINE. A few months later it renamed itself About.com. In 2001 the magazine publisher Primedia bought it. The New York Times Company bought About.com in 2005, and IAC bought it in 2012. IAC later broke the site into separate brands under a new company called Dotdash.

tagline: Lookup Chips for the Internet's Routers
dek: NetLogic made the chips that let routers decide in an instant where each packet of internet traffic should go.
lede: Every packet crossing the internet has to be looked up against a table before a router knows where to send it. NetLogic Microsystems, from Mountain View, made the chips that did those lookups at full speed. Its network search processors sat inside the switches and routers of the big equipment makers. When NetLogic went public in July 2004, the telecom bust was ending, and traffic from broadband and mobile data was starting to climb again.

sections.heading: Searching at Line Speed
sections.body: NetLogic began as a California limited liability company and incorporated in Delaware in 2000. Its chips held large tables of addresses and rules and could match a packet against all of them in a single step. That let networking gear classify traffic, enforce security rules and route packets without slowing down. NetLogic sold to a small number of large equipment makers, so each design win mattered a great deal.

sections.heading: Broadcom's Fifty Dollars
sections.body: NetLogic priced its IPO at $12 a share in July 2004 on Nasdaq. It grew by adding product lines, including multicore processors for networking gear when it bought RMI in 2009. In September 2011 Broadcom agreed to buy NetLogic for $50 a share, a 57 percent premium over its last close. The deal was valued at about $3.7 billion and closed in February 2012.

cover.artwork: Chinese and Tartar Boys Quarreling over a Game of Go

dek: Niu sold sleek lithium-battery electric scooters in China and abroad, each connected to the rider's phone.
lede: China's cities run on electric scooters, and most of them were heavy, slow and powered by lead-acid batteries. Niu, a Beijing startup, sold a lighter kind: designed like a gadget, powered by removable lithium batteries and linked to an app that showed battery life and location. When Niu listed on Nasdaq in October 2018, it was four years old and selling hundreds of thousands of scooters a year. It wanted to be the premium brand in a market full of cheap ones.

sections.heading: A Search Engineer's Scooter
sections.body: Li Yinan, a former chief technology officer at Baidu, founded Niu in 2014 with Hu Yilin. Niu sold its first scooters online. It designed its own battery packs and software, and every scooter reported its data back to the company. The pitch to riders was style and convenience. The pitch to investors was a consumer brand with the data of a tech company.

sections.heading: Riding Out the Price War
sections.body: Niu priced its American depositary shares at $9 each in October 2018. Sales grew in China, and Niu pushed into Europe and later the United States. Competition grew too, and prices fell. In 2026 Niu sold 434,687 units in the second quarter, up about 24 percent from a year earlier, but swung to a loss. It still trades on Nasdaq under NIU.

dek: Brightcove gave media companies and brands the tools to host, play and make money from video on their own sites.
lede: Brightcove's founder had been chief technology officer of Macromedia, the company behind Flash. Jeremy Allaire started the Boston company in 2004 to give broadcasters, publishers and big brands their own video players, hosting and ad tools, so they did not have to hand their audience to YouTube. When Brightcove went public in February 2012, video was spreading to phones, tablets and connected TVs, and every media company needed to play it everywhere.

sections.heading: Video Without YouTube
sections.body: Allaire had co-founded Allaire Corporation, which merged into Macromedia, where he served as chief technology officer. At Brightcove he built a cloud service that customers paid for by subscription. It stored their videos, played them in a branded player and inserted ads. News sites, TV networks and corporate marketers signed on. The bet was that serious video owners wanted control of their content and their viewers.

sections.heading: Sold to Bending Spoons
sections.body: Brightcove priced its IPO at $11 a share in February 2012 on Nasdaq. It grew steadily but faced rising competition from cheaper video tools and from the big cloud providers. In November 2024 it agreed to be acquired by Bending Spoons, the Italian owner of Evernote, for $4.45 a share in cash. The deal, worth about $233 million, closed in February 2025, and Brightcove became private.

tagline: The Chips Behind the HDMI Plug
dek: Silicon Image built the digital links that carry pictures from computers and players to flat screens, including HDMI.
lede: The cable between your TV and your game console owes a lot to Silicon Image. In 1999 the Cupertino company sold chips built on PanelLink, its technology for sending a picture digitally from a computer to a flat-panel screen. Most monitors then were bulky glass tubes driven by analog signals. When Silicon Image went public in October 1999, flat screens were expensive and rare. The company was betting they would take over, and that every one would need a digital connection.

sections.heading: From PanelLink to HDMI
sections.body: David Lee founded Silicon Image in 1995 and led it as chief executive through the IPO. PanelLink became the basis of DVI, the digital standard for computer monitors. Silicon Image then joined with TV makers to create HDMI, which carried high-definition video and audio over one cable to TVs. It sold chips that used these standards and earned licensing fees from other makers who adopted them.

sections.heading: Sold to Lattice
sections.body: Silicon Image priced its IPO at $12 a share in October 1999 on Nasdaq. HDMI became the standard plug on TVs, players and consoles. As chips that handled HDMI became cheaper and more common, Silicon Image looked for new growth in wireless video and mobile links. In 2015 Lattice Semiconductor bought the company in a cash tender offer, and Silicon Image's shares stopped trading in March 2015.

cover.theme: one of the first photographs (the making of an image)

dek: Modem Media designed websites and online marketing for large corporations as they moved their brands onto the internet.
lede: Modem Media named itself after the device that got people online, and it did so in 1987, years before the web. Douglas Ahlers and G.M. O'Connell started the Connecticut company to do marketing for interactive media. By the late 1990s it was one of the biggest agencies building websites and online campaigns for large corporations. When it went public in February 1999, it was majority owned by True North Communications, a traditional ad holding company, and the web was the hottest place to spend a marketing budget.

sections.heading: An Agency Ahead of the Web
sections.body: Ahlers and O'Connell founded Modem Media in 1987. It later merged with Poppe Tyson, an agency in the True North family, and for a time traded under the name Modem Media.Poppe Tyson. The agency planned online strategy, built sites and ran digital ad campaigns. It billed clients for the work and staffed up as fast as corporate web budgets grew.

sections.heading: Into Digitas
sections.body: Modem Media priced its IPO at $16 a share in February 1999 on Nasdaq. Part of the proceeds repaid money owed to True North. The dot-com crash cut demand for agency work. By 2003 it had about $61 million in revenue. In July 2004 Digitas, the Boston marketing firm, agreed to buy Modem Media in a stock deal worth about $200 million, which closed that October.

fate: Merged with TriQuint to form Qorvo, 2015
tagline: The Radio Inside Every Cell Phone
dek: RF Micro Devices made the radio chips that let cell phones reach the nearest tower.
lede: Some of the most important chips in the first mobile phone boom came from Greensboro, North Carolina, far from Silicon Valley. RF Micro Devices made the radio frequency parts that amplify a phone's signal and send it to the nearest tower. It built them from gallium arsenide, a material that handles high frequencies better than ordinary silicon. When RF Micro went public in June 1997, cell phones were turning from car-mounted luxuries into things people carried in a pocket.

sections.heading: Gallium Arsenide in Greensboro
sections.body: William Pratt, Powell Seymour and Jerry Neal founded RF Micro Devices in 1991. They licensed a gallium arsenide transistor process and designed power amplifiers and other radio chips around it. The parts were small and efficient, which meant longer battery life and smaller phones. Phone makers needed several such chips in every handset. RF Micro's bet was that wireless would grow fast enough to make a specialist chipmaker in North Carolina a large company.

sections.heading: Becoming Qorvo
sections.body: RF Micro priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 1997 on Nasdaq. Its sales rose with the spread of mobile phones, and its customers grew to include most of the large handset makers. The work got harder as phones packed in more radio bands and buyers pushed prices down. In 2015 RF Micro merged with TriQuint Semiconductor, a rival radio chipmaker, to form Qorvo.

cover.theme: a thunderstorm over the Alps (energy sent through the air)
cover.artwork: Valley of Aosta: Snowstorm, Avalanche, and Thunderstorm

tagline: Tape Drives for the Backup Room
dek: Overland Data built tape backup drives and libraries that companies used to keep copies of their data safe.
lede: Before cloud backup, a company's safety net was a rack of magnetic tape. Overland Data, from San Diego, made the drives and robotic loaders that copied servers onto cartridges every night so the data could survive a crash or a fire. Its customers were IT departments that had more files to protect every year. When it went public in February 1997, corporate networks were growing fast, and so were the hours it took to back them up.

sections.heading: Robots That Swap Tapes
sections.body: Overland's products ranged from single tape drives to libraries that held many cartridges and swapped them with a mechanical arm. A library let an office back up large amounts of data overnight without anyone changing tapes by hand. Overland sold under its own name and also built products that larger computer makers sold under their brands. That second channel brought volume but tied Overland to a few big customers.

sections.heading: Disks, Then a Merger
sections.body: Overland Data priced its IPO at $10 a share in February 1997 on Nasdaq.
