It later renamed itself Overland Storage and added disk-based backup and storage systems as tape lost ground to cheaper hard drives. Profits were hard to find in a crowded market. In December 2014 Overland merged into Sphere 3D, a virtualization company, and its shares left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a wagon train at rest (overland travel)

dek: InterVU delivered video clips across the internet for websites when most viewers still connected by modem.
lede: InterVU sold internet video in 1997, when most people watched the web through a dial-up modem. The small company from Solana Beach, near San Diego, ran a network that stored and streamed video for websites, so a news site or a record label could add clips without building its own servers. It had launched that network in December 1996. When InterVU went public in November 1997, online video was jerky and postage-stamp sized, and InterVU was betting that would change.

sections.heading: A Network for Clips
sections.body: InterVU was incorporated in Delaware in August 1995, and Harry Gruber led it as chairman and chief executive. Its service took video from content owners, encoded it and delivered it to viewers from InterVU's own servers. Websites paid for that delivery. Content owners avoided the cost of running their own video servers. The business depended on faster connections arriving before its cash ran out.

sections.heading: Folded Into Akamai
sections.body: InterVU priced its IPO at $9.50 a share in November 1997 on Nasdaq. It raised more money in later offerings as it expanded its network. In early 2000 Akamai, the content delivery company, agreed to buy InterVU in an all-stock deal to add streaming media to its service. The acquisition closed in April 2000, near the top of the dot-com market, and InterVU became part of Akamai.

dek: Acacia built optical chips and modules that pushed more data down each strand of fiber between data centers and cities.
lede: Acacia's stock jumped 35 percent on its first day in May 2016, in the year's first venture-backed tech IPO. The Maynard, Massachusetts company made the chips and modules that turn data into pulses of light and send them across fiber optic lines, long haul and inside data centers. Cloud giants and telecom carriers needed far more bandwidth every year without laying new cable. Acacia sold them a way to squeeze more data out of the fiber they already had.

sections.heading: Silicon That Speaks Light
sections.body: Acacia was founded in 2009 and shipped its first products in 2011. It combined two hard technologies. One was a digital signal processor that cleaned up the signal as light traveled hundreds of miles. The other was silicon photonics, which built optical parts with the same factories that make computer chips. Acacia packed both into modules that network equipment makers plugged into their gear. Its biggest customers were a handful of large equipment makers.

sections.heading: Cisco Raises Its Bid
sections.body: Acacia priced its IPO at $23 a share in May 2016 on Nasdaq, at the top of its range. In July 2019 Cisco agreed to buy Acacia for about $2.6 billion. The deal stalled while it waited for approval in China. In January 2021 Cisco raised its offer to $115 a share, about $4.5 billion. The purchase closed on March 1, 2021.

cover.theme: a lighthouse on the rocks (light across distance)

tagline: The Chip That Felt the Wii Swing
dek: InvenSense made tiny motion sensors that let game controllers, phones and cameras know how they were moving.
lede: When you swung a Nintendo Wii remote fitted with Wii MotionPlus, a tiny InvenSense gyroscope measured the turn. The Sunnyvale company built motion sensors on silicon: chips with microscopic moving parts that sense rotation and tilt. Nintendo accounted for a big share of its sales, and its prospectus warned that Wii sales were falling. When InvenSense went public in November 2011, smartphones were the next market, and the company wanted its sensors in every one.

sections.heading: Gyroscopes on a Chip
sections.body: Steve Nasiri founded InvenSense in California in 2003. Gyroscopes had been large and costly. InvenSense used its own manufacturing process to put them on chips small and cheap enough for consumer gadgets. It then combined gyroscopes with accelerometers in single packages, with software to fuse their readings. The first big win was gaming. Next came camera image stabilization and phones, where motion sensing powered screen rotation and games.

sections.heading: Phones, Then TDK
sections.body: InvenSense priced its IPO at $7.50 a share in November 2011 on the New York Stock Exchange. Its sensors went into popular smartphones, and its revenue grew fast. Competition from larger chipmakers squeezed prices, and Nasiri left the company in 2012. In December 2016 Japan's TDK agreed to buy InvenSense for about $1.3 billion, and the deal closed in 2017. It now operates as TDK InvenSense.

cover.artwork: Acrobats at the Cirque Fernando (Francisca and Angelina Wartenberg)

dek: Qwest ran fiber-optic cable beside old railroad tracks and sold long-distance capacity to a data-hungry country.
lede: Qwest's network began as a railroad's side project. Philip Anschutz owned the Southern Pacific, and its telecom arm laid fiber-optic lines along the tracks, linked at the rail junctions. Qwest turned those rights of way into a national fiber network. When it filed to go public in 1997, the internet was driving up demand for bandwidth, and phone companies were hunting for capacity. Qwest offered investors a new, all-digital network built for that traffic.

sections.heading: A Billionaire's Rail Lines
sections.body: The railroad already owned a long strip of land across the West. Putting digital fiber beside the rails gave Qwest a cheap path from city to city. Qwest, founded in 1996 and based in Denver, stretched that idea into a coast-to-coast network. It sold capacity to other carriers and offered its own long-distance service. Anschutz kept control. After the 1997 offering, his Anschutz Company still held about 84 percent of the stock.

sections.heading: From $22 to a Fraud Case
sections.body: Qwest priced its shares at $22 in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as QWST. The stock climbed with the telecom boom. In 2000 Qwest took over US West, one of the regional Bell phone companies, in a deal worth about $48 billion. Then the boom ended. Regulators said Qwest had inflated its results from 1999 to 2002, and former CEO Joseph Nacchio was convicted of insider trading in 2007. CenturyLink bought Qwest in 2011 in a deal valued at $22.4 billion, including debt.

cover.theme: a railroad trestle (fiber along the rails)
cover.artwork: Secret Town Trestle, near Gold Run, from the series "Central Pacific Railroad"

fate: Bought Broadcom in 2016 and took its name; still public (NASDAQ: AVGO)
tagline: The Chip Unit That Swallowed Broadcom
dek: Avago made the analog and wireless chips inside phones and networks, then bought its way into becoming Broadcom.
lede: The company now called Broadcom started life in 1961 as a chip division of Hewlett-Packard. It moved to Agilent in the 1999 split. In 2005 KKR and Silver Lake bought it for about $2.7 billion and named it Avago. By its 2009 offering it sold chips for phones, factories and networks from bases in San Jose and Singapore. Markets were still shaky from the financial crisis, and few tech companies dared to go public.

sections.heading: A Spinoff of a Spinoff
sections.body: Avago had no founder in the usual sense. It was Hewlett-Packard's old chip division, passed to Agilent, then sold to private equity. The new owners set it up with headquarters in Singapore and San Jose. The bet was focus. Avago made analog, optical and radio chips, including the filters that let a phone pick a clean signal out of the air. Hock Tan became chief executive in 2006 and ran the company with a sharp eye on profit margins.

sections.heading: Small Fish, Big Appetite
sections.body: Avago priced its offering at $15 a share in August 2009, at the top of its range, and raised about $648 million. The shares closed their first day at $16.18. Then Tan started buying. Avago bought LSI in 2014. In 2016 it bought Broadcom for about $37 billion and took the bigger company's name. Broadcom later bought CA Technologies, Symantec's enterprise business and VMware. It still trades on Nasdaq under Avago's old ticker, AVGO.

cover.theme: big fish eating little fish (the acquirer)

tagline: Selling the Top of the Search Page
dek: GoTo.com let advertisers bid for the top spot in search results and pay only when someone clicked.
lede: GoTo.com put a price on the top of the search page. Advertisers bid on a keyword, the highest bidder showed up first, and they paid only when someone clicked. Rival search engines made their money from banner ads. GoTo's model turned out to be the one that would pay for search across the web. When the Pasadena company went public in June 1999, it had been running for about a year and was losing money fast.

sections.heading: An Idealab Brainstorm
sections.body: Bill Gross ran Idealab, a Pasadena incubator that spun out one company after another. GoTo.com was incorporated in September 1997 and opened in 1998. It let advertisers name what they would pay to appear at the top of the results, and every click cost that amount. Idealab owned about 24 percent of the company going into the offering. The bet was that ads ranked by price could still be useful to the person searching, and could pay for search itself.

sections.heading: Yahoo's Billion-Dollar Answer
sections.body: GoTo.com priced 6 million shares at $15 on June 18, 1999, above its planned range, and the stock jumped on its first day. It soon found its real business: supplying paid listings to bigger portals. In 2001 it renamed itself Overture Services. Yahoo came to rely on Overture for about a fifth of its revenue. In 2003 Yahoo bought the company for about $1.63 billion in cash and stock. Overture's system lived on as Yahoo Search Marketing.

dek: BEA sold the middleware that let big companies tie their old computer systems to each other and to the web.
lede: BEA's name is just its founders' initials: Bill Coleman, Ed Scott and Alfred Chuang, three Sun Microsystems veterans. They started the company in 1995 with a shopping trip. Their big early prize was Tuxedo, Novell's software for keeping huge streams of transactions moving in order. When BEA went public in April 1997, companies were trying to hook their old mainframe systems up to the new web. They needed software in the middle, and BEA sold it.

sections.heading: Buying the Middle Layer
sections.body: BEA began by acquiring the two largest resellers of Tuxedo, then Tuxedo itself. It kept buying other middleware companies. The bet was that big companies would never throw out their old systems. They would pay for software that let those systems talk to each other and to the web. In 1998 BEA bought WebLogic, a San Francisco startup that had built the first standards-based Java application server. WebLogic became BEA's best-known product.

sections.heading: Six Dollars, Then Oracle
sections.body: BEA priced 5 million shares at $6 in April 1997 and raised about $30 million. The stock closed its first day at $6.25. It was a quiet start. Then WebLogic took off with the dot-com boom, and BEA grew past $1.5 billion in yearly revenue. In October 2007 Oracle offered $6.7 billion, and BEA turned it down. Oracle came back with $8.5 billion. The deal closed in April 2008, and BEA's products became part of Oracle's middleware line.

cover.artwork: View of Ponte Lugano on the Anio, from Views of Rome

fate: Acquired by Liberty Interactive (QVC), 2015 ($2.4B); shut down 2023
dek: Zulily ran fresh flash sales every day on clothes, toys and home goods for moms and their kids.
lede: Zulily's founders came from Blue Nile, the online diamond seller, and they built a store that changed its shelves every day. Each morning brought new flash sales on children's clothes, toys and home goods, open for only a few days. Moms came back to see what was new. When the Seattle company filed to go public in 2013, it had 2.6 million active customers and $331 million in revenue. Investors were still deciding whether flash sales could last.

sections.heading: Two Blue Nile Veterans
sections.body: Mark Vadon had founded Blue Nile. Darrell Cavens had worked there with him. They started Zulily in December 2009 and launched the site in January 2010. The bet was on moms who shopped for fun and liked a surprise. Zulily gave them a new store every day, stocked with deals from brands they did not see at the mall. The daily drop gave shoppers a reason to open the site again the next morning.

sections.heading: A 71 Percent Debut
sections.body: Zulily priced its shares at $22 in November 2013 and listed on Nasdaq as ZU. The stock closed its first day at $37.70, up 71 percent. Growth slowed after that. In 2015 Liberty Interactive bought Zulily for $2.4 billion and put it beside QVC. In 2023 Liberty's successor, Qurate, sold it to the private equity firm Regent. Less than eight months later the site went dark and the company wound down. Beyond Inc. bought the brand in 2024 for $4.5 million.

cover.artwork: Lilies, from an untitled series of Large Flowers

tagline: A Marketplace for Every Purchase Order
dek: Commerce One built online marketplaces where big companies could buy supplies from each other over the internet.
lede: At the top of the bubble in 2000, Commerce One was worth $21.5 billion. Its pitch was business-to-business trade. Companies spent fortunes buying office supplies, parts and services through paper catalogs and fax machines. Commerce One offered software to do that buying online, plus a hosted exchange, MarketSite, where buyers and sellers could meet. When it filed to go public in 1999, B2B was the hottest phrase on Wall Street.

sections.heading: A Father and Son Start-Up
sections.body: Tom Gonzales and his son, Thomas Gonzales Jr., started the company in 1994 as DistriVision. It renamed itself Commerce One in 1997, after Mark Hoffman became chief executive. The company sold BuySite software that let employees order approved goods from their desks. MarketSite linked those buyers to suppliers on a shared network. The bet was that corporate buying would move online the way consumer shopping had started to, and that whoever ran the exchanges would collect a cut.

sections.heading: A 190 Percent Pop, Then Bankruptcy
sections.body: Commerce One priced its shares at $21 in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as CMRC. The stock rose 190 percent on its first day. By 2000 the company was worth $21.5 billion. Then the dot-com crash hit, and few of the online exchanges drew the trade they promised. Revenue shrank and losses piled up. Commerce One filed for bankruptcy in October 2004. A Novell subsidiary bought part of its patents that December for $15.5 million.

tagline: Software on Wheels, and Then Wings
dek: XPeng builds smart electric cars in China, with driver-assist software it writes itself, and is working on flying cars.
lede: XPeng owns a flying-car company. It also builds robots and robotaxis, but its core business is electric cars that can steer, park and change lanes with software written in-house. The Guangzhou company was six years old when it went public in New York in August 2020. Tesla's stock was soaring, and investors were hunting for the Chinese electric carmakers that might follow. XPeng arrived weeks after its rival Li Auto, and raised $1.5 billion.

sections.heading: An Internet Founder Bets on Cars
sections.body: Xia Heng and He Tao started XPeng in Guangzhou in August 2014. He Xiaopeng, who had sold his mobile browser company to Alibaba, backed them early and became chairman. The company carries his name. The bet was that a car could be a computer first. XPeng put its engineers on driver-assist software, voice control and over-the-air updates. It opened offices in Mountain View, California, and later Munich, to hire engineers for that work.

sections.heading: A 41 Percent First Day
sections.body: XPeng priced its American depositary shares at $15 on August 26, 2020, above its planned range. The shares opened at $23.10 and closed the first day at $21.22, up 41 percent. In 2021 it added a listing in Hong Kong. Volkswagen bought a 4.99 percent stake in 2023 for $700 million. In 2025 XPeng delivered 429,445 cars and posted its first quarterly profit. It still trades in New York and Hong Kong.

cover.theme: a kite in flight (flying cars, lift-off)

tagline: The Sock Puppet Spent the Money
dek: Pets.com sold dog food, cat litter and pet toys online and shipped them to your door.
lede: Pets.com's most famous employee was a sock puppet. The dog with a microphone starred in a $1.2 million Super Bowl ad in January 2000, a few weeks before the company went public. Pets.com sold pet food and supplies online and delivered them to the door. The trouble was in the box: bags of kibble and litter are heavy and cheap, so shipping ate the profit. Investors still bought in, at the very top of the dot-com boom.

sections.heading: Amazon Bought Half
sections.body: Greg McLemore started Pets.com, and the site launched in November 1998. Early in 1999 Julie Wainwright took over as chief executive. That March, in the first venture round, Amazon bought a 54 percent stake. The bet was that pet owners, who buy the same food every month, would happily let a website do the hauling. The company spent heavily on marketing to win them. The sock puppet, created by the agency TBWA\Chiat\Day, first appeared in August 1999.

sections.heading: Nine Months on Nasdaq
sections.body: Pets.com sold 7.5 million shares at $11 in February 2000, raising $82.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as IPET. A month later the dot-com crash began. The company kept losing money on most orders, and new funding dried up. On November 7, 2000, Pets.com announced it would shut down. Its stock closed that day at 19 cents. PetSmart bought the Pets.com name and web address that December, and the liquidation finished in January 2001.

fate: Bankrupt, 2001; assets sold to Cable & Wireless
dek: Exodus ran giant, guarded data centers where companies parked the servers that kept their websites online.
lede: By 2000, Exodus was worth about $32 billion for renting out floor space. Its Internet Data Centers were secure, air-conditioned buildings full of other companies' servers, wired straight into the internet's main lines. If you ran a busy website, you did not want your servers in a closet down the hall. When Exodus filed to go public in early 1998, the web was growing faster than companies could build places to host it.

sections.heading: Two Engineers and a Server Room
sections.body: K.B. Chandrasekhar and B.V. Jagadeesh founded Exodus in 1994. That October it began selling internet connections to businesses. It soon found a better product: hosting. Exodus built data centers with backup power, cooling and fast links to many networks, and charged customers to keep their machines there. The bet was that every serious website would need a professional home. Exodus built a chain of those buildings and tied them together with its own backbone network.

sections.heading: Thirty-Two Billion, Then Chapter 11
sections.body: Exodus priced its shares at $15 in March 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as EXDS. As the web boomed, so did the stock, and the company kept building. In September 2000 it agreed to buy Global Crossing's hosting unit for $6.5 billion in stock. By the January 2001 closing, that stock was worth $1.95 billion. Dot-com customers were failing, and many stopped paying. Exodus filed for Chapter 11 in September 2001, and Cable & Wireless bought its assets.

cover.theme: the Exodus story, the Red Sea closing
cover.artwork: The Submersion of Pharaoh's Army in the Red Sea

dek: SendGrid let developers send password resets, receipts and newsletters by email without landing in the spam folder.
lede: Every app sends email nobody thinks about until it fails to arrive: the password reset, the receipt, the shipping notice. SendGrid made sure those messages got through. Developers added a few lines of code, and SendGrid handled the servers and the hard work of staying out of spam folders. When the Denver company went public in November 2017, developer tools sold through an API were a proven business, and Twilio had shown the way.

sections.heading: Email Without the Blacklists
sections.body: Isaac Saldana, Jose Lopez and Tim Jenkins founded SendGrid in 2009 and went through the Techstars accelerator in Boulder. The bet was that developers hated running their own email servers. Getting mail delivered meant constant fights with spam filters and blacklists. SendGrid turned all of that into a service. Developers paid by volume, so the company grew as its customers grew. It later added marketing email tools for newsletters and campaigns.

sections.heading: A Year Later, Twilio Called
sections.body: SendGrid priced its shares at $16 in November 2017 and began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on November 16, under the ticker SEND. It stayed public for about 14 months. In October 2018 Twilio, which sold text and voice tools to the same developers, agreed to buy SendGrid in an all-stock deal worth about $2 billion. The deal closed on February 1, 2019. SendGrid lives on as Twilio's email service.

tagline: A Stylist and an Algorithm, Boxed
dek: Stitch Fix mailed you clothes picked by a stylist and a computer, and you kept only what you liked.
lede: Stitch Fix started in 2011 as Rack Habit, run out of Katrina Lake's apartment in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The idea was a box of clothes chosen for you. A stylist, guided by data about your size, taste and budget, picked the pieces. You kept what fit and sent back the rest. When the company went public in November 2017, malls were emptying and investors wanted to know which online sellers could make shopping personal and still turn a profit.

sections.heading: From Rack Habit to a Fix
sections.body: Lake founded the company with Erin Morrison Flynn, a former J.Crew buyer. They soon moved it to San Francisco. The bet was that many people disliked shopping but liked getting dressed well. Stitch Fix asked customers detailed questions, then used algorithms to suggest items that human stylists chose from. Every return taught the system more about what each person wanted.

sections.heading: A Flat Debut, a Long Rebuild
sections.body: Stitch Fix priced its shares at $15 in November 2017, valuing it at about $1.6 billion, and the stock closed its first day at $15.15. Lake handed the CEO job to Elizabeth Spaulding in 2021, then returned as interim chief in 2023. Matt Baer, a former Macy's executive, took over that June. The company left the United Kingdom to focus on America. It still trades on Nasdaq as SFIX, with about 2.3 million active clients in late 2025.

fate: Acquired by Sun Microsystems, 2000 ($2B in stock)
tagline: A Web Server in a Blue Cube
dek: Cobalt sold small, cheap Linux server boxes that let a business or web host get online in minutes.
lede: Cobalt's best-known product was a small blue cube called the Qube. Plug it in, answer a few questions, and a small office had a web server, email and file sharing, all running on Linux. Its rack-mounted cousin, the RaQ, let hosting companies stack hundreds of cheap servers. When Cobalt went public in November 1999, Linux was the newest darling of Wall Street, and every company with a website needed somewhere to run it.

sections.heading: Linux Before It Was Safe
sections.body: Vivek Mehra co-founded the company in 1996 as Cobalt Microserver and renamed it Cobalt Networks in June 1998. The Qube came out that March, and the RaQ followed in September. The bet was that most businesses did not want a general-purpose server and a full-time administrator. They wanted an appliance that did a few jobs well and cost little. Cobalt built its machines on free Linux software, which kept prices low.

sections.heading: A 618 Percent Day
sections.body: Cobalt priced its shares at $22 on November 5, 1999. On its first day the stock rose as much as 618 percent above that price. Ten months later, in September 2000, Sun Microsystems agreed to buy Cobalt for $2 billion in stock, and the deal closed that December. Many of Cobalt's engineers left soon after. Sun shut down the Cobalt product line in December 2003. The RaQ 550 was the last of the blue boxes.

tagline: Online Banking for Main Street Banks
dek: Q2 gave small community banks and credit unions the slick online and mobile banking their big rivals had.
lede: Hank Seale had spent his career selling technology to small banks before he started Q2. He knew their problem. Big national banks spent fortunes on websites and phone apps, and the local bank down the street could not keep up. Q2 sold those small banks and credit unions a cloud-based digital branch. When the Austin company went public in March 2014, 334 institutions used it, and customers were starting to choose banks by their apps.

sections.heading: A Banker's Software Veteran
sections.body: Seale co-founded Regency Voice Systems in 1991, which sold voice banking to community banks, and later founded Q-Up. He started Q2 in Austin in 2005. The bet was that regional and community banks would pay for one secure platform that ran online banking, mobile apps and more for them. Q2 hosted the software itself, so a small bank did not need a big tech team.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars on the Big Board
sections.body: Q2 priced its shares at $13 in March 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as QTWO. At the time it had 334 installed customers, up from 249 two years earlier. Over the next decade it kept adding products, including lending tools and software for banks' business customers. It also began selling to larger banks and to fintech companies. Q2 still trades on the New York Stock Exchange under QTWO.

dek: Eloqua let marketers track every prospect's clicks and emails, then hand the warmest leads to sales.
lede: Eloqua's software watched which emails a prospect opened and which web pages they read, then scored how ready they were to buy. Marketers had long been judged by how many leads they produced. Eloqua wanted them judged by revenue. The company called this Revenue Performance Management. It started in Toronto and later based itself in Vienna, Virginia. When it went public in August 2012, cloud marketing software was booming and big software companies were shopping for it.

sections.heading: From Toronto, a Lead Score
sections.body: Steven Woods, a former Bain & Company strategist, co-founded Eloqua in 2000 and served as its chief technology officer. The bet was that business-to-business selling was moving online. Buyers did their own research long before they called a salesperson. Eloqua gave marketers tools to send campaigns, track every response and nurture prospects until they were ready to talk. It ran its engineering in Toronto and its sales and headquarters near Washington, D.C.

sections.heading: Six Months on Nasdaq
sections.body: Eloqua priced its shares at $11.50 in August 2012 and listed on Nasdaq as ELOQ. Its stay was short. In December 2012 Oracle agreed to buy the company for about $871 million, as Oracle and Salesforce raced to build marketing clouds. The deal closed in February 2013, about six months after the offering. Eloqua became Oracle Eloqua, the center of Oracle's marketing software.

dek: Rally gave software teams a shared online board to plan and track their work in short, fast cycles.
lede: Rally spent its first three years mostly on research, and released its first cloud product in late 2004. It was built for Agile, a way of writing software in short sprints instead of giant, years-long plans. Big companies were adopting Agile, and their teams were spread across the world. Rally gave them one place to plan, track and see the work. When the Boulder company went public in April 2013, it had about 1,000 customers.

sections.heading: Born as F4 Technologies
sections.body: Ryan Martens founded the company in 2001, and it was incorporated in Delaware that July as F4 Technologies. It later took the name Rally Software. The bet was that Agile would spread from small teams to the largest companies, and that those companies would need software to manage it. Rally sold its tools as a cloud service. By its offering, its customers included 34 of the Fortune 100.

sections.heading: Two Years Public
sections.body: Rally priced its shares at $14 in April 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as RALY. It kept growing but kept losing money, like many cloud companies of its size. In 2015 CA Technologies agreed to buy Rally for about $480 million in cash, or $19.50 a share. CA folded Rally into its tools for managing software development.

fate: Taken private by Silver Lake, 2006 ($1.2B); sold to Micro Focus, 2016 ($540M)
tagline: Keeping Track of Every Mainframe Change
dek: Serena sold software that tracked every change programmers made to the code running a company's mainframes.
lede: Serena had been selling software for 18 years when it went public in the dot-com rush of early 1999. Its software did a dull, vital job. Big companies ran their banks, payrolls and airlines on mainframe code that programmers changed every day. Serena's tools tracked each change, so a bad edit could be found and undone. With the Year 2000 deadline approaching, every company with old code was combing through it line by line.

sections.heading: Comparing Code Since 1980
sections.body: Doug Troxel founded the company in 1980. Its first product, COMPAREX, compared files and showed what had changed between two versions. Later came ChangeMan and StarTool, which managed how code moved from a programmer's desk into the systems a business ran on. The bet was that mainframes would stay at the heart of big companies for decades. Every change to that code carried risk, and Serena sold the safety net.

sections.heading: Two Buyouts Later
sections.body: Serena priced 6 million shares at $13 in February 1999, raising $78 million, and listed on Nasdaq as SRNA. It kept buying smaller tool makers and moved beyond the mainframe. In 2006 Silver Lake took the company private in a buyout worth about $1.2 billion, or $24 a share. A decade later, in May 2016, Micro Focus bought Serena for $540 million and folded its products into its own software line.

cover.artwork: Souvenir of the Environs of Lake Nemi

fate: Renamed Telaria, 2017; merged with Rubicon Project (now Magnite), 2020
dek: Tremor Video sold and measured the video ads that play before online clips, for brands and their agencies.
lede: Tremor Video bet on the few seconds you wait before an online video starts. That pre-roll slot was where TV ad budgets were moving, and Tremor helped brands buy it, place it and prove it worked. When the New York company went public in June 2013, YouTube and online video were exploding, and advertisers wanted the same kind of audience numbers they got from television. Tremor promised to deliver them through its own software.

sections.heading: From Banners to Pre-Roll
sections.body: Tremor was organized in 2005. At first it delivered video ads both inside banner spaces on web pages and inside video streams. Over time it shifted to in-stream ads, the kind that play before or during a clip. In late 2010 it bought ScanScout, another video ad company. The bet was that brands would pay more for ads people actually watched, and that software could match each ad to the right viewer.

sections.heading: Selling Half, Keeping Half
sections.body: Tremor priced 7.5 million shares at $10 in June 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as TRMR. Ad tech stocks soon fell out of favor. In 2017 Tremor sold its business that worked for advertisers and kept the side that served publishers, renaming itself Telaria. In April 2020 Telaria merged with Rubicon Project. That June the combined company took a new name, Magnite.

fate: Acquired by News Corp, 2005 ($650M); now owned by Ziff Davis
dek: Snowball ran IGN and other websites for young people who grew up online, starting with video gamers.
lede: Snowball.com had a name for its audience: Generation i, people aged 13 to 30 who treated the internet as part of daily life. Its biggest site was IGN, the Imagine Games Network, which covered video games with news, reviews and guides. Snowball wanted to build a whole network around that crowd. When it went public in March 2000, it was the very top of the dot-com boom, and ad-supported websites for teenagers looked like a fortune.

sections.heading: Born Inside a Magazine Company
sections.body: IGN launched on September 29, 1996, as five websites inside Imagine Media, a magazine publisher founded by Chris Anderson. Gaming fans came for news and reviews, and they came back every day. Imagine spun the web business out, and it took the name Snowball. The bet was that gamers were just the first of many young audiences. Snowball added sites for other interests and sold ads and goods to all of them.

sections.heading: IGN Outlasted Snowball
sections.body: Snowball priced its shares at $11 in March 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as SNOW. The dot-com crash had already begun, and ad money soon dried up. Snowball shut or sold most of its sites and kept the one that worked. In May 2002 it renamed itself IGN Entertainment. News Corp bought IGN for $650 million in 2005. In 2013 News Corp sold it to Ziff Davis, which still owns IGN.

fate: Taken private, 2016; merged with Tongcheng to form Tongcheng-Elong
tagline: China's Hotel Rooms by Phone and Web
dek: eLong let Chinese travelers book hotel rooms and flights through a call center and a website.
lede: eLong's ticker was LONG, the Chinese word for dragon. The Beijing company booked hotel rooms for China's business travelers, mostly through a big call center backed by a website. In 2004 China's middle class was starting to travel. IAC, the American owner of Expedia and Hotels.com, saw the opening and bought into eLong before its offering. eLong went public that October as a bet on Chinese travel.

sections.heading: Expedia's Way into China
sections.body: Justin Tang was one of the co-founders of eLong.com in 1999, after working as an investment banker in New York. He later became its chairman and CEO. The bet was that Chinese travelers would book rooms the way Americans had learned to, by calling one number or visiting one site. IAC bought a large stake and the right to take control. That made eLong the vehicle for Expedia's push into China.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Tongcheng
sections.body: eLong priced its American depositary shares at $13.50 in October 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as LONG. It spent the next decade fighting a larger rival, Ctrip, and a wave of new travel apps. In 2015 Expedia sold its stake to Ctrip and other investors. eLong was taken private and left Nasdaq in May 2016. It later merged with Tongcheng to form Tongcheng-Elong, which listed in Hong Kong in 2018.

cover.theme: a dragon (long, the Chinese word for dragon)

fate: Acquired by Mitel, 2015 ($560M); name revived as a private company, 2017
dek: Mavenir sold software that let mobile carriers run voice calls and texts over their new 4G LTE networks.
lede: The first 4G LTE networks were built for data, and they had no native way to carry an ordinary phone call. Mavenir sold the fix. Its software let carriers run voice over LTE and over Wi-Fi, plus texting and other services, on standard computers instead of costly custom hardware. When the Texas company went public in November 2013, carriers around the world were upgrading to LTE and looking for ways to move voice calls onto it.

sections.heading: Phone Calls as Software
sections.body: Mavenir was founded in 2005 near Dallas and began earning revenue in 2007. Before its offering it raised about $105 million from investors. Pardeep Kohli led it as president and chief executive. The bet was that carriers would run more of their networks as software. Mavenir's products handled voice over LTE, known as VoLTE, and Voice over Wi-Fi. Carriers could launch new services faster and with less special equipment.

sections.heading: Sold, Split and Reborn
sections.body: Mavenir priced its shares at $10 in November 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as MVNR. The offering raised about $44.5 million. In 2015 Mitel Networks bought Mavenir for $560 million and renamed it Mitel Mobile. Mitel then sold that unit to Xura for $350 million. In 2017 Siris Capital merged Xura and two other companies and brought back the Mavenir name. It remains a private company.

dek: WebTrends turned a website's raw traffic logs into reports that showed who visited and what they did.
lede: Every web server keeps a diary. Each page request lands in a log file, line after line, unreadable to most people. WebTrends turned those logs into charts a manager could understand: how many visitors came, where they came from, and which pages they read. By early 1999, more than 20,000 customers had bought its software, including over a third of the Fortune 500. Companies had built websites in a hurry and now wanted to know if anyone used them.

sections.heading: Two Founders in Portland
sections.body: Elijahu Shapira and W. Glen Boyd built WebTrends in Portland, Oregon. The company was incorporated in 1993 and reorganized in Oregon in 1997. The bet was that every business with a website would soon need numbers to judge it, and that most of them would rather install a program than hire an analyst. WebTrends sold packaged software that a company could install on its own server and run itself.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to NetIQ
sections.body: WebTrends sold 3.5 million shares at $13 in February 1999, including 500,000 from its two founders. The web was booming, and so was demand for ways to measure it. Two years later, in 2001, WebTrends merged into NetIQ, a maker of systems management software. The WebTrends name outlived the deal. It kept selling web analytics for years as rivals, Google Analytics among them, made basic traffic reports free.

cover.theme: a spider's web (web logs, the web)
cover.artwork: Arachne Being Turned into a Spider by Minerva

tagline: Free Home Pages, Paid by Email Deals
dek: Xoom.com gave people free home pages and email, then sold them products through email offers.
lede: Xoom.com was adding about 20,000 members a day in the fall of 1998. It gave them free web pages, email and chat. Then it emailed them deals, and that was the business: 69 percent of its revenue in the first nine months of 1998 came from e-commerce sold to its own members. By its December offering, Xoom.com had about 4.5 million members and reached over 13 percent of web users. Portal mania was in full swing.

sections.heading: Born as Atomsoft
sections.body: The company was incorporated in Delaware in April 1996 as Atomsoft. It became Xoom in February 1998 and Xoom.com that October. Chris Kitze was chairman and Laurent Massa was chief executive. The bet was that free services would build a huge community, and that a community could be sold to. Members agreed to receive offers by email, and Xoom.com sold them software, computer accessories and consumer electronics. Nearly 30 percent of its revenue came from outside the United States.

sections.heading: A Year Later, NBC
sections.body: Xoom.com priced 4 million shares at $14 in December 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as XMCM. Internet stocks were soaring that winter. In 1999 NBC combined Xoom.com with its stake in the Snap portal to form a new public company, NBC Internet, or NBCi. Xoom.com's members became part of NBC's push onto the web. NBCi did not last. NBC took it back in 2001.

tagline: The Operating System Apple Didn't Buy
dek: Be built BeOS, a fast operating system for audio and video that tried to win a place beside Windows.
lede: In 1996 Apple needed a new operating system and looked hard at BeOS. It chose NeXT instead, and Steve Jobs came back with it. Be, led by former Apple executive Jean-Louis Gassée, carried on alone. BeOS could play several videos and audio tracks at once without stuttering, something Windows and the Mac struggled with. When Be went public in July 1999, it was still betting that people would install a second operating system for media work.

sections.heading: Built for Media
sections.body: Gassée founded Be in 1990 with Steve Sakoman, another Apple veteran, who became its chief technology officer. They built BeOS from scratch. It used multiple processors at once, protected each program's memory, and handled audio, video and images with ease. Be first sold its own computer, the BeBox, then moved the software to ordinary PCs. The bet was that a clean, modern system could win over creative users. Few software makers wrote programs for it.

sections.heading: Six Dollars a Share
sections.body: Be priced 6 million shares at $6 in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as BEOS. The money bought time but not users. In 2000 Be turned toward software for internet appliances, small devices for browsing the web. That market never took off. In 2001 Be sold its technology and intellectual property to Palm for about $11 million, and the company wound down. Fans still keep BeOS alive through an open-source rebuild called Haiku.

cover.artwork: The Peasant Attacked by Bees, from The Caprices

dek: Rogue Wave sold ready-made building blocks of C++ and Java code so programmers did not have to write them.
lede: Rogue Wave's founder studied ocean waves before he sold software. Thomas Keffer was an oceanography professor at the University of Washington, and his company carried the name of a giant, sudden ocean wave. The company sold libraries of tested C++ and later Java code, the basic parts that programmers otherwise rewrote for every project. When it went public in November 1996, object-oriented programming was spreading fast through big companies.

sections.heading: From Oceanography to C++
sections.body: Keffer started Rogue Wave in 1989 and ran it as an unincorporated business until 1991, when it incorporated in Oregon. It was based in Corvallis, home of Oregon State University, where Keffer had earned his Ph.D. The bet was that programmers would buy well-made parts instead of building everything themselves. Rogue Wave's libraries handled data structures, math and database access, and worked across many kinds of computers.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars in Corvallis
sections.body: Rogue Wave sold its shares at $12 in November 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as RWAV. The offering raised about $29.4 million, including shares sold by existing holders. The company later moved its headquarters to Boulder, Colorado. In 2003 Quovadx, a health care software company, bought Rogue Wave. The Rogue Wave name lived on as a developer tools brand for years after.

dek: MindSpring sold easy dial-up internet access to ordinary people, many of them online for the first time.
lede: MindSpring sold internet access to people who had never been online. It shipped its own easy software, ran its own local dial-up numbers, and answered the phone when customers got stuck. The Atlanta company started service in June 1994, and two years later it had about 34,500 subscribers. In the fall of 1996 it raised more money to buy 66,000 subscriber accounts from PSINet, a deal that would take it from a regional player to a national one.

sections.heading: A Year of Planning
sections.body: Charles Brewer spent May 1993 to January 1994 working out the idea. He had been chief executive of AudioFax, a fax software company, and before that a venture capitalist. MindSpring was incorporated in Georgia in February 1994. The bet was on beginners. Online services like AOL kept people inside their own walls. MindSpring gave them the open internet, with friendly software and support for people who had little or no online experience.

sections.heading: Eight Dollars, Then EarthLink
sections.body: MindSpring went public on March 14, 1996, at $8 a share, on Nasdaq as MSPG. That October it sold 2.25 million more shares to help pay for the PSINet accounts, which also came with access to PSINet's national network. MindSpring kept growing by buying subscribers from smaller providers. In 2000 it merged with EarthLink, a larger rival. The combined company kept the EarthLink name and moved its headquarters to Atlanta.

fate: Taken private by Thoma Bravo, 2022 ($6.9B); public again on Nasdaq (SAIL) since 2025
dek: SailPoint showed big companies exactly who could open which apps and files, and helped them take access away.
lede: SailPoint has gone public twice, both times with Thoma Bravo as its main owner. Its software answers a plain question that big companies struggle with: who has access to what. Employees join, switch jobs and leave, and their logins pile up across hundreds of apps. SailPoint tracks those rights and flags the ones that should not exist. When the Austin company first went public in November 2017, a run of data breaches had made that question urgent.

sections.heading: Identity Veterans in Austin
sections.body: Mark McClain founded SailPoint in Austin in 2005 with Kevin Cunnington, after both had worked in identity management software. In 2007 it released IdentityIQ, which it said created a new category called identity governance. In 2010 it combined governance with provisioning, the work of setting up and removing access. The bet was that auditors and security teams would demand proof of who could reach sensitive data. Thoma Bravo invested and owned about 60 percent going into the offering.

sections.heading: Public, Private, Public Again
sections.body: SailPoint priced 20 million shares at $12 in November 2017 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as SAIL. It moved its products to the cloud over the next few years. In 2022 Thoma Bravo took the company private again for about $6.9 billion. In February 2025 SailPoint returned to the market, this time on Nasdaq, at $23 a share. It still trades under its old ticker, SAIL.

dek: Time Warner Telecom ran fiber networks in big cities and sold phone and data lines to businesses.
lede: Time Warner Telecom began inside a cable company. Time Warner Cable started the business in 1993, using fiber it had laid in cities to sell phone lines to businesses. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 opened local phone markets to competition, and the company rushed in. By the end of 1998 it ran networks in 19 metro areas, with 6,968 route miles of fiber. It sold dedicated lines, local and long distance calls, and data to big business customers.

sections.heading: Fiber Under the Cable
sections.body: The company was a competitive local exchange carrier, a newcomer allowed to take on the old Bell phone companies. It used the Time Warner name and shared the cost of building fiber with its parent's cable systems. That gave it a head start in places where Time Warner already had cable. The bet was that businesses, phone carriers and internet providers would pay for fast, reliable lines that did not run through the local Bell.

sections.heading: Twenty Years to Level 3
sections.body: Time Warner Telecom priced 18 million shares at $14 in May 1999, raising $252 million, and listed on Nasdaq as TWTC. It survived the telecom crash that sank many rivals. In 2008 it renamed itself tw telecom. Its fiber network kept growing through new builds and acquisitions. In 2014 Level 3 Communications bought tw telecom in a deal valued at about $7.3 billion, including debt.

cover.artwork: N.W. Corner of Dearborn and Monroe Streets, Chicago, Showing the Post Office

fate: Taken private by Digital Colony and EQT, 2020 ($14.3B incl. debt)
dek: Zayo bought and built fiber networks, then leased the bandwidth to carriers, cloud companies and big businesses.
lede: Zayo was built to buy things. Its founders started it in 2007 with a plan to roll up the fiber networks left over from the telecom bust, and by 2014 it had bought many of them. The biggest was AboveNet, bought for about $2.2 billion. By its October 2014 offering, Zayo's fiber ran over 81,000 route miles and reached 4,200 cell towers and 756 data centers. Video, cloud computing and phones were driving demand.

sections.heading: A Roll-Up in Boulder
sections.body: Dan Caruso and John Scarano started Zayo in Boulder, Colorado, in 2007. The company was founded with a stated thesis: build a bandwidth infrastructure platform and take part in the consolidation of the industry. The bet was that fiber, once laid, lasts for decades, and that whoever owned the most of it in the right places could lease it again and again. Zayo bought networks from failed and struggling carriers and tied them together.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars, Then Private
sections.body: Zayo priced its shares at $19 in October 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ZAYO, raising about $400 million. It kept buying networks, in the United States and Europe. In 2019 it agreed to sell itself. The deal closed in March 2020, when Digital Colony and EQT took Zayo private in a deal worth about $14.3 billion, including debt.

cover.theme: an aqueduct (infrastructure that carries the flow)
cover.artwork: Segovia, The Aqueduct from Market, from Castilian Days

dek: MapQuest gave anyone free driving directions on the web, ready to print and take along in the car.
lede: The web's favorite map started life in 1967 as a map shop inside a Chicago printing company. R.R. Donnelley & Sons made road atlases and travel guides from a plant in Pennsylvania farm country. By the time MapQuest filed to go public in 1999, that same team had put its maps online. Millions of drivers typed in two addresses, hit print, and set off with a sheet of turn-by-turn directions on the passenger seat.

sections.heading: From Atlas to Address Bar
sections.body: The mapping unit spent decades drawing maps for atlases and travel guides. Donnelley spun it out in 1994 as GeoSystems Global, and in 1996 the company opened MapQuest, a free website for maps and directions. The bet was simple. Give the maps away and sell the traffic to advertisers. Then license the same engine to other websites and businesses that needed maps of their own. The company kept its headquarters in Mountville, Pennsylvania.

sections.heading: A Billion-Dollar Map
sections.body: MapQuest priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999, above the $10 to $12 range it first set. The money was useful, but the sale came fast. In December 1999, AOL agreed to buy MapQuest for about $1.1 billion in stock, and the deal closed in 2000. Phones with GPS and Google Maps later took most of its audience. In 2019 the site changed owners again when Verizon sold MapQuest to System1.

dek: Rivian builds electric pickups and SUVs for people who like mud, plus delivery vans for Amazon.
lede: Rivian was worth more than Ford on its first day of trading, after delivering only a handful of trucks. The electric truck maker went public in November 2021, at the peak of a market hungry for anything that ran on batteries. It had a pickup, an SUV, and an order from Amazon for 100,000 electric delivery vans. Investors paid for the future, and they paid a great deal.

sections.heading: Twelve Years in the Garage
sections.body: RJ Scaringe founded the company in 2009, soon after earning a doctorate at MIT. He spent years reworking the plan before Rivian settled on electric trucks for outdoor adventure. The company built a flat battery platform it called a skateboard, which could carry different bodies on top. It bought a former Mitsubishi plant in Normal, Illinois. Amazon and Ford invested, and in 2019 Amazon ordered 100,000 vans. The R1T pickup reached its first customers in September 2021.

sections.heading: The Biggest Debut in Years
sections.body: Rivian priced its shares at $78 in November 2021, well above its first range of $57 to $62. The offering raised about $11.9 billion, the largest American IPO since Facebook. The stock opened at $106.75 and closed the first day at $100.73. That fever did not last. Supply problems and slow production pulled the shares far below the offer price. In 2024 Volkswagen agreed to invest up to $5 billion in a joint venture. Rivian still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a wild river in the redwoods (Rivian, named for a river)
cover.artwork: Big River, from the Rancherie, Mendocino, California

dek: Brocade sold the switches that let rows of servers share one big pool of storage over fiber.
lede: One of Brocade's founders co-wrote the Fibre Channel standard, then built a company to sell the switches it needed. By 1999, big companies were drowning in data stuck on disks bolted to single servers. Brocade's switches tied many servers to many storage arrays over fast fiber links, a setup called a storage area network. When the San Jose company filed to go public, it was selling the plumbing for a new kind of data center.

sections.heading: A Racer, an Engineer, a Builder
sections.body: Brocade started in August 1995. Seth Neiman was a venture capitalist, a former Sun Microsystems executive, and a professional race car driver. Kumar Malavalli co-wrote the Fibre Channel specification. Paul Bonderson came from Intel and Sun. Their bet was that storage would split away from the servers that used it. If it did, every data center would need a switch in the middle. Brocade's SilkWorm switches aimed to be that switch.

sections.heading: The SilkWorm Years
sections.body: Brocade priced its IPO at $19 a share on May 25, 1999, and traded on Nasdaq as BRCD. Storage networks spread fast, and Brocade became the leading maker of Fibre Channel switches. In 2008 it bought Foundry Networks to move into Ethernet gear. Broadcom agreed to buy Brocade in November 2016 for $5.9 billion, or $12.75 a share. The deal closed in November 2017, and Broadcom sold off the Ethernet business to Arris.

cover.theme: a woman tying silk thread (Brocade, SilkWorm, fiber)
cover.artwork: Tying Thread, from the series "Women's Handicrafts: Models of Dexterity"

fate: Taken private by founder Rob Glaser, 2022
dek: RealNetworks let people hear and then watch live audio and video on the web, years before broadband.
lede: Before RealAudio, sound on the web meant waiting for a whole file to download. Rob Glaser's player started talking almost at once, over an ordinary dial-up modem. Radio stations, ball games and news broadcasts poured onto the web through it. When the Seattle company filed to go public in 1997, millions of people had installed its free player. Microsoft had just bought a stake in it, and would soon become its fiercest rival.

sections.heading: A Microsoft Veteran's Second Act
sections.body: Glaser spent about ten years at Microsoft before leaving to start Progressive Networks in Seattle in 1994. In April 1995 it shipped RealAudio, which streamed sound in real time instead of making people download first. RealVideo followed. The bet was to give the player away and sell the server software to broadcasters and websites. The company took the name RealNetworks in 1997, shortly before it filed for its offering.

sections.heading: Streaming Before Its Time
sections.body: RealNetworks priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in November 1997 and traded on Nasdaq as RNWK. It rode the dot-com boom, then lost ground as Microsoft bundled Windows Media Player into Windows. Real sued, and Microsoft paid $761 million to settle in 2005. Apple's iTunes and later YouTube took the audience. In 2022 Glaser bought out the other shareholders at $0.73 a share and took the company private.

cover.artwork: A Mountainous Landscape with a Stream

tagline: Detonating the Mail Before It Arrives
dek: FireEye caught hackers' newest attacks by opening suspicious files in a safe virtual machine and watching what happened.
lede: FireEye's product opened every suspicious file in a fake computer and waited to see if it exploded. Antivirus tools of 2013 looked for the fingerprints of known attacks. FireEye watched behavior instead, so it could catch attacks no one had seen before. That fall, reports of state-backed hackers inside American companies filled the news. The Milpitas company filed to go public into a market that wanted exactly what it sold.

sections.heading: A Sandbox for Malware
sections.body: Ashar Aziz, a former Sun Microsystems engineer, founded FireEye in 2004. His idea was to run incoming web traffic and email attachments inside virtual machines, cut off from the real network. If a file tried to break in, the trap caught it. FireEye sold this as hardware appliances that sat in a customer's network. It was costly gear, aimed at banks, governments and big companies that feared targeted attacks.

sections.heading: Two Names, One Watchman
sections.body: FireEye priced its IPO at $20 a share in September 2013, after raising its range from $12 to $14. The stock closed its first day at $36, up 80 percent. Months later it bought Mandiant, the incident response firm led by Kevin Mandia, for about $1 billion. In 2021 FireEye sold its product business and name for $1.2 billion and renamed itself Mandiant. Google bought Mandiant in September 2022 for $5.4 billion, or $23 a share.

cover.theme: a giant watchful head guarding the waters (a guardian eye)

dek: FreeMarkets ran online auctions where suppliers bid prices down to win factory orders from big manufacturers.
lede: On its first day of trading, FreeMarkets stock climbed more than 440 percent. The Pittsburgh company ran a strange kind of auction. Buyers set the job, such as die-cast pistons for an engine, and suppliers bid against each other in real time to go lower. A graph on the screen showed the price dropping minute by minute. By December 1999 the dot-com boom had reached its peak, and business-to-business marketplaces were the newest craze.

sections.heading: A McKinsey Man in Steel Country
sections.body: Glen Meakem had worked at McKinsey on industrial sourcing, then at General Electric. In 1995 he and Sam Kinney started the company that became FreeMarkets. Their bet was that big buyers paid too much for parts because they only talked to a few suppliers at a time. FreeMarkets found suppliers, prepared the bid, and ran the event on its BidWare software. Clients included General Electric, Emerson Electric, Navistar and Owens Corning.

sections.heading: Five Times the Price by Lunch
sections.body: FreeMarkets priced its IPO at $48 a share on December 10, 1999. By that afternoon the stock traded above $260 on Nasdaq, one of the biggest first-day jumps of the boom. The high did not hold. When the bubble burst, the shares fell with the rest of the B2B sector. In January 2004 Ariba agreed to buy FreeMarkets in a stock deal worth about $493 million, and FreeMarkets CEO Dave McCormick became Ariba's president.

fate: Taken private by Naver and SoftBank, 2020; now part of LY Corporation
dek: LINE gave hundreds of millions of people across Asia a free way to chat, call, and send cartoon stickers.
lede: LINE launched in Japan in June 2011, three months after the earthquake and tsunami of March 2011. The free chat app spread fast, carried by cartoon stickers of a bear named Brown and a rabbit named Cony. By March 2016 it had 218 million monthly users, most of them in Japan, Taiwan, Thailand and Indonesia. That summer the Tokyo company listed in New York and Tokyo in the same week.

sections.heading: A Korean Parent in Tokyo
sections.body: The company began as the Japanese arm of NHN, the Korean firm behind the search engine Naver, which ran online games in Japan. LINE grew from that team. The bet was that a messaging app could become the front door to a whole phone life. LINE sold stickers, games, music and payments inside the app. Japan still produced most of its revenue, and Naver kept control of the company after the offering.

sections.heading: Two Bells, One Week
sections.body: LINE priced its global offering at $32.84 per American share and ¥3,300 per share in Japan in July 2016, one of the year's largest tech IPOs. It traded on the New York Stock Exchange as LN. Growth outside its four core markets proved hard. In 2020 Naver and SoftBank bought out the public shareholders and delisted the stock. LINE then merged with Yahoo Japan's parent, now called LY Corporation.

dek: drkoop.com put the trusted name of a former Surgeon General on a free health website for consumers.
lede: The most famous doctor in America lent his name and his beard to a website. C. Everett Koop had been Surgeon General under Ronald Reagan, the man who warned the country about smoking and AIDS. In 1999 his Austin company promised to bring that same trust to the web, with health news, chat rooms, drug interaction checks and a lifelong personal medical record. The prospectus opened with his photograph. Investors loved the name.

sections.heading: Personal Medical Records, Inc.
sections.body: The company started in Texas in July 1997 under the name Personal Medical Records, Inc. It became Empower Health, then drkoop.com in early 1999. Donald Hackett ran it as CEO, with Koop as chairman. The bet was that patients would come to the site for advice and stay for its tools and stores. Revenue would come from ads, sponsorships and sales of drugs and health products through partners.

sections.heading: The House Call Ends
sections.body: drkoop.com priced its IPO at $9 a share in June 1999 and traded on Nasdaq as KOOP. The stock soared in its first weeks. But the site spent heavily on marketing and portal deals, and it never earned close to what it spent. By 2000 its own auditors doubted it could survive. The company moved to Santa Monica and kept searching for money. In December 2001 it shut down and filed for Chapter 7 liquidation.

cover.theme: a doctor at his work (the house call)

fate: Merged with Software.com to form Openwave, 2000
tagline: The Web on a Tiny Green Screen
dek: Phone.com built the browser and server software that first put the internet on ordinary cell phones.
lede: Eight years before the iPhone, people could already read email and news on a cell phone, through a browser from a company most of them never heard of. Phone.com wrote the UP.Browser, a tiny program that fit inside basic handsets with a few lines of text on screen. Carriers ran its UP.Link servers to feed those phones. When the Redwood City company went public in June 1999, the mobile web was a few lines of monochrome text.

sections.heading: From Pen Computers to Phones
sections.body: Alain Rossmann had run EO Corporation, which made an early pen-based handheld computer. In December 1994 he started the company that became Unwired Planet, renamed Phone.com in April 1999. His bet was that the cheap phone in everyone's pocket would beat any special device for getting online. To make that happen, Unwired Planet formed the WAP Forum with Ericsson, Motorola and Nokia, and much of the WAP standard was based on its technology.

sections.heading: Openwave and After
sections.body: Phone.com priced its IPO at $16 a share on June 10, 1999, and traded on Nasdaq as PHCM. It became one of the hottest stocks of the boom as investors bet on the wireless internet. In 2000 it merged with Software.com to form Openwave Systems. Smartphones later made its products obsolete. Openwave sold its product lines in 2012 and became Unwired Planet, a patent licensing company, and later Great Elm Capital Group.

fate: Taken private by Elliott's Evergreen Coast Capital, 2017 ($38.50 a share)
dek: Gigamon copied network traffic and sent it to the security and monitoring tools that needed to see it.
lede: Every security tool in a data center wants to see the same traffic, and there are only so many places to plug in. Gigamon sold the box that solved that fight. Its gear took copies of everything moving across a network, sorted them, and sent each tool only the slice it needed. By 2013 Gigamon counted more than 1,000 customers, including 60 of the Fortune 100. The Milpitas company filed to go public as networks grew too fast to watch.

sections.heading: Four Founders and a Tap
sections.body: Gigamon was founded in 2004 by four people, among them Ted Ho, who became CEO, and Patrick Leong, a former Ciena engineer who became chief technology officer. It sold its first products in 2005. Their bet was that monitoring would need a network of its own. Gigamon called its product a Traffic Visibility Fabric, a layer that sat between the live network and the tools that watched it, from security scanners to performance monitors.

sections.heading: The Watchers' Network
sections.body: Gigamon priced its IPO at $19 a share in June 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as GIMO. Rising fear of cyberattacks kept demand strong for a few years. Then growth slowed in 2017, and activist investor Elliott Management took a stake. In October 2017 Gigamon agreed to be bought by Elliott's tech arm, Evergreen Coast Capital, for $38.50 a share in cash. The deal closed in December 2017.

cover.theme: an aqueduct crossing a railroad (traffic over traffic)
cover.artwork: The Arcueil Aqueduct at Sceaux Railroad Crossing

dek: Paylocity runs payroll and HR in the cloud for companies too big for a spreadsheet and too small for SAP.
lede: Steve Sarowitz learned payroll at a small Chicago service bureau, then started his own company in 1997 to do it better. Paylocity aimed squarely at the middle: firms with 20 to 1,000 employees. By 2013 it handled pay, taxes, benefits and time sheets for about 6,850 clients, all through the web. In early 2014, cloud software was the hottest corner of the stock market.

sections.heading: Built for the Middle
sections.body: Before Paylocity, Sarowitz worked at Robert F. White, a Chicago-based independent payroll firm, and later as an executive at other payroll companies. He founded Paylocity in 1997. The bet was that medium-sized businesses wanted the same tools as big ones, delivered over the internet and sold by subscription. Steve Beauchamp became CEO, and Sarowitz moved to executive chairman. Payroll came first, then HR, benefits, time tracking and talent tools.

sections.heading: A Steady Climb from Illinois
sections.body: Paylocity priced its IPO at $17 a share in March 2014 and listed on the Nasdaq Global Select Market as PCTY. Then it did what payroll companies do. It kept adding clients and kept them for years. Revenue grew fast for a decade while the company added more modules for HR teams. Paylocity moved its headquarters to Schaumburg, Illinois, and it still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: factory workers (the people on the payroll)

fate: Bankrupt, 2001; assets sold to Williams Communications ($25M)
dek: iBEAM used satellites to beam streaming video and audio to servers near viewers, around the internet's traffic jams.
lede: iBEAM's plan to fix slow web video went through space. In 2000, streaming a clip meant stutters and buffering, because every stream crossed a crowded internet. The Sunnyvale company broadcast content by satellite to its own servers sitting at the edge of the network, close to viewers. From there, each stream had only a short trip left. Microsoft recommended iBEAM to companies using Windows Media. The company went public weeks after the dot-com crash began.

sections.heading: Skipping the Traffic
sections.body: iBEAM was founded in March 1998 and began selling its internet broadcasting service in October 1999. Its network combined land lines with satellite links. A single satellite broadcast could reach many edge servers at once, which made it cheap to send the same live event to a large audience. The bet was that streaming media would explode and that media companies would pay someone else to carry it.

sections.heading: Falling to Earth
sections.body: iBEAM priced its IPO at $10 a share in May 2000 and traded on Nasdaq as IBEM. The timing was poor. The market for internet stocks was already sliding, and the customers iBEAM counted on were running out of money too. The company kept losing cash. In October 2001 it filed for bankruptcy. In December 2001 Williams Communications bought substantially all of its assets for $25 million in cash.

cover.theme: a shooting star (a beam from the sky)
cover.artwork: Shooting Stars, from Mélodies de Désiré Dihau

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners, 2019 ($1.9B)
dek: Mindbody gave yoga studios, gyms and salons software to run their business, and gave customers an app to book.
lede: Mindbody's first big customer bought the software on the very first phone call. Rick Stollmeyer was running the company from his garage in San Luis Obispo, California. Bob Murphy and his wife ran five yoga studios in New York and needed one schedule for all of them. The two men became partners. By 2015, Mindbody served about 42,000 studios, gyms and spas, with 24 million active consumers booking classes and appointments through them.

sections.heading: From a Garage to the Front Desk
sections.body: Mindbody started in 2001 as desktop software for yoga and Pilates studios. Stollmeyer and Murphy spent hours behind studio front desks, fixing bugs and learning the work. In 2004 they rebuilt the business around the web. They would sell the software by monthly subscription instead of a one-time license. The first subscription version shipped in February 2005. The bigger bet was a marketplace, where consumers found classes and the studios got paid.

sections.heading: Vista Comes Calling
sections.body: Mindbody priced its IPO at $14 a share in June 2015 and listed on Nasdaq as MB. It kept adding studios and bought fitness-tracking startup FitMetrix and salon software maker Booker. Losses lingered, though, and the stock swung hard. In December 2018 Vista Equity Partners agreed to buy Mindbody for $36.50 a share in cash, about $1.9 billion. The deal closed in February 2019, and Mindbody left the public market.

cover.theme: a dancer stretching at the barre (a studio class)

dek: Alpha and Omega designs power chips that move electricity efficiently inside laptops, phones, TVs and servers.
lede: Every laptop needs dozens of tiny switches to turn battery power into the exact voltages its chips want. Alpha and Omega Semiconductor built a business on those parts, called power MOSFETs. The company designed them in Sunnyvale, had the wafers made at outside foundries, and packaged the chips in its own plant in Shanghai. When it went public in April 2010, the electronics industry was climbing back from the recession, and AOS had just swung to a profit.

sections.heading: Silicon Valley Design, Shanghai Packaging
sections.body: Mike Chang founded the company, which was incorporated in Bermuda in September 2000, and he served as its CEO. AOS ran its research and U.S. sales from Sunnyvale. It did not own a wafer fab. Instead, it ran its own MOSFET processes at partner foundries and kept packaging in-house in Shanghai. The bet was that owning the process and the package, without owning a fab, would let a small company win on cost and speed.

sections.heading: From First to Last Volt
sections.body: AOS priced its IPO at $18 a share in April 2010 and listed on Nasdaq as AOSL. It later changed its mind about fabs. In 2012 it bought a wafer fab in Hillsboro, Oregon, and in 2016 it formed a joint venture to build a plant in Chongqing, China. Its chips went into PCs, phones, servers and home appliances. Alpha and Omega Semiconductor still trades on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a turbine in a power house (power electronics)
cover.artwork: The Turbine, Power-House, New York City

dek: Qutoutiao was a Chinese news app that rewarded readers with points for reading articles and recruiting friends.
lede: Qutoutiao paid people to read. Its users earned loyalty points for opening articles, watching videos, and bringing friends to the app, and the points turned into small amounts of cash. The scheme worked fast. The Shanghai app launched in June 2016 and soon had about 62 million monthly users, each spending about 55 minutes a day in it. Barely two years after launch, the company sold shares in New York.

sections.heading: Points for Every Page
sections.body: Qutoutiao means something like "fun headlines." Founder Eric Tan built a news aggregator that picked stories for each user with a recommendation engine. The rivals were Jinritoutiao and Tencent's Kuaibao. Qutoutiao's edge was its loyalty program, which turned reading and referrals into rewards. The company earned its money from ads shown between the articles. Tencent was a strategic investor, and an affiliate of JD.com bought shares in the IPO.

sections.heading: The Points Ran Out
sections.body: Qutoutiao priced its IPO at $7 per American share in September 2018 and listed on Nasdaq as QTT. Paying for attention proved expensive. As China's ad market cooled and regulators tightened rules on online content, user growth stalled and losses mounted. The share price collapsed. In April 2023 the company's shares were removed from Nasdaq. It still files annual reports with the SEC.

cover.artwork: Untitled (Portrait of a Man Reading a Newspaper and Wearing a Top Hat)

fate: Taken private by Permira, 2022 ($80 a share)
dek: Mimecast protected, backed up and archived company email from the cloud, so attacks and outages never reached the inbox.
lede: Email was the front door for most attacks on a company, and Mimecast stood in the doorway. Every message passed through its cloud before it reached a mail server. Mimecast scanned it for malware and phishing, saved a copy, and kept mail flowing if the company's own server went down. Two South Africans built it from London. By 2015 it had more than 600 employees in four countries and revenue growing over 30 percent a year.

sections.heading: One Service for Every Inbox
sections.body: Peter Bauer and Neil Murray founded Mimecast in 2003 to make email safer. Their first service was Mimecast Email Security, delivered from the cloud at a time when most companies ran their own mail servers and bolted on separate tools. The bet was that one service could handle security, continuity and archiving together. Bauer became CEO, and Murray became chief technology officer. The company opened offices in the United States, Australia and South Africa.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars to Eighty
sections.body: Mimecast priced its IPO at $10 a share in November 2015 and listed on Nasdaq as MIME. Revenue for its fiscal year ended March 2015 was $116.1 million. As companies moved their mail to Microsoft's cloud, Mimecast sold protection on top of it, and the stock climbed for years. In 2022 the private equity firm Permira bought Mimecast for $80 a share in cash, about $5.8 billion, and took it private.

tagline: The Spam Box in the Closet
dek: Barracuda sold small and midsize businesses simple, affordable boxes and cloud services to block spam and attacks.
lede: Barracuda made its name with an appliance that IT staff could plug in and forget. The Barracuda Spam Firewall sat in a closet and stopped junk mail before it reached anyone's inbox. It was priced for small and midsize businesses. By 2013 the Campbell, California company counted more than 150,000 customers in over 100 countries since its start, and it sold backup, firewalls and cloud services too.

sections.heading: Built for the Overworked Admin
sections.body: Dean Drako, Zachary Levow and Michael Perone founded Barracuda in 2003. Their vision was to solve everyday IT problems simply and cheaply, with strong customer support. The bet was on the mainstream market that big security firms ignored. The spam firewall came first. Barracuda then added web filters, network firewalls, backup and storage, sold through thousands of partners. Francisco Partners bought a stake in the company before its offering.

sections.heading: A Round Trip on Wall Street
sections.body: Barracuda priced its IPO at $18 a share in November 2013 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as CUDA. Its appliance business faced pressure as customers moved to the cloud, and the stock struggled. In 2017 Thoma Bravo agreed to buy Barracuda for $27.55 a share in cash, about $1.6 billion. The deal closed in February 2018. Thoma Bravo later sold the company to KKR in 2022.

cover.theme: a predator fish in the water (the barracuda)
cover.artwork: A Youth Rescued from a Shark

tagline: The Phone System Behind the Carrier
dek: BroadSoft sold phone companies the software to run business phone and video calling over the internet.
lede: Office phones around the world rang through BroadSoft's software, and almost nobody using them knew its name. The Maryland company sold to phone carriers and cable companies. They used its BroadWorks platform to offer businesses hosted phone systems, voicemail and conferencing over internet lines, with no switchboard in the office. By 2010 the old telephone network was giving way to internet calling, and BroadSoft filed to go public as one of the quiet winners of that shift.

sections.heading: Selling Through the Carriers
sections.body: Michael Tessler and Scott Hoffpauir founded BroadSoft in November 1998. Tessler became CEO and Hoffpauir chief technology officer. The company began earning revenue in 2001, and it raised about $70.9 million from investors before its offering. The bet was that phone carriers would run their business customers' phone systems for them. BroadSoft sold through service providers worldwide, including some of the largest telecom equipment makers.

sections.heading: Cisco Picks Up
sections.body: BroadSoft priced its IPO at $9 a share in June 2010 and listed on Nasdaq as BSFT. Hosted calling grew, and BroadSoft added cloud services of its own for business messaging and meetings. In October 2017 Cisco agreed to buy BroadSoft for $55 a share in cash, about $1.9 billion. The deal closed in February 2018, and BroadWorks became part of Cisco's collaboration business.

cover.theme: two men in conversation (a phone call)

dek: ArcSight gathered security alerts and logs from across a company's network and spotted the attacks hiding in them.
lede: A big company's network produces millions of alerts a day, from firewalls, servers, routers and apps that do not talk to each other. ArcSight collected them all in one place and looked for the patterns that meant an attack. Its customers ran security command centers built around its screens. In February 2008, the Cupertino company went public as the financial crisis was starting, one of the few tech IPOs that year.

sections.heading: Wahoo Becomes ArcSight
sections.body: The company was incorporated in May 2000 as Wahoo Technologies and renamed ArcSight in 2001. Co-founder Hugh Njemanze, a veteran of the search company Verity, became its chief technology officer. Robert Shaw became CEO in August 2001. ArcSight sold its first product, ArcSight ESM, in June 2002. The bet was that companies would buy one console to make sense of all their security data. Revenue grew from $32.8 million in fiscal 2005 to $69.8 million in fiscal 2007.

sections.heading: HP Takes Aim
sections.body: ArcSight priced its IPO at $9 a share in February 2008 and listed on Nasdaq as ARST. Compliance rules and rising attacks kept sales growing through the recession. In September 2010 HP made a tender offer for ArcSight at $43.50 a share in cash, about $1.5 billion. The deal closed in October 2010. The ArcSight product later passed to Micro Focus and then to OpenText.

cover.theme: a rainbow arcing over a cathedral (an arc in sight)
cover.artwork: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows: the Rainbow

fate: Merged with MedicaLogic, 2000; now part of WebMD
dek: Medscape gave doctors, nurses and pharmacists free medical news, journal articles and continuing education on the web.
