lede: More than 210,000 physicians had signed up for Medscape by mid-1999. The New York site gave them free medical news, original articles by leading physicians, and courses that counted toward their license requirements. Drug companies paid for much of it. Genentech alone supplied about 27 percent of 1998 revenue. When Medscape went public that fall, health websites were among the hottest bets of the boom.

sections.heading: A Medical Publisher Goes Online
sections.body: Peter Frishauf, a medical publisher, founded Medscape, which was incorporated in New York in March 1996 and began operating the next month. Venture investor Alan Patricof joined as chairman that year. The bet was that professionals would trade the medical journal pile on their desks for a website. Medscape.com had more than 1.2 million registered members by June 1999, including 600,000 nurses, pharmacists and other health workers.

sections.heading: Merged, Then Absorbed
sections.body: Medscape priced its IPO at $8 a share in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as MSCP. CBS agreed to buy 600,000 shares in the offering. In 2000 Medscape merged with MedicaLogic, an electronic medical records company, to form MedicaLogic/Medscape. The combination struggled as the dot-com bust hit. WebMD bought the Medscape business in 2001, and Medscape remains one of the main websites for doctors today.

cover.theme: an anatomy plate from the Encyclopédie (medical reference)

fate: Acquired by Dun & Bradstreet, 2003 ($7 a share)
dek: Hoover's gave businesspeople and investors quick, readable profiles of thousands of companies, first in books and then online.
lede: Hoover's started as a book publisher called The Reference Press, printing thick handbooks of company profiles. Its writers turned annual reports into plain summaries: what a company did, who ran it, who it competed with. By 1999 that work lived on the web as Hoover's Online, free for basic profiles and paid for the deep ones. The Austin company went public that summer, when every investor suddenly wanted to research stocks from home.

sections.heading: A Bookstore Founder's Handbook
sections.body: Gary Hoover, who had earlier founded the BookStop chain of bookstores, started the company in 1990. His longtime friend and business partner Patrick Spain joined within weeks and later became CEO. The staff wrote and published reference books on companies and industries. As the web grew, the bet shifted. Hoover's would sell its database online, earn money from ads and subscriptions, and license content to newspapers such as The Washington Post and the Los Angeles Times. Subscribers could read detailed profiles of more than 3,500 companies.

sections.heading: Into the Dun & Bradstreet Files
sections.body: Hoover's priced its IPO at $14 a share in July 1999 and traded on Nasdaq as HOOV. Ad revenue faded after the dot-com bust, and the company leaned on paid subscriptions from businesses. In early 2003 Dun & Bradstreet, the giant of business credit data, bought Hoover's for $7 a share in cash. Hoover's kept its name for years afterward as D&B's company research service.

cover.theme: the Manhattan skyline (a city of companies)

dek: Pegasystems sells software that automates customer service and back-office work at large banks, insurers and other big companies.
lede: Pegasystems had made money every quarter for eleven years before it went public. That was rare for a software company in 1996. The Cambridge, Massachusetts firm sold rules-based software to some of the world's largest banks, mutual funds and credit card companies. When a customer called about a disputed charge or an account change, Pega's software decided what should happen next and who should do it.

sections.heading: A Chess Player's Logic
sections.body: Alan Trefler founded Pegasystems in 1983 and incorporated it in Massachusetts that April. He was a nationally ranked chess player, and the company built its products around rules: logic that captured how a business should handle each case. The bet was that big service firms would buy software to standardize the millions of small decisions their staff made every day. Pega had been profitable in every quarter since early 1985.

sections.heading: Forty Years and Counting
sections.body: Pegasystems priced its IPO at $12 a share in July 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as PEGA. The company stayed independent through every cycle since, and Trefler led it for decades. Its product grew into a platform for building business apps with little code, and later added AI. In 2022 a Virginia jury ordered Pega to pay rival Appian about $2 billion in a trade-secrets case, and an appeals court threw out the verdict in 2024. Pega still trades on Nasdaq.

fate: Acquired by Maxim Integrated, 2013 ($23 a share)
dek: Volterra made power chips that fed precise, steady voltage to processors in servers, networking gear and storage systems.
lede: Fast processors are picky eaters. They need large currents at low, exact voltages, and they need it to change in a blink when the workload does. Volterra, started by engineers trained at Berkeley, designed the integrated voltage regulators that handled that job. Its chips sat inside gear from Cisco, IBM, Hewlett-Packard and NEC. About 90 percent of its revenue came from outside the United States, where most of those systems were built.

sections.heading: Born in Berkeley
sections.body: The company was incorporated in August 1996 as Berkeley Integrated Technologies and took the name Volterra in 1997. Its co-founders included Anthony Stratakos, who became chief technology officer, Craig Teuscher, who ran sales, and Greg Hildebrand, who became chief financial officer. The bet was that power delivery, long built from separate parts, could be squeezed into smarter chips. A handful of large customers supplied most of its early revenue.

sections.heading: Maxim Takes Charge
sections.body: Volterra priced its IPO at $8 a share in July 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as VLTR. Demand from servers and data centers grew, and the company became one of the specialists in power for high-end processors. In August 2013 Maxim Integrated launched a tender offer for Volterra at $23 a share in cash. The deal closed that October, and Volterra became part of Maxim.

cover.theme: a Tuscan hill town (Volterra, the Tuscan city)
cover.artwork: San Gimignano, Piazza Cavour cis della cisterna

dek: EarthWeb ran websites where programmers and IT workers found code, answers, and later jobs, which became Dice.
lede: EarthWeb's stock more than tripled on its first day, in a week when New York's internet companies could do no wrong. The Manhattan startup ran a network of websites for computer professionals, with directories of Java code, technical references and a paid library called ITknowledge.com. Advertisers who wanted to reach programmers paid to be there. In November 1998, Silicon Alley had its first real stars, and EarthWeb was one of them.

sections.heading: Three Founders, One Audience
sections.body: Jack Hidary, his brother Murray Hidary and Nova Spivack started the company, first known as IdentiNet, and began operating as EarthWeb in October 1996. Jack Hidary became CEO. Their bet was a narrow one. EarthWeb would own a single crowd: developers, network engineers and the managers who bought technology. It earned money from ads, sponsorships, and subscriptions to premium technical content.

sections.heading: From Content to Careers
sections.body: EarthWeb priced its IPO at $14 a share in November 1998 and traded on Nasdaq as EWBX. In 1999 it bought Dice.com, a tech jobs board, and the job listings soon mattered more than the content. EarthWeb sold its content sites in 2000 and renamed itself Dice Inc. Debt from the boom years forced a Chapter 11 filing in 2003. Dice came out of bankruptcy and returned to the market in 2007 as Dice Holdings.

cover.artwork: Men Playing a Game of Dice

dek: Visigenic sold middleware that let programs talk to any database and to each other across a network.
lede: The founder of Informix started Visigenic to connect everything Informix's rivals had built. Corporate software in 1996 was a tangle of databases from Oracle, Sybase, Microsoft and others, and applications that could not talk to each other. Visigenic sold the connectors. VisiODBC let one program read many databases. VisiBroker let objects running on different machines call each other over a network, using the CORBA standard. Netscape and Microsoft were among its partners.

sections.heading: The Informix Founder Returns
sections.body: Roger Sippl had founded Informix, the database company, and co-founded Vantive. He started Visigenic in San Mateo in February 1993 and served as its CEO. The first business was database connectivity. In 1996 Visigenic bought PostModern Computing Technologies, which made distributed object software, and that became VisiBroker. The bet was that the internet would turn corporate software into pieces spread across many machines, all needing a common language.

sections.heading: Folded Into Borland
sections.body: Visigenic priced its IPO at $7.50 a share in August 1996 and traded on Nasdaq as VSGN. Database makers and operating system vendors threatened to build the same connections into their own products. In late 1997 Borland agreed to buy Visigenic in a stock deal, giving holders 0.81988 of a Borland share for each Visigenic share. The merger closed in early 1998, and VisiBroker lived on inside Borland's tools.

cover.theme: a bridge over a canal (connecting systems)

dek: SanDisk makes the flash memory inside memory cards, USB drives, phones and the solid-state drives in data centers.
lede: SanDisk went public twice, thirty years apart. The flash memory company first listed in 1995, then sold itself to Western Digital in 2016. In February 2025 Western Digital spun it back out as its own company. This filing is the next step. Western Digital handed some of its remaining SanDisk shares to its lenders to pay down debt, and they sold them to the public in June 2025, as demand for memory in AI data centers climbed.

sections.heading: From Camera Cards to Data Centers
sections.body: Eli Harari, Sanjay Mehrotra and Jack Yuan founded the company in 1988 to build storage from flash memory chips. Flash had no moving parts and kept data without power. SanDisk's cards went into early digital cameras, then phones, and its patents earned royalties from rivals. Western Digital bought SanDisk in 2016, betting that flash would replace spinning hard drives. Nine years later it split the businesses again, giving its shareholders 80.1 percent of the new SanDisk.

sections.heading: A Sale, Not a Debut
sections.body: SanDisk began trading on Nasdaq as SNDK in February 2025. This prospectus covers a secondary offering. Western Digital exchanged 18.5 million SanDisk shares for debt held by affiliates of J.P. Morgan and BofA, and those lenders sold the shares at $38.50 each on June 5, 2025. SanDisk raised no money from the sale. The company stays based in Milpitas, California, and still trades on Nasdaq.

fate: Acquired by Cambium Learning, 2020 ($30 a share)
tagline: The Yellow Box at the Airport
dek: Rosetta Stone taught languages through software that used pictures and immersion instead of grammar drills and translation.
lede: Rosetta Stone taught Spanish without a word of English. Its software showed a picture and a spoken phrase, again and again, until learners worked out the meaning the way a child does. The company called the method Dynamic Immersion. Its yellow boxes were sold at airport kiosks and advertised everywhere. In April 2009, with the financial crisis still raging and almost no companies going public, the Virginia company listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: A Family Business in Harrisonburg
sections.body: Allen Stoltzfus started the business in 1992 in Harrisonburg, Virginia, as Fairfield Language Technologies, run with members of his family. Many of its employees still worked in Harrisonburg when it went public. The bet was that computers could teach languages the natural way, through sight and sound. In January 2006 a new holding company bought the family firm, Fairfield & Sons, and took the Rosetta Stone name. The headquarters moved to Arlington, Virginia.

sections.heading: Immersion Meets the App Store
sections.body: Rosetta Stone priced its IPO at $18 a share in April 2009 and listed on the NYSE as RST. Free phone apps such as Duolingo soon undercut its pricey boxed courses. The company shifted to subscriptions and leaned on its Lexia reading business for schools. In 2020 Cambium Learning, owned by Veritas Capital, bought Rosetta Stone for $30 a share. The language business was sold to IXL Learning in 2021.

cover.theme: a stone carved with hieroglyphs (the Rosetta Stone)

dek: Intelsat runs a fleet of communications satellites that carry TV channels, airline Wi-Fi, and military and corporate networks.
lede: Intelsat put the first commercial communications satellite in orbit in 1965, when it was a club of governments. Nearly fifty years later it was a private company in Luxembourg, carrying TV channels and data for media firms, telecom carriers and the U.S. military. It also carried a mountain of debt from years of private equity ownership. In April 2013 Intelsat went public, mainly to raise cash to pay some of it down.

sections.heading: From Treaty to Takeover
sections.body: Intelsat began in 1964 as an intergovernmental organization to build a global satellite system, and in 1965 it launched Early Bird. For decades member countries owned it together. In 2001 it was privatized. Buyout firms then bought it, sold it and loaded it with borrowing. The bet behind the IPO was that steady long-term contracts for satellite capacity could carry that debt while the company invested in new, faster satellites.

sections.heading: Bankruptcy, Then a Merger
sections.body: Intelsat priced its IPO at $18 a share in April 2013 and listed on the NYSE as I. Competition from fiber and new satellite networks pushed prices down, and the debt never shrank enough. In May 2020 Intelsat filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It came out in early 2022 as a private company owned by its former creditors. In July 2025 the European satellite operator SES completed its purchase of Intelsat.

cover.theme: figures gazing up at the moon (looking to orbit)

dek: StarMedia gave Spanish and Portuguese speakers a home page on the web built for them, in their own language.
lede: StarMedia ran a web portal for Latin America out of offices in New York. Its sites spoke Spanish and Portuguese, and they offered news, email, chat and search to a region where few people were online yet. On its first day of trading in May 1999, the stock jumped from $15 to about $26. Within a week it closed above $61. Investors were paying up for a continent of users who had not logged on yet.

sections.heading: Two Founders, One Continent
sections.body: Fernando Espuelas and Jack Chen founded StarMedia in 1996. Their bet was simple. Americans had Yahoo, AOL and Excite, and Latin America had nothing like them built for its own languages. StarMedia set out to be the first stop for Spanish and Portuguese speakers going online. It raised venture money, sold ads across the region, and spent hard to win users before the American giants arrived. Speed mattered more to the founders than profit.

sections.heading: Trouble in Mexico
sections.body: StarMedia priced its offering at $15 a share in May 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. Less than a year later the dot-com crash began. In November 2001 the company said its results for 2000 and 2001 could not be trusted, because two Mexican subsidiaries had booked revenue they had not earned. Nasdaq delisted the stock in February 2002. StarMedia sold its portal to the Spanish company eresMas for about $8 million and filed for bankruptcy in December 2003.

cover.theme: palms over a bay near Rio (a home page for Latin America)
cover.artwork: Praÿa Rodriguez, near Rio de Janeiro, plate one from Paysages, volume 1 of Voyage pittoresque dans le Brésil

fate: Taken private by Vista Equity Partners and Elliott, 2022 ($16.5B)
dek: Citrix let companies run Windows programs on one central server and show them on almost any screen, anywhere.
lede: Citrix started life as Citrus, until another company claimed the name. Its founder, a former IBM developer named Ed Iacobucci, wanted one powerful server to run Windows programs for many people at once, each on a cheap or distant machine. Microsoft liked the idea enough to license its code to him and take a stake. When Citrix went public in December 1995, its stock doubled on the first day. This filing came six months later, for a second sale of shares.

sections.heading: A Renamed Fruit
sections.body: Iacobucci founded the company in Richardson, Texas, in April 1989, then moved it to Coral Springs, Florida. The new name blended Citrus and UNIX. Citrix shipped its first products in 1991. Its WinFrame and WinView software, built under license from Microsoft, let a company keep its Windows programs on a central server. Remote workers, branch offices and even non-Windows machines could all reach the same applications over a network.

sections.heading: Thirty Dollars by the Close
sections.body: Citrix priced its first shares at $15 in December 1995. They closed the first day at $30. This 1996 filing raised more money from that eager market. The company later moved to Fort Lauderdale and grew into a fixture of corporate IT, as its products became the standard way to deliver apps and desktops from a data center. In September 2022, Vista Equity Partners and Elliott's Evergreen Coast Capital took Citrix private in a $16.5 billion deal and merged it with TIBCO.

cover.theme: a window onto distant woods (apps reached from afar)

tagline: A Hundred Searches in the Crowd
dek: Baidu built the search engine most people in China used to find things on the web.
lede: On its first day of trading in August 2005, Baidu's stock rose from $27 to more than $122. That gain of about 354 percent was one of the largest first-day jumps since the dot-com bubble. Investors were buying a five-year-old Beijing company that answered the questions of China's fast-growing population of internet users, in Chinese. Google was still a small player in China, and Baidu already led the market.

sections.heading: A Name From a Poem
sections.body: Robin Li and Eric Xu founded Baidu in Beijing in January 2000. Li had worked on search technology in the United States, including a patented method for ranking pages by the links that pointed to them. The name comes from a Song dynasty poem about searching for someone in a festival crowd a hundred, a thousand times. Baidu began by selling search to Chinese portals, then built its own site and made money from paid search results.

sections.heading: From $27 to $122
sections.body: Baidu sold American depositary shares at $27 each on Nasdaq on August 5, 2005. They closed the day at $122.54. In the years after, Google pulled back from mainland China, and Baidu became the default search engine for hundreds of millions of people. It expanded into maps, cloud services and self-driving cars. Baidu added a second listing in Hong Kong in 2021 and still trades on Nasdaq under the ticker BIDU.

dek: EarthLink sold home internet access over the phone line, and won members by treating them well.
lede: Sprint handed EarthLink 130,000 of its own internet customers in 1998, along with cash and credit, in return for about 30 percent of the company. EarthLink was a four-year-old internet service provider from Pasadena, selling dial-up access to homes and small businesses. It had gone public in January 1997 at $13 a share. This filing came in May 1998, as the Sprint deal closed, for a new sale of shares at an assumed price of $58.50.

sections.heading: Busy Signals and Setup Disks
sections.body: Sky Dayton founded EarthLink in 1994, when getting online meant modems, phone numbers and setup disks. His bet was that a provider could win by making the internet simple and by keeping its members happy, at a time when rivals were known for busy signals and slow help lines. EarthLink grew through direct mail and partner deals. By April 1998 it had passed 500,000 members, and the Sprint alliance promised at least 150,000 new members a year.

sections.heading: Sprint, MindSpring, Windstream
sections.body: EarthLink first sold shares at $13 in January 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as ELNK. The 1998 offering in this filing followed the Sprint deal. In 2000 EarthLink merged with MindSpring and moved its headquarters to Atlanta. As broadband replaced dial-up, the company shifted toward selling network services to businesses. In 2017 the telecom company Windstream bought EarthLink in an all-stock deal.

cover.theme: a heart-shaped map of the world (a link to the whole earth)

fate: Acquired by Yahoo, 1999 ($3.57B); shut down in the U.S., 2009
dek: GeoCities gave anyone a free home page, filed on a street in a themed online neighborhood.
lede: By May 1998, people had built more than 1.9 million free websites on GeoCities, up from about 10,000 in October 1995. The company called them Homesteaders. Each site sat on a numbered street in a themed neighborhood, so a fan page about movies lived near other movie pages. In April 1998 GeoCities drew more than 14 million visitors. That made it one of the most visited sites on the web when it filed to go public that summer.

sections.heading: Neighborhoods of Strangers
sections.body: David Bohnett and John Rezner started the company in 1994 as Beverly Hills Internet. The idea was a city of personal pages, organized by interest. Homesteaders got free space and simple tools, and in return GeoCities sold ads on the pages they built. By the time of the filing, Homesteaders had made an estimated 15 million pages. Many of them were the first thing their authors had ever published.

sections.heading: Bought, Then Bulldozed
sections.body: GeoCities priced its offering at $17 a share in August 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as GCTY. Five months later, in January 1999, Yahoo agreed to buy it for about $3.57 billion in stock. The deal closed that May. Under Yahoo the neighborhoods faded, and users moved on to blogs and social networks. Yahoo shut down GeoCities in the United States in October 2009, and volunteer archivists rushed to save as many pages as they could.

cover.theme: a small town and its streets (a city of home pages)
cover.artwork: View of the Town of Maassluis

dek: Value America sold computers, appliances and almost anything else online, shipped straight from the maker to your door.
lede: Value America owned no warehouse. When a customer ordered a printer or a toaster on its website, the order went straight to the manufacturer, which shipped the product. Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures and FedEx founder Frederick W. Smith both backed the idea. When the Charlottesville company went public in April 1999, its stock closed the first day at $55, more than double the offer price. That valued a three-year-old company with no profits at about $2.4 billion.

sections.heading: Convergence Commerce
sections.body: Craig Winn and Rex Scatena founded Value America in March 1996 and moved it to Charlottesville, Virginia, in 1998. Winn called the model convergence commerce. Brands would pay to present their products well online, and the store would skip the cost of stocking them. Customers would get low prices and a wide range of goods, from computers to kitchen supplies. The plan depended on dozens of manufacturers filling orders quickly and accurately on Value America's behalf.

sections.heading: Seventeen Months Later
sections.body: Value America priced its shares at $23 in April 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. The model broke under real orders. Shipments ran late, bills went wrong, and manufacturers struggled to keep up. The company cut its catalog back to computer products and office supplies, then replaced its leadership. On August 11, 2000, Value America filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. In October 2000, the distributor Merisel bought what was left, including its supply chain system.

cover.theme: a galloping mail coach (straight from the maker to the door)

dek: NXP makes the chips inside car systems, contactless cards and phones, spun out of the Dutch electronics giant Philips.
lede: Five private equity firms bought most of Philips' chip business in 2006, two years before the financial crisis. KKR, Bain Capital, Silver Lake, Apax and AlpInvest renamed it NXP. The buyout left the Dutch chipmaker with heavy debt, and the crisis cut deep into chip sales. In August 2010 NXP came to Nasdaq and priced its shares at $14. It was a modest start for a company that later drew a takeover bid worth $44 billion.

sections.heading: A Spinout From Eindhoven
sections.body: Philips had made semiconductors for decades from its home in Eindhoven. In September 2006 it sold an 80.1 percent stake in the division to the buyout group. The new company kept the Philips engineers and customers and took a new name. NXP's bet was to focus on chips that connect and control things, such as car electronics, identification cards, and the near-field radios that let a phone or card talk to a reader.

sections.heading: The Deal That Died
sections.body: NXP sold 34 million shares at $14 each on Nasdaq in August 2010. The stock rose as car and payment chips took off. In December 2015 it completed a merger with Freescale, the former Motorola chip unit. In October 2016 Qualcomm agreed to buy NXP for about $44 billion. The deal waited for approval from Chinese regulators that never came, and Qualcomm walked away in July 2018. NXP still trades on Nasdaq as NXPI.

cover.theme: a Dutch canal boat (a Netherlands company setting off)
cover.artwork: Canal with a Large Boat and a Bridge

dek: VA Linux built servers and workstations that ran the free Linux operating system, for companies building the web.
lede: VA Linux priced its shares at $30 and watched them close the first day at $239.25. That gain of 698 percent, on December 9, 1999, set a record for a first-day pop. The Sunnyvale company sold computers loaded with Linux, the free operating system that hobbyists had built and big companies were starting to trust. Investors wanted any piece of open source they could buy, and VA Linux was the purest one on offer.

sections.heading: Servers for the Open Web
sections.body: Larry Augustin, a Stanford graduate student, started the company with fellow students, and it dates its founding to January 1995. VA built Intel-based servers and workstations tuned for Linux, and sold them to the internet companies multiplying across Silicon Valley. Its engineers also worked on Linux itself. The bet was that free software would run the web, and that someone had to sell the reliable machines it ran on. VA also owned Linux.com, a hub for the community.

sections.heading: From Servers to T-Shirts
sections.body: The record debut faded fast. Within months VA agreed to buy Andover.net, owner of Slashdot, and the dot-com crash soon followed. Dell, IBM and HP began selling Linux servers too. In 2001 VA left the hardware business and became VA Software, then SourceForge, after its site for open-source projects. It later sold geek gifts as ThinkGeek and renamed itself Geeknet. In 2015 GameStop bought Geeknet for about $140 million.

cover.theme: fireworks bursting over a cathedral spire (a record first day)
cover.artwork: Firework around the Antwerp Cathedral, plate 41 from Casperius Gevartius, Pompa Introitus Honori Serenissimi Principis Ferdinandi

fate: Acquired by SBI Group, 2003; now part of Publicis Groupe
dek: Razorfish designed websites and online services for big companies that needed help showing up on the internet.
lede: Razorfish redesigned Charles Schwab's online trading system and built the screens for Road Runner, the cable internet service owned by Time Warner and its partners. The New York firm also worked on theglobe.com and IBM's server pages. Two friends had started it in 1995. When it filed to go public in early 1999, every big company wanted a website, and few knew how to make one. Razorfish sold strategy, design and the code to make it all work.

sections.heading: Two Friends in Manhattan
sections.body: Jeff Dachis and Craig Kanarick founded Razorfish in New York in 1995. They called the work digital communications solutions: consulting, information architecture, user interfaces and the custom software beneath them. The bet was that companies would pay premium fees for a firm that understood both design and technology. Razorfish grew by winning large clients and by buying other agencies in the United States and Europe, and became a name brand for the Silicon Alley scene.

sections.heading: A Long Line of Owners
sections.body: Razorfish raised $48 million on Nasdaq in April 1999, at $16 a share. When the dot-com crash hit in 2000, its clients cut their web budgets, and the firm shrank hard. In 2003 SBI Group bought it and renamed it SBI.Razorfish. The agency then passed to aQuantive in 2004, to Microsoft in 2007 through its aQuantive purchase, and to Publicis Groupe in 2009 for $530 million. Razorfish still operates inside Publicis.

cover.artwork: Carp in the Tone River (Tonegawa no koi), section of a sheet from the series "Cutout Pictures of Famous Places in Edo (Edo meisho harimaze zue)"

dek: AVG gave away antivirus software to millions of people, then sold upgrades to the ones who wanted more.
lede: AVG had about 106 million active users when it filed to go public, and most of them paid nothing. The company began in 1991 in Czechoslovakia as Grisoft and gave away a basic antivirus program to anyone who wanted it. That free product brought in customers for almost nothing. AVG then sold paid security suites, small business tools and search partnerships on top. In February 2012 it listed on the New York Stock Exchange, a rare Czech-born software company on Wall Street.

sections.heading: Grisoft Gives It Away
sections.body: Jan Gritzbach and Tomáš Hofer founded Grisoft in 1991, soon after the fall of communism in Czechoslovakia. Its antivirus product, AVG, became the company's name in 2008. The bet was freemium before the word was common. A free scanner earned trust and downloads around the world, and a share of those users would pay for stronger protection. The company kept its engineers in the Czech Republic and set up its legal home in Amsterdam.

sections.heading: Two Czech Rivals Merge
sections.body: AVG sold shares at $16 on the New York Stock Exchange in February 2012. Growth slowed as people moved from PCs to phones and as Microsoft built free protection into Windows. AVG spent on mobile security and other new products to keep up. In July 2016 Avast, its old rival from Prague, agreed to buy AVG for $1.3 billion. The combined company later merged with NortonLifeLock in 2022 to form Gen Digital.

cover.theme: Saint Michael crushing the dragon (a guardian against viruses)
cover.artwork: St Michael Triumphing Over the Dragon

dek: DivX squeezed full-length movies small enough to download, and got its format built into millions of DVD players.
lede: DivX began as a hack. Around 1998 a French programmer named Jérôme Rota pulled apart a Microsoft video codec and made it shrink whole movies small enough to pass around the internet. A San Diego company turned that trick into a business. By its 2006 filing, people had downloaded the DivX codec more than 180 million times. Consumer electronics makers paid to put a DivX Certified logo on their DVD players, and about 8.5 million certified devices shipped in a single quarter of 2005.

sections.heading: From Montpellier to San Diego
sections.body: Jordan Greenhall recruited Rota in 2000, and the two built DivXNetworks in San Diego, renamed DivX in 2005. They rewrote the codec as their own software and gave it away to consumers. The money came from licensing. Chipmakers built DivX playback into their chips, and device makers paid a fee for each certified player they shipped. The bet was that a format fans already loved could become a standard that the electronics industry paid to support.

sections.heading: A Format Changes Hands
sections.body: DivX priced its offering at $16 a share in September 2006 and listed on Nasdaq. Streaming soon pulled viewers away from downloaded files and discs. In 2010 Sonic Solutions bought DivX, and the next year Rovi bought Sonic. Rovi sold DivX in 2014 to Blackstone and Parallax Capital for $75 million. NeuLion bought it in 2015, and Fortress Investment Group took over key DivX assets in 2018. DivX still operates from San Diego.

cover.theme: a grid of photographic frames of a moving hand (video, frame by frame)

tagline: The Web on a Palm V
dek: OmniSky sold a clip-on modem and a monthly plan that put email and the web on Palm handhelds.
lede: The pictures inside OmniSky's prospectus show a Palm V snapping onto a small wireless modem, with E*Trade on its screen. This was the mobile internet of 2000, years before the iPhone. The Palo Alto company had launched its service nationally only in May, after a beta test that reached about 5,500 subscribers. Users could read email, check stocks and browse a trimmed-down web from anywhere with a signal. OmniSky went public that September, as the dot-com market was already falling.

sections.heading: AirWeb, Renamed
sections.body: OmniSky was incorporated in May 1999 as AirWeb Corporation and took its new name that November. Patrick McVeigh, Barak Berkowitz and Michael Dolbec were among its co-founders. The bet was that people would pay a monthly fee for the internet in their pocket. OmniSky bundled the modem, the wireless network access and software tuned for small screens, so a Palm owner could get online without dealing with a phone carrier.

sections.heading: A Short Flight
sections.body: OmniSky priced its offering at $12 a share in September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. The money ran out fast. Wireless networks were slow, the hardware was costly, and phones with their own browsers were coming. In November 2001 the company said it could not finish its financial statements. OmniSky went into bankruptcy, and in December 2001 EarthLink bought its business.

cover.theme: wild geese crossing the moon (messages carried through the sky)
cover.artwork: Wild Geese Flying Across Full Moon

dek: New Focus made lasers and optical parts that phone companies used to push more data through fiber.
lede: New Focus spent its first ten years making precise optical tools for scientists' labs. Then the telecom boom arrived, and the same skills became hot property. Its tunable lasers let fiber-network builders test and run their equipment, and its customers included Lucent, Nortel, Corning and Alcatel. When the Santa Clara company went public in May 2000, carriers were laying fiber as fast as they could, and investors were paying almost any price for photonics.

sections.heading: From the Lab Bench
sections.body: Milton Chang, Timothy Day and Robert Marsland were among the co-founders of New Focus in April 1990. The company first sold advanced photonics tools to researchers. By 2000 it was turning a decade of that know-how toward optical networking, selling to more than 50 customers. The bet was that phone companies would need far more components to light their fiber, and that New Focus could build them in volume.

sections.heading: After the Light Went Out
sections.body: New Focus priced its offering at $20 a share in May 2000 and listed on Nasdaq. Within a year the telecom bubble burst. Carriers stopped buying, and orders for optical parts collapsed across the industry. New Focus cut staff and closed plants. In 2004 the British optical company Bookham bought New Focus, merging two of the survivors of the crash.

cover.theme: clouds caught through a lens (light brought into focus)
cover.artwork: Music - A Sequence of Ten Cloud Photographs, No. II

dek: Cavium designed processors that let network gear move and secure traffic at high speed.
lede: Cavium's best chips used the MIPS design, the same architecture that once powered the Nintendo 64. The Mountain View company packed many of those cores onto one chip, called OCTEON, and sold it to the makers of routers, switches and security boxes. Its customers included Cisco, Aruba Networks, Citrix and F5. When Cavium went public in May 2007, it had more than 100 customers. Every one of those boxes needed a fast brain to sort and secure the traffic passing through it.

sections.heading: A Chip Full of Cores
sections.body: Syed Ali and Raghib Hussain were among the founders of Cavium in November 2000. They saw that network equipment needed more than raw speed. It also had to encrypt, inspect and sort traffic as it passed. Cavium built processors with many cores and special engines for those jobs. The bet was that equipment makers would rather buy that power on a chip than design it themselves, and the OCTEON family began shipping in volume.

sections.heading: Bought by Marvell
sections.body: Cavium priced its offering at $13.50 a share in May 2007 and listed on Nasdaq. Over the next decade it grew by acquisition, adding storage and server chips, including the purchase of QLogic in 2016. Cavium also built ARM-based server processors called ThunderX. In July 2018 Marvell Technology completed its purchase of Cavium in a deal worth about $6 billion.

cover.artwork: Grotto and Friars, from The Ruins of Rome

dek: Glu made games for mobile phones, from Monopoly to Diner Dash, sold through phone carriers.
lede: Before the App Store, a mobile game reached you through your phone carrier's menu, and Glu sold through more than 150 carriers and distributors. Its catalog included Diner Dash, Monopoly, Sonic the Hedgehog and World Series of Poker, squeezed onto small screens and keypads. The San Mateo company filed to go public in late 2006. Three months after its March 2007 offering, Apple released the first iPhone, and the business of mobile games began to change.

sections.heading: Cyent, Sorrent, Glu
sections.body: The company was incorporated in May 2001 as Cyent Studios and became Sorrent later that year, before taking the Glu name. It licensed famous brands and built games that could run on hundreds of different phone models. The bet was that phones would become the world's largest game console, and that a publisher with strong brands and carrier deals would win the shelf space on every handset.

sections.heading: The Kardashian Years
sections.body: Glu priced its offering at $11.50 a share in March 2007 and listed on Nasdaq. The iPhone and Android moved games from carriers to app stores, and Glu had to rebuild around free-to-play games. Its 2014 hit Kim Kardashian: Hollywood brought in huge revenue from in-game purchases. Later hits included Design Home. In April 2021 Electronic Arts bought Glu for about $2.4 billion.

cover.artwork: Chrysanthemum festival, from the series "Precious Children's Games of the Five Festivals (Kodakara gosetsu asobi)"

dek: MIPS designed processor cores and licensed them to chipmakers for game consoles, printers and set-top boxes.
lede: The processor inside the Nintendo 64 came from MIPS, and so did the one in Sony's first PlayStation. MIPS made no chips of its own. It designed processor cores and licensed them to semiconductor partners such as NEC and Toshiba, which built and sold the silicon. When MIPS went public in June 1998, it was a unit of Silicon Graphics, the workstation maker. SGI sold part of its stake in the offering and kept control of the company.

sections.heading: Out From Silicon Graphics
sections.body: MIPS Computer Systems was founded in 1984 to build fast, simple RISC processors, a design approach that came out of Stanford research. Silicon Graphics, its biggest customer, bought the company in 1992. MIPS Technologies, incorporated that June, became the processor design arm. The bet was to license designs instead of making chips, collecting fees and royalties from every partner that shipped a MIPS-based product.

sections.heading: Patents Worth More
sections.body: MIPS priced its offering at $14 a share in June 1998, and Silicon Graphics received the proceeds from the shares it sold. SGI later spun off the rest of its stake. MIPS cores spread into routers, set-top boxes and printers, but ARM won the phone market. In 2013 Imagination Technologies bought MIPS's business, while a group led by ARM bought most of its patents.

cover.theme: a clockmaker at his bench (precise little machines)

dek: AppFolio gave small and midsize property managers one cloud system for rent, repairs, accounting and tenants.
lede: AppFolio's founders had sold a company to Citrix before. Klaus Schauser co-founded Expertcity, the maker of GoToMyPC, Then he turned to a plain, overlooked market: the people who manage apartments and rental houses. AppFolio built cloud software for managers with 20 to 3,000 units. It counted the U.S. market at $5 billion or more. When the Goleta company went public in June 2015, most of its customers were still moving off spreadsheets and old desktop programs.

sections.heading: From GoToMyPC to Rent Checks
sections.body: Schauser and Jon Walker co-founded AppFolio in 2006, near Santa Barbara. Their bet was that vertical software, built for one trade, could beat general tools. AppFolio Property Manager handled leasing, maintenance, accounting and online rent payments in one place, and worked on a phone as well as a desktop. The company also sold MyCase, practice management software for small law firms, using the same playbook in a second industry.

sections.heading: A Steady Climber
sections.body: AppFolio priced its offering at $12 a share in June 2015 and listed on Nasdaq as APPF. It kept adding customers and services, such as tenant screening and payments, which grew revenue per unit managed. Over the following years the stock rose many times over its offer price. AppFolio still trades on Nasdaq and is still based in the Santa Barbara area.

cover.theme: an apartment building drawn in plan (property managed from above)
cover.artwork: Ontario Apartment Building, Chicago, Illinois, Isometric

dek: Be Free ran affiliate programs, so online stores could pay other sites a cut of each sale they sent.
lede: One customer, barnesandnoble.com, brought Be Free 78 percent of its revenue in 1997. The Massachusetts company ran the affiliate program behind the bookseller's site. Thousands of smaller websites posted links to books, and Be Free tracked every click and paid each site a commission when a visitor bought. By its November 1999 offering, Be Free had spread that model to many more online merchants and portals, including GeoCities. Online stores were spending heavily for traffic, and Be Free counted the results.

sections.heading: Freedom of Information, Inc.
sections.body: Be Free was incorporated in January 1996 under the name Freedom of Information. It became a service that let e-merchants recruit and manage tens of thousands of partner sites. Its BFAST service handled the tracking, reporting and payments, and B-INTOUCH did the same for email referrals. The bet was that stores would rather pay for sales than for banner views. Barnesandnoble.com's share of revenue fell to 40 percent in the first half of 1999 as new clients signed on, with GeoCities alone bringing in 15 percent.

sections.heading: Sold to ValueClick
sections.body: Be Free priced its offering at $12 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. Like most internet stocks, it rose fast and then fell hard when the bubble burst and many of its merchant clients cut back or closed. Affiliate marketing itself survived and became a standard part of online retail. In 2002 the online advertising company ValueClick bought Be Free.

cover.theme: swallows swooping over a river (links flying free)

fate: Taken private by Baring Private Equity Asia, 2021
dek: Virtusa wrote and maintained software for big banks and phone companies, with engineers in Sri Lanka and India.
lede: Virtusa ran its business from a Massachusetts office park, but much of its work happened in Colombo, Sri Lanka, and in Hyderabad and Chennai, India. Its engineers built and maintained software for clients such as JPMorgan, British Telecommunications and Bear Stearns. When Virtusa went public in August 2007, offshore IT services had become a big industry, led by Indian giants. Virtusa pitched itself as a smaller, specialized rival with a Sri Lankan base.

sections.heading: Technology Providers, Inc.
sections.body: Kris Canekeratne, a Sri Lankan-born engineer, founded the company in Massachusetts in November 1996 as Technology Providers, Inc. It later took the name Virtusa. The bet was that a firm with strong engineering in Sri Lanka could win complex software work from large Western companies. Virtusa focused on banks, insurers and telecom companies, and built most of its development centers in South Asia to keep costs down.

sections.heading: Bought for Two Billion
sections.body: Virtusa priced its offering at $14 a share in August 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as VRTU. The financial crisis hit its banking clients the next year, but the company kept growing and later bought Polaris, an Indian financial software firm. In February 2021 Baring Private Equity Asia completed its purchase of Virtusa in a deal valued at about $2 billion, and the stock left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a ship under furled sails (work sent across the ocean)
cover.artwork: Ship with Sails Furled and Arrow Pointing to the Right

tagline: The Palm OS, On Its Own
dek: PalmSource made Palm OS, the software inside Palm handhelds, and licensed it to Sony, Samsung, Garmin and others.
lede: Palm OS ran on the best-selling handhelds in the world, and Palm decided the software should live in its own company. PalmSource was born as a Palm subsidiary in December 2001. It licensed Palm OS to device makers including Sony, Samsung, Garmin, Kyocera and Lenovo, as well as to palmOne, the hardware company left behind. Palm handed PalmSource shares to its own stockholders in October 2003. This filing, in early 2004, sold about 20 percent more stock to new investors.

sections.heading: Splitting the Palm
sections.body: Palm split its operating system group from its hardware business so that rival device makers would trust the platform. The bet was that Palm OS could become to handhelds and smartphones what Windows was to PCs, licensed to many brands and earning a fee on each device. The filing named its main rivals plainly: Microsoft and Symbian, both spending heavily to win the smartphone.

sections.heading: Sold to Japan
sections.body: PalmSource sold shares at $18 in its 2004 offering, after trading on Nasdaq since the spin-off. The new money did not change the trend. Licensees were slow to adopt its next-generation system, and smartphones moved toward other platforms. In 2005 the Japanese software company Access agreed to buy PalmSource for about $324 million. Access later built a Linux-based successor, but Palm OS never regained its lead.

cover.theme: a glasshouse of tall palms (Palm OS)
cover.artwork: The Interior of the Palm House on the Pfaueninsel Near Potsdam

dek: Bankrate compared mortgage, loan and savings rates from banks across the country, free for anyone to read.
lede: Bankrate began as a printed newsletter called Bank Rate Monitor, that tracked what banks paid and charged. The company that filed this S-1 in March 1999 was called Intelligent Life Corporation. It ran Bankrate.com and smaller sites such as theWhiz.com and Consejero.com. Banks paid to appear in its rate tables, and advertisers paid to reach readers shopping for a mortgage or a CD. Consumers got the rates for free.

sections.heading: A Newsletter Turned Website
sections.body: Intelligent Life was incorporated in Florida in 1993 and bought the assets of the rate-tracking business. It surveyed financial institutions for their rates and published them in print, in Bank Rate Monitor and Consumer Mortgage Guide, and then on the web. The bet was that people would compare rates online before they walked into a bank, and that lenders and advertisers would pay to be there when they did.

sections.heading: Three Lives on the Market
sections.body: The company priced its offering at $13 a share in May 1999 and soon renamed itself, first ilife.com and then Bankrate. After the dot-com crash it narrowed its focus to Bankrate.com. Apax Partners took Bankrate private in 2009, and it returned to the stock market in 2011. In 2017 the marketing company Red Ventures bought Bankrate for about $1.4 billion.

cover.theme: a weather vane (which way rates are blowing)

fate: Acquired by Monex Group, 2011 (as TradeStation Group)
dek: Omega Research sold TradeStation, software that let traders write, test and run their own trading rules.
lede: TradeStation let a trader type a rule in near-plain English, test it against years of market history, and then watch it fire signals live. Omega Research, run by two brothers in Miami, released it in 1991. Its EasyLanguage made strategy programming open to people who were not programmers. When the company went public in October 1997, day traders and online brokers were multiplying, and Omega Research sold the tools serious traders used to look for an edge.

sections.heading: The Cruz Brothers
sections.body: William and Ralph Cruz founded Omega Research in Florida in 1982. Their products included TradeStation, OptionStation and SuperCharts. The bet was that individual traders would pay for the kind of charting and back-testing tools that professional desks built for themselves. The company sold software licenses and data services, and it grew with the spread of fast PCs and real-time market data into homes and small trading firms.

sections.heading: From Software to Broker
sections.body: Omega Research priced its offering at $11 a share in October 1997 and listed on Nasdaq. In 2000 it bought an online brokerage, onlinetradinginc.com, so customers could send orders straight from its software. The company renamed itself TradeStation Group in 2001 and became a broker as much as a software maker. In 2011 the Japanese online brokerage Monex Group bought TradeStation Group.

cover.theme: faces on the stock exchange floor (traders and their tools)
cover.artwork: Physiognomy of the Stock Exchange. The despair of the baissier and the triumph of the haussier - or crying and laughing, plate 440 from Actualités

dek: FTD.com let people order flowers online and have a local FTD florist deliver them the same day.
lede: Florists began wiring flower orders to each other in 1910, and that network became FTD. Eighty-nine years later its parent set up FTD.com to move the business online. Customers picked a bouquet on the website or called 1-800-SEND-FTD, and a member florist near the recipient made and delivered it. The winged Mercury Man was already one of the best-known logos in retail. FTD.com went public in September 1999, as dot-com flower sellers raced to own Mother's Day.

sections.heading: A 1910 Network, Online
sections.body: FTD.com was founded by FTD, the floral services company, to run its consumer website and toll-free number. It owned no greenhouses or vans. Orders flowed to independent florists in FTD's network, who did the arranging and delivery. The bet was that a trusted old brand, plus a ready-made delivery system in nearly every town, could beat rivals such as 1-800-Flowers and a wave of startups that were spending heavily to win customers online.

sections.heading: Back Into the Fold
sections.body: FTD.com priced its offering at $8 a share in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq. It spent heavily on advertising, then cut back as the dot-com market cooled. Its parent kept control of the company throughout, and the shares held by the public were a small slice. In 2002 FTD Inc. bought out the public shareholders and folded FTD.com back into the company.

cover.theme: winged Mercury in flight (the FTD messenger)

tagline: The Sports Page With an Eye
dek: SportsLine ran CBS SportsLine, a website with live scores, news and fantasy games for sports fans.
lede: The CBS eye sat on SportsLine's home page. In 1997 the Fort Lauderdale startup signed a deal with CBS, and its site became CBS SportsLine, promoted on the network's broadcasts of events such as the NCAA basketball tournament and the 1998 Winter Olympics. Fans came for live scores, stats, news and fantasy leagues they could play all season. When SportsLine went public in November 1997, few websites had a television network pushing viewers their way.

sections.heading: Michael Levy's Sports Wire
sections.body: Michael Levy founded the company in Florida in February 1994. The bet was that sports fans wanted more scores, numbers and news than a newspaper or a nightly highlight show could give them, and that they would come back every day. SportsLine sold advertising and merchandise and charged for premium content and fantasy games. The CBS deal traded a stake in the company for promotion that SportsLine could never have afforded to buy.

sections.heading: Back to the Network
sections.body: SportsLine priced its offering at $8 a share in November 1997 and listed on Nasdaq. The stock soared in the internet boom and fell after the crash, as ESPN and others built rival sites. The company renamed itself SportsLine.com, cut costs and leaned harder on its CBS partnership. In 2004 Viacom, then the parent of CBS, bought the rest of SportsLine. The site later became CBSSports.com.

cover.theme: two boxers squaring off before a crowd (sport, live)

dek: Onsale ran live online auctions for refurbished and closeout computers and electronics, with bids updating as you watched.
lede: On Onsale's website, the current high bidders' initials and hometowns updated on the page as the auction ran. The Mountain View company sold refurbished and closeout computers, printers and electronics this way, around the clock, more than a year before eBay became a household name. More than 30,000 people registered as bidders in a single quarter of 1996. When Onsale went public in April 1997, it was one of the first companies to prove that strangers would bid real money on a web page.

sections.heading: Jerry Kaplan's Auction House
sections.body: Jerry Kaplan, who had earlier founded the pen-computing company GO, started Onsale with Alan Fisher in July 1994. The bet was that the web could clear surplus goods faster and at better prices than catalog liquidators. Manufacturers and distributors had warehouses full of last year's models. Onsale took that stock and sold it in timed auctions, where the urge to win pushed prices up and the live updates kept bidders coming back.

sections.heading: Becoming Egghead
sections.body: Onsale priced its offering at $6 a share in April 1997 and listed on Nasdaq. In November 1999 it merged with Egghead.com, the former software chain that had closed its stores to sell online, and the combined company took the Egghead.com name. Price wars with other online retailers drained its cash. Egghead.com filed for bankruptcy in August 2001, and Amazon bought its brand and web address at auction that December.

cover.theme: bidders crowding an auction preview (the live auction)
cover.artwork: Preview at the Auction House Drouot

tagline: Cell Towers on the Open Range
dek: Western Wireless brought cell phone service to small towns and open country across the rural American West.
lede: Western Wireless ran cell networks in 57 rural areas of the American West, places the big carriers had passed over. It sold service under the Cellular One brand to more than 240,000 subscribers. It also owned new licenses for PCS, the digital cellular service that was just arriving. The Issaquah, Washington, company was run by John Stanton, a veteran of the early cell phone business. When it went public in May 1996, it was betting that ranchers and truckers needed phones too.

sections.heading: John Stanton's Rural Bet
sections.body: Western Wireless was incorporated in January 1994, built from Stanton's earlier cellular ventures. The company bought licenses in rural service areas, where fewer people lived but long highways and spread-out towns made a mobile phone more useful. Roaming fees from travelers passing through added to revenue. At the same time, Western Wireless bought PCS licenses for larger cities, a second business that it kept separate from the rural one.

sections.heading: VoiceStream and Alltel
sections.body: Western Wireless priced its shares at $23.50 in May 1996 and listed on Nasdaq. In 1999 it spun off its PCS business as VoiceStream Wireless. Deutsche Telekom bought VoiceStream in 2001, and it became T-Mobile USA. Western Wireless kept its rural networks and expanded abroad. In 2005 Alltel bought Western Wireless, adding its rural Western coverage to Alltel's own network.

cover.theme: a lone rock tower on the plains (a cell tower out West)
cover.artwork: Dial Rock, Red Buttes, Laramie Plains

fate: Merged with Alltel's wireline business to form Windstream, 2006
dek: Valor ran local phone service in rural Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Arkansas, and paid investors a large dividend.
lede: Valor promised its new shareholders $1.44 a share in dividends every year, on a stock sold at $15. That 9.6 percent yield was the whole pitch. The Irving, Texas, company owned about 548,000 telephone lines, mostly in rural parts of Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Arkansas. It was the seventh-largest local phone company in the country outside the Bell system. When it went public in February 2005, investors were hungry for steady income, and small-town phone lines produced steady cash.

sections.heading: Lines Bought From GTE
sections.body: Valor was built in 2000 by buying rural telephone businesses from GTE Southwest, now part of Verizon. In many of its towns, Valor was the only company offering a full set of phone, long distance and internet services. The bet was that rural lines would shrink slowly, if at all, and that careful cost control could turn them into dependable cash. Its main threats were cable companies and cell phones, which could pull customers away from the copper line.

sections.heading: The Birth of Windstream
sections.body: Valor priced its offering at $15 a share in February 2005 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. A year and a half later, in July 2006, it merged with the wireline business that Alltel spun off. The combined company took the name Windstream and became one of the largest rural phone companies in the country. The registrant behind this filing continued as Windstream.

cover.theme: two neighbors meeting on a country road (local lines)

tagline: Groceries at the Door, Billions Too Soon
dek: Webvan let you order groceries online and had them driven to your door within a 30-minute window you picked.
lede: The man who built Borders bookstores wanted to end the weekly trip to the supermarket. Louis Borders started Webvan in 1996 with a plan to sell groceries online and deliver them from giant automated warehouses. By the fall of 1999 the company served the San Francisco Bay Area and had plans for many more cities. Investors loved the idea. When Webvan filed to go public, it had a famous founder, a big vision, and almost no revenue.

sections.heading: Warehouses Before Customers
sections.body: Webvan's bet was scale. A normal grocer adds stores one at a time. Webvan built huge, highly automated distribution centers first, each one meant to replace dozens of supermarkets. Customers picked a delivery window online, and a Webvan van brought the bags to the kitchen. The model only worked if each warehouse ran near full. That needed a lot of customers, fast, in city after city. Webvan raised hundreds of millions of dollars from top venture firms to build them.

sections.heading: From $8 Billion to Zero
sections.body: Webvan priced its IPO at $15 a share in November 1999. The stock opened at $26 on Nasdaq and closed the first day at $24.875, up 66 percent. That gave the company a market value of about $8 billion. In 2000 it bought rival HomeGrocer. Orders never caught up with the cost of the warehouses, and the dot-com crash closed the door to new money. Webvan shut down and filed for bankruptcy in July 2001.

cover.theme: a delivery wagon outside a general store (home delivery)
cover.artwork: Untitled (S.K. Fisk store with delivery wagon)

tagline: Many Colors in One Glass Thread
dek: Ciena let phone companies send many beams of light down one fiber, multiplying how much traffic a cable could carry.
lede: Ciena's big idea was to split light into colors and send them all down the same glass fiber at once. Each color carried its own stream of data. In the mid-1990s, long-distance carriers were running out of room on their fiber networks, and laying new cable was slow and costly. Ciena's systems let a carrier get many times more out of fiber it already owned. When the Maryland company filed to go public, it had only just started shipping.

sections.heading: More Room in the Same Fiber
sections.body: David Huber, an optical engineer, founded the company in 1992. Patrick Nettles came on as CEO and steered it toward the carriers. The technology is called wavelength division multiplexing. The bet was that internet and phone traffic would grow faster than anyone could dig trenches for new fiber. Sprint became an early customer and used Ciena's gear to expand its long-distance network. Sales grew fast in Ciena's first year of shipping.

sections.heading: A Record Debut
sections.body: Ciena priced its IPO at $23 a share in February 1997, raising more than $120 million. Shares jumped on the first day, and the debut ranked among the richest for a young company up to then. The telecom boom that followed lifted Ciena much higher, and the bust of 2001 knocked it down hard. The company survived, bought Nortel's optical business in 2010, and kept selling networking gear to carriers and cloud companies. It still trades on the NYSE as CIEN.

cover.theme: a rainbow over the sea (light split into colors)

dek: Fortinet sold one network box that did the work of a firewall, antivirus, and intrusion blocker together.
lede: Ken Xie had already built and sold one firewall company when he started his second. NetScreen, his first, went to Juniper. With Fortinet he and his brother Michael bet that companies were tired of buying a separate device for every kind of threat. Their FortiGate boxes ran on custom chips and packed many defenses into one appliance. Fortinet filed to go public in 2009, when the IPO market had barely woken up from the financial crisis.

sections.heading: Two Brothers, Custom Chips
sections.body: The Xie brothers founded Fortinet in 2000 in Silicon Valley. Most security vendors ran their software on general-purpose processors. Fortinet designed its own chips to speed up the heavy work of scanning traffic. That let one FortiGate handle firewall, antivirus, VPN, and intrusion prevention at once without slowing the network. The pitch suited small and midsize businesses that had no big security team. Fortinet also sold to carriers and large enterprises.

sections.heading: Priced Above the Range
sections.body: Fortinet priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in November 2009, above its planned range of $9 to $11. It raised $156 million and was the first security IPO since 2007. The stock rose about 33 percent on its first day on Nasdaq. Fortinet kept growing through the next decade as firewalls moved into cloud and remote work. Ken Xie still runs the company as CEO, and it trades on Nasdaq as FTNT.

cover.artwork: Siege of the Citadel of Saint Martin on the Isle de Ré

dek: Global Crossing laid undersea fiber cables to carry internet and phone traffic between continents.
lede: Global Crossing went from a single undersea cable plan to a $5 billion stock market value in about 18 months. Gary Winnick, a Los Angeles investor, founded it in 1997 to lay fiber across the Atlantic and sell the capacity to carriers. The internet was growing, and traffic between continents seemed sure to explode. When the Bermuda company filed to go public in 1998, its first cable, Atlantic Crossing, was still being finished.

sections.heading: Fiber on the Ocean Floor
sections.body: Undersea cables had long been built by groups of phone companies working together. Winnick's idea was to build them privately and sell capacity to anyone who wanted it. Atlantic Crossing linked the United States and Europe. Plans followed for cables to Asia and Latin America, adding up to a global network. The bet needed huge amounts of debt and steady demand. Global Crossing borrowed heavily to build both.

sections.heading: Boom, Then the Biggest Bust
sections.body: Global Crossing priced its IPO at $19 a share in August 1998, selling 21 million shares and raising $399 million. It closed its first day at $25.50, worth about $5.15 billion. Through 1999 it bought Frontier Communications and expanded fast. Too many companies laid too much fiber, and prices for capacity collapsed. Global Crossing filed for bankruptcy in January 2002, one of the largest in U.S. history. It emerged in 2003 and was acquired by Level 3 Communications in 2011.

dek: 3dfx made the Voodoo graphics chips that gave PC gamers smooth, fast 3D worlds for the first time.
lede: Three engineers from Silicon Graphics left to put workstation-class 3D graphics into a gamer's home PC. Their company, 3dfx, built the Voodoo chip. Add-in cards using it made games like Quake look and move in ways a normal PC could not. In 1997 the 3D graphics card was a brand new product category, and 3dfx led it. When the company filed to go public that spring, Voodoo was fast becoming the name every PC gamer knew.

sections.heading: Silicon Graphics for the Living Room
sections.body: Ross Smith, Gary Tarolli, and Scott Sellers founded 3dfx in 1994 with backing from the TechFarm incubator. Silicon Graphics machines cost a fortune. The founders bet that falling memory prices would let them build a cheap chip that did one job well: draw textured 3D triangles at high speed. They first aimed at arcade machines, then at PC add-in cards. Their Glide programming interface gave game developers a direct path to the hardware.

sections.heading: Voodoo to Nvidia
sections.body: 3dfx priced its IPO at $11 a share in June 1997. Voodoo2 followed in 1998 and kept the company on top for a while. In 1999 3dfx bought board maker STB Systems and began selling its own cards, which put it in competition with its former customers. Nvidia and ATI pulled ahead. In December 2000, Nvidia agreed to buy 3dfx's core assets, brands, and patents for $70 million in cash plus one million shares. The remaining company later went bankrupt.

cover.artwork: Mirror View, Yosemite Valley, Mariposa County, Cal.

tagline: The ARPANET Builder, Sold by Regulators
dek: Genuity ran one of the biggest internet backbones, carrying traffic and hosting websites for large businesses.
lede: Genuity's network traced back to BBN, the Cambridge firm that built the first routers of the ARPANET. By 2000 it belonged to GTE and carried a large share of America's internet traffic. Then GTE agreed to merge with Bell Atlantic, and regulators stood in the way. Bell Atlantic could not own a long-distance internet backbone. So GTE sold most of Genuity to the public in one of the largest IPOs the market had seen.

sections.heading: BBN's Wires, GTE's Money
sections.body: GTE bought BBN in 1997 to get into the internet business. It joined BBN's backbone with Genuity, a web hosting company it had also acquired, and kept the Genuity name. The combined company sold dial-up access, private networks, and hosting to big companies and other internet providers. GTE kept a small stake and the option to take control again later. The plan depended on traffic growing fast enough to fill an expensive new fiber network.

sections.heading: $1.9 Billion, Then a Slide
sections.body: Genuity priced its IPO at $11 a share in June 2000, below its planned range of $12 to $14. It sold 173.9 million shares and raised about $1.9 billion. The stock fell 14.5 percent on its first day. Verizon, the company formed by the merger, never took back control. As the telecom bust deepened, Genuity ran short of cash. It filed for bankruptcy in November 2002, and Level 3 Communications bought most of its business in February 2003.

cover.theme: a Roman aqueduct (a backbone that carries the flow)

tagline: The Guard at the Network's Gate
dek: Check Point sold the firewall that stood between a company's network and the open internet.
lede: Gil Shwed was in his twenties when he wrote the firewall that made Check Point. He and two partners started the company in Ramat Gan, Israel, in 1993, the year the web began to spread. Companies were plugging their networks into the internet for the first time and had no idea who was knocking. Check Point's FireWall-1 checked every connection against rules the company set. By its 1996 IPO, Check Point held about 40 percent of the world firewall market, by IDC's count.

sections.heading: Three Founders in Ramat Gan
sections.body: Shwed, Marius Nacht, and Shlomo Kramer founded Check Point in 1993. Their product, FireWall-1, used a method Shwed patented called stateful inspection. It tracked each connection as it passed through the firewall, which made it both safer and faster than older filters. Check Point sold mostly through partners and resellers, including Sun Microsystems. That let a small Israeli team reach big customers around the world quickly.

sections.heading: Thirty Years on Nasdaq
sections.body: Check Point went public on Nasdaq on June 28, 1996, at $14 a share, with Goldman Sachs leading the deal. It became one of the largest security companies in the world and stayed independent. Its firewall line grew into network, cloud, and email security products. Gil Shwed ran the company as CEO for three decades before handing the job to Nadav Zafrir in 2024. Check Point still trades on Nasdaq as CHKP.

fate: Taken private by Silver Lake and GIC, 2025 ($1.7B)
dek: Zuora let companies sell subscriptions instead of one-time products, handling the billing, pricing, and revenue math.
lede: Tien Tzuo liked to call his company's stock an "index fund of the subscription economy." He coined that phrase for the shift from buying things once to paying for them every month. Software, newspapers, and even cars were moving to subscriptions by 2018. Each change needed billing systems that could handle upgrades, trials, and renewals. Zuora built that plumbing. It filed to go public as investors were paying up for cloud software that brought in money every month.

sections.heading: Out of Salesforce
sections.body: Tzuo had been an early Salesforce executive and saw how hard subscription billing was for that company. He founded Zuora in 2007 with K. V. Rao and Cheng Zou. Old billing software was built to send one invoice for one sale. Zuora ran in the cloud and tracked every customer's plan as it changed over time. Salesforce's Marc Benioff was an early backer. Customers came from software, media, and manufacturing.

sections.heading: Up 43 Percent, Then Private
sections.body: Zuora priced its IPO at $14 a share in April 2018, above a raised range of $11 to $13. It opened on the NYSE at $20 and closed there, up about 43 percent. Growth slowed in the years that followed, and the stock spent long stretches below its IPO price. In October 2024, Silver Lake and GIC agreed to buy the company for $10 a share. The deal, worth about $1.7 billion, closed in February 2025.

cover.theme: the same stacks, painted season after season (recurring)

fate: Agreed to be acquired by Amazon, April 2026 (pending)
dek: Globalstar ran a fleet of low satellites that let people call and text from places with no cell towers.
lede: Globalstar went bankrupt before it ever went public as Globalstar, Inc. The original partnership, backed by Loral and Qualcomm, launched dozens of satellites in low orbit to make phone calls possible anywhere on Earth. Too few people bought the phones, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2002. Thermo Capital bought the business in 2004. Two years later the new company filed to go public, selling satellite phones and data service to ships, oil fields, and rural customers.

sections.heading: A Constellation Reborn
sections.body: Globalstar's satellites sat much lower than old communications satellites. That cut the delay on calls and let handsets stay small. The first network cost billions of dollars to build. After bankruptcy wiped out most of that debt, the new owners could run the same satellites at a much lower cost. The plan was simple: sell service to people who worked far from towers, and later add simple trackers and messengers for hikers and fleets.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Amazon
sections.body: Globalstar priced its IPO at $17 a share in November 2006. Its aging satellites soon had trouble with two-way voice, and the stock fell far below its offer price. A second-generation constellation went up between 2010 and 2013. In 2022 Apple began using Globalstar for emergency texts from iPhones, and in 2024 Apple took a 20 percent stake in a Globalstar unit. In April 2026, Globalstar agreed to be acquired by Amazon.

cover.theme: a celestial globe (stars around the Earth)
cover.artwork: Celestial Globe, Cover of the set of eight Pictures of Foreign Countries

tagline: Top Universities, Taught Through a Screen
dek: 2U built and ran online degree programs for well-known universities, from marketing to classes to student support.
lede: The founder of the Princeton Review bet that elite universities would put whole graduate degrees online if someone else did the hard work. John Katzman started 2U in 2008 with Chip Paucek and Jeremy Johnson. 2U paid to build each program and find the students, then split tuition with the school. When it filed to go public in 2014, eight of its nine university partners ranked among the top 75 national universities in U.S. News.

sections.heading: Paying Up Front for Tuition
sections.body: Most universities had no budget or skill to run a national online program. 2U offered to fund the platform, the marketing, and the student support. In return it took a large share of tuition for years. Its live online classes kept sections small and faces on screen. The model cost a lot at the start of each program and paid off only as students enrolled and stayed. 2U's prospectus estimated its early students would bring in more than $475 million in total tuition.

sections.heading: From edX to Chapter 11
sections.body: 2U priced its IPO at $13 a share in March 2014 and listed on Nasdaq as TWOU. For several years it grew fast and signed many more schools. In 2021 it bought edX, the online course platform started by Harvard and MIT, for $800 million. Growth slowed, new rules on revenue-sharing deals loomed, and the debt from the edX deal weighed on it. 2U filed for bankruptcy in July 2024 and left Nasdaq that September as a private company.

cover.theme: a scholar at his desk (learning anywhere)

tagline: Phone Calls Carried Over the Internet
dek: iBasis carried international phone calls over internet lines for other carriers, at a fraction of old prices.
lede: Many of the international calls people made around 2000 crossed the ocean as internet packets, and they never knew it. iBasis was one of the companies that carried them. It sold this service wholesale to phone carriers, which passed the calls on to their own customers. Old international calling ran on costly dedicated circuits. When iBasis filed to go public in 1999, internet calling was cheap, a little rough, and growing fast.

sections.heading: A Network Behind the Carriers
sections.body: Ofer Gneezy and Gordon VanderBrug started iBasis in 1996 in the Boston area, and it began service in May 1997. They placed gateways in cities around the world that turned voice into data and back again. Carriers handed iBasis calls to hard-to-reach countries, and iBasis routed them over the internet. The bet was that voice would become just another kind of data. Getting the call quality right was the hard part.

sections.heading: Ending Up Dutch
sections.body: iBasis priced its IPO at $16 a share in November 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as IBAS. The stock rose in the bubble and fell hard after it. The company kept going and grew into one of the largest wholesale carriers of international voice traffic. In 2007 it combined with the international wholesale arm of KPN, the Dutch phone company, which took a majority stake. KPN bought the rest of iBasis in December 2009 and took it off Nasdaq.

cover.theme: an echo across canyon rocks (a voice carried far)

dek: KongZhong sold text-message news, ringtones, pictures, and games to China's mobile phone users through the carriers.
lede: KongZhong went from founding to Nasdaq in about two years. Two former Sohu executives, Yunfan Zhou and Nick Yang, started it in Beijing in May 2002. China had more mobile phones than any other country, and most of them could do little beyond calls and text. KongZhong sold small things to those phones: news alerts, pictures, ringtones, and simple games. When it filed to go public in 2004, this business was one of the hottest corners of China's internet.

sections.heading: Two Founders From Sohu
sections.body: Zhou and Yang had worked at Sohu, one of China's big web portals, before starting KongZhong. The company sold its services through China Mobile and other carriers, which billed users and took a cut. It added WAP, picture messages, and Java games as phones got better. The bet was that China's phone owners would pay small sums, often, for things to read and play. The risk was that a single carrier controlled the gate and could change the rules at any time.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars an ADS
sections.body: KongZhong priced its IPO at $10 per American depositary share in July 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as KONG. Carrier rule changes soon hit its messaging revenue. Over the next decade the company moved into mobile and online games, which became the core of its business as smartphones replaced simple handsets. In 2017 a buyer group of company insiders took KongZhong private, and its shares left Nasdaq that April.

cover.theme: geese in flight (KongZhong means 'in the air')

tagline: Measuring the Vacuum Inside Chip Factories
dek: MKS made the gauges and controllers that measure pressure and gas flow inside the machines that build chips.
lede: Every chip is made in a near-perfect vacuum, and MKS Instruments sold the tools that measure how near. Its pressure gauges and gas flow controllers sit inside the machines that etch and coat silicon wafers. Chip equipment makers bought them by the thousand. MKS had been making these instruments since the 1960s. When it went public in March 1999, the chip industry was climbing out of a slump and about to boom.

sections.heading: Gauges for Every Gas
sections.body: MKS started in 1961 near Boston. Its early specialty was the capacitance manometer, a gauge that reads tiny pressures with great accuracy. As chipmaking grew, so did the need to control gases precisely inside sealed chambers. MKS built a wide line of gauges, valves, and flow controllers. Most of its sales went to semiconductor equipment makers such as Applied Materials. The rest went to other industries that worked in a vacuum.

sections.heading: From Gauges to Lasers
sections.body: MKS priced its IPO at $14 a share in March 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as MKSI. Over the next 25 years it grew by buying other companies.
