It bought Newport, a laser and optics maker, in 2016 and Atotech, a chemicals company, in 2022. Those deals moved MKS well beyond chip tools. The company still trades on Nasdaq as MKSI, now under the name MKS Inc.

cover.theme: an experiment with the air pump (vacuum)
cover.artwork: A Philosopher Shewing an Experiment on the Air Pump

dek: Switchboard put the white and yellow pages online, so anyone could find a person or business for free.
lede: Before Google Maps and before Yelp, people found a plumber or an old friend's number on Switchboard. The site put national white pages and yellow pages online, free to search. It grew inside Banyan Systems, a Massachusetts networking company, and became its own company in 1996. America Online used it for its directory service. When Switchboard filed to go public in late 1999, it was still majority owned by Banyan.

sections.heading: Born Inside Banyan
sections.body: Dean Polnerow built Switchboard as a project at Banyan, and he stayed on as president when it was spun into its own company. Printed phone books were thick, local, and out of date by the time they arrived. Switchboard offered every listing in the country, searchable in seconds. It made money from ads and from licensing its directory to other web portals. Merchants could pay for better placement, much like a big yellow pages ad.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars, Then InfoSpace
sections.body: Switchboard priced its IPO at $15 a share in March 2000, the same month the Nasdaq peaked. The crash soon cut its ad revenue, and the stock fell far below its offer price. Switchboard trimmed costs, leaned on licensing deals, and kept its directory business going for four more years. In 2004 InfoSpace, another directory and search company, bought Switchboard for $7.75 a share in cash.

cover.theme: a city street plan (a directory of a city)
cover.artwork: Plate 110 from The Plan of Chicago, 1909

tagline: The Classroom Moves Into the Browser
dek: Blackboard gave colleges one website where professors posted syllabi, readings, and grades, and students turned in work.
lede: Blackboard's core software began as a class tool built by students at Cornell. Michael Chasen and Matthew Pittinsky started Blackboard in Washington in 1997 as consultants on education technology standards. In 1998 they bought CourseInfo, the Cornell project, and turned it into a product. By 2004 a generation of college students logged into Blackboard to find their homework. When the company filed to go public that year, it sold to thousands of schools.

sections.heading: Two Consultants and a Cornell Project
sections.body: Blackboard's first job was advising a group of universities on standards for online learning. The founders saw that every campus would need software to run courses on the web. CourseInfo gave them a working system that faculty already used. Blackboard sold it to colleges as yearly licenses, then added campus card systems for dorm doors and dining halls. Its customers ranged from community colleges to large state universities.

sections.heading: From Nasdaq to Providence
sections.body: Blackboard priced its IPO at $14 a share in June 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as BBBB. It bought its main rival, WebCT, in 2006 and became the giant of college course software. Newer rivals and free open-source tools kept up the pressure. In 2011 the private equity firm Providence Equity Partners took Blackboard private in a deal worth about $1.64 billion. Blackboard later combined with Anthology in 2021.

cover.artwork: The Lesson of the Professor, plate five from Les Comédiens de Société

tagline: Wiring the Storage Room With Fiber
dek: Gadzoox sold Fibre Channel hubs and switches that linked servers to shared pools of disk storage.
lede: Gadzoox started out making electronic test equipment and pivoted to storage networks in 1995. Its bet was that servers would stop keeping their own disks and share big pools of storage instead. Linking them needed a fast new kind of network called Fibre Channel. Gadzoox sold the hubs and switches in the middle. When it filed to go public in 1999, storage area networks were the hot new idea in the data center.

sections.heading: From Test Gear to Fibre
sections.body: Gadzoox was founded in April 1992 in Silicon Valley. Since October 1995 it had focused entirely on Fibre Channel products. Its hubs and switches connected servers to disk arrays and tape libraries at high speed. It sold mostly through big storage and computer makers, such as Compaq, which put Gadzoox gear inside their own systems. The bet was that every large company would build a storage network, and that Gadzoox could become a leading supplier of the plumbing.

sections.heading: A Hot Debut, Then Chapter 11
sections.body: Gadzoox priced its IPO at $21 a share in July 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as ZOOX. The storage boom carried the stock through its first year. Larger switch makers such as Brocade and McDATA took most of the market as it grew. Gadzoox's sales fell when the tech bust hit, and its losses mounted. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in San Jose on August 22, 2002.

cover.artwork: Marguerite at the Spinning Wheel, from Faust

dek: Sequans designed the radio chips that let phones, hotspots, and connected devices talk to 4G wireless networks.
lede: Sequans bet on two versions of 4G wireless at once and sold chips for both. In 2011, carriers were still split between WiMAX and LTE, and nobody knew which would win. The Paris company already supplied 7 of the 10 largest WiMAX carriers in the world. It was also shipping LTE chips. Sequans filed to go public in the United States as one of the few independent 4G chip designers left outside the giants.

sections.heading: Juniper to the Banlieue
sections.body: Georges Karam had run cable access at Juniper Networks before he founded Sequans in 2003 with Bertrand Debray. Their company was fabless: it designed chips and paid factories to make them. The founders bet that 4G would need new radio silicon, and that a small, focused team could design it faster than big companies. Their chips went into USB sticks, home routers, and early 4G devices. WiMAX had early backers such as Clearwire in the United States and UQ in Japan.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars, Then IoT
sections.body: Sequans priced its IPO at $10 per American depositary share in April 2011 and listed on the NYSE as SQNS. LTE soon won, WiMAX faded, and big rivals took most phone business. Sequans moved toward low-power LTE chips for meters, trackers, and other connected devices. In 2023 Renesas launched a tender offer for the company, but the deal fell through. Sequans still trades on the NYSE as SQNS.

cover.theme: ships at anchor by a lighthouse (a signal that guides)
cover.artwork: Four-Master and Two Three-Masters Anchored near a Fortified Island with a Lighthouse, from The Sailing Vessels

tagline: Faster Data Over the Same Copper
dek: Aquantia made chips that pushed much faster Ethernet over the copper cables already in buildings and data centers.
lede: Most office buildings are full of copper Ethernet cable that tops out at one gigabit. Aquantia's chips let that same wire carry 2.5, 5, or 10 gigabits. It was cheaper than pulling new cable, and Wi-Fi access points and data centers needed the speed. Aquantia also put its chips into cars, where networks were getting faster too. When it filed to go public in 2017, it was a rare venture-backed chip company headed for Wall Street.

sections.heading: Ten Gigabits on Old Wire
sections.body: Aquantia was founded in San Jose in 2004 to build the physical-layer chips, called PHYs, that send Ethernet signals down a cable. Running 10 gigabits over ordinary copper took heavy signal processing. Aquantia's engineers worked out how to do it at lower power than rivals. The company sold to makers of switches, servers, and network cards. Later it pushed multi-gigabit speeds for Wi-Fi gear and for networks inside cars.

sections.heading: Nine Dollars to Marvell
sections.body: Aquantia priced its IPO at $9 a share in November 2017 and listed on the NYSE as AQ. The company kept growing its automotive and Wi-Fi business and won design slots in new multi-gigabit networking gear. In 2019 Marvell Technology agreed to buy Aquantia for $13.25 a share in cash. The deal closed that September, and Aquantia's shares left the NYSE.

cover.theme: a cascade of water (Aqua, data flowing)

tagline: A Tiny Inverter Under Every Panel
dek: Enphase made small inverters that sit under each solar panel, turning sunlight into household power more safely and reliably.
lede: Enphase had to cut its IPO price nearly in half to get public at all. In March 2012 the solar industry was in a slump, and investors had soured on anything with panels. Enphase sold microinverters, small boxes that sit under each solar panel and turn its power into the kind a house can use. Older systems used one big inverter for the whole roof. If one panel was shaded, the whole string suffered. Enphase's design fixed that.

sections.heading: One Panel at a Time
sections.body: Martin Fornage and Raghu Belur founded the company in 2006 in Petaluma, California. Enphase put a small computer-controlled inverter on every panel. That made each panel work on its own, let owners track output panel by panel online, and avoided the high-voltage wiring of older setups. Home installers liked it because it was simpler to design and safer to work on. The bet was that this approach would win the rooftop market.

sections.heading: Six Dollars to the S&P 500
sections.body: Enphase priced its IPO at $6 a share in March 2012 and listed on Nasdaq as ENPH. The price was far below its planned range of $10 to $12. The first years were hard, and the stock sank further. A new CEO, Badri Kothandaraman, cut costs and moved to cheaper chip-based designs. Sales and profits rose sharply. Enphase added batteries and joined the S&P 500 in 2021. It still trades on Nasdaq as ENPH.

cover.theme: a falcon at sunrise (sunlight turned into power)
cover.artwork: Falcon on a Pine Tree with the Rising Sun

dek: Streamline delivered groceries, dry cleaning, and errands each week to a box in suburban families' garages.
lede: Streamline.com put a refrigerator and a freezer in its customers' garages. Once a week, a driver let himself in and filled them with groceries the family had ordered online. Nobody had to be home. The Boston-area company aimed at busy suburban families and offered far more than food. It picked up dry cleaning, returned bottles, and dropped off rental videos. When Streamline went public in June 1999, it was betting that people would hand over a garage key to save a Saturday.

sections.heading: The Streamline Box
sections.body: Timothy DeMello founded Streamline in 1993. The company called its home setup the Streamline box: a refrigerator, a freezer, and a storage unit installed on the customer's property. Unattended delivery let Streamline plan efficient routes instead of chasing narrow time windows. Orders came from a warehouse with separate temperature zones. Customers paid for the service, and Streamline hoped to earn more from each family by handling every weekly errand.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars to Peapod
sections.body: Streamline priced its IPO at $10 a share in June 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as SLNE. It expanded beyond Boston into Washington, D.C., and Chicago. The cost of new markets outran sales, and investors stopped funding online grocers in 2000. In September 2000 Streamline sold its Washington and Chicago operations to Peapod for $11.6 million. It stopped all service on November 22, 2000.

cover.theme: a market woman with her basket (groceries delivered)

tagline: Power Chips Carved From One Stone
dek: Monolithic Power Systems makes chips that manage and convert power inside laptops, servers, cars, and phones.
lede: Monolithic Power Systems went public while its founder was being sued over his own inventions. Michael Hsing had worked at Micrel, and Micrel claimed that MPS chips infringed patents naming Hsing as an inventor. MPS made analog power chips, the parts that turn a battery or wall current into the exact voltages a device needs. Its customers in 2004 included Dell, LG Electronics, and Motorola. The company was small, based in Los Gatos, and growing fast.

sections.heading: One Chip, Fewer Parts
sections.body: Hsing founded MPS in 1997. The name points to its approach: put as much of a power system as possible onto a single, monolithic chip. That meant fewer parts, smaller boards, and better efficiency for notebook computers and LCD screens. MPS designed its own manufacturing processes and worked with outside foundries to build the chips. The bet was that power management would get harder as devices shrank and demanded more.

sections.heading: From $8.50 to the S&P 500
sections.body: MPS priced its IPO at $8.50 a share in November 2004 and listed on Nasdaq as MPWR, with Goldman Sachs leading the deal. Hsing stayed on as CEO for the next two decades. The company moved from notebooks into servers, cars, and data centers, where AI chips need huge amounts of carefully controlled power. MPS joined the S&P 500 in 2021. It still trades on Nasdaq as MPWR.

cover.artwork: Obelisk and Granite Lotus Column, Karnac

dek: Applied Optoelectronics makes the lasers and optical parts that move data through data centers and cable TV networks.
lede: Applied Optoelectronics makes its own laser chips, from the raw material up, in a Houston suburb. Most optics companies buy those chips from someone else. Thompson Lin founded the company in 1997 in Sugar Land, Texas. Its lasers go into transceivers, the small modules that turn electrical data into light and back. By 2013, giant internet companies were building data centers stuffed with them. AAOI filed to go public as that build-out began.

sections.heading: Owning the Whole Chain
sections.body: Lin, an engineer with a Ph.D., founded the company in February 1997 and has run it as CEO since. AAOI grows its laser wafers, packages the chips, and assembles finished modules. It sells to cable TV operators, which use optics to carry signals across their networks, and to data center operators, which became its biggest market. Doing every step in-house cost more up front, but let AAOI control quality and cost as speeds rose.

sections.heading: Riding the Data Center Waves
sections.body: AAOI priced its IPO at $10 a share in September 2013 and listed on Nasdaq as AAOI. It raised about $30.8 million. The stock swung hard over the next decade, rising and falling with the spending plans of a few huge cloud customers. Its fortunes turned again as AI data centers needed faster optical links. Applied Optoelectronics still trades on Nasdaq as AAOI.

tagline: Faxes That Land in Your Inbox
dek: eFax began as JetFax, which built the brains of office print-fax-copy machines, and later turned faxes into email.
lede: eFax.com went public under another name and sold another product. In 1997 it was JetFax, a Menlo Park company that designed the software and electronics inside multifunction office machines. Those boxes printed, faxed, copied, and scanned in one unit. JetFax licensed its technology to 25 companies, including Hewlett-Packard, Xerox, Samsung, and Intel. Two years later it renamed itself after the free service that made it famous: a fax number that delivered faxes to email.

sections.heading: The Brains Inside the Box
sections.body: JetFax was incorporated in 1988. Its embedded systems let printer and copier makers add fax and scan features without building them from scratch. It also sold desktop software and its own branded machines. The bet was that offices would trade separate printers, faxes, and copiers for one device. That market grew, but big hardware makers held most of the profit. JetFax needed a new idea.

sections.heading: Free Fax Numbers
sections.body: JetFax priced its IPO at $8 a share in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as JTFX. In 1999 the company launched eFax, which gave anyone a free fax number and sent incoming faxes to their email as attachments. Users signed up in large numbers, and the company renamed itself eFax.com. Free service was hard to turn into revenue. In 2000 eFax merged into JFAX.COM, its paid rival, which later became j2 Global and kept the eFax brand alive.

fate: Sold Mediasite to Enghouse, then bankrupt, 2024
dek: Sonic Foundry made Sound Forge, the PC audio editor, then video tools, and later lecture-capture software for universities.
lede: A generation of home musicians and radio editors learned to cut audio on a program from Madison, Wisconsin. Sound Forge let anyone record, edit, and polish digital sound on a Windows PC. Sonic Foundry built it and sold it alongside tools like CD Architect for burning audio CDs. In 1998 the web was starting to carry sound and video. When Sonic Foundry went public that April, it was a small software maker with a loyal following among creators.

sections.heading: Desktop Audio for Everyone
sections.body: Rimas Buinevicius and Monty Schmidt led the company as CEO and president. Professional audio editing once needed costly dedicated hardware. Sonic Foundry bet that ordinary PCs had become fast enough to do the job in software. Sound Forge sold to musicians, game studios, and broadcasters. The company also saw a future in preparing audio and video for the internet, and it built services around that idea.

sections.heading: From Sound Forge to Mediasite
sections.body: Sonic Foundry priced its IPO at $7.50 a share in April 1998 and listed on the American Stock Exchange as SFO. It added the Vegas video editor and other creative tools. In 2003 it sold its desktop software line to Sony and kept Mediasite, a system that records and streams university lectures. Mediasite carried the company for two decades. In early 2024 Sonic Foundry sold Mediasite to Enghouse and then filed for bankruptcy.

cover.theme: a blacksmith at the forge (Sound Forge)

dek: Whittman-Hart sold IT consulting to big companies, then merged into marchFIRST, the dot-com era's ill-fated web services giant.
lede: This filing belongs to a Chicago consulting firm that would later bet everything on the dot-com boom and lose. In 1996 Whittman-Hart was a fast-growing IT services company. It planned, built, and ran computer systems for corporations, billing by the hour. It had grown revenue every year since its founding in 1984. It had gone public that spring at $16 a share. By August, the stock traded near $29.50, and the company filed this S-1 for a second offering.

sections.heading: Billable Hours in Chicago
sections.body: Robert Bernard was chairman and CEO, and he was 35 when this filing went in. Whittman-Hart sold consultants who worked on client/server, midrange, and enterprise systems. Its pitch was strategic IT work that made clients more productive and more competitive, and most of its revenue came from professional fees billed by the hour. This August 1996 offering priced at $28.50 a share and included shares sold by existing holders.

sections.heading: The Merger That Named It
sections.body: Whittman-Hart kept growing for four more years on Nasdaq as WHIT. In March 2000 it merged with USWeb/CKS, a web design and marketing firm, to form marchFIRST. The new company promised to build entire online businesses for its clients. The dot-com crash began weeks later, and clients cancelled projects. marchFIRST ran out of money and filed for bankruptcy in April 2001.

fate: Acquired by Rovi, 2016 ($1.1B); the combined company took the TiVo name
tagline: The Box That Paused Live Television
dek: TiVo let people pause live TV, skip the parts they hated, and watch shows on their own schedule.
lede: TiVo went public six months after it shipped its first box. The company was called Teleworld until July 1999, and it had a single bold idea: a hard drive under the television that recorded shows for you. You could pause a live broadcast, rewind it, and come back later. In 1999 most people still taped shows on VHS or missed them. TiVo bet that viewers wanted control of the clock, and that the TV industry would learn to live with it.

sections.heading: A Hard Drive Under the TV
sections.body: Mike Ramsay and Jim Barton, two veterans of Silicon Graphics, started the company in 1997. Their box recorded TV to a disk and paired it with a program guide, so you picked shows by name instead of by channel and time. A monthly subscription paid for the guide. The name became a verb almost overnight. People said they would TiVo a show, the way they said they would Xerox a page.

sections.heading: Eighty-Seven Percent on Day One
sections.body: TiVo first aimed to sell shares for $11 to $13. Demand pushed the price to $16 on September 30, 1999. The stock opened at $13.94 and closed its first day at $29.94, up 87 percent. Then came years of losses as cable companies built their own recorders. TiVo fought them with patents and won large settlements. In September 2016 Rovi bought TiVo for about $1.1 billion and took its name.

cover.theme: Muybridge's frozen frames of a bird in flight (pausing time)

dek: Ameritrade let ordinary investors buy and sell stocks cheaply, first by phone and then on the web.
lede: One of the biggest brokers of the online boom was run from Omaha, Nebraska, a thousand miles from Wall Street. Joe Ricketts started the business in 1975 as a discount broker, selling trades for less than the full-service firms charged. By the time it filed to go public in early 1997, the web was turning stock trading into something anyone could do from a desk at home. Ameritrade bet that price would win, and that most investors did not want advice.

sections.heading: A Discount Broker on the Plains
sections.body: Ricketts opened his firm the year Wall Street ended fixed trading commissions. That change let brokers compete on price, and he chose to compete on nothing else. His firm took orders and filled them, with no research and no stock tips. For years its customers placed those orders by phone. When the web arrived, Ameritrade moved its customers online and kept cutting the price.

sections.heading: From Fifteen Dollars to Schwab
sections.body: Ameritrade Holding went public in March 1997 at $15 a share. The online trading boom of the late nineties made it one of the busiest brokers in the country. In 2006 it bought TD Waterhouse and became TD Ameritrade. Charles Schwab, its oldest rival in discount trading, bought the company in an all-stock deal that closed in October 2020. The price was about $22 billion.

cover.theme: a bull in the ring (a bull market for everyone)

tagline: Shovels for the AI Gold Rush
dek: Supermicro built the server boards and racks that data centers filled with chips, and later with AI.
lede: Supermicro priced its IPO below the range, at $8 a share, and gained just 9.5 percent on day one. Few people noticed. The San Jose company built server motherboards and systems in Silicon Valley, a place most hardware makers had left for cheaper factories in Asia. It sold building blocks that customers could mix into the machines they needed. Fifteen years later, those machines became the racks that held the chips of the AI boom.

sections.heading: Building Blocks in San Jose
sections.body: Charles Liang started the company in 1993 with his wife, Sara Liu. Liang was an engineer, and he ran Supermicro as one. The company designed boards, chassis, and power supplies that fit together in many ways. A customer could order a server close to custom without waiting months. Supermicro kept much of its design and assembly in San Jose, which let it move fast when a new chip came out.

sections.heading: Eight Dollars, Then a Boom
sections.body: Supermicro sold 8 million shares at $8 on March 29, 2007, below its planned range of $9.50 to $11.50. The stock closed the day at $8.76. For years it grew quietly. Then demand for AI servers exploded, and the shares soared through 2023 and early 2024. A short seller's report, an auditor's resignation, and late filings followed in 2024. Supermicro stayed listed, and it still trades on Nasdaq as SMCI.

cover.theme: gold miners (selling shovels in a gold rush)
cover.artwork: Untitled (Gold Miners in Front of a Pond)

fate: Bankrupt, 2001; assets sold to Cable & Wireless
tagline: The Landlord of the Early Web
dek: Exodus ran the giant data centers where the early web's biggest sites kept their servers.
lede: At its peak in 2000, Exodus was worth about $32 billion, and it made its money renting rooms full of other people's computers. Its data centers held the servers of the web's busiest companies, wired to fast networks and kept cool, powered, and guarded around the clock. When it filed to go public in early 1998, most companies still kept their servers in a closet down the hall. Exodus bet they would rather hand that job to someone else.

sections.heading: Servers Need a Home
sections.body: K.B. Chandrasekhar and B.V. Jagadeesh, two engineers who came to the United States from India, started the company in 1994. They saw a simple need. Web companies were growing faster than they could build server rooms. Exodus built the rooms for them, with backup power, cooling, and links to many networks, and charged rent by the rack. A customer could add servers as fast as its traffic grew.

sections.heading: Eighty-Four Percent, Then Chapter 11
sections.body: Exodus priced its IPO at $15 a share on March 19, 1998, above a range it had already raised. The stock closed the first day at $27.63, up 84 percent. It became one of the hottest stocks of the bubble. When dot-com customers went broke, Exodus was left with costly data centers and heavy debt. It filed for bankruptcy in September 2001. Cable & Wireless bought most of its data centers that winter.

cover.theme: the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus)
cover.artwork: The Submersion of Pharaoh's Army in the Red Sea

fate: Fully acquired by USA Interactive, 2003 ($1.1B); brand now owned by Expedia Group
tagline: Hotel Rooms Bought by the Block
dek: Hotels.com bought hotel rooms in bulk and resold them to travelers for less, first by phone and then online.
lede: Before it had a famous web address, this company was a phone number: 1-800-96-HOTEL. David Litman and Robert Diener started it in Dallas in 1991. They bought rooms from hotels ahead of time, in bulk and at a discount, then resold them to travelers. When it went public in February 2000 as Hotel Reservations Network, it had deals with about 1,500 hotels in 40 markets. The web was turning a call center into a booking site.

sections.heading: A Toll-Free Number in Dallas
sections.body: Litman and Diener's trick was to take on risk. They committed to blocks of rooms in busy cities, so hotels gave them lower rates. Travelers called the 800 number and got a deal. Moving the business to the web cut the cost of each booking. In 1999 USA Networks, the company behind Home Shopping Network and Ticketmaster, bought the business. The founders stayed on to run it.

sections.heading: A Parent Buys It Back
sections.body: Hotel Reservations Network sold 5.4 million shares at $16 in February 2000, under the ticker ROOM. USA Networks kept most of the company. The stock closed its first day at $26. In 2002 the company renamed itself after its best asset, Hotels.com. In 2003 its parent, by then called USA Interactive, bought the rest of the shares in a stock deal worth about $1.1 billion. The brand now belongs to Expedia Group.

tagline: A Legend Played in Internet Cafes
dek: Shanda ran China's most popular online game and turned millions of internet cafe players into paying customers.
lede: Shanda's biggest hit came from South Korea. Shanda licensed The Legend of Mir II and ran it in China, where it became the country's most popular online game. Players logged on by the thousands from crowded internet cafes and paid for time in a fantasy world. When Shanda filed to sell shares in America in 2004, China's online game market was young and growing fast. Shanda bet it could own that market.

sections.heading: Brothers in Shanghai
sections.body: Tianqiao Chen and his brother Danian started the business in Shanghai in December 1999. Chen's wife, Chrissy Luo, was also a founder. The turn came in November 2001, when they launched Mir II, a game licensed from Korea. Its success drew a venture investment from a SoftBank fund in 2003. By then Shanda had also released The World of Legend, the first online game it built itself.

sections.heading: Eleven Dollars, Then Four Times That
sections.body: Shanda sold American depositary shares at $11 each in May 2004, on Nasdaq under the ticker SNDA. Within months the stock had roughly quadrupled, and Tianqiao Chen became one of the richest people in China. The company kept buying games and studios. In February 2012 shareholders approved a buyout by the three founders, who paid about $740 million for the quarter of the company they did not already own.

cover.theme: a legendary duel on a bridge (The Legend of Mir)
cover.artwork: The Young Yoshitsune defeats Benkei at Gojo Bridge

tagline: A Credit Bureau's Coders in Chennai
dek: Cognizant wrote and maintained software for big American companies, using teams of engineers in India.
lede: Cognizant started as the in-house programming shop of Dun & Bradstreet, the credit-report company. In 1994 it set up a software team in India to work on its parent's systems. Then it began selling that work to other companies. When it went public in June 1998, corporations everywhere were racing to fix the Year 2000 bug before the calendar ran out. Cognizant bet that once clients sent their code to India for that deadline, they would keep sending it.

sections.heading: Born Inside Dun & Bradstreet
sections.body: Kumar Mahadeva, a former McKinsey consultant and Dun & Bradstreet strategy executive, led the team that built the business. Francisco D'Souza was there from the start. The model was simple. A small team worked with the client in America, and a larger team of engineers in India did most of the coding. The time difference let work go on around the clock. Y2K repairs paid the early bills.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars and a Long Climb
sections.body: Cognizant sold its first shares at $10 on June 19, 1998, on Nasdaq under the ticker CTSH. Its parent, IMS Health, kept control. When the Y2K deadline passed, Cognizant moved on to new software projects, and it grew faster than most of its rivals for years. It joined the S&P 500 and the Fortune 500. Cognizant is still public and employs more than 300,000 people.

tagline: A Flight Recorder for Every Laptop
dek: Carbon Black watched every laptop and server in a company, so security teams could stop attacks and trace them.
lede: Carbon Black spent its first twelve years under another name. It began in 2002 as Bit9, a Massachusetts company that blocked any program not on an approved list. In 2014 it bought a small startup called Carbon Black, whose software recorded everything that happened on a computer, and in 2016 it took that name. When it went public in 2018, companies were losing faith in old antivirus tools. Carbon Black bet they would move their defenses to the cloud.

sections.heading: From Whitelist to Black Box
sections.body: Bit9's first idea was strict. Instead of hunting for known viruses, it let only trusted software run. The Carbon Black deal added a second idea. Its sensor kept a record of every process on a machine, like a flight recorder, so investigators could replay an attack. The company joined the two and moved them onto its own cloud platform. By the end of 2017 it had more than 3,700 customers.

sections.heading: Nineteen Dollars, Then VMware
sections.body: Carbon Black priced its IPO at $19 a share on May 4, 2018, and listed on Nasdaq as CBLK. It kept growing but kept losing money, and larger rivals crowded the market. In August 2019 VMware agreed to buy it for $26 a share. The deal valued Carbon Black at about $2.1 billion and closed in October 2019. Broadcom later bought VMware, and Carbon Black came along.

dek: Verio bought dozens of local internet providers and joined them into one national service for small businesses.
lede: Verio assembled its network by buying it, one local internet provider at a time. In the mid-1990s thousands of small companies sold web access and hosting in their own towns, and none had the money to grow. Verio, based in Englewood, Colorado, set out to buy the best of them and join them under one name. When it went public in May 1998, small businesses were just starting to need websites and email. Verio wanted to be their provider.

sections.heading: A Roll-Up From Colorado
sections.body: Verio was incorporated on March 1, 1996, for one purpose: to buy independent internet providers that served business customers. Its pitch to small and medium businesses was simple. They had no tech staff of their own, so Verio would run their connections, web hosting, and email. Local teams kept their customers, while Verio supplied the money, the national network, and the back office.

sections.heading: Sixty Dollars From Tokyo
sections.body: Verio sold shares at $23 in May 1998, on Nasdaq under the ticker VRIO. It kept buying smaller providers and became one of the largest web hosting companies in the country. In May 2000 Japan's NTT Communications agreed to buy Verio for $60 a share in cash. The deal, worth about $5.5 billion, closed later that year, and Verio became NTT's American internet arm.

tagline: Locks for Digital Music and Movies
dek: InterTrust built software to control how songs, films, and documents were copied and paid for online.
lede: InterTrust's patents turned out to be worth more than its products. Victor Shear started the company in 1990 to solve a problem most people had not noticed yet: once a song or a book is digital, anyone can copy it for free. InterTrust built a system to wrap content in a secure container with rules about who could open it and what they owed. When it went public in October 1999, Napster was months old and the record labels were scared.

sections.heading: A Container With Rules
sections.body: Shear's idea was called digital rights management, or DRM. InterTrust's DigiBox container held a file along with instructions for its use. A buyer might get to play a song three times, or read a report but not print it. Payment ran through the same system. InterTrust spent most of the 1990s writing software and filing patents on these ideas, long before it had many paying customers.

sections.heading: Patents Worth a Fortune
sections.body: InterTrust sold shares at $18 on October 27, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as ITRU. The stock soared during the bubble and then collapsed. Its software never caught on widely. Its patents did matter, and in 2001 InterTrust sued Microsoft over them. In January 2003 Sony and Philips bought InterTrust for about $453 million. In 2004 Microsoft settled the patent case for $440 million.

cover.theme: Saint Peter with his keys (who holds access)

tagline: Storage That Grew Box by Box
dek: Isilon built storage systems that held huge video and media files and grew by adding another box.
lede: Isilon was built for files too big for ordinary storage. Video, medical scans, and research data were piling up in the early 2000s, and the usual systems choked as they grew. Isilon's answer was a cluster: buy a few boxes, and when you need more room, add another, and it joins the rest as one large pool. The Seattle company went public in December 2006, as studios, broadcasters, and labs were moving their work from tape and film to disk.

sections.heading: One Pool, Many Boxes
sections.body: Sujal Patel and Paul Mikesell founded Isilon in January 2001 to store and manage digital content. They spent the first two years writing OneFS, the operating system that tied every box into a single file system. Each new box added space and speed at once. If one failed, the others kept the data safe. That made it simple to grow from a few terabytes to far more.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars to EMC
sections.body: Isilon priced its IPO at $13 a share on December 15, 2006, on Nasdaq under the ticker ISLN. The stock jumped on its first day. A year later the company had to restate its revenue, and its chief executive left. Patel took over and steadied the business. In late 2010 EMC bought Isilon for about $2.25 billion. Dell later bought EMC, and Isilon's technology lives on in Dell's storage line.

cover.theme: rocks that hold against the sea (storage that lasts)

dek: Hortonworks sold support and tools for Hadoop, the free software big companies used to store and crunch huge data sets.
lede: Hortonworks gave away its software and still went public three years after it started. Its product was Hadoop, a free, open-source system for spreading huge data sets across cheap servers. Engineers at Yahoo had done much of the work to build it. In 2011 a group of them left to form a company around it, named after an elephant from a Dr. Seuss book. When it went public in December 2014, every large company was told it needed a big data plan.

sections.heading: Spun Out of Yahoo
sections.body: Hortonworks launched in 2011 with Yahoo as a backer. Its founders included Yahoo's Hadoop leaders, Eric Baldeschwieler and Arun Murthy, and Rob Bearden, who became chief executive. The company kept all of its code open source. It earned money by selling support subscriptions to banks, retailers, and phone companies that ran Hadoop. Its rival Cloudera sold some paid software of its own on top.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then a Merger
sections.body: Hortonworks priced its IPO at $16 a share on December 12, 2014, and listed on Nasdaq as HDP. The stock jumped on its first day. Revenue grew fast, but losses stayed high, and the cloud began to replace the data centers where Hadoop ran. In January 2019 Hortonworks completed an all-stock merger with Cloudera. In 2021 two private equity firms took the combined company private.

tagline: Scanning for Holes From the Cloud
dek: Qualys scanned company networks for security holes from the cloud, so nobody had to install scanning software.
lede: Qualys sold security as a web service years before the phrase cloud computing caught on. Its scanners lived on its own servers and probed customers' networks from the outside, looking for weak spots an attacker might use. Customers logged in through a browser and read the results. When Qualys went public in September 2012, it had over 5,800 customers in more than 100 countries. Cloud software had finally become a category investors understood.

sections.heading: No Software to Install
sections.body: Qualys was incorporated at the end of 1999. Its main product, QualysGuard, checked computers and websites for known flaws and missing patches. Because the service ran in Qualys's own data centers, it was always up to date, and customers did not need to buy hardware or hire experts to run it. Philippe Courtot led the company as chairman and chief executive for most of its first two decades.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and Still Going
sections.body: Qualys priced its IPO at $12 a share on September 28, 2012, and listed on Nasdaq as QLYS. It kept adding tools on the same cloud platform, from asset tracking to compliance checks, and sold them to the same customers. The company has been profitable for years, which is unusual among security software makers. Qualys is still public and is based in Foster City, California.

cover.artwork: The Sentinel, 3270 feet, Yosemite Valley, Mariposa County, Cal., No. 6

dek: Retek's software told big retailers what to stock, where to ship it, and how to price it.
lede: Retek's IPO left its parent company holding about 88 percent of the shares. That parent was HNC Software, a maker of fraud-detection tools, which had bought Retek in 1996. Retek wrote the systems large chains used to plan what to stock, move goods through warehouses, and set prices. When it went public in November 1999, retailers were racing to sell online, and every one of them needed to know what was on its shelves.

sections.heading: Merchandise by the Numbers
sections.body: Retek Information Systems was founded in 1995 and acquired by HNC a year later. HNC joined it with Retek Logistics, a maker of warehouse software founded in 1985. The core product, the Retek Merchandising System, tracked items from purchase order to sale. Big chains used it to see which stores were selling what. The company was based in Minneapolis, home to some of the country's largest retailers.

sections.heading: A Bidding War for the Shop
sections.body: Retek sold shares at $15 on November 18, 1999, on Nasdaq under the ticker RETK. HNC later passed its remaining stake to its own shareholders, and Retek stood alone. Growth slowed after the dot-com bust. In early 2005 SAP and Oracle both tried to buy the company. Oracle won, and it completed the purchase that spring. Retek's software became part of Oracle's retail business.

cover.artwork: The Pastry Shop, plate ten from Landscapes and Interiors

fate: Merged with Scient, 2001; the combined company went bankrupt in 2002
tagline: Thirty-Four Web Shops Under One Roof
dek: iXL built websites and online strategies for big companies that had no idea what to do with the internet.
lede: In its first three years, iXL bought 34 companies. The Atlanta firm stitched together small web design shops, programmers, and consultants into one national agency for the Fortune 1000. Big companies in 1999 knew they needed a web strategy and had no one in-house to build it. iXL sold them both the plan and the code. When it went public in June 1999, web consultancies were among the hottest stocks on Nasdaq, and iXL was one of the largest.

sections.heading: A Roll-Up of Web Builders
sections.body: Bert Ellis, an Atlanta media executive, founded iXL in March 1996 and made its first acquisitions two months later. The plan was speed through buying. Each new shop brought designers, engineers, and clients in another city. iXL then offered the whole set of services: strategy, design, and the systems behind a site. Its customers were large companies that wanted to be on the web fast.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars Into the Bust
sections.body: iXL sold shares at $12 on June 3, 1999, on Nasdaq under the ticker IIXL. The stock climbed through the rest of the bubble. When the dot-com crash came in 2000, clients cut their web budgets, and iXL laid off staff and lost heavily. In November 2001 it merged with Scient, a San Francisco rival, to form Scient Inc. The combined company filed for bankruptcy in July 2002.

cover.theme: a kneeling mason (builders of the web)

dek: E.piphany let big companies study their customer data and send each customer the right offer.
lede: E.piphany's co-founder Steve Blank later wrote a famous book on how startups find customers. His own company sold software to do just that for large ones. It pulled data from a company's existing systems, built a profile of each customer, and let marketers design campaigns around what they found. When it went public in September 1999, every big business wanted to know its customers online the way a corner shop knew its regulars.

sections.heading: From Data to Campaigns
sections.body: Eliot Wegbreit and Steve Blank started the company in November 1996 as Epiphany Marketing Automation. It took the name E.piphany in April 1999. Its E.4 System gathered customer data that was scattered across a company's software and outside sources. Marketers could see who bought what, then plan and run campaigns aimed at each group. E.piphany sold licenses to large and medium businesses, plus consulting and support.

sections.heading: Sixteen Dollars, Then a Long Fall
sections.body: E.piphany priced its IPO at $16 a share on September 22, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as EPNY. The stock soared in its first months, as investors chased anything tied to the web. It fell hard after the crash, and larger rivals like Siebel and Oracle crowded the market. In 2005 SSA Global, a business software maker, bought E.piphany, and the company left the public market that September.

cover.theme: the Epiphany (the Magi's moment of revelation)

tagline: Small Parts for the Fiber Boom
dek: E-Tek made the tiny glass parts that steer and split light inside fiber optic networks.
lede: Some of E-Tek's parts sold for $200 apiece and were small enough to fit in a palm. Inside a fiber optic network, they did the quiet work: letting light pass one way only, splitting it, and combining many colors of light onto a single strand of glass. In 1998 telephone companies were laying fiber as fast as they could to keep up with the internet. E-Tek went public that December, betting every new strand of fiber would need its parts.

sections.heading: One-Way Valves for Light
sections.body: Theresa Pan and J.J. Pan founded the company, which was incorporated in Florida in 1983 and moved to California in 1987. E-Tek began making optical isolators in 1989. An isolator works like a one-way valve for light, keeping signals from bouncing back down the fiber. The company added couplers and parts for wavelength division multiplexing, which lets one fiber carry many signals at once in different colors.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars to JDS Uniphase
sections.body: E-Tek sold shares at $12 on December 2, 1998, on Nasdaq under the ticker ETEK. The founders kept about a third of the company. As the fiber boom took off in 1999, E-Tek's sales and stock both soared. In early 2000 JDS Uniphase, the largest maker of optical parts, agreed to buy E-Tek in an all-stock deal. The purchase closed in the summer of 2000, near the peak of the boom.

cover.theme: a mill spinner among threads (optical fiber)
cover.artwork: Sadie Pfeifer, a Cotton Mill Spinner, Lancaster, South Carolina

dek: Cheap Tickets sold discount airfares from empty seats airlines did not want to advertise.
lede: One of the biggest discount airfare sellers in America was based in Honolulu. Cheap Tickets sold seats airlines could not fill at full price. Carriers did not want to cut their public fares, so they sold this extra capacity quietly through Cheap Tickets, which passed the savings on to vacationers. In 1998 it sold about 960,000 airline tickets through call centers, stores, and its website. When it went public in March 1999, the web was about to become its main counter.

sections.heading: Fares You Could Not See
sections.body: Michael Hartley started the company in Hawaii in 1986. Before that he had founded and sold a charter airline. His business rested on contracts with more than 30 airlines, including American, Continental, Northwest, and US Airways. The airlines handed over unpublished fares on seats that would otherwise fly empty. Cheap Tickets sold them to leisure travelers, who cared about price more than flexibility.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars to Cendant
sections.body: Cheap Tickets priced its IPO at $15 a share on March 19, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as CTIX. Online travel grew fast, but so did rivals like Expedia, Travelocity, and the airlines' own sites. In 2001 Cendant, the travel and hotel company, bought Cheap Tickets for about $425 million. The brand later passed to Orbitz, and today it belongs to Expedia Group.

cover.theme: a flock of cranes in flight (cheap travel)

dek: iPrint let small businesses design and order business cards, stationery, and logo mugs online.
lede: Ordering business cards used to mean a trip to the print shop and a week of waiting. iPrint moved the whole job into a web browser. Customers designed cards, letterhead, checks, mugs, and t-shirts on its site, and iPrint sent the orders to commercial printers it had picked. The Redwood City company went public in March 2000, the same month the Nasdaq peaked. It bet that every small office would buy its printing online.

sections.heading: A Print Shop With No Presses
sections.body: Royal Farros founded iPrint in February 1996 and launched the online service in January 1997. The company owned no printing presses. Its software handled design and ordering, then routed each job electronically to an outside print vendor. That cut the back-and-forth of a traditional print order. iPrint also ran private-label print shops on other companies' websites, and lost money as it grew.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars at the Peak
sections.body: iPrint sold shares at $10 on March 8, 2000, on Nasdaq under the ticker IPRT. The dot-com crash began weeks later. In October 2001 it merged with Wood Associates, a seller of promotional merchandise, and took the name iPrint Technologies. Losses continued. In 2002 shareholders voted to transfer the company's assets through an assignment for the benefit of creditors, a way to wind down outside bankruptcy court.

cover.artwork: The Etcher's Press - The Printmaker's Shop

dek: CrossWorlds connected big companies' separate software systems so an order or a customer record flowed between them.
lede: By the late 1990s a large company might run SAP for its books, Siebel for its sales team, and a dozen homegrown systems besides, and none of them spoke to each other. CrossWorlds sold the translator. Its software carried a business process, such as a new order, across every system it touched. Katrina Garnett founded the company in 1996. It went public in June 2000, three months after the Nasdaq peaked, when investors were starting to turn away from software stocks.

sections.heading: Connectors Between Islands
sections.body: Garnett incorporated CrossWorlds in March 1996, and it shipped its first products in November 1997. The company built ready-made connectors for popular business applications and process modules for common jobs, like taking an order or updating a customer record. Instead of writing custom code to link every pair of systems, a company could plug each one into CrossWorlds once. Rivals such as TIBCO and webMethods sold similar ideas.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars, Then Big Blue
sections.body: CrossWorlds priced its IPO at $10 a share on June 2, 2000, and listed on Nasdaq as CWLD. The timing was hard. Corporate software budgets shrank after the dot-com crash, and the company kept losing money. In late 2001 IBM agreed to buy CrossWorlds, and the deal closed in January 2002. IBM folded its software into the WebSphere family of business integration products.

cover.artwork: The Angel of the Ninth Sphere, or Primum Mobile, plate 49 from Planets and Spheres

tagline: Memory and Graphics on One Chip
dek: NeoMagic made graphics chips for laptops that packed memory onto the same chip, saving space and battery.
lede: NeoMagic's trick was to put memory and graphics on the same piece of silicon. In 1997 laptops were heavy, hot, and short on battery, and every separate chip inside them took space and power. NeoMagic's MagicGraph chips combined a large block of memory with the logic that drew the screen. Notebook makers could build thinner machines that lasted longer. The Santa Clara company went public in March 1997, four years after it was founded, betting laptops were the future of the PC.

sections.heading: A Design Win in Every Notebook
sections.body: Kamran Elahian and Prakash Agarwal started the company in May 1993. Elahian had co-founded several chip companies before. NeoMagic's chips integrated large DRAM with analog and logic circuits on one die, which was hard to manufacture and hard to copy. The company sold to notebook PC makers. Each new laptop model that chose its chip, a design win, could mean hundreds of thousands of units.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and a Fade
sections.body: NeoMagic sold shares at $12 in March 1997, on Nasdaq under the ticker NMGC. For a few years its chips were inside a large share of the world's laptops. Then bigger rivals caught up, and Intel began building graphics into its own chipsets. NeoMagic left the notebook market and tried chips for phones and handheld devices. Nasdaq delisted the stock in 2008, and the company stopped filing with the SEC in 2013.

cover.artwork: Two Magicians with Two Boys, from Scherzi

tagline: Amplifiers for the Cell Phone Boom
dek: Powerwave built the power amplifiers that let cell towers push signals out to millions of phones.
lede: Powerwave's biggest early market was South Korea. In the mid-1990s Korea was building one of the first digital cell networks in the world, and every base station needed amplifiers to boost its radio signal. Powerwave, an Irvine, California company that had started life as Milcom International, made those amplifiers. When it went public in December 1996, cell phones were turning from a luxury into something everyone carried. Powerwave bet that every new tower would need its gear.

sections.heading: From Milcom to Powerwave
sections.body: Alfonso Cordero founded the company, which was incorporated in Delaware in January 1985 as Milcom International. It took the Powerwave name in June 1996, just before the IPO. Its products were radio frequency power amplifiers for wireless networks. An amplifier has to boost a signal without distorting it, and that gets harder as more calls share the same tower. Powerwave sold to the equipment makers who built networks for the carriers.

sections.heading: Eleven-Fifty and a Long Ride
sections.body: Powerwave sold shares at $11.50 in December 1996, on Nasdaq under the ticker PWAV. It grew with each new generation of cell networks and bought rivals to get bigger. Prices for wireless gear kept falling, and a few giant equipment makers held most of the buying power. Losses mounted. Powerwave filed for bankruptcy in January 2013, and Nasdaq removed its shares that March.

cover.theme: a storm breaking on the coast (Powerwave)

tagline: The Last Mile to the Phone Company
dek: AFC made equipment that connected homes and offices to the phone company's switch over copper, fiber, or cable.
lede: Donald Green had already co-founded one big telecom equipment maker, Tellabs, before he started this one. In 1992 he set up Advanced Fibre Communications in Petaluma, California, to rebuild the last stretch of the phone network, the lines between a central office and the homes it served. Its UMC system could run over copper, fiber, coaxial cable, or radio. When AFC went public in October 1996, phone companies were starting to rewire for data as well as voice.

sections.heading: One Box for Every Wire
sections.body: Green founded AFC with Jim Hoeck and John Webley in May 1992. The company spent two years on development and began shipping the UMC system in January 1994. It was a digital loop carrier, a box that gathered many phone lines and linked them to the central office switch. Ameritech and GTE were early buyers. Before the IPO, AFC settled a costly lawsuit with DSC Communications, a larger rival.

sections.heading: Twenty-Five Dollars, Then Home
sections.body: AFC priced its IPO at $25 a share on October 1, 1996, raising $112.5 million, and listed on Nasdaq as AFCI. Its sales grew as phone companies upgraded their networks for the internet, and AFC later added gear for broadband data and video over the same lines. In 2004 Tellabs, the company Green had co-founded in 1975, bought AFC for about $1.9 billion. The deal closed that December.

dek: 21Vianet ran data centers across China that any network or company could plug into.
lede: In China, most data centers belonged to the big state phone carriers. 21Vianet built its business by belonging to none of them. Its data centers connected to every major network, so a website or game company could reach users on all of them from one place. When the Beijing company went public in April 2011, it was the largest carrier-neutral data center provider in China by revenue, with sites in 33 cities and over 39,000 servers under management.

sections.heading: Wired to Every Carrier
sections.body: Sheng Chen and Jun Zhang started the business in 1999. Chen became chairman and chief executive. China's internet traffic was split among rival carriers, and moving data between their networks was slow. 21Vianet's answer was neutrality. It linked its data centers to all the major carriers and to its own network, and it rented space, power, and bandwidth to companies that needed fast access across China.

sections.heading: Fifteen Dollars and the Cloud
sections.body: 21Vianet sold American depositary shares at $15 each on April 21, 2011, on Nasdaq under the ticker VNET. It later became Microsoft's partner for running Azure and Office 365 inside China, where foreign companies cannot operate those services alone. The company changed its name to VNET Group. It still trades on Nasdaq as VNET and keeps building data centers for China's cloud and AI demand.

cover.theme: bamboo spreading along a stream (a network grown across China)

dek: Agilent made the instruments that scientists and engineers use to test chips, networks, blood and chemicals.
lede: Hewlett-Packard started in 1939 by selling an audio oscillator, a box that measured sound. Sixty years later, HP cut that measuring business loose and called it Agilent. The new company took the test gear, the chip unit, the chemical analyzers and the medical equipment, while HP kept the computers and printers. Agilent priced its IPO at $30 a share in November 1999. It raised about $2.1 billion, all of it paid back to HP.

sections.heading: HP Splits Itself in Two
sections.body: In March 1999 HP decided it had grown too wide to run as one company. The computer and printer side faced fast, cheap rivals. The instrument side sold oscilloscopes, signal analyzers and lab machines to engineers and chemists who cared more about precision than price. Agilent became the home for the instrument side. Its pitch to investors was simple: the tools that test the internet's chips and fiber deserved a company of their own, with its own stock to pay its own engineers.

sections.heading: Sixty Seven Percent by Lunch
sections.body: Agilent sold 72 million shares at $30 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange under the single letter A. The stock touched $50 within its first hours of trading. HP handed its remaining shares to its own stockholders in 2000. Agilent later sold its medical unit and its chip business, and in 2014 it spun off its electronic test arm as Keysight. What stayed was the life sciences and chemistry lab business. Agilent still trades on the NYSE under the ticker A.

fate: Iridium LLC bankrupt, 1999; network revived, now Iridium Communications (NASDAQ: IRDM)
dek: Iridium promised a phone that worked anywhere on Earth, carried by a ring of satellites overhead.
lede: The company took its name from element 77, because the first design called for 77 satellites circling the planet like electrons. Iridium wanted to let a person dial from a glacier, a desert or a ship at sea. Motorola engineers had dreamed it up and Motorola owned a large stake. In June 1997 Iridium World Communications sold stock at $20 a share so the public could own a piece of the network before a single call went through.

sections.heading: Sixty Six Moons of Motorola
sections.body: The plan shrank to 66 satellites in low orbit, each one passing calls to the next until they reached a ground station. Iridium World Communications was a Bermuda holding company. Its only job was to own shares of Iridium LLC, the partnership building the system. The bet was that travelers, oil crews, soldiers and executives would pay for a phone with no dead zones. Rockets carried the satellites up through 1997 and 1998, and service opened in November 1998.

sections.heading: Bankrupt, Then Reborn
sections.body: The offering was so popular that Iridium raised it from 10 million shares to 12 million, bringing in $240 million on Nasdaq under IRIDF. Then the phones arrived: heavy handsets that cost thousands of dollars and failed indoors. Few people signed up. Iridium LLC filed for bankruptcy in August 1999, less than a year after launch. A group of investors bought the network for $25 million in 2000. The satellites stayed up, and the business now trades as Iridium Communications on Nasdaq.

cover.theme: Icarus falling from the sun (a network that fell to Earth)

dek: Weibo gave hundreds of millions of Chinese users a public feed for news, gossip and celebrity posts.
lede: Twitter was blocked in China, so a Beijing web portal built its own. Sina launched Weibo in August 2009, and within a few years it was where China argued, joked and broke news. Movie stars posted there. Train crashes and scandals surfaced there before the state media covered them. By the time Weibo filed to go public in 2014, Alibaba owned a large stake, and Sina wanted Wall Street to put a price on China's loudest public square.

sections.heading: A Portal Builds a Feed
sections.body: Sina was one of China's original web portals, a site of news headlines and email. Under chief executive Charles Chao, it saw that people wanted to talk back. Weibo, which means microblog, let users post short messages, photos and video and follow anyone. Sina invited celebrities to join first, and their fans followed them in. The bet was that a huge, public, mobile audience could be sold to advertisers, the way Twitter and Facebook were selling theirs in the United States.

sections.heading: A Weak Start, a Long Run
sections.body: Weibo priced on April 17, 2014, at $17 a share, the bottom of its range, and cut the offering to 16.8 million shares. It opened below that price on Nasdaq. Then buyers came in, and the stock closed just over $20, up about 19 percent. Weibo kept growing as China moved onto smartphones. In 2021 it added a second listing in Hong Kong. Weibo still trades on Nasdaq under WB.

cover.theme: a songbird on a plum branch (chatter)

tagline: A Computer in Your Shirt Pocket
dek: Palm made the PalmPilot, the pocket organizer that put a calendar and address book in everyone's hand.
lede: On its first day of trading, Palm was worth almost twice as much as the company that owned it. Shares priced at $38 touched $165 and closed at $95.06, giving Palm a market value of $53.4 billion. Its parent, 3Com, still held 94 percent of the stock, yet 3Com itself was worth only about $28 billion that afternoon. It was March 2, 2000, eight days before the Nasdaq peaked, and the market had decided the future fit in a palm.

sections.heading: A Block of Wood
sections.body: Jeff Hawkins founded Palm in 1992 with Donna Dubinsky and Ed Colligan. Hawkins is said to have carried a wooden block cut to pocket size to test how a handheld should feel. Early handhelds had failed because they tried to do too much. The PalmPilot, launched in 1996, did a few things well: calendar, contacts, notes, and a quick sync with a desktop computer. U.S. Robotics bought Palm in 1995, and 3Com bought U.S. Robotics in 1997.

sections.heading: Pilot, Treo, Pre, HP
sections.body: 3Com handed its remaining Palm shares to its own stockholders later in 2000. Then the bubble burst, and Palm's stock fell with everything else. The company split its software arm off as PalmSource in 2003. It found a second hit with the Treo smartphone and a third try with the Pre and its webOS software in 2009. By then the iPhone owned the market. Hewlett-Packard bought Palm in 2010 for about $1.2 billion.

dek: HomeGrocer let busy families order groceries online and have them delivered by the company's own trucks.
lede: Amazon put its money behind a Seattle-area startup that promised to bring milk, bread and bananas to your door. HomeGrocer took orders on the web, picked them in its own warehouses and drove them out in its own trucks, inside a window the customer chose. In March 2000 it sold stock at $12 a share, raising about $288 million. Its bigger rival Webvan was already public, and investors were betting that online grocery would be the next giant market.

sections.heading: A Warehouse Instead of a Store
sections.body: Terry Drayton started HomeGrocer in Kirkland, Washington, in 1997 with a small group of cofounders. The idea was to skip the supermarket. A single warehouse could serve a whole metro area, and drivers could carry the bags all the way to the kitchen. HomeGrocer opened in Seattle and then moved into Portland, Southern California and other western cities. Each new city needed its own warehouse and fleet, and each one cost tens of millions of dollars before it earned a cent.

sections.heading: Swallowed by Webvan
sections.body: HomeGrocer listed on Nasdaq in March 2000, days before the dot-com market began to crack. Three months later Webvan agreed to buy it in an all-stock deal valued at about $1.2 billion, and stockholders approved it that September. The combined company kept the Webvan name. It was still burning cash faster than it could raise it. Webvan shut down and filed for bankruptcy in July 2001.

cover.artwork: A Fruit Market, from The Houghton Gallery

dek: Youku gave Chinese viewers a free place to stream TV shows, films and homemade videos.
lede: Youku's stock jumped 161 percent on its first day, the best debut on the New York Stock Exchange since Baidu in 2005. Shares sold at $12.80 closed at $33.44. YouTube was blocked in China, and Youku had become the place where hundreds of millions of people watched clips, dramas and movies for free. Its December 2010 offering raised $203 million and valued a company that had never turned a profit at more than $3 billion.

sections.heading: Excellent and Cool
sections.body: Victor Koo, a former president of the portal Sohu, founded Youku in Beijing in 2006. The name means roughly excellent and cool. Youku started as a home for user videos, then spent heavily on licensed Chinese TV series and films, which kept viewers watching for hours. Ads before and during videos paid the bills. The bet was that Chinese viewers would move from television to screens they carried, and that the biggest library would win the audience.

sections.heading: Merger, Then Alibaba
sections.body: Youku listed on the NYSE under YOKU and priced above its planned range of $9 to $11. Rising license costs ate its margins, and its fiercest rival was Tudou, another video site. In 2012 the two merged in an all-stock deal and became Youku Tudou. Alibaba bought a large stake in 2014. In 2016 Alibaba bought the rest at $27.60 a share, in a deal valued at about $4.8 billion, and took the company private.

cover.theme: a box at the theater (a nation watching)
cover.artwork: A Box at the Kabuki Theater, from the illustrated book "Guide to the Actors' Dressing Rooms (Yakusha gakuya tsu)"

tagline: Taking the Hiss Out of Sound
dek: Dolby made the sound technology that kept tapes, films and phones clear, and charged a small fee on each device.
lede: For forty years, Ray Dolby's company made money every time someone else built a tape deck, a film projector or a DVD player. Dolby built some studio and cinema gear, but most of its money came from ideas. It licensed the methods that cut hiss from tapes and filled movie theaters with surround sound, and it collected a fee on each machine. When it went public in February 2005, the name was printed on hundreds of millions of devices, and its founder still controlled the company.

sections.heading: A Lab in London
sections.body: Ray Dolby, an American engineer, started Dolby Laboratories in London in 1965. His first product cut the background hiss from recording studio tape. He later moved the company to San Francisco. Dolby noise reduction spread to cassette decks in homes and cars. Then came film: Dolby Stereo changed how movies sounded, and Dolby Digital became a standard for DVDs and home theater. The bet was that licensing an idea to every manufacturer beat building one product yourself.

sections.heading: Pricing Above the Range
sections.body: Dolby had planned to sell shares at $13.50 to $15.50. Demand pushed the price to $18, and the stock began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under DLB on February 17, 2005. Ray Dolby sold shares in the deal too, yet he kept control through a second class of stock. He died in 2013. Dolby moved into streaming and phones with Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision, and it still trades on the NYSE under DLB.

cover.theme: an evening at the concert (sound, heard clearly)

fate: Renamed Monster Worldwide, 2003; acquired by Randstad, 2016
tagline: The Yellow Pages Grew a Monster
dek: TMP placed yellow page and help-wanted ads, then built Monster, one of the first big job sites.
lede: The company that owned Monster.com started out selling ads in the yellow pages. Andrew McKelvey founded it in 1967, and by 1996 TMP was the world's largest yellow page advertising agency. It also wrote help-wanted ads for employers, which gave it a reason to buy a small job site called The Monster Board. TMP went public in December 1996 at $14 a share. Monster was a footnote in the filing, and it became the reason anyone remembers the company.

sections.heading: Ads in the Phone Book
sections.body: McKelvey built TMP around national advertisers that needed listings in thousands of local phone books. The second business was recruitment advertising: placing job ads in newspapers for big employers. Both paid commissions. In 1995 TMP bought the company behind The Monster Board, one of the earliest job sites on the web, started by Jeff Taylor. The bet was that help-wanted ads would move from newsprint to screens, and that an ad agency already serving the employers could carry them there.

sections.heading: From TMPW to Randstad
sections.body: TMP sold shares at $14 on December 12, 1996, and listed on Nasdaq as TMPW. Monster grew into the best-known job site of the dot-com era, with a Super Bowl ad and a purple mascot. In 2003 the company spun off its staffing arm, sold off older lines and renamed itself Monster Worldwide. LinkedIn and Indeed later took much of its audience. The Dutch staffing firm Randstad bought Monster in 2016 for about $429 million.

fate: Renamed Leaf Group, 2016; acquired by Graham Holdings, 2021 ($8.50 a share)
tagline: Articles Written to Order for Search
dek: Demand Media paid freelancers to write the how-to articles people were searching for, then sold ads beside them.
lede: Demand Media let software decide what to write. Its algorithms studied what people typed into search engines, and freelancers wrote articles to match, at a few dollars a piece, for sites like eHow. The pages ranked well on Google and carried ads. When the Santa Monica company went public in January 2011, it also ran a large domain name registrar, and investors were betting the content machine could keep growing as fast as the web did.

sections.heading: A Content Factory
sections.body: Richard Rosenblatt and Shawn Colo started Demand Media in 2006. They bought eHow and other sites, and they bought eNom, a registrar that sold web addresses. The content studio was the bold part. It found questions with steady search traffic and ad value, then assigned them to an army of freelance writers and video makers. The bet was that cheap pages, made in huge numbers and aimed at search, could earn more in ads than they cost to make.

sections.heading: Google Changes the Rules
sections.body: Demand Media priced at $17 a share, above its $14 to $16 range, and closed its first day on the NYSE at $22.65, up 33 percent. Within weeks Google changed its ranking system to push down low-quality pages, and eHow's traffic suffered. A year after the IPO the stock had fallen about 60 percent. The company spun off its domain business in 2014 and renamed itself Leaf Group in 2016. Graham Holdings bought it in 2021 for $8.50 a share.

cover.artwork: Maple Leaves in Shimosa Province (Shimosa, momiji), section of sheet no. 7 from the series "Cutout Pictures of the Provinces (Kunizukushi harimaze zue)"

fate: Acquired by Cisco, 2009 ($35 a share, about $2.9B)
dek: Starent built the gear that let wireless carriers move internet traffic to and from millions of phones.
lede: Every time a phone loaded a web page in 2007, the data passed through a box most people never heard of. Starent Networks made those boxes. Its gateways sat inside wireless carriers' networks and handled the traffic between the radio towers and the internet. Starent went public that June, the same month the first iPhone went on sale. Mobile data was about to explode, and Starent sold the equipment carriers needed to keep up.

sections.heading: Built for Traffic Jams
sections.body: Ashraf Dahod founded Starent in Tewksbury, Massachusetts, in August 2000. It took the company until 2003 to ship its first commercial product. Starent's platform was built to manage huge numbers of mobile data sessions at once, and to add new services like video and messaging through software. The bet was that carriers would soon carry far more data than voice, and that the gear they already owned was not built for it. Starent's chief customers were large mobile operators.

sections.heading: Cisco Pays Up
sections.body: Starent priced at $12 a share in June 2007 and listed on Nasdaq under STAR. Smartphones arrived just as its gear was ready, and the business grew with them. In October 2009 Cisco agreed to buy Starent for $35 a share in cash, nearly three times the offering price, in a deal valued at about $2.9 billion. The sale closed in December 2009, and Starent became part of Cisco's mobile networking group.

fate: Acquired by Oracle, 2016 ($10.30 a share, about $532M)
dek: Opower got people to use less electricity by showing them how their bills stacked up against their neighbors'.
lede: Opower's best product was a piece of paper. Utilities mailed it to homes, and it showed how much power you used compared with the neighbors next door. People who saw that they used more tended to cut back. By the time Opower went public in April 2014, 93 utilities in eight countries used its software, and its data covered 52 million homes and businesses. The company sold the idea that a nudge could work like a power plant.

sections.heading: Once Called Positive Energy
sections.body: Dan Yates and Alex Laskey started the company in 2007 in the Washington, D.C., area under the name Positive Energy. Their first product was the home energy report, built on behavioral science research. Utilities paid because regulators rewarded them for cutting demand, and saved power was cheaper than building new plants. Opower later added web and mobile tools for utility customers. The bet was that utilities, slow buyers of technology, would pay for cloud software that made customers both thriftier and happier.

sections.heading: Oracle Buys the Nudge
sections.body: Opower sold shares at $19 on April 4, 2014, and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as OPWR. Growth slowed as utilities took a long time to sign and renew contracts, and the company kept losing money. The stock drifted well below its offering price. In 2016 Oracle bought Opower in a cash tender offer at $10.30 a share, a deal valued at about $532 million, and folded it into its utilities business.

fate: Acquired by IBM, 2010 ($27 a share, about $1.7B)
tagline: A Data Warehouse in a Box
dek: Netezza sold ready-made machines that let companies search mountains of data much faster than older systems.
lede: Netezza started life as Intelligent Data Engines, a name that said exactly what it built. The Massachusetts company sold a single machine that combined the database, the servers and the storage, tuned to answer big questions about big piles of data. Companies wheeled it in and plugged it in. By the spring of 2007 Netezza had sold more than 230 of these appliances to 101 customers, and it went public that July.

sections.heading: Hardware for Hard Questions
sections.body: Jit Saxena and Foster Hinshaw founded the company in August 2000, and it took the name Netezza that November. Large companies stored years of sales, calls and transactions in data warehouses, but asking those systems a complex question could take hours. Netezza's appliance pushed much of the work down into custom hardware close to the disks. The bet was that buyers would trade the flexibility of mixing parts from several vendors for a box that was faster, cheaper to run and simple to set up.

sections.heading: Bought by Big Blue
sections.body: Netezza priced at $12 a share in July 2007 and listed on NYSE Arca under NZ. The company kept growing through the financial crisis as businesses collected more data than ever. In September 2010 IBM agreed to buy Netezza for $27 a share in cash, more than double the offering price, in a deal valued at about $1.7 billion. The sale closed that November, and IBM sold the product under its own name.

fate: Acquired by Ivanti, 2020 ($7.05 a share, about $872M)
tagline: Locking Down the Phone in Your Pocket
dek: MobileIron let companies secure the apps and data on employees' phones, even phones the employees owned.
lede: Once workers started bringing their own iPhones to the office, IT departments lost control of where company email and files lived. MobileIron sold the fix. Its software let a company secure work apps, documents and settings on a phone while leaving the owner's photos and texts alone. MobileIron had been founded in 2007, the year the iPhone came out. By its IPO in June 2014, bring your own device had become a standard office policy.

sections.heading: Work Apps, Personal Phones
sections.body: Ajay Mishra and Suresh Batchu founded the company in Mountain View in July 2007 as Mobile Iron, two words. It released its platform commercially in 2009 and added tools for securing individual apps and content in 2012. The software worked across Apple, Android and other phones. The bet was that mobile would become the main way people worked, and that every company would need one place to set rules for all its devices.

sections.heading: From MOBL to Ivanti
sections.body: MobileIron sold 11.1 million shares at $9 each on June 12, 2014, and listed on Nasdaq as MOBL. Rivals moved in fast: VMware bought AirWatch, and Microsoft and others bundled similar tools into their own products. MobileIron grew, but it struggled to turn a profit, and the stock spent long stretches below its offering price. Ivanti, a private IT software company, bought MobileIron in December 2020 for $7.05 a share, about $872 million.

fate: Merged with Phone.com to form Openwave, 2000
tagline: The Mail Room of the Early Internet
dek: Software.com made the email systems that internet providers and phone companies used to run millions of mailboxes.
lede: John MacFarlane registered the domain name Software.com in 1992, planning to sell software downloads. He ended up building the mail room for the internet instead. His Santa Barbara company wrote the server software that phone companies and internet providers used to run email for their customers. By March 1999 it had licensed more than 37 million mailboxes. Three months later Software.com went public, just as email was becoming the reason most people got online.

sections.heading: A Domain Name First
sections.body: MacFarlane started the business as a partnership in January 1993 and incorporated it in October 1994. Its products, Post.Office and InterMail, were built on internet standards, so they could grow from thousands of accounts to millions without changing the plumbing. Customers were the big carriers and service providers, not the people reading the mail. The bet was that every company handing out email addresses would rather license a proven system than build its own.

sections.heading: Phone.com Calls
sections.body: Software.com sold shares at $15 on June 24, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as SWCM. A year later it agreed to merge with Phone.com, which made the software for browsing the web on mobile phones. Each Software.com share became 1.6105 Phone.com shares.
