The deal closed in November 2000, and the combined company took the name Openwave Systems. Openwave later sold off its product lines and became Unwired Planet in 2012.

cover.theme: pigeons gathered on a fence (messages carried)

fate: Acquired by Vision Solutions (Thoma Bravo), 2010 ($10.55 a share)
tagline: A Spare Server, Always Up to Date
dek: Double-Take kept a live copy of a company's servers elsewhere, so work could continue when disaster struck.
lede: After September 11 and Hurricane Katrina, companies started asking what would happen if their main office went dark. Double-Take Software had an answer. Its software copied every change on a business's key servers to a second machine, across the hall or across the country, as the changes happened. If the first server died, the second could take over. In December 2006 the company went public, calling itself the leading supplier of replication software for Microsoft servers.

sections.heading: Fifteen Years as NSI
sections.body: The company began in New Jersey in 1991 as NSI Software. It released its replication software in 1995 and spent a decade improving it with customer feedback. The product sat on the server, watched for changed files and sent only those changes to the backup. That kept the copy current without heavy network traffic. NSI moved to Southborough, Massachusetts, and in July 2006 renamed itself after its product. The bet was that smaller companies wanted disaster recovery without a mainframe budget.

sections.heading: From DBTK to Thoma Bravo
sections.body: Double-Take priced at $11 a share in December 2006 and began trading on Nasdaq under DBTK. It sold mostly through resellers and partners, and its focus on Windows servers fit the market as virtual machines spread. In May 2010 it agreed to be bought by Vision Solutions, a company controlled by the private equity firm Thoma Bravo, for $10.55 a share in cash. The deal closed that summer, and the stock left Nasdaq.

cover.theme: a reflection on water (a live copy)

dek: Launch gave young music fans videos, news and personalized radio online, paid for by brands chasing them.
lede: Launch began as a music magazine you put in your computer's CD-ROM drive. A former Capitol Records executive and a securities lawyer started it in 1994, and by 1999 it had moved onto the web at launch.com, with music videos, artist interviews and personal home pages for about a million registered users. Its pitch was Generation Y. When Launch went public in April 1999, it sold advertisers like Coca-Cola a direct line to teenagers.

sections.heading: From Capitol Records to the Web
sections.body: David Goldberg left Capitol Records and cofounded Launch in February 1994 with Robert Roback, who had been practicing securities law in Chicago. The first Launch on CD-ROM shipped in May 1995. As connections got faster, the company moved its videos and features online. The bet was that young fans would spend hours with music on their computers, and that record labels and big brands would pay to reach them there.

sections.heading: Ninety Two Cents
sections.body: Launch sold 3.4 million shares at $22 in April 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as LAUN. Then the dot-com market collapsed, ad budgets dried up, and record labels fought online music in court. In 2001 Yahoo bought Launch in a cash tender offer at 92 cents a share, and its streaming radio became part of Yahoo Music. Goldberg later became chief executive of SurveyMonkey.

cover.artwork: Women and Children Viewing the Fireworks

dek: Andover.net owned Slashdot and other sites where programmers and Linux fans got news and free software.
lede: Andover.net owned Slashdot, the site that called itself "News for Nerds. Stuff that Matters." Its readers argued in the comments all day about Linux, open source and the tech industry. In December 1999 Linux was the hottest word on Wall Street, and Andover.net went public with a network built for exactly that crowd. It even sold its shares through an online auction, a method that let ordinary investors bid alongside the big funds.

sections.heading: A Software Shop Buys Slashdot
sections.body: The company started in Massachusetts in 1992 as Andover Advanced Technologies, a small packaged software publisher. It moved toward an advertising business on the web and, between June and August 1999, bought Slashdot.org, Freshmeat.net and Animation Factory. Its network also included ThinkGeek. Slashdot's readers wrote much of its content by commenting on posted stories. The bet was that programmers made a loyal audience that tech advertisers would pay to reach.

sections.heading: Sold by Auction, Sold Again
sections.body: Andover.net priced its offering at $18 a share on December 8, 1999, through WR Hambrecht's OpenIPO auction, and listed on Nasdaq as ANDN. Two months later VA Linux Systems, which had just staged a record IPO of its own, agreed to buy it for stock. The deal closed in June 2000. Slashdot changed owners several times after that, and the site still runs.

cover.theme: reading the morning paper (news for nerds)

tagline: The Web, Packed for the Road
dek: AvantGo loaded news and web pages onto Palm handhelds so people could read the internet away from a connection.
lede: Before Broadcom made the ticker AVGO famous, it belonged to a small San Mateo company that put the web in your pocket. AvantGo's software copied news, stock quotes and other web pages onto Palm and Pocket PC handhelds whenever you synced them. You could read the internet on the train, with no connection at all. In the fall of 2000, AvantGo went public as the hope for a mobile internet was colliding with a falling Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Once Called Bombardier
sections.body: The company was incorporated in June 1997 as Bombardier Software and became AvantGo in January 1998. It released its first software that May. AvantGo ran two businesses. Its free consumer service let publishers send channels of content to handhelds. Its enterprise software let companies push their own data to mobile workers in the field. The bet was that handhelds, and soon wireless phones, would become a main way people reached the web.

sections.heading: From AVGO to Sybase
sections.body: AvantGo priced at $12 a share in late September 2000 and listed on Nasdaq under AVGO. The dot-com crash soon cut its stock to a fraction of that. Smartphones with real browsers were still years away, and handhelds stayed a niche. In early 2003 Sybase bought AvantGo for about $1.03 a share in cash and folded it into its mobile software unit.

cover.theme: a mail coach on the road (news that travels)

dek: Bluestone made Java application server software that let companies open their databases to customers over the web.
lede: Bluestone Software spent most of its life as a Unix consulting and staffing firm in New Jersey. Then it built a product called Sapphire/Web, and everything changed. Sapphire/Web was a framework for Java application servers, the software layer that sits between a company's stored records and the people who need to reach them on the web. By the fall of 1999 more than 500 customers, from AT&T to Eli Lilly, had bought it, and Bluestone went public.

sections.heading: From Unix Staffing to Java
sections.body: The company was incorporated in New Jersey in 1989 as Bluestone Consulting. Its early business was information technology consulting on Unix systems and placing technical staff. In the mid-1990s it turned its expertise into packaged software, and from 1996 on it sold Sapphire/Web through a direct sales force and resellers. The bet was that every big company would need to put its old databases on the web, and that a dedicated application server would handle the load better than custom code.

sections.heading: Into Hewlett-Packard
sections.body: Bluestone sold 4 million shares at $15 on September 24, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as BLSW. The internet boom lifted every company with web infrastructure to sell. In October 2000 Hewlett-Packard agreed to buy Bluestone in an all-stock deal, giving 0.2433 pre-split HP shares for each Bluestone share. HP wanted its XML and mobile technology for its own internet software push. The deal closed in early 2001.

cover.theme: a stone quarry (Bluestone and its Sapphire)

dek: Manhattan Associates wrote the software that tells warehouse workers what to pick, pack and ship, and in what order.
lede: Despite the name, Manhattan Associates was born in Atlanta. Its first product, PkMS, shipped in 1990 and did one job in great detail: it ran the inside of a distribution center. It tracked every box from the receiving dock to a shelf, then to a picker, a packer and a truck. In 1998 retailers and manufacturers were racing to move goods faster with less inventory on hand, and Manhattan went public to sell them the tool.

sections.heading: PkMS and the Pick Ticket
sections.body: Alan Dabbiere led the company, and his firm Pegasys Systems contributed the software and staff that became Manhattan Associates. PkMS managed receiving, stock locating, picking, order checking, packing and shipping in complex distribution centers. Customers bought it to turn inventory faster, cut errors and get orders out the door sooner. The bet was that the warehouse, long run on paper and habit, would become a place where software made money for its owner.

sections.heading: Still Shipping Software
sections.body: Manhattan Associates sold shares at $15 on April 24, 1998, and listed on Nasdaq as MANH. It grew from warehouse software into a wider supply chain suite, covering transportation, inventory and store systems, and later moved its products to the cloud. Online shopping made fast, accurate warehouses matter more each year. Manhattan Associates is still independent and still trades on Nasdaq under MANH.

cover.theme: the old and new New York skyline (Manhattan)

tagline: Getting Paid to Look at Ads
dek: Cybergold paid people small amounts of cash for reading ads, joining offers and trying products online.
lede: Cybergold started under the name Cyber-Bucks, which explains the whole idea. Instead of hoping people would notice an ad, advertisers paid Cybergold only when a member did something specific, like reading an offer or signing up for a trial, and Cybergold passed real cash to the member. By the middle of 1999 the Bay Area company had about 2.6 million members. That September it went public as one of the web's attention merchants.

sections.heading: Earn and Spend
sections.body: Nathaniel Goldhaber, a venture investor, became chief executive when the company was formed in California in October 1994. Meaningful revenue only began in March 1997. Cybergold called its system Earn and Spend: members earned cash for responding to offers, and could spend it on digital goods through Cybergold's own micropayment system. The bet was that advertisers would rather pay for actions than for eyeballs, and that consumers would trade a little attention for a little money.

sections.heading: Folded Into MyPoints
sections.body: Cybergold sold 5 million shares at $9 in September 1999 and listed on Nasdaq as CGLD. Its rivals, like MyPoints, paid members in points instead of cash. In 2000 MyPoints agreed to buy Cybergold, giving 0.48 of a MyPoints share for each Cybergold share, and the merger closed that summer. A year later United Airlines' venture arm bought MyPoints itself.

cover.artwork: Danae and the Shower of Gold

dek: Pervasive sold small database engines that software makers built into accounting, payroll and other business programs.
lede: Pervasive Software began by buying a database from Novell. In April 1994 the new Austin company, then called Btrieve Technologies, acquired Btrieve, a compact database engine that shipped with Novell's NetWare. Thousands of business programs already used Btrieve to store their records, often without the end user ever knowing. When it went public in September 1997, Pervasive was selling the invisible part inside other companies' software.

sections.heading: Bought From Novell
sections.body: The company was incorporated in January 1994 as Btrieve Technologies and renamed itself Pervasive Software in June 1996. Its engines, Btrieve and Scalable SQL, were made for software developers who wanted a reliable database that needed almost no upkeep at a customer's office. Much of its revenue came from upgrades sold into the NetWare installed base. The bet was that packaged business software would keep spreading, and that each copy would need an embedded database underneath.

sections.heading: Taken Private by Actian
sections.body: Pervasive sold 4 million shares at $10 in September 1997, half of them from existing holders, and listed on Nasdaq as PVSW. NetWare lost ground to Windows NT, so the company added data integration tools and other products to keep growing. It stayed public for more than fifteen years. In 2013 Actian, a database company, bought Pervasive for $9.20 a share in cash and took it private.

cover.theme: a sudden rain shower (pervasive, everywhere at once)

dek: Ambarella designs the chips that turn raw camera images into sharp, compact video, from action cameras to cars.
lede: When surfers and skiers strapped GoPro cameras to their helmets, an Ambarella chip did the hard work. It took the flood of raw pixels from the sensor and squeezed it into high-definition video small enough to store and share. Ambarella's chips also went into security cameras from Bosch and devices from Samsung. In October 2012 the small Santa Clara chip designer went public at $6 a share, a modest price for a company sitting inside the decade's favorite gadget.

sections.heading: Video, Compressed
sections.body: Fermi Wang and Les Kohn founded Ambarella in 2004, setting it up as a Cayman Islands company with its main office in Silicon Valley. It first earned product revenue in 2006. Ambarella did not own factories. It designed system-on-chip processors that handled video compression and image processing at low power, then had them built by contract manufacturers. The bet was that cameras would show up everywhere, in pockets, on helmets, on walls and in cars, and all of them would need efficient video chips.

sections.heading: From Action Cams to AI
sections.body: Ambarella sold shares at $6 in October 2012 and listed on Nasdaq under AMBA. GoPro's own IPO in 2014 drew attention to its suppliers, and Ambarella's stock rose well above its offering price. As GoPro's growth slowed, Ambarella moved toward security cameras and cars, building chips that run computer vision to spot people, lanes and objects. Ambarella still trades on Nasdaq under AMBA.

fate: Taken private by Fenway Partners, 2007 ($24.25 a share)
dek: 1-800 Contacts let people reorder their contact lenses by phone or online for less than the eye doctor charged.
lede: The company's name was also its phone number, and its whole pitch. Contact lens wearers used to buy refills from the eye doctor who wrote the prescription, often at a steep markup. 1-800 Contacts let them call a toll-free line in Utah, or later click a website, and get the same lenses shipped to the door for less. When it went public in February 1998, soft lenses were growing more popular every year among teenagers and young adults.

sections.heading: A Toll-Free Number in Utah
sections.body: John Nichols started the business in March 1991. Jonathan Coon joined as president, and the two formed 1-800 Contacts as a Utah company in February 1995. They spent heavily on advertising to make the number stick in people's heads, then kept customers by making reorders easy. The bet was that lenses were a commodity, and that buyers would pick convenience and price over loyalty to their optometrist's front desk.

sections.heading: Sold, Then Sold Again
sections.body: 1-800 Contacts sold shares at $12.50 in February 1998 and listed on Nasdaq under CTAC. More and more of its orders moved to the web, and it became one of the larger online retailers of its era. In 2007 a group led by the private equity firm Fenway Partners bought the company for $24.25 a share in cash and took it private. It has changed private owners several times since then.

fate: Acquired by Intermedia Communications, 1997 ($13 a share)
dek: Digex sold fast internet lines and web server hosting to businesses and government agencies in the web's early years.
lede: Digex started life as Digital Express Group, founded in 1990 by a group of early internet enthusiasts in Maryland. By 1996 it had stopped chasing home dial-up users and sold only to businesses and government agencies, which needed fast, always-on connections and a safe place to run their web servers. It had built its own high-speed backbone around the continental United States. That October, as companies rushed to get online, Digex went public at $10.125 a share.

sections.heading: Businesses Only
sections.body: The company took its first major outside investment in March 1995 and then turned its focus entirely to business customers. It sold leased-line connections, hosting for customers' web servers, and security products. In the first half of 1996 it brought in an experienced management team and finished a DS-3 backbone ring across the country. Its line and server accounts grew from about 65 in April 1995 to roughly 1,050 by the time of its filing.

sections.heading: Bought Within a Year
sections.body: Digex listed on Nasdaq under DIGX in October 1996. Less than a year later, in June 1997, the telecom carrier Intermedia Communications agreed to buy it through a cash tender offer at $13 a share. Intermedia built Digex into a large web hosting business and later sold part of it to the public again. Through Intermedia, the Digex business ended up inside WorldCom.

cover.theme: a relay station on the road (digital express)

fate: Acquired by Salesforce, 2013 ($33.75 a share, about $2.5B)
dek: ExactTarget gave marketers software to send, track and tune email, text and social campaigns to their customers.
lede: ExactTarget first filed to go public in December 2007, then waited more than four years while the financial crisis came and went. When it finally listed in March 2012, the Indianapolis company sent marketing email, text messages and social posts for more than 4,700 clients. It ran on rented servers in Indianapolis and Las Vegas and sold its software by subscription. In a city better known for car racing, it had grown into one of the biggest cloud companies in the Midwest.

sections.heading: Email From the Midwest
sections.body: Scott Dorsey, Chris Baggott and Peter McCormick started the company in Indianapolis in 2000 as ExactTarget, LLC. Their first product helped small marketers write and send email newsletters without a programmer. Over time ExactTarget added mobile messaging, social media tools and data features, and moved up to big brands and agencies. The bet was that marketing would move from mass ads to one-to-one messages, and that marketers would pay a monthly fee for the software to send them.

sections.heading: Salesforce Comes Calling
sections.body: ExactTarget sold 8.5 million shares at $19 in March 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as ET. It sold more stock in a follow-on offering that September. In June 2013 Salesforce agreed to buy ExactTarget for $33.75 a share in cash, about $2.5 billion, and completed the deal that July. The business became the core of Salesforce Marketing Cloud, and its Indianapolis offices became a major Salesforce hub.

cover.artwork: Archery (Sha), from the series "Informal Versions of the Six Accomplishments in the Floating World (Ukiyoe rikugei ryaku)"

fate: Taken private by founder Scott Blum, 2001; sold to Rakuten, 2010
tagline: Selling at Cost, Losing on Purpose
dek: Buy.com sold computers, books and electronics online at prices so low it often lost money on the sale.
lede: Buy.com's plan was to sell things for less than they cost and make the money back somewhere else. The Southern California store priced computers, software, books and music at or below what it paid for them, and counted on ads and volume to cover the gap. It went public in February 2000, in the last weeks of the dot-com boom. Investors bid the stock to almost three times the offer price on its first day.

sections.heading: The Lowest Price Online
sections.body: Scott Blum started Buy.com in 1997, after founding a computer storage company. The idea was simple. Shoppers comparing prices online would find Buy.com first, because its prices were the lowest. Sales grew fast, past half a billion dollars a year, but the losses grew with them. Blum stepped back from running the company before the offering. He still owned close to half of it when the stock began to trade.

sections.heading: Thirteen Dollars, Then Pennies
sections.body: Buy.com priced at $13 a share on February 8, 2000, and traded on Nasdaq as BUYX. The stock touched $35 on day one. Within a year the dot-com crash had pushed it below a dollar. In November 2001 Blum bought the company back for about $23.6 million and took it private. Japan's Rakuten bought Buy.com in 2010 and later renamed it Rakuten.com.

dek: Network Solutions was the one place on earth where you could register a .com name.
lede: If you wanted a .com address in 1997, you had one place to get it. Network Solutions ran the registry for .com, .net and .org under a contract with the National Science Foundation, and it charged $100 for two years. Every new web business paid the toll. The company was a small Virginia unit of defense contractor SAIC. When it went public that September, it was selling the land the whole commercial internet was about to build on.

sections.heading: A Consulting Shop Gets the Keys
sections.body: Emmit McHenry and three partners started Network Solutions in Washington, D.C., in 1979 as a technology consulting firm. In 1993 it won a government contract to register internet domain names, a quiet job when few people used the web. SAIC bought the company in 1995. That same year Network Solutions began charging for names. As the web took off, a sleepy clerical contract turned into a monopoly on the most valuable addresses in the world.

sections.heading: Twenty-One Billion for an Address Book
sections.body: Network Solutions priced at $18 a share in September 1997 and began trading on Nasdaq as NSOL on September 26. SAIC kept about three-quarters of the company. Competition for registrations arrived in 1999, but the stock had already soared. In March 2000, near the top of the bubble, VeriSign agreed to buy the company for about $21 billion in stock. Network Solutions lives on as a web-hosting brand owned by Newfold Digital.

cover.theme: a spider (the keeper of the web)

fate: Acquired by Intel, 2017 ($15.3B); re-listed 2022, still public (NASDAQ: MBLY)
dek: Mobileye taught cars to see the road with one camera and a chip, so they could brake in time.
lede: A Hebrew University professor bet that one cheap camera could do the work of radar. Amnon Shashua's company, Mobileye, built a chip called EyeQ that read lanes, cars and people from a windshield camera and warned the driver in time to stop. By 2014 automakers had put it in millions of cars. When Mobileye went public that summer, investors valued it at about $5.3 billion.

sections.heading: A Professor and a Windshield
sections.body: Shashua founded Mobileye in Jerusalem in 1999 with businessman Ziv Aviram. The industry wanted radar and lasers to spot obstacles. Shashua argued that computer vision alone could do it, if the software was good enough and the chip was cheap enough. Mobileye sold its EyeQ chips and software to the suppliers that build parts for carmakers. Its systems warned of lane drift, measured the distance to the car ahead, and later hit the brakes.

sections.heading: Sold Once, Listed Twice
sections.body: Mobileye priced at $25 a share on July 31, 2014, above its raised range, and closed its first day on the New York Stock Exchange at $37, up 48 percent. In 2017 Intel bought the company for $15.3 billion. Five years later Intel took Mobileye public again, pricing a new offering at $21 a share in October 2022. It trades on Nasdaq under its old symbol, MBLY, with Intel still the majority owner.

cover.theme: an eye opening in a flower (machine vision)
cover.artwork: There Was Perhaps a First Vision Attempted in the Flower, plate 2 of 8 from "Les Origines"

dek: Marvell designed the chips that move data in and out of hard drives, networks and, later, data centers.
lede: On its first day of trading, Marvell's stock rose 278 percent. The chip company had been started five years earlier by a husband, a wife and a brother. Its chips read and wrote the data on hard disk drives, a dull job every computer needed done. In June 2000 the dot-com market was already cracking. Investors still lined up for a profitable chip designer with a product inside millions of PCs.

sections.heading: Two Brothers and Weili Dai
sections.body: Sehat Sutardja, his wife Weili Dai and his brother Pantas Sutardja founded Marvell in 1995. Sehat was an engineer with a Berkeley doctorate. The company designed mixed-signal chips: parts that turn the faint analog signals on a spinning disk into clean digital data. Marvell did not own factories. It designed chips and paid others to make them, a model that kept costs low. Hard drive makers became its first big customers.

sections.heading: From Disk Drives to the Cloud
sections.body: Marvell priced 6 million shares at $15 each on June 27, 2000, raising $90 million on Nasdaq as MRVL. The stock closed the day near four times the offer. The founders ran the company until 2016, when they left after an audit-committee review of its accounting. A new chief executive, Matt Murphy, steered Marvell toward chips for data centers and networks. It remains a public company, still on Nasdaq as MRVL.

cover.artwork: Fireworks at Ryogoku (Ryogoku hanabi), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo"

dek: Handspring made the Visor handheld and the Treo, an early phone that also ran your calendar and email.
lede: The people who invented the PalmPilot quit Palm to build a better one. Jeff Hawkins, Donna Dubinsky and Ed Colligan left in 1998, unhappy with where Palm's owner, 3Com, was taking it. They licensed Palm's own software and launched the Visor, a cheaper handheld with a slot on the back for add-ons. By June 2000, Handspring was selling a lot of them, and Wall Street wanted in.

sections.heading: A Slot for Everything
sections.body: Handspring started in Mountain View in June 1998. Its Visor ran the Palm operating system, synced over USB, and had a Springboard slot that took modules: a GPS, a camera, an MP3 player, even a cell phone. The bet was that a handheld could become whatever its owner needed. In early 2002 the company stopped making Visors and launched the Treo, a phone with a keyboard and an organizer built in.

sections.heading: Back Home to Palm
sections.body: Handspring priced 10 million shares at $20 on June 20, 2000, raising about $200 million. It traded on Nasdaq as HAND and closed its first day near $27, up 35 percent. Then handheld sales slumped and the stock fell hard. In 2003 Palm's hardware business bought Handspring and kept the Treo. The founders went back to the company they had left, and the Treo became one of the first popular smartphones.

cover.artwork: Upraised Right Hand, with Palm Facing Outward: Study for Saint Peter

tagline: Free Antivirus for Half a Billion
dek: Qihoo 360 gave China free antivirus software, then earned its money from the browser and search box it shipped alongside.
lede: Qihoo 360 gave away the thing everyone else sold. In China, antivirus software was a paid product until Zhou Hongyi made his free. Hundreds of millions of people installed it, and Qihoo turned that reach into a web browser, a search box and an ad business. When it listed in New York in March 2011, China's internet was the hottest trade on Wall Street. Qihoo's shares more than doubled on the first day.

sections.heading: Give Away the Shield
sections.body: Zhou Hongyi and Qi Xiangdong founded Qihoo in Beijing in 2005. Zhou had sold an earlier startup to Yahoo. Qihoo's bet was that security software could be free if the company owned the user's desktop. Its 360 Safe Guard cleaned up malware, and its free antivirus followed. Then came the 360 browser and a homepage of links that millions saw every day. Advertising and online games paid the bills.

sections.heading: Wall Street, Then Shanghai
sections.body: Qihoo priced 12.1 million American depositary shares at $14.50 on March 29, 2011, above its $10.50 to $12.50 range. They began trading on the New York Stock Exchange as QIHU the next day and closed up 134 percent. Five years later, a group led by Zhou took the company private in a deal worth about $9.3 billion. In 2018 it relisted on the Shanghai Stock Exchange as 360 Security Technology.

fate: Rescued by Coupang, 2023; delisted from NYSE, 2024
tagline: Every Boutique in One Shop Window
dek: Farfetch let shoppers anywhere buy from hundreds of small luxury boutiques through a single website.
lede: A Portuguese shoe designer saw that the best fashion boutiques in Paris, Milan and Tokyo could not reach shoppers outside their own streets. José Neves built Farfetch to give them all one shop window. The boutiques kept their stock. Farfetch took the orders, handled the website, and earned a commission on every sale. By September 2018 luxury was finally moving online, and Farfetch came to New York to raise money for the shift.

sections.heading: Boutiques Without Borders
sections.body: Neves founded Farfetch in 2007 and launched the site in 2008, with offices in London and engineers in Portugal. The bet was that a marketplace would beat a store. Farfetch held almost no inventory of its own. It connected small boutiques and big brands to shoppers in nearly every country, and charged them a cut. As luxury houses grew more comfortable online, Farfetch also sold them its technology to run their own sites.

sections.heading: From $28 to a Rescue
sections.body: Farfetch priced at $20 a share on September 20, 2018, above its range, and raised $885 million. It opened on the New York Stock Exchange as FTCH and closed its first day at $28.45, up 42 percent. Big acquisitions and steady losses followed. By late 2023 the company was running out of cash. South Korea's Coupang stepped in with a $500 million rescue, and Farfetch's shares left the NYSE in early 2024.

cover.theme: a milliner in her shop (boutique fashion)

tagline: A Verdict on Every Used Car
dek: CarGurus told used-car shoppers whether a listed price was a great deal or a bad one.
lede: Every car on CarGurus comes with a verdict: great deal, good deal, fair, high, or overpriced. The site compares each listing against similar cars nearby and tells the shopper where it falls. That one feature brought buyers who did not trust dealer prices, and dealers paid to be in front of them. CarGurus came from a co-founder of TripAdvisor, and it applied the same idea to cars: trust the data and the crowd.

sections.heading: TripAdvisor for the Car Lot
sections.body: Langley Steinert started CarGurus in 2006, after co-founding TripAdvisor. It began as a place for car fans to swap advice. Steinert then turned it into a search engine for used-car listings, ranked by price and dealer reviews. The money came from dealers, who paid a monthly subscription to list their cars. The bet was that shoppers would come back to the site that told them the truth about price.

sections.heading: Boston's Big Tech IPO of 2017
sections.body: CarGurus priced 9.4 million shares at $16 on October 11, 2017, above its $13 to $15 range. It opened on Nasdaq as CARG at $29 the next day and closed at $27.58, up 72 percent. It was Boston's first tech IPO of the year. The company later added financing and a business that buys cars directly from owners. CarGurus remains public on Nasdaq under CARG.

cover.artwork: Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove - No. 2 (Chikurin shichiken sono ni), from the series "Popular Versions of Sages (Fuzoku kenjin ryaku)"

fate: Taken private by Clearlake Capital and Insight Partners, 2024 ($4.4B)
dek: Alteryx let business analysts clean, blend and study their data by dragging boxes, with no programming.
lede: Alteryx bet that the person who needs the answer should be able to get it without waiting on a programmer. Its software turned data work into a canvas of boxes and arrows. An analyst could pull in spreadsheets and databases, join them, clean them and run a forecast in an afternoon. When it went public in March 2017, companies were drowning in data and short of people who could code.

sections.heading: Twenty Years in Irvine
sections.body: Dean Stoecker, Libby Duane Adams and Ned Harding started the company in 1997 in Southern California, first selling maps and census data for marketing. The work showed them how much time analysts spent preparing data before they could study it. They rebuilt the product around that problem and renamed the company Alteryx. Customers paid a yearly subscription for each analyst. The bet was that millions of spreadsheet users wanted more power without learning to program.

sections.heading: Analysts Go Private
sections.body: Alteryx priced at $14 a share in March 2017 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as AYX. Growth was strong for several years as more companies bought licenses for their analysts. As software moved to the cloud, the desktop product slowed. In December 2023 Clearlake Capital and Insight Partners agreed to buy Alteryx for about $4.4 billion, including debt, at $48.25 a share. The deal closed in March 2024.

cover.theme: an astrolabe (instruments that read the world)
cover.artwork: The Astrolabe - Amerigo Vespucci, from Nova Reperta

dek: DTS made the surround sound that filled movie theaters and home theaters, starting with Jurassic Park.
lede: The first movie with a DTS soundtrack was Jurassic Park. In 1993 the dinosaurs roared out of theater speakers on every side, played from a CD synced to the film. Universal, the studio behind the film, had invested in the small company that year. A decade later DTS sound was in theaters, DVD players and home receivers, and it had an Oscar for its playback system. In July 2003 the company went public on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: Sound on a Separate Disc
sections.body: Digital Theater Systems was founded in 1990 in Southern California. Engineer Terry Beard was behind its early work. The company's trick was to put a movie's sound on a separate disc and keep it in step with the film using a timecode. That gave theaters several clean channels of sound, each from its own speakers. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gave DTS a Scientific and Engineering award for the theater system.

sections.heading: From the Cinema to the Living Room
sections.body: Digital Theater Systems priced 3.84 million shares at $17 on July 9, 2003, and began trading on Nasdaq as DTSI the next day. Shares rose fast enough that the company sold more stock in November at $25.75. In 2005 it changed its name to DTS. Its money came more and more from licensing its sound to makers of home theater gear and phones. In 2016 Tessera bought DTS for $42.50 a share in cash, about $850 million.

cover.artwork: The Actor Ichikawa Ebizo III as the Thunder God, an Incarnation of Sugawara Michizane, in the Play Sugawara Denju Tenarai Kagami, Performed at the Ichimura Theater in the Eighth Month, 1776

tagline: Performance Reviews Move to the Web
dek: SuccessFactors put employee goals, reviews and pay decisions online, so managers could see how their people were doing.
lede: Lars Dalgaard spent years as a manager at Unilever and Novartis before he started a software company. In most offices, performance reviews lived in binders and spreadsheets. His company, SuccessFactors, moved all of it into a browser. By November 2007 it had more than 1,400 customers and two million users in over 150 countries. It was still losing money when it went public.

sections.heading: A Unilever Manager's Fix
sections.body: Dalgaard founded SuccessFactors in May 2001 and ran it from San Mateo, California. The product tracked goals, reviews, pay and succession plans in one place. Customers paid a subscription and used it through a web browser, with no software to install. The bet was that big companies would trust a young startup with sensitive data about their people. American Airlines was among the early names on its customer list.

sections.heading: SAP Buys a Cloud
sections.body: SuccessFactors priced 10.79 million shares at $10 on November 19, 2007, and listed on Nasdaq as SFSF. The stock closed its first day at $13.25, up 33 percent. The company later moved its listing to the New York Stock Exchange. In December 2011, SAP agreed to buy SuccessFactors for $40 a share in cash, about $3.4 billion. The deal closed in February 2012, and Dalgaard went on to run SAP's cloud business.

cover.artwork: The Summit, from Ascent of Mont Blanc

dek: Paycom ran payroll, hiring, time clocks and HR for businesses from one online system.
lede: Chad Richison learned payroll as a salesman for ADP. In 1998 he started his own payroll company in Oklahoma City, and he built it to run online from the start. Paycom kept every part of a worker's record in one database, from the job application to the last paycheck. By 2013 it had 840 employees and $107.6 million in revenue. In April 2014 it went public on the New York Stock Exchange.

sections.heading: One Database, One Paycheck
sections.body: Richison began his career in sales at ADP and then moved to another payroll firm, Payroll 1, before founding Paycom. His bet was that businesses wanted one system for everything to do with their workers: hiring, time, pay, benefits and HR. Most rivals stitched separate programs together. Paycom built a single database and sold the whole thing as a subscription. Its own trained sales force sold it directly to mid-sized companies.

sections.heading: The Bell in New York
sections.body: Paycom priced 6.645 million shares at $15 in April 2014 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as PAYC. Private equity firm Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe was its largest outside owner. Paycom kept growing as a public company and later launched Beti, a tool that lets employees check and approve their own paychecks. It remains public on the NYSE under PAYC.

cover.artwork: Earning their money, from the series "The Camera's Story of Raftman's Life on the Wisonsin"

dek: Lightspan sold schools reading and math lessons that kids could play at home on a Sony PlayStation.
lede: Lightspan sent kids home with a PlayStation. Its K-8 curriculum came on game discs, and school districts bought consoles so students could practice reading and math in the living room. The idea was to connect school to home through the one machine kids already wanted to use. By early 2000 more than 873 school districts in 46 states had bought it. Lightspan was also building websites for teachers and parents, and the dot-com market was paying for that.

sections.heading: Game Consoles for Class
sections.body: John Kernan and Carl Zeiger founded Lightspan in 1993, and both had started education technology companies before. For three years the company mostly built its product, Lightspan Achieve Now. It covered language arts, reading and math. Lightspan sold it only to schools and districts, which used it in class and sent it home. The prospectus warned that the business depended on Sony and on a steady supply of PlayStation consoles.

sections.heading: Twelve Dollars and a Merger
sections.body: Lightspan priced 7.5 million shares at $12 in February 2000 and listed on Nasdaq as LSPN. Cable company Cox and computer maker Gateway bought shares alongside the offering. The dot-com crash soon followed, and the company kept losing money. In September 2003 PLATO Learning, a Minneapolis maker of school software, agreed to merge with Lightspan. The deal closed that November, and Lightspan's stock stopped trading.

cover.theme: a lamp lit for study (the light of learning)
cover.artwork: The Light, from the third album of L'Estampe originale

dek: NeoPhotonics made the optical chips and modules that push internet traffic through fiber networks as pulses of light.
lede: NeoPhotonics started life making nanoparticles. In 2002 it spun off that business, took a new name, and bet everything on photonic integrated circuits: chips that steer light the way ordinary chips steer electricity. By 2011 its modules carried data at 10, 40 and 100 gigabits a second inside the networks of phone and cable companies. Smartphones and online video were filling those networks faster than carriers could add capacity.

sections.heading: From NanoGram to Light
sections.body: The company was incorporated in Delaware in 1996 as NanoGram Corporation. Tim Jenks became chief executive in 1998. In November 2002 it spun out two companies, renamed itself NeoPhotonics, and focused on optical parts for communications networks. It built many of its products in its own factories in Shenzhen, China. By its IPO it sold more than 300 products, including ROADMs, which shift bandwidth around a network as traffic changes.

sections.heading: Ten Years to Lumentum
sections.body: NeoPhotonics priced 7.5 million shares at $11 in February 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as NPTN. The next decade brought tough price competition in optical parts. The company turned to faster products for data centers and long-haul links, including 400-gigabit modules. In November 2021 Lumentum agreed to buy NeoPhotonics for $16 a share in cash. The deal closed in August 2022, and the stock left the NYSE.

cover.theme: fireflies in the dark (points of light)

fate: Still public (NYSE: SSTK); merger with Getty Images called off, 2026
dek: Shutterstock sold stock photos, illustrations and video clips for a flat subscription instead of a price per picture.
lede: Shutterstock sold pictures the way a gym sells memberships. In 2003, when stock photos were licensed one at a time for steep fees, it launched with a simple subscription: pay a flat amount, download what you need. Nine years later its library held more than 20 million images from over 35,000 contributors in 125 countries. In 2011 customers paid for more than 58 million downloads. In October 2012 the New York company went public.

sections.heading: One Price, Many Pictures
sections.body: Jon Oringer, a software developer in New York, started Shutterstock in 2003. The bet was that small businesses, bloggers and marketers wanted lots of decent images, cheaply and fast, more than they wanted a few perfect ones. Photographers uploaded their work and earned a cut each time it was downloaded. In 2011 it made $120.3 million in revenue, and about two-thirds came from outside North America.

sections.heading: The Getty Deal That Died
sections.body: Shutterstock priced 4.5 million shares at $17 in October 2012 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange as SSTK. It later built a business licensing its library as data. In January 2025 it agreed to combine with its old rival, Getty Images. Britain's competition regulator demanded that Shutterstock sell its editorial business first. In mid-2026 the merger agreement was terminated, and Shutterstock remains public on the NYSE.

dek: iGate, first called Mastech, supplied software engineers and offshore programming to big American companies.
lede: Mastech grew its revenue every year from 1986 to its IPO, and made a profit every year since 1987. Sunil Wadhwani and Ashok Trivedi built the IT services firm in Pittsburgh. They recruited skilled programmers and placed them with large companies that could not hire fast enough. In December 1996 the Year 2000 bug was looming, and every big company needed people to fix its old code.

sections.heading: Programmers for Hire
sections.body: Mastech sold a single source for software work: building client/server systems, moving old programs to new machines, installing ERP packages, and fixing Year 2000 date problems. Its model was to staff projects with trained engineers at client sites and to move more work offshore. By 1996 it had offices in Pittsburgh, Washington, San Francisco, Toronto, Singapore, London and Tokyo. Wadhwani and Trivedi kept about 78 percent of the stock after the offering.

sections.heading: Mastech Becomes iGate
sections.body: Mastech priced its IPO at $15 a share in December 1996 and listed on Nasdaq as MAST. In 2000 it renamed itself iGate and leaned into internet services and offshore delivery from India. It spun its staffing business back out as Mastech in 2008. In 2011 iGate bought the larger Indian outsourcer Patni Computer Systems. Four years later France's Capgemini bought iGate for about $4 billion.

cover.artwork: The Holy Family Leaving by a City Gate, plate seven from The Flight into Egypt

dek: DemandTec helped big retailers set prices, promotions and markdowns using data on how shoppers actually behave.
lede: Target, Wal-Mart and Safeway all paid DemandTec to help decide what to charge. The San Carlos company sold software that studied how shoppers responded to prices and promotions, then recommended what retailers should do next. Best Buy and Office Depot rounded out its biggest U.S. accounts. When it went public in August 2007, customers used the software as a service over the internet.

sections.heading: Modeling the Shopper
sections.body: DemandTec was incorporated in Delaware in November 1999. Its software modeled shopper demand to guide four decisions: regular prices, promotions, markdowns, and trade deals with brands. Retailers paid a subscription, and so did consumer products companies such as Kraft, Nestlé USA and Procter & Gamble. By 2007, 35 retailers and more than 100 brands used it. Retailers brought in 94 percent of its revenue.

sections.heading: Into IBM's Smarter Commerce
sections.body: DemandTec priced 6 million shares at $11 in August 2007 and listed on Nasdaq as DMAN. It had posted a small net loss of $1.5 million in its latest fiscal year. In December 2011 IBM agreed to buy DemandTec for $13.20 a share in cash. The deal closed in February 2012, and the stock left Nasdaq. IBM folded DemandTec into its Smarter Commerce software for retailers and brands.

cover.theme: market women at their stalls (retail pricing)

dek: Egreetings let people send free animated greeting cards by email, with a gift suggestion attached.
lede: Egreetings started as Virtual Mall in 1994 and charged people to send digital cards. In November 1998 it made the cards free. The new plan was to pay for them with ads, sponsorships and the gifts people bought on the way out. Its site held more than 5,000 cards with graphics, animation and music. Every card sent was an ad for the service. The San Francisco company went public in December 1999.

sections.heading: Say More, Give More
sections.body: The pitch on the prospectus was three steps: choose a free greeting, write a personal message, pick a gift and send. Cards sat in channels such as birthdays, so Egreetings could match a gift to the moment. NBC licensed content to the company and bought a stake. So did Gibson Greetings, a paper card maker. When American Greetings agreed to buy Gibson, its rival became Egreetings' largest stockholder.

sections.heading: Ten Dollars to Eighty-Five Cents
sections.body: Egreetings priced 6 million shares at $10 on December 16, 1999, and listed on Nasdaq as EGRT. Free cards were easy to send and hard to profit from, and the online ad market collapsed in 2000. In February 2001 AmericanGreetings.com made a tender offer for the company at $0.85 a share in cash. The deal closed in March 2001, and Egreetings joined its old competitor.

cover.artwork: Thou Art the Star that Guides Me (valentine)

tagline: Test the Network Before It Breaks
dek: OPNET's software simulated computer networks, so engineers could see how changes would perform before making them.
lede: OPNET let network engineers crash a network without breaking anything. Its software built a model of a company's network and its applications, then ran them forward to show where traffic would jam. Phone carriers, internet providers and large companies used it to plan upgrades and chase slowdowns. By August 2000 it had licensed its software to more than 600 organizations, and the company in Washington, D.C., was ready for Nasdaq.

sections.heading: MIL 3 and a Simulator
sections.body: Marc Cohen and Alain Cohen started the company as MIL 3 in Maryland in 1986. Marc was chief executive and Alain ran the technology. Their product, OPNET, used predictive simulation to test network designs under many conditions. The company changed its name to OPNET Technologies in February 2000. Revenue had grown to $19.2 million in its latest fiscal year, and it had been profitable for most of its history.

sections.heading: Netted by Riverbed
sections.body: OPNET priced 4 million shares at $13 on August 1, 2000, and listed on Nasdaq as OPNT. It came through the dot-com crash and grew into tools for watching how applications perform across a network. In late 2012 Riverbed Technology bought OPNET through a tender offer. Each OPNET share received $36.55 in cash plus 0.2774 of a Riverbed share. The stock left Nasdaq in December 2012.

cover.theme: a youth with a fishing net (the network)

tagline: Every Call to the Right Person
dek: Genesys wrote the software that sent each incoming call to the right agent in big companies' call centers.
lede: Charles Schwab, BT and BellSouth used Genesys software to decide which agent picked up each call. It linked a company's phone switches to its computers, so a call could be routed by who the caller was and what they needed. Gregory Shenkman and Alec Miloslavsky started the company in San Francisco in 1990. By its IPO it had licensed its products to more than 125 companies worldwide.

sections.heading: Phones Meet Computers
sections.body: Gregory Shenkman and Alec Miloslavsky founded Genesys in October 1990. At first it earned money from one-off consulting jobs. In 1991 it shipped its platform software, which let a company's computers see and steer its phone calls. The industry called this computer telephony integration. Genesys aimed first at formal call centers in phone companies, banks and tech firms. It turned its first profitable quarters in late 1996 and early 1997.

sections.heading: Into Alcatel's Network
sections.body: Genesys priced 2.5 million shares at $18 in June 1997 and listed on Nasdaq as GCTI. Shenkman was chief executive and Miloslavsky was chief technical officer. Call centers grew fast through the late 1990s, and so did Genesys. In late 1999 French telecom giant Alcatel agreed to buy the company, and the deal closed in early 2000. The business still operates today under the Genesys name.

cover.artwork: The First Day, plate 2, from Creation of the World

dek: Everspin makes magnetic memory chips that are as fast as RAM but keep their data when the power cuts out.
lede: Most fast computer memory forgets everything the instant the power fails. Everspin's chips store each bit in a tiny magnet, so the data stays put. That makes them useful in places where losing the last second of work is expensive: storage systems and factory machines. Everspin was born in 2008 as a spin-off from Freescale Semiconductor. When it went public in October 2016, its ticker said exactly what it sold: MRAM.

sections.heading: Out of Freescale
sections.body: Freescale spun out its MRAM business as Everspin in June 2008, and the new company shipped products from day one. MRAM stands for magnetoresistive random access memory. Everspin processed its own magnetic layers at a 200mm plant in Chandler, Arizona. It also signed GLOBALFOUNDRIES to build its denser chips on 300mm wafers. The bet was that MRAM would win in systems that cannot afford to lose data in a power failure.

sections.heading: A Ticker Named MRAM
sections.body: Everspin priced 5 million shares at $8 in October 2016 and listed on Nasdaq under the symbol MRAM. The company had a history of losses and warned investors of it in the prospectus. GLOBALFOUNDRIES, its manufacturing partner, could also build Everspin's technology into its own chips and pay royalties. Everspin kept selling its chips into industrial and data-storage systems. Everspin remains a public company on Nasdaq, still trading as MRAM.

cover.artwork: Awa Province: Naruto Whirlpools (Awa, Naruto no fūha), from the series Famous Places in the Sixty-Odd Provinces (Rokujūyoshmeisho zue)

fate: Acquired by Adesto Technologies, 2018 ($8.50 a share)
dek: Echelon made LonWorks, chips and software that let lights, thermostats and machines talk to each other on one network.
lede: Echelon wanted every switch, sensor and motor in a building to share one language. Its LonWorks technology put a small networking chip inside ordinary devices, so a thermostat could talk to a fan and a light could answer a motion sensor. Honeywell, Johnson Controls, Hitachi and Raytheon built it into their products. Apple's early chairman, Mike Markkula, sat on its board. In July 1998 Echelon went public, ten years and many losses after it started.

sections.heading: One Network for Every Device
sections.body: Echelon began operations in Palo Alto in February 1988. Its products let equipment makers and systems integrators build open control networks in buildings, factories and transport systems. Devices from different makers could work together without custom wiring. The company sold chips, software and tools to those makers and earned more as they shipped. It lost money every year from 1993 to 1997, while the market slowly caught up.

sections.heading: Seven Dollars and a Long Road
sections.body: Echelon priced 5 million shares at $7 in July 1998 and listed on Nasdaq under the symbol ELON. The company later sold its networking technology into electric meters and street lighting. In June 2018 chip maker Adesto Technologies agreed to buy Echelon for $8.50 a share in cash. The deal closed that September, and Echelon left Nasdaq after twenty years of trading there.

fate: Sold Fallout to Bethesda, 2007; deregistered with the SEC, 2014
dek: Interplay published PC games such as Fallout, Descent and Battle Chess in the 1990s.
lede: The company that published Fallout went public at $5.50 a share. Interplay, run by founder Brian Fargo out of Irvine, California, made PC games with a following: Battle Chess, Descent, Earthworm Jim, Star Trek: Starfleet Academy. Its role-playing division, Black Isle Studios, had just released Fallout. Its prospectus opened with a slogan, "By gamers. For gamers." By June 1998 the company needed the money to pay down debt.

sections.heading: Fargo's Studio
sections.body: Brian Fargo founded Interplay in 1983 and ran it as chief executive from the start. The company built and published games for PCs and consoles, and it licensed its games to online services such as America Online. Universal Studios became a major investor and held two seats on the board. Interplay's hits earned it a strong name with players. Its spending on new games kept it short of cash.

sections.heading: Selling the Wasteland
sections.body: Interplay priced 5 million shares at $5.50 in June 1998 and listed on Nasdaq as IPLY. It used the money to repay debt. Losses continued, and France's Titus Interactive took control in 2001. Fargo left the next year. In 2007 Interplay sold the Fallout franchise to Bethesda Softworks. The company shrank to a small rights holder and stopped filing reports with the SEC in 2014.

tagline: Testing Chips in the Lion City
dek: STATS tested and packaged other companies' chips, from a factory floor in Singapore.
lede: Before a chip goes into a phone or a network switch, someone has to test it and seal it in a package. In 2000, much of that work for Texas Instruments and Nortel happened in Singapore, at ST Assembly Test Services. STATS ran 165 testers and 364 wire bonders there. Singapore Technologies, the state-linked group, owned 90.6 percent of it. In January 2000 STATS went public in both New York and Singapore.

sections.heading: Mixed-Signal Specialists
sections.body: ST Assembly Test Services was incorporated in Singapore on October 31, 1994. It did the back-end work of chipmaking: testing finished chips and assembling them into packages. It built particular skill in testing mixed-signal chips, which handle analog and digital signals together. Communications chips made up 62.1 percent of its revenue in the first nine months of 1999. Its sister company, Chartered Semiconductor, was an important customer from the start.

sections.heading: Two Listings, One Merger
sections.body: STATS sold 153 million shares at S$3.554 each, or US$21 per American depositary share, in January 2000. The ADSs traded on Nasdaq as STTS, and the shares listed on the Singapore Exchange. In 2004 it merged with U.S. rival ChipPAC to form STATS ChipPAC. A Temasek unit raised its stake through a tender offer in 2007, and the Nasdaq listing ended that year. China's JCET acquired the company in 2015.

cover.theme: a lion on a column (Singapore, the Lion City)

tagline: Light Strong Enough to Cut Steel
dek: IPG Photonics makes fiber lasers that cut, weld and mark metal in factories around the world.
lede: IPG Photonics started in Russia in 1990, in the last days of the Soviet Union. Physicist Valentin Gapontsev bet that lasers built from optical fiber could replace the big gas lasers that cut and weld metal. Fiber lasers were smaller, lasted longer and used less power. By 2006 IPG had plants in Massachusetts, Germany and Russia, and its sales had passed $100 million in nine months. That December, it went public on Nasdaq.

sections.heading: From Fryazino to Massachusetts
sections.body: Gapontsev began IPG's operations in Russia in 1990 and incorporated the company in Delaware in 1998. Its main factories sat in Oxford, Massachusetts; Burbach, Germany; and Fryazino, Russia. IPG made almost every part of its lasers itself, including the diodes that pump light into the fiber. Its target was the materials-processing market, long held by CO2 gas lasers and crystal lasers. In 2005 it had net sales of $96.4 million.

sections.heading: A Laser Maker on Nasdaq
sections.body: IPG first filed to go public in 2000 and withdrew. It tried again and priced 9 million shares at $16.50 on December 12, 2006. The stock listed on Nasdaq as IPGP. Gapontsev, other directors and funds tied to Merrill Lynch sold some of their shares in the deal. Fiber lasers went on to take a large share of industrial cutting and welding. IPG remains public on Nasdaq under IPGP.

cover.theme: a blacksmith's forge (cutting and welding metal)

dek: YY ran live voice and video rooms in China where people sang, played games and bought virtual gifts for performers.
lede: On YY, fans paid real money for virtual gifts and sent them to singers they had never met. The Guangzhou company started as a voice chat tool for online gamers and grew into a stage. Hosts sang and talked to rooms full of listeners, and YY took a cut of every gift. By August 2012 it had 70.5 million monthly users. That November it went public in New York.

sections.heading: From Gamer Chat to Stage
sections.body: David Xueling Li, a former chief editor at NetEase, co-founded the company with Lei Jun, who later became chairman of Xiaomi. It began with Duowan.com, a gaming website. In July 2008 it launched YY Client, a program for real-time group voice, text and video chat. Users organized themselves into channels. The bet was that people would pay for status and virtual items inside those rooms. YY reached 400.5 million registered accounts by September 2012.

sections.heading: YY Becomes JOYY
sections.body: YY priced 7.8 million American depositary shares at $10.50 in November 2012 and listed on Nasdaq as YY. Live streaming grew into its main business. It spun off the game-streaming site Huya, and in 2020 it renamed itself JOYY. It later sold its Chinese YY Live business to Baidu and focused on Bigo Live, an app used mostly outside China. JOYY remains public on Nasdaq, now based in Singapore.

cover.theme: a singer performing to a crowd (live streaming)
